xa: Visakhapatnam also hosts **NSTL**, the **Naval Dockyard** and the **Rambilli** submarine base.
⚠ **Boeing India**'s **₹413 crore** deal is for **P-8I** MRO, not marine gas turbines.
**Kalyani Strategic Systems** and **BDL** are investing in AP.

52.s:
Match List-I (AP defence unit) with List-II (Purpose):
List-I
a. BEL Palasamudram
b. BEL Machilipatnam
c. Rambilli
d. Naval Dockyard, Visakhapatnam
List-II
i. Opto-electronics and night vision
ii. Eastern Naval Command refit yard
iii. Missile and radar systems integration
iv. New Eastern Naval Command base for submarines, incl. nuclear boats
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
52.x: BEL Palasamudram (Sri Sathya Sai district) integrates missile and radar systems (iii); BEL Machilipatnam makes opto-electronics and night-vision devices (i); Rambilli (Anakapalli district) is the new submarine base (iv); the Naval Dockyard, Visakhapatnam is the ENC refit yard (ii).
52.tq: Palasamudram = missiles/radars; Machilipatnam = night vision.
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**BEL Palasamudram** = **missile + radar** systems integration; **BEL Machilipatnam** = **opto-electronics/night vision**.
**Rambilli** = new **submarine base** incl. nuclear boats; **Naval Dockyard Visakhapatnam** = **ENC refit yard**.
xa: Rambilli is in **Anakapalli district**.
**ADA complex** in **Sri Sathya Sai district**: **₹15,803 crore**.
**Bharat Forge** set up India's **first private marine gas turbine** MRO at **Visakhapatnam**.

52.s: Which of the following activities is associated with NSTL, Visakhapatnam?
o: Development of torpedoes such as Varunastra, mines and autonomous underwater vehicles
Manufacture of defence chips for export
Production of stealth frigates and destroyers
Integration of fighter aircraft and flight testing only
52.x: NSTL is DRDO’s naval weapons laboratory, associated with torpedoes such as Varunastra, mines and AUVs.
52.tq: Link a specialised laboratory with its weapons and systems.
xs: **NSTL Visakhapatnam** is DRDO's **naval weapons lab** for **torpedoes (Varunastra)**, **mines** and **AUVs** — option **(1)**.
Defence **chips** are still **imported**, and warships are built in shipyards, not at NSTL.
xa: The **Naval Dockyard** at Visakhapatnam is the **Eastern Naval Command** refit yard.
**Bharat Forge** MGT MRO is at Visakhapatnam.
**ADA** aircraft integration and flight testing is in **Sri Sathya Sai** district.

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to recent defence-export developments?
52.x: The Philippines is associated with BrahMos, Indonesia with Astra, and the UAE was in talks with India.
52.tq: Start from the sure buyer-product pair and verify the remaining associations.
xs: **Philippines — BrahMos; Indonesia — Astra; UAE — in talks** — option **(1)**.
**Indonesia** (Astra) is dated **Jul 2026**; the **UAE** talks **Jun 2026**.
xa: Exports rose from **₹686 crore** to **₹23,622 crore** (~**34-fold**).
India still imports **jet engines** + **defence chips**.
The **BrahMos** unit at **Lucknow** is in the **UP corridor**.

52.s: Swathi Weapon Locating Radar and Akash control centres are associated with:
52.x: Swathi Weapon Locating Radar and Akash control centres are associated with Bharat Electronics Limited.
52.tq: Match defence systems with the organisation responsible for them.
xs: **Swathi** WLR and **Akash** control centres are **BEL** (**Bharat Electronics Limited**) products — option **(3)**.
**Navantia** is the Spanish partner of **L&T**; **HVF Avadi** licence-builds the **T-90**; **HAL** builds **Tejas**, **Dhruv** and **Su-30 MKI**.
xa: **BEL** and **HAL** set up the **DIO**, which runs **iDEX**.
**BEL Palasamudram** (Sri Sathya Sai district) integrates **missile + radar** systems.
**BEL Machilipatnam** works on **opto-electronics / night vision**.

52.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. ATAGS is a licence-built Russian gun.
2. The Su-30MKI is a Russian design licence-built by HAL at Nashik.
3. The T-90 'Bhishma' is licence-built at the Heavy Vehicles Factory, Avadi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
52.x: Statement 1 is wrong: ATAGS is an indigenous design (DRDO-ARDE with industry). Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Su-30MKI (HAL Nashik) and T-90 (HVF Avadi) are licence-built Russian platforms. So '2 and 3 only'.
52.tq: Licence-built: Su-30MKI, T-90. Indigenous: ATAGS, Arjun, Tejas, Akash, Pinaka.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **ATAGS** is an **indigenous design** (**DRDO-ARDE** with industry).
Statement 2 is correct: **Su-30 MKI** is a Russian design **licence-built by HAL** (**Nashik**).
Statement 3 is correct: **T-90 'Bhishma'** is licence-built at **HVF, Avadi**.
xa: Exam angle: UPSC **2026** keyed only "**Su-30 MKI**" as made in India from {Su-30 MKI, T-90 Mk-III, Akula}.
BPSC **2025** keyed both **Arjun** and **ATAGS** as Make in India platforms.
**Akula** boats were **leased from Russia**; the **F-35** is American — not made in India.

52.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of indigenous designs?
o: ATAGS, Arjun, Tejas, Akash and Pinaka
52.x: ATAGS, Arjun, Tejas, Akash and Pinaka are identified as indigenous designs. Su-30MKI and T-90 are licence-built, while Akula and F-35 are not made in India.
52.tq: Classify every item before accepting an all-inclusive option.
xs: **ATAGS, Arjun, Tejas, Akash and Pinaka** are all **indigenous designs** — option **(1)**.
**Su-30 MKI** and **T-90** are **licence-built** Russian platforms; **Akula** and **F-35** are **not made in India**.
xa: **ATAGS** = DRDO-**ARDE** with industry; **Arjun** = DRDO-**CVRDE**; **Tejas** = **ADA** design, built by **HAL**.
**Dhruv ALH** and **HTT-40** are **HAL** products.
Akula boats were **leased from Russia**; the F-35 is **American**.

52.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between GTRE and the MGT 'Samudra'?
o: GTRE is developing it from the Kaveri engine
GTRE is developing it from the K9 Vajra-T engine
HAL is developing it from the P-8I engine
DRDO is developing it from the Arjun tank engine
52.x: The Gas Turbine Research Establishment is developing the MGT 'Samudra' from the Kaveri engine.
52.tq: Separate the developer from the platform or engine used as the technological base.
xs: **GTRE** is developing the marine gas turbine "**Samudra**" from the **Kaveri** engine — option **(1)**.
**K9 Vajra-T** is a South Korean-linked gun and **P-8I** is the Boeing aircraft under MRO — neither is Samudra's source.
xa: **Bharat Forge** is setting up India's first private **MGT MRO** at **Visakhapatnam**.
Imports of **jet engines** and **defence chips** remain a weakness.
**Boeing India** got a **₹413 crore** P-8I MRO contract under **'Buy Indian with 100% indigenous content'**.

53.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the energy intensity of GDP?
o: GDP produced per unit of energy; a falling value shows growth decoupling from energy use
Energy imports as a share of GDP; a falling value shows self-reliance
Energy used per unit of GDP; a rising value shows growth decoupling from energy use
Energy used per unit of GDP; a falling value shows growth decoupling from energy use
53.x: D is right: energy intensity is energy used per unit of GDP, and a falling value means growth is decoupling from energy use. A inverts the ratio, B describes import dependence, and C reverses the direction of change.
53.tq: Intensity = energy / GDP; falling = decoupling.
xs: **Energy intensity** = **energy used per unit of GDP**; a **falling** value shows **growth decoupling** from energy use — option **(4)**.
Option (1) inverts the ratio, and option (3) reverses the direction of change.
xa: **Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
⚠ **Energy shortage** in **MU**; **peak shortage** in **MW**.
NDC intensity targets (vs **2005**): **45% by 2030**, **47% by 2035**.

53.s: Which combination correctly identifies the institutional tools associated with improving energy efficiency under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001?
o: BEE and NMEEE, working through ESCOs
CEA and IEA, working through DISCOMs only
NITI Aayog and APERC, working through NHPC
MoEFCC and IUCN, working through BESS providers
53.x: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency and the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency under NAPCC work through Energy Service Companies under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.
53.tq: Match the institutions with the policy mechanism rather than with electricity planning bodies.
xs: **BEE** and **NMEEE** (under **NAPCC**) work through **ESCOs** under the **Energy Conservation Act 2001** — option **(1)**.
**CEA** does demand forecasting (NGAP, EPS) and **IEA** publishes the **World Energy Outlook** — not efficiency tools under the Act.
xa: The **Draft National Electricity Policy 2026** sets GHG-intensity targets for **208 industrial units** under the same Act.
Emission intensity is **down 36%** below **2005**.
**ESCOs** = Energy Service Companies.

53.s: Peak demand on an electricity grid is defined as:
o: The average power drawn over a full day
The highest power drawn in a 15-minute interval
The total electricity generated in a month
The maximum annual energy produced by renewable sources
53.x: Peak demand is the highest power drawn from the grid during a 15-minute interval.
53.tq: Distinguish instantaneous or interval-based peak power from aggregate energy generation.
xs: **Peak demand** is the **highest power drawn** on the grid in a **15-minute interval** — option **(2)**.
**Peak shortage** = unmet peak demand (**MW**); **energy shortage** = unmet energy requirement (**MU**).
xa: Record peak: **270.8 GW** (**May 2026**).
**Evening peak (6-11 p.m.)**: cooling demand after solar output drops.
NGAP: peak demand to reach **459 GW by 2035-36**.

53.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes energy shortage from peak shortage?
o: Energy shortage occurs only in summer, whereas peak shortage occurs only in winter.
Energy shortage is measured in MW, whereas peak shortage is measured in MU only.
Energy shortage is unmet energy requirement, whereas peak shortage is unmet peak demand.
Energy shortage refers to fuel imports, whereas peak shortage refers to renewable generation.
53.x: Energy shortage refers to unmet energy requirement and is expressed in MU or percentage terms. Peak shortage refers to unmet peak demand and is expressed in MW or percentage terms.
53.tq: Separate the two similar terms by their measurement and meaning.
xs: **Energy shortage** = **unmet energy requirement**; **peak shortage** = **unmet peak demand** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses the units: energy shortage is in **MU**, peak shortage in **MW**.
xa: **Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
Shortage fell from **4.2% (FY14)** to **0.03% (2025)**, **zero by Nov 2025**.
**Energy security**: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability.

53.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four A's on which energy security rests?
53.x: The four A's are availability, accessibility, affordability and acceptability. Accumulation is not included.
53.tq: Find the look-alike term that is absent from the standard four-part formulation.
xs: **Accumulation** is not one of the four A's — option **(3)**.
Energy security rests on the **Four A's**: **availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability**.
xa: **Energy intensity** = energy used per unit of **GDP**; a falling value = growth **decoupling**.
**Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
⚠ **Energy shortage** in **MU**; **peak shortage** in **MW**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour.
II. One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules.
III. Electricity cost is charged per unit, where the unit is kWh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: All three are correct: 1 kWh is a 1 kW device running for 1 hour, which is 3.6 × 10⁶ J, and electricity bills are charged per kWh.
53.tq: Recall 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s.
n: One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
Electricity cost is charged per unit in kWh. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
xs: **All three — I, II and III** — are correct — option **(2)**.
I: **1 kWh** = energy of a **1 kW** device in **1 hour**.
II: **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ joules**; III: electricity is **charged per unit**, the unit being **kWh**.
xa: **Energy shortage** is counted in **MU** (million units); **peak shortage** in **MW**.
**Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
**Energy intensity** = energy used per unit of **GDP**.

53.s: The annual publication titled “Energy Statistics” is brought out by which organisation?
o: Central Electricity Authority under the Ministry of Power
Central Statistics Office, now functioning as the National Statistics Office under MoSPI
53.x: Energy Statistics was published by the Central Statistics Office (CSO), now the National Statistics Office (NSO) under MoSPI.
53.tq: Identify the correct publishing authority rather than a related sectoral body.
xs: The annual "**Energy Statistics**" is published by the **Central Statistics Office (CSO)**, now the **National Statistics Office, MoSPI** — option **(2)**.
APPSC **2019** keyed **CSO** as the answer.
**CEA** publishes the **NGAP** and **Electric Power Survey**; **NITI Aayog** publishes **IESS 2047**.
xa: Coverage: reserves + potential, installed capacity, production, **imports/exports**, consumption, **energy balance**.
Fuels covered: **coal, lignite, crude oil, natural gas, electricity**.
⚠ **IESS 2047** = NITI Aayog; **NGAP** + **EPS** = CEA; **WEO** = IEA; Energy Statistics = CSO/NSO.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the India Cooling Action Plan:
1. It aims to cut cooling demand by 20-25% by 2037-38.
2. It aims to cut refrigerant demand by 40-50% by 2037-38.
3. It was launched in 2019 by MoEFCC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the refrigerant-demand cut is 25-30% (cooling energy 25-40%). So '1 and 3 only'.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **cooling demand** cut **20-25%** by **2037-38**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **refrigerant demand** cut is **25-30%**.
Statement 3 is correct: launched in **2019** by **MoEFCC**.
xa: Cooling energy to be cut **25-40%**.
AC ownership grows **15-20%** a year.
Peak demand rose **37%**: **183 GW** (Dec 2020) → over **250 GW**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Households use about 50% of India's electricity.
2. Household electrification in India is about 99%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statement 1 is wrong: industry, not households, uses about 50% of electricity. Statement 2 is correct: household electrification is about 99%. So '2 only'.
53.tq: Industry ~50% of electricity; electrification ~99%.
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — option **(2) 2 only**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **industry**, not households, uses ~**50%** of electricity.
Statement 2 is correct: household electrification is **~99%** (**Apr 2026**).
xa: **Saubhagya** connected **26 million** households.
Industry was also the largest energy sector in the IESS **2012** base (**2,367 TWh**).
Urban population grows ~**2.5%** a year.

53.s:
Match List-I (Report) with List-II (Publisher):
List-I
a. India Energy Security Scenarios (IESS) 2047
b. India Energy Outlook
c. Electric Power Survey
d. Energy Statistics (annual)
List-II
i. Central Electricity Authority
ii. NITI Aayog
iii. CSO, now NSO (MoSPI)
iv. International Energy Agency
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
53.x: IESS 2047 is NITI Aayog's (ii); the India Energy Outlook is an IEA special report of the World Energy Outlook (iv); the Electric Power Survey is CEA's official demand forecast (i); Energy Statistics is published by CSO, now NSO under MoSPI (iii; APPSC 2019).
53.tq: IESS = NITI; WEO/IEO = IEA; EPS + NGAP = CEA; Energy Statistics = CSO/NSO.
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(3)**.
**IESS 2047** = **NITI Aayog**; **India Energy Outlook** = **IEA**.
**Electric Power Survey** = **CEA**; **Energy Statistics** = **CSO**, now **NSO (MoSPI)** (APPSC 2019).
xa: **NGAP** is also by **CEA**: peak **459 GW** by **2035-36**.
IEA also publishes the **World Energy Outlook**.
IESS 2047: per-capita energy **521 kgoe (2014) → 1,055-1,184 kgoe (2040)**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the World Energy Outlook 2022:
1. India's coal generation and oil imports are projected to peak around 2030.
2. India's gas imports are projected to double.
3. It is published by NITI Aayog.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the World Energy Outlook is published by the International Energy Agency.
53.tq: Find the swapped publisher in a statement set.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **WEO 2022** sees India's **coal generation** and **oil imports** peaking around **2030**.
Statement 2: India's **gas imports double**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **World Energy Outlook** is published by the **IEA**, not NITI Aayog.
xa: The IEA also publishes the **India Energy Outlook**, an India-specific WEO special report.
⚠ **IESS 2047** = NITI Aayog; **NGAP** + **EPS** = CEA; **WEO** = IEA.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Generation Adequacy Plan (NGAP) 2026–27 to 2035–36:
1. It is prepared by the Central Electricity Authority.
2. It projects peak demand of 459 GW by 2035–36.
3. It projects installed capacity of 1,121 GW.
4. It projects 70% of capacity from non-fossil sources.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: All four statements are correct. The CEA's NGAP covers 2026–27 to 2035–36 and gives all the stated projections.
53.tq: Use the all-inclusive option when every listed feature belongs to the same plan.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**NGAP 2026-27 to 2035-36** is by **CEA**: peak demand to **459 GW by 2035-36**.
Capacity **1,121 GW**, **70%** non-fossil.
xa: Peak demand grows **5.58%/yr**.
Coal still **51%** of generation; storage need **174 GW/888 GWh**.
Storage split: **94 GW** pumped storage + **80 GW** BESS (**17 May 2026**).

53.s: According to the NITI Aayog projection based on the India Energy Security Scenarios, energy demand between 2012 and 2040 was expected to increase by:
o: 3.5–4.0 times, while electricity demand increases three-fold
53.x: The projection indicated that total energy demand would rise 2.7–3.2 times from 2012 to 2040, while electricity demand would increase 4.5-fold.
53.tq: Preserve the paired projection values and avoid reversing the total-energy and electricity figures.
xs: IESS: energy demand up **2.7-3.2 times** (**2012-2040**), electricity up **4.5-fold** — option **(1)**.
Option (3) swaps the two figures.
xa: IESS 2047 is by **NITI Aayog**.
Separately, energy demand is expected to **triple by 2047**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh's Resource Adequacy Plan for 2025–26 to 2035–36:
1. It is a state-wise plan prepared by the CEA framework.
2. It seeks about 5,588 MW of new thermal capacity for Andhra Pradesh.
3. APERC cleared the first 1,600 MW under the plan.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: All three statements are correct. The plan is part of the CEA's resource adequacy process, recommends about 5,588 MW of thermal capacity, and APERC cleared the first 1,600 MW.
53.tq: Verify the authority, state-specific requirement and approved first tranche together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **CEA Resource Adequacy Plan for AP** (**2025-26 to 2035-36**) is one of CEA's **state-wise** plans.
It recommends ~**5,588 MW** new thermal capacity; **APERC** cleared the first **1,600 MW**.
xa: AP electricity requirement grows **6.90% CAGR**; peak demand **7.10%**.
APERC approval was dated **6 Aug 2026**.

53.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the significance of nuclear energy in India's energy system?
o: It provides 24×7 baseload power and can reduce fossil-fuel imports.
It is used exclusively for off-grid household lighting.
It operates only during evening peak hours and increases fossil imports.
53.x: Nuclear power provides round-the-clock baseload electricity and can reduce dependence on fossil-fuel imports.
53.tq: Select the option that links the technology with its stated system-level benefits.
xs: **Nuclear** provides **24x7 baseload** and **cuts fossil imports** — option **(1)**.
So options (3) and (4), which deny baseload or say it raises imports, are wrong.
xa: Nuclear installed capacity: **8.78 GW**.
NITI scenario: nuclear's share of generation **3%** → **5-8%** by **2070**.
Crude oil import dependence is **~88%**.

53.s: Which source supplies approximately 55% of India’s energy mix and over 74% of its power generation?
53.x: Coal supplies about 55% of the energy mix and more than 74% of power generation.
53.tq: Match the quantitative share with the correct fuel source.
xs: **Coal** supplies **55% of the energy mix** and **over 74% of power generation** (2025-26) — option **(1)**.
India is the world's **second-largest coal consumer**; coal leads installed capacity (**230 GW**).
xa: **Solar** is second in installed capacity (**157 GW, ~29%**) and the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC **2021**).
**Nuclear** has only **8.78 GW** of installed capacity.
NITI scenario: coal's share of generation **~74% → 6-10%** by **2070**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India's energy demand is expected to triple by 2047.
2. India is the world's largest coal consumer.
3. India is the world's third-largest energy consumer.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: India is the world's second-largest coal consumer. So '1 and 3 only'.
53.tq: India: 3rd in energy, 2nd in coal.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: energy demand is expected to **triple by 2047**.
Statement 2 is wrong: India is the world's **second-largest coal consumer**.
Statement 3 is correct: India is the **third-largest energy consumer**.
xa: Coal = **55% of the energy mix**, over **74%** of power generation.
**Solar** is the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC 2021).
Installed capacity: coal **230 GW**, solar **157 GW**, wind **56.8 GW**.

53.s: India’s per-capita electricity consumption increased from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to approximately what level in FY 2025?
53.x: Per-capita electricity consumption rose from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to 1,460 kWh in FY 2025.
53.tq: Use the time labels carefully and select the correct terminal value.
xs: Per-capita electricity consumption rose from **957 kWh (FY 2014)** to **1,460 kWh (FY 2025)** — option **(1)**.
Older notes gave **1,181 kWh**, "about half the world average".
xa: Per-capita **generation** in **2024**: India **1,418 kWh**, China **7,097**, USA **12,701**.
India's per-capita electricity ≈ **a fifth** of China's and **a ninth** of the USA's.
IESS 2047 projects **2,911-2,924 kWh** per capita.

53.s: India’s per-capita energy consumption is approximately what fraction of the world average?
53.x: India’s per-capita energy consumption is reported as only one-third of the world average.
53.tq: Separate the current world-gap ratio from older references to one-half of the world average.
xs: India's per-capita energy is only **one-third of the world average** — option **(2)**.
⚠ "**About half** the world average" is an older figure for per-capita **electricity** (**1,181 kWh**).
xa: Consumption is **low** with a large **urban-rural disparity**.
Per-capita electricity ≈ **a fifth** of China's, **a ninth** of the USA's.

53.s: The policy objective of raising per-capita electricity consumption is linked to the Human Development Index primarily because:
o: Electricity consumption is unrelated to social development indicators
Higher electricity consumption automatically eliminates urban-rural disparity
A minimum level of per-capita consumption is needed for a minimally acceptable level of well-being
HDI measures only the availability of commercial energy
53.x: Per-capita electricity consumption acts as a proxy for energy use, and a certain minimum level is required to ensure a minimally acceptable level of well-being.
53.tq: Apply the development-indicator relationship to the policy objective.
xs: A **certain minimum level of per-capita consumption** is needed to ensure a **minimally acceptable level of well-being** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2016** key).
Per-capita electricity, a proxy for all energy, **correlates with HDI**, so policy aims to raise it.
xa: India's per-capita electricity rose from **957 kWh** to **1,460 kWh** (FY 2014 → FY 2025).
Consumption is **low per capita** with a large **urban-rural disparity**.
Energy security rests on the **Four A's**: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability.

53.s: Which one of the following best describes the pattern of India’s per-capita energy consumption?
o: High per-capita consumption with negligible regional disparity
High rural consumption with negligible urban consumption
Low per-capita consumption accompanied by a large urban-rural disparity
Uniform consumption across urban and rural areas
53.x: India has low per-capita consumption and a large disparity between urban and rural areas.
53.tq: Use the paired qualifiers—low level and large disparity—to identify the precise description.
xs: India has **low per-capita consumption** with a **large urban-rural disparity** — option **(3)**.
Per-capita energy is only **one-third of the world average**.
xa: Per-capita electricity ≈ **a fifth** of China's and **a ninth** of the USA's.
Household electrification is **~99%**.
**Saubhagya** connected **26 million** households.

53.s: Which statement best describes the projected sectoral pattern of energy demand by 2040?
o: Transport becomes the only sector with increasing demand.
Industry remains the largest sector, with 8,764 TWh under BAU, while cooking demand falls as clean fuels replace biomass.
Cooking remains the largest sector because biomass use expands.
Buildings become the largest sector and industry demand disappears.
53.x: Cooking demand is expected to fall as clean fuels replace biomass, while industry remains the largest sector with 8,764 TWh under business as usual in 2040.
53.tq: Contrast the declining cooking trend with the continuing industrial lead.
xs: By **2040** **industry** stays the largest sector (**8,764 TWh** BAU), while **cooking** demand **falls** as **clean fuels replace biomass** — option **(2)**.
Cooking does not grow (option 3), and industry does not disappear (option 4).
xa: **2012** base: industry **2,367 TWh**, cooking **1,072**, transport **929**; total **4,926**.
IESS 2047 is by **NITI Aayog**: energy demand up **2.7-3.2 times** (2012-2040), electricity up **4.5-fold**.
Import dependence projected **31%** → **36-55%**.

53.s: Which of the following combinations best represents the emerging drivers of India's peak electricity demand?
o: Electric vehicles, farm pumps, appliances, cooling and data centres
Declining appliance ownership and reduced telecom activity
Only household lighting in rural areas
Only coal mining and railway electrification
53.x: Electric vehicles, farm pumps, appliances, cooling demand, data centres and telecom operations all contribute to rising electricity demand.
53.tq: Group the closely related demand-side drivers rather than selecting an exclusive cause.
xs: **EVs, farm pumps, appliances, cooling** and **data centres** drive peak demand — option **(1)**.
EVs, pumps and appliances lifted peak demand **37%**, from **183 GW (Dec 2020)** to **over 250 GW (Apr 2026)**.
xa: **Data centres + telecom** need **continuous power**.
**AC ownership** grows **15-20%** a year.
Jan-Feb **2026** demand hit a **five-year high**.

53.s: India's peak electricity demand rose by approximately 37%, from 183 GW in December 2020 to over what level in April 2026?
53.x: Peak demand increased from 183 GW in December 2020 to more than 250 GW in April 2026, representing a rise of about 37%.
53.tq: Match the percentage change with the correct end-point figure.
xs: Peak demand rose **37%** from **183 GW (Dec 2020)** to **over 250 GW (Apr 2026)** — option **(1)**.
Drivers: **EVs, farm pumps, appliances**.
xa: All-time high: **270.8 GW** in **May 2026**, ~**90 GW** above **2019**.
**25 Apr 2026**: **256.1 GW**, about a third met by RE.
CEA's **NGAP** projects peak demand of **459 GW by 2035-36** (**5.58%/yr**).

53.s: Which of the following correctly describes the change in India's non-fossil capacity share?
o: It rose from 40% in 2015 to 60% in 2035 only through nuclear power.
It rose from 32% in 2014 to 51% in 2025 and crossed the 50% target five years early.
It fell from 51% in 2014 to 32% in 2025.
It remained unchanged at 32% between 2014 and 2025.
53.x: The non-fossil capacity share increased from 32% in 2014 to 51% in 2025, reaching the 50% target five years ahead of schedule.
53.tq: Check direction, years and the early-achievement detail together.
xs: Non-fossil capacity share rose from **32% (2014)** to **51% (2025)**, reaching the **50%** target **five years early** — option **(2)**.
The **50%** target came from the **Aug 2022** updated NDC (for **2030**).
xa: The **2031-35 NDC** raises the non-fossil target to **60%**.
First NDC (**2015**) targeted **40%** non-fossil by **2030**.
CEA's NGAP sees **70%** non-fossil in **1,121 GW** of capacity by **2035-36**.

53.s: NITI Aayog's study 'Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero' projects which change in India's electricity generation mix?
o: Renewables' share rising from about 20% (2024-25) to about 80% by 2070, with coal falling from about 74% to 6-10%
Renewables' share rising from about 40% to about 60% by 2047, with coal falling to about 30%
Renewables' share rising from about 20% to about 50% by 2050, with coal unchanged at about 74%
Renewables' share rising from about 74% to about 95% by 2070, with coal eliminated entirely
53.x: The NITI study projects renewables' share of generation rising from about 20% in 2024-25 to about 80% in 2070, coal falling from about 74% to 6-10% and nuclear rising from 3% to 5-8%. The other options misstate the starting point, the end year or the coal share.
53.tq: NITI net-zero scenario: RE 20% to 80%, coal 74% to 6-10% by 2070.
xs: NITI's "**Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero**": renewables' generation share **~20% (2024-25) → ~80% (2070)**; coal **~74% → 6-10%** — option **(1)**.
Nuclear rises from **3%** to **5-8%**.
xa: Coal today = **over 74%** of power generation and **55%** of the energy mix.
NGAP: coal still **51%** of generation by **2035-36**.
**Nuclear** = **24x7** baseload; cuts fossil imports.

53.s: Which of the following correctly compares India's per-capita electricity consumption with that of China and the United States?
o: It is about one-ninth of China's and one-fifth of the USA's.
It is about one-fifth of China's and one-ninth of the USA's.
It is approximately equal to both countries.
It is about one-half of China's and one-third of the USA's.
53.x: India's per-capita electricity consumption is about one-fifth of China's and one-ninth of the USA's.
53.tq: Preserve the direction and denominator of each comparative ratio.
xs: India's per-capita electricity ≈ **one-fifth of China's** and **one-ninth of the USA's** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) swaps the two fractions.
xa: Per-capita generation **2024**: India **1,418 kWh**, China **7,097**, USA **12,701**.
OECD average: a little above **8,000 kWh**.
Per-capita electricity consumption: **1,460 kWh** (FY **2025**).

53.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the peak demand recorded in May 2026?
o: It was 256.1 GW, about one-third above the 2019 level
It was 237 GW, about 90 GW below the 2019 level
It was 250 GW, about 20 GW above the 2019 level
It was 270.8 GW, about 90 GW above the 2019 level
53.x: The May 2026 peak demand was an all-time high of 270.8 GW, approximately 90 GW above the 2019 level.
53.tq: Match the all-time-high figure with its correctly stated historical comparison.
xs: **May 2026** peak was **270.8 GW**, an **all-time high**, ~**90 GW above the 2019 level** — option **(4)**.
**256.1 GW** was **25 Apr 2026**; **237 GW** the **2025** non-solar figure; **250 GW** the **2024** solar-hours record.
xa: The record pushed **long-duration storage** (**over 8 hours**) to the centre of policy.
Peak demand had risen **37%** from **183 GW (Dec 2020)**.
On **25 Apr 2026** non-solar hours saw a **2% (4,243 MW)** deficit.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's electricity shortage:
1. The shortage declined from 4.2% in FY14 to 0.03% in 2025.
2. The shortage reached zero by November 2025 according to the Economic Survey 2025–26.
3. Earlier assessments had reported shortages in the range of 10–15%.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: All three statements are correct. The shortage was historically in the 10–15% range, then declined to 0.03%, followed by zero shortage by November 2025.
53.tq: Combine the long-term trend with the historical comparison and endpoint.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 2: shortage reached **zero by Nov 2025**.
Statement 3: older notes record **10-15%** shortages.
xa: Some notes give the same fall as **2016** to **2026**.
Exam angle: "**near-zero peak deficit**"; the **evening non-solar peak** is the new gap.

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 2026 El Niño-related conditions:
1. June rainfall was among the lowest recorded since 1901.
2. Rainfall was 20% below normal by 6 July.
3. The conditions affected wind and hydropower output.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: All three statements are correct. The rainfall deficit associated with El Niño affected renewable generation, including wind and hydropower.
53.tq: Combine the date, magnitude and consequence of the weather event.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**El Niño 2026**: June rainfall among the lowest since **1901**, **20%** below normal by **6 July**.
It **dented wind and hydro** output.
xa: **AP angle**: El Niño-driven peaks led to AP's roadmap of **1,600 MW** thermal + **2,000 MW** of BESS.
Heatwaves strain grids; poor storage and slow transmission strand renewables.
Rules: **15-day coal stock** and **12-month** advance plans (**9 Sep 2026**).

53.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the coverage of Energy Statistics:
1. It includes data on coal, lignite, crude oil and natural gas.
2. It includes electricity consumption and the energy balance.
3. It is restricted to production data and excludes imports and exports.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the publication also covers imports and exports.
53.tq: Locate the false exclusion statement by checking the publication’s full range of indicators.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: it covers **coal, lignite, crude oil, natural gas** and electricity.
Statement 2 is correct: it covers **consumption** and the **energy balance**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it also covers **imports/exports**, reserves and installed capacity.
xa: Publisher: **CSO**, now **NSO, MoSPI** (APPSC **2019** key: CSO).
The **Electric Power Survey** is **CEA**'s official long-term electricity demand forecast.

53.s: Which one of the following correctly pairs the cause of the evening peak (6-11 p.m.) with Delhi's response to it?
o: Peak solar output; a ban on power exchanges
Industrial shutdown; a 15-day coal stock rule only
Cooling demand after solar output drops; time-of-day tariffs and smart meters
Cooling demand after solar output drops; exclusive dependence on pumped hydro
53.x: C is right: the 6-11 p.m. evening peak comes from cooling demand after solar output drops, and Delhi responds with time-of-day tariffs and smart meters. Solar output is low in the evening (A); industrial shutdown and a coal-stock rule are neither the cause nor Delhi's tool (B); exclusive dependence on pumped hydro is not stated (D).
53.tq: Evening peak = cooling after sunset; answer = ToD tariffs + smart meters.
xs: The **evening peak (6-11 p.m.)** comes from **cooling after solar output drops**; **Delhi** uses **ToD tariffs** + **smart meters** — option **(3)**.
Solar output is low in the evening (option 1); the **15-day coal stock** is a general rule, not Delhi's response (option 2).
xa: **El Niño 2026** dented **wind and hydro** output.
**Regional imbalance**: poor storage + slow transmission strand renewables.
Rules: **15-day coal stock**; **12-month** advance power plans.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about India's fuel position:
1. India's crude-oil import dependence is about 88%.
2. India has the fourth-largest coal reserves (about 344 bt), and coal is about 55% of primary energy.
3. India has about 17% of the world's population but about 7% of world oil reserves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: India holds only about 0.4% of world oil reserves (0.6% of gas); the 7% figure is its share of coal reserves. So '1 and 2 only'.
53.tq: 17% people vs 0.6% gas, 0.4% oil, 7% coal.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: crude oil import dependence **~88%**.
Statement 2 is correct: **4th largest** coal reserves (~**344 bt**); coal ~**55%** of primary energy.
Statement 3 is wrong: India has only **0.4% of oil** reserves; **7%** is its share of **coal**.
xa: India holds **17%** of world population but only **0.6% of gas** reserves.
Natural gas: ~**50-51%** imported.
FY26 coal output: **1,040.08 MT**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about India's fuel position:
1. Approximately 50–51% of natural gas or LNG is imported.
2. LNG imports were estimated at 28–29 MMT in 2026.
3. LPG shortages were reported during the 2026 gas crisis.
4. The Strait of Hormuz was identified as a risk to LPG supplies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: All four statements correctly describe the reported natural-gas and LPG supply situation.
53.tq: Check each fuel-related statement before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Natural gas / LNG ~**50-51%** imported; LNG imports **28-29 MMT** in **2026**.
**LPG shortages** came in the **2026 gas crisis**, with **Strait of Hormuz** risk.
xa: India holds only **0.6%** of world gas reserves.
IEA **WEO 2022**: India's gas imports **double**.
Crude oil import dependence **~88%**.

53.s: Which authority has been allowed to import coal under the Andhra Pradesh energy roadmap?
53.x: APGENCO has been allowed to import coal under the Andhra Pradesh energy roadmap.
53.tq: Ask which operational entity, rather than regulator or central agency, performs the specified action.
xs: **APGENCO** has been allowed to **import coal** — option **(2)**.
**APERC** is the regulator that approved **1,600 MW**; **NHPC** partners the **500 MW/1,000 MWh** VGF storage.
xa: Roadmap: **15-day coal stock** required.
**1,500 MW/6,000 MWh BESS** for the evening peak.
Thermal-plant coal **imports down 27.4%** nationally.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about India's NDC targets (versus 2005):
1. The first NDC (2015) targeted a 33-35% cut in intensity and 40% non-fossil capacity by 2030.
2. The updated NDC (Aug 2022) targeted a 45% cut in intensity and 50% non-fossil capacity by 2030.
3. The 2031-35 NDC targets a 47% cut in intensity and 50% non-fossil capacity by 2035.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the 2031-35 NDC sets 47% by 2035 with a 60% non-fossil capacity target. So '1 and 2 only'.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: first NDC (**2015**) — intensity **33-35%** and non-fossil **40%** by **2030**.
Statement 2 is correct: updated NDC (**Aug 2022**) — **45%** intensity and **50%** non-fossil by **2030**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **2031-35 NDC** sets **47% by 2035** with **60%** non-fossil capacity.
xa: Emission intensity is already **down 36%** below **2005**.
Non-fossil capacity: **32% (2014)** → **51% (2025)**; **50%** reached five years early.

53.s: The COP31 goal described as “35 by 35” seeks to make electricity account for what share of final energy by 2035?
53.x: The “35 by 35” goal seeks to raise electricity's share to 35% of final energy by 2035.
53.tq: Read the target directly from the compact numerical slogan.
xs: **COP31 "35 by 35"**: electricity = **35%** of final energy by **2035** — option **(3)**.
Today only ~**one-fifth** of India's energy use is electricity.
xa: Per-capita energy **2024**: **7,893 kWh**.
The **2031-35 NDC** targets **47%** intensity cut by **2035** and **60%** non-fossil.
IESS: electricity demand up **4.5-fold** (2012-2040).

53.s: Which scheme was associated with connecting approximately 26 million households?
53.x: The Saubhagya programme is associated with connecting approximately 26 million households.
53.tq: Match the programme with its quantitative achievement.
xs: **Saubhagya** connected **26 million** households — option **(2)**.
**NGAP** is CEA's generation adequacy plan; **COP31** is linked to "**35 by 35**".
xa: Other schemes: **RDSS**, **DDUGJY**, **IPDS**.
Household electrification is **~99%**.

53.s: India's aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses declined from 22.62% in FY14 to approximately what level in FY25?
53.x: AT&C losses fell from 22.62% in FY14 to 15.04% in FY25, alongside measures such as RDSS, IPDS, smart meters and time-of-day tariffs. 10.04%, 18.62% and 12.50% are not the reported FY25 figure.
xs: **AT&C losses** fell from **22.62% (FY14)** to **15.04% (FY25)** — option **(1)**.
They are listed with **RDSS**, **DDUGJY**, **IPDS** and **Saubhagya** as measures against the deficit.
xa: Other measures: **ToD tariffs**, **smart meters**, **BESS**, **pumped storage**.
**National Electricity Plan 2023 (CEA)**: non-fossil **485 GW** (**62.4%**) of **777 GW** by **2029-30**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The National Electricity Plan 2023 (CEA) projects 777 GW of capacity by 2029-30, of which 485 GW (62.4%) is non-fossil.
2. The Draft National Electricity Policy 2026 was issued by NITI Aayog.
3. The same plan projects 900 GW by 2031-32.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
53.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Draft National Electricity Policy 2026 is from the Ministry of Power; it replaces the 2005 policy and proposes 100 GW of pumped storage by 2047. So '1 and 3 only'.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **NEP 2023 (CEA)**: **777 GW by 2029-30**, non-fossil **485 GW (62.4%)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **Draft National Electricity Policy 2026** is from the **Ministry of Power**.
Statement 3 is correct: **900 GW by 2031-32**.
xa: The draft policy replaces the **2005** policy and targets **100 GW of pumped storage by 2047**.
**Saubhagya** connected **26 million** households.

53.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched with the Andhra Pradesh energy roadmap of September 2026?
o: Central VGF project with NHPC — 1,500 MW/6,000 MWh
Coal-based procurement — 1,600 MW through tariff-based competitive bidding
53.x: The central VGF project with NHPC is 500 MW/1,000 MWh. The 1,500 MW/6,000 MWh BESS is planned for the evening peak.
53.tq: Find the swapped capacity and storage figure in a closely related pair.
xs: **Central VGF with NHPC — 1,500 MW/6,000 MWh** is wrong — option **(2)**; the VGF project is **500 MW/1,000 MWh**.
**1,500 MW/6,000 MWh** is the **BESS for the evening peak**.
**15-day coal stock** and **1,600 MW** via tariff-based competitive bidding are correctly matched.
xa: **APGENCO** is allowed to import coal.
AP angle: **El Niño**-driven peaks → **1,600 MW** thermal + **2,000 MW** of BESS.
The roadmap is dated **9 Sep 2026**.

53.s: An energy crisis, in the sense used in discussions of conventional energy resources, refers to:
o: A rise in electricity consumption during solar hours
A temporary fall in renewable-energy generation only
The danger that fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum may run out
A shortage limited to nuclear fuel imports
53.x: Energy crisis refers to the danger of exhaustion of fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum.
53.tq: Identify the underlying resource-depletion meaning rather than a short-term grid event.
xs: An **energy crisis** is the danger that **fossil fuels** like **coal and petroleum** will **run out** — option **(3)** (UKPSC **2006** key).
Fossil fuels still dominate: **coal** = **55%** of the energy mix.
xa: India has **17%** of world population but only **0.6% of gas**, **0.4% of oil** and **7% of coal** reserves.
Crude oil import dependence is **~88%**.
**Solar** is the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC **2021**).

53.s: India's emissions intensity has declined by what percentage below the 2005 level, according to the stated achievement?
53.x: Emissions intensity has declined by 36% below the 2005 level.
53.tq: Distinguish the achieved reduction from the future 2030 NDC target.
xs: **Emission intensity** is **down 36%** below **2005** — option **(2)**.
NDC target is **45% by 2030**; IESS modelled **45-53%**.
xa: Non-fossil capacity reached **51%** in **2025**.
Efficiency tools: **BEE** + **NMEEE** under the **Energy Conservation Act 2001**.

53.s: The evening peak has become central to India’s storage push primarily because:
o: Renewable energy cannot contribute during daylight hours
Coal supplies less than one-tenth of power generation
The remaining deficit occurs mainly during non-solar evening hours
Electricity demand is highest only during solar hours
53.x: Although solar-hour supply has improved, the non-solar evening peak still creates a deficit, making storage important for meeting that period’s demand.
53.tq: Infer the policy response from the timing of the remaining grid deficit.
xs: The remaining deficit now falls in **non-solar evening hours**, so **storage** is needed — option **(3)**.
On **25 Apr 2026** solar hours had no shortage but non-solar hours a **2% (4,243 MW)** deficit.
xa: NGAP storage need: **174 GW/888 GWh** = **94 GW** pumped storage + **80 GW** BESS.
**Draft National Electricity Policy 2026**: **100 GW** of pumped storage by **2047**.
Delhi uses **ToD tariffs** and smart meters for the **6-11 p.m.** peak.

53.s: Regional imbalances in renewable electricity may arise because of:
o: Uniform renewable generation across all regions
53.x: Poor storage and slow transmission can strand renewable power in some regions, while heatwaves can place additional stress on grids.
53.tq: Select the option expressing the infrastructure-related cause of regional imbalance.
xs: **Poor storage** and **slow transmission** strand renewables, causing **regional imbalance** — option **(2)**.
**Heatwaves** add strain on grids.
xa: **El Niño 2026** dented **wind and hydro** output.
NGAP storage need: **94 GW** pumped storage + **80 GW** BESS.
The **single national grid** is a listed measure against deficit.

54.s: India is described as the world’s ______ largest holder of coal reserves in the current estimate referred to.
54.x: The current estimate identifies India as the world’s fifth-largest holder of coal reserves; an older estimate had placed it fourth.
54.tq: Distinguish the current ranking from the older alternative ranking.
xs: India is the world's **fifth** largest holder of coal reserves (2025-26) — option **(2)**.
⚠ Older notes say **4th** (~**344 bt**) — option (1) is the outdated figure.
xa: ⚠ Coal: **fifth-largest reserves** but **third-largest producer**.
Coal import share is still **~26%**.
India holds **7%** of world coal reserves vs **17%** of population.

54.s: Which country is identified as a key supplier of LNG to India?
54.x: Qatar is identified as a key LNG supplier to India.
54.tq: Distinguish the major LNG supplier from countries listed mainly in the crude-import movement.
xs: **Qatar** is India's key **LNG** supplier — option **(1)**.
Natural gas / LNG import share is **~47-51%**.
xa: The **Strait of Hormuz** carries a fifth of global **LNG** trade.
**Coking coal** for steel comes mainly from **Australia** and **Indonesia**.
**CBO** in CGD aims to substitute **LNG** imports.

54.s:
Consider the following pairs (fuel : approximate import share):
1. Crude oil : about 88%
2. Coal : about 26%
3. Lithium : about 26%
4. Natural gas/LNG : about 47-51%
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
54.x: Pairs 1-3 are correct (coal imports are ~26% even though India is the third-largest producer). Pair 3 is wrong: lithium import dependence is about 90%. So '1, 2 and 4 only'.
54.tq: Import share: crude ~88% > gas ~50% > coal ~26%; lithium ~90%.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 4** are correctly matched — option **(2)**.
Pair 1 is correct: crude oil import dependence is **~88%** (**88.5%**, PPAC, July 2026).
Pair 2 is correct: coal imports are **~26%** despite India being the **third-largest producer**.
Pair 3 is wrong: **lithium** import dependence is **~90%**.
Pair 4 is correct: natural gas/LNG imports are **~47-51%**.
xa: India has **17%** of world population but only **0.6%** gas, **0.4%** oil, **7%** coal reserves.
⚠ Coal: **fifth-largest reserves** (older: 4th) but **third-largest producer**.
Of **26** sedimentary basins, only **7** produce.

54.s: In 2026, India is described as the world's ______ largest oil consumer.
54.x: India is the third-largest oil consumer and also the third-largest energy consumer in the world. Second, fourth and fifth are incorrect.
54.tq: India: 3rd in energy, 3rd in oil consumption.
xs: India is the world's **third** largest oil consumer (**2026**) — option **(2)**.
It is also the **3rd largest energy consumer**.
xa: Crude import dependence: **88.5%** (**PPAC**, **July 2026**).
⚠ In coal, India is the **third-largest producer** but has the **fifth-largest reserves**.
India holds only **0.4%** of world oil reserves.

54.s: According to PPAC data, India's crude oil import bill in July 2026 rose year-on-year by approximately:
54.x: PPAC reported that the crude import bill of $13.7 billion in July 2026 was up 41% year-on-year. The 13.3% rise refers to import volume and 10% to petroleum product exports.
54.tq: Bill 41, volume 13.3.
xs: **PPAC**: the July 2026 crude import **bill** (**$13.7 billion**) rose **41%** YoY — option **(2)**.
**13.3%** is the rise in import **volume**; **10%** the rise in product exports.
xa: Volume: **21.4 MMT**.
Crude basket **$82.04/bbl** vs **$70.95** a year earlier.
The **41-MT** strategic storage plan followed the 2026 Hormuz disruption.

54.s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct regarding India’s hydrocarbon storage position?
o: LPG semi-strategic caverns have a capacity of approximately 0.14 MT.
India’s underground natural-gas storage capacity is greater than its crude-oil storage capacity.
India has no underground natural-gas storage facility mentioned in the assessment.
The total oil stock is approximately 74 days.
54.x: The assessment states that there is no underground natural-gas storage. LPG semi-strategic caverns are about 0.14 MT and total oil stock is about 74 days.
54.tq: Find the statement that directly contradicts the stated absence of underground natural-gas storage.
xs: The false statement is **underground natural-gas storage exceeding crude storage** — option **(2)**: India has **no underground natural-gas storage**.
LPG semi-strategic caverns ~**0.14 MT** and total oil stock ~**74 days** are correct.
xa: The proposed **41 MT** programme adds **9 MT LNG** (**56 days**).
SPR Phase I: **5.33 MMT** (**9.5 days**).
IEA norm: **90 days**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about methanol as a fuel:
1. It can be made from high-ash coal, agri-residue, biomass, natural gas and CO2 from thermal plants.
2. It cannot be used in cooking applications.
3. It is a low-carbon hydrogen-carrier fuel.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: besides replacing petrol/diesel in transport, DG sets and boilers, methanol can partly replace LPG and kerosene in cooking. So '1 and 3 only'.
54.tq: Methanol: many feedstocks, many uses incl. cooking.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: methanol can be made from **biomass**, **high-ash coal**, **agri-residue**, **CO2 from thermal plants**, **natural gas**.
Statement 2 is wrong: methanol can partly replace **LPG** and **kerosene** in **cooking**.
Statement 3 is correct: methanol is a low-carbon **hydrogen-carrier fuel**.
xa: **DME** = two methanol molecules minus one water molecule; can **substitute propane in LPG**.
**M15** (15% methanol) cuts gasoline imports by at least **15%**.
**20% DME in LPG** saves **₹6,000 crore/yr**.
NITI's Methanol Economy aims: cut oil import bill, cut **GHG**, use coal + **municipal solid waste** (APPSC-G1 2024: all three).

54.s: The principal objective of introducing Compressed Biogas Obligation in the City Gas Distribution sector is to
o: increase coal imports for power generation
replace all petrol vehicles with electric vehicles
substitute imports of liquefied natural gas
increase the import of LPG cylinders
54.x: The CBO is intended to promote compressed biogas and substitute LNG imports.
54.tq: Identify the stated import-substitution objective rather than a general clean-energy benefit.
xs: The **Compressed Biogas Obligation** in CGD aims to **substitute LNG imports** — option **(3)**.
Obligation: **1% / 3% / 4%** of CNG/PNG in **FY26 / FY27 / FY28**; **5%** from **2028-29**.
xa: Natural gas / LNG import share: **~47-51%**.
**Qatar** is the key LNG supplier.
No underground **natural-gas** storage exists in India.

54.s:
Match the major crude-oil supplier with its approximate share of India’s crude imports in 2025:

List-I (Supplier)
A. Russia
B. Iraq
C. Saudi Arabia
D. United States of America

List-II (Share)
1. About 8%
2. About 15%
3. About 20%
4. About 35%

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
54.x: Russia accounted for about 35%, Iraq about 20%, Saudi Arabia about 15% and the United States about 8% of India’s crude imports in 2025.
54.tq: Start with Russia’s largest share and use the descending supplier pattern to complete the code.
xs: Correct code: **A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1** — option **(1)**.
Crude shares **2025**: **Russia ~35%**, **Iraq ~20%**, **Saudi Arabia ~15%**, **USA ~8%**.
xa: **Russia** has been the **largest** supplier in recent years.
**West Asia + Africa** supply ~**65%** (**Dec 2025**).
India's imports from **OPEC** have fallen **below 50%** (older notes: **80%**).

54.s: With reference to India’s sedimentary basins, which one of the following is correct?
o: All 26 basins are currently producing hydrocarbons.
Only 7 sedimentary basins exist, all of which are producing.
Of 26 sedimentary basins, only 7 are producing.
Of 26 sedimentary basins, 19 are producing and 7 are non-producing.
54.x: India has 26 sedimentary basins, of which only 7 are producing according to the stated figures.
54.tq: Watch the reversal between the total number of basins and the number that are producing.
xs: Of India's **26 sedimentary basins**, **only 7** produce hydrocarbons — option **(3)**.
So neither "all 26 producing" nor "19 producing" fits the notes.
xa: **Hydrocarbon Vision 2025** calls for **appraisal of all sedimentary basins**.
**HELP** (single licence for all hydrocarbons) and **OALP** drive upstream exploration.
The **KG Basin** (offshore, East Coast) is one of India's most prolific hydrocarbon zones.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about the Strait of Hormuz:
1. It lies between Iran and Oman.
2. It carries about one-fifth of global LNG trade.
3. It carries about half of world crude-oil trade.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
54.x: Statement 1 is correct: the strait lies between Iran and Oman. Statement 2 is correct: about a fifth of global LNG trade passes through it. Statement 3 is wrong: it carries about 15 million bbl/day, roughly 34% (about one-third) of world crude trade, not half. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' leaves out the true LNG statement, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
54.tq: Hormuz: Iran-Oman, ~15 mb/d = ~34% of crude trade, one-fifth of LNG.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **Strait of Hormuz** lies **between Iran and Oman**.
Statement 2 is correct: it carries **a fifth** of global **LNG** trade.
Statement 3 is wrong: it carries ~**15 million bbl/day**, about **34%** of world crude trade — not half.
xa: **Iran** effectively closed it in **early March 2026**.
The closure led to a **41%** jump in India's July crude bill and an **LPG** crunch.

54.s: The increase in international oil prices is most directly associated with which combination of macroeconomic effects in India?
o: A rise in exports and elimination of the current account deficit
Lower inflation and a narrower trade deficit
A wider trade deficit and higher inflation
A fall in import expenditure and currency appreciation
54.x: Higher oil prices increase import costs, thereby widening the trade deficit and contributing to inflation.
54.tq: Apply the import-cost transmission mechanism to macroeconomic outcomes.
xs: Higher oil prices cause a **wider trade deficit** and **higher inflation** — option **(3)**.
Oil is the **biggest driver** of the **trade deficit/CAD**, and global volatility feeds **domestic inflation**.
xa: India's crude basket: **$82.04/bbl** in **July 2026** vs **$70.95** a year earlier.
Fiscal angle: **subsidy and excise** pressure when prices spike.

54.s: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026 was associated with which combination of developments?
o: A 4.1% rise in the crude bill, an ethanol shortage and a 500 MT fuel system
A 14% fall in the July crude bill, an LPG surplus and a proposed 4.1 MT system
A 41% rise in coal exports, a gas surplus and cancellation of strategic storage
A 41% rise in the July crude bill, an LPG crunch and a proposed 41 MT strategic fuel system
54.x: The disruption was linked to a 41% jump in the July crude bill, an LPG crunch and a proposed 41 MT strategic fuel system.
54.tq: Keep the percentage, commodity effect and storage quantity together; altered units are the trap.
xs: The **Hormuz** closure (**Mar 2026**) brought a **41%** jump in the **July crude bill**, an **LPG crunch** and a proposed **41 MT strategic fuel system** — option **(4)**.
**Iran** effectively closed the strait (between **Iran and Oman**) in **early March 2026**.
xa: July 2026 crude import bill: **$13.7 billion**.
The **41 MT** plan = **28 MT crude + 9 MT LNG + 4 MT LPG**.
Hormuz carries ~**15 million bbl/day** (~**34%** of world crude trade) and a fifth of global **LNG** trade.

54.s: India has about 17% of the world's population. Approximately what share of the world's oil reserves does it hold?
54.x: India holds only about 0.4% of world oil reserves. 0.6% is its share of gas reserves and 7% its share of coal reserves; 4% is not a stated figure.
54.tq: Reserves vs 17% population: gas 0.6, oil 0.4, coal 7.
xs: India holds only **0.4%** of world **oil** reserves — option **(1)**.
**0.6%** is its share of **gas** reserves and **7%** of **coal** reserves.
xa: This gap explains crude import dependence of **88.5%** (**PPAC**, **July 2026**).
Only **7** of **26** sedimentary basins produce.
**ONGC Videsh (OVL)** buys **equity oil** and gas abroad to offset the gap.

54.s:
Which of the following statements about India’s crude suppliers is correct?
1. Russia was the largest supplier in recent years.
2. Iraq and Saudi Arabia were among the major suppliers.
3. West Asia and Africa together supplied approximately 65%.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
54.x: Russia was the largest supplier in recent years; Iraq and Saudi Arabia were major suppliers; and West Asia and Africa together accounted for approximately 65% of supplies.
54.tq: Use the broad regional share to confirm the individual supplier statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Russia** was the largest supplier in recent years (~**35%** in **2025**).
**Iraq** (~**20%**) and **Saudi Arabia** (~**15%**) are major suppliers; **West Asia + Africa** supply ~**65%**.
xa: Other top suppliers: **UAE**, **USA** (~**8%**).
**IOC** signed new **2027** deals with **Algeria** + more US crude.
India's imports from **OPEC** have fallen **below 50%**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements regarding OPEC and OPEC+:
1. OPEC produces about 40% of global oil.
2. OPEC and Russia agreed to an unprecedented 10% output cut in 2020.
3. OPEC’s share of India’s crude imports has remained above 80% in recent years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: OPEC’s share of India’s imports has fallen below 50%, although older figures referred to a much higher share.
54.tq: Spot the outdated percentage in the third statement while retaining the two supported facts.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **OPEC** holds ~**40%** of global oil.
Statement 2: in **2020** **OPEC + Russia** agreed an unprecedented **10% output cut**.
Statement 3 is wrong: India's imports from OPEC have fallen **below 50%** (**Aug 2025**); **80%** is an older figure.
xa: **Russia** is now India's largest crude supplier (~**35%**).
**West Asia + Africa** supply ~**65%**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about India's Phase I Strategic Petroleum Reserves:
1. Actual stocks of about 3.37 MT (64% utilisation) give only about 5 days of cover.
2. The IEA norm for strategic reserves is 60 days of cover.
3. They are underground rock caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur with 5.33 MMT capacity (about 9.5 days at full).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the IEA norm is 90 days. So '1 and 3 only'.
54.tq: SPR Phase I: 5.33 MMT, 9.5 days full, ~5 days actual vs IEA 90.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: actual stocks ~**3.37 MT** (**64%** utilisation) give only ~**5 days** of cover.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **IEA norm** is **90 days**.
Statement 3 is correct: Phase I caverns at **Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur** hold **5.33 MMT** = **9.5 days** at full.
xa: **Phase II**: **Chandikhol (Odisha)** and **Padur (Karnataka)**; proposed **Bikaner**, **Rajkot**.
Proposed strategic fuel programme: **41 MT** = **28 MT crude + 9 MT LNG + 4 MT LPG**.
LPG semi-strategic caverns hold only ~**0.14 MT**; no underground gas storage.

54.s: Which one of the following correctly matches a strategic petroleum reserve site with its State and capacity?
54.x: Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh has a stated capacity of 1.33 MMT. Mangaluru and Padur are in Karnataka, while Padur’s capacity is 2.5 MMT.
54.tq: Check the place–State–capacity triple; the wrong options swap either the State or the capacity.
xs: **Visakhapatnam — AP — 1.33 MMT** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Mangaluru** (**1.5 MMT**) and **Padur** (**2.5 MMT**) are in **Karnataka**, not AP or Odisha.
xa: ⚠ **Padur** is in both **Phase I** and **Phase II**.
Phase II: **Chandikhol (Odisha)** and **Padur** approved.
Visakhapatnam also hosts the **HPCL** refinery and **IIPE**.

54.s:
Which of the following sites are associated with Phase II of India’s strategic petroleum reserve programme?
1. Chandikhol
2. Padur
3. Bikaner
4. Rajkot
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
54.x: Phase II was approved for Chandikhol in Odisha and Padur in Karnataka. Bikaner and Rajkot were proposed sites, not approved Phase II sites.
54.tq: Separate approved sites from merely proposed sites; this is a common status-based trap.
xs: **Phase II** was approved at **Chandikhol (Odisha)** and **Padur (Karnataka)** — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**Bikaner (Rajasthan)** and **Rajkot (Gujarat)** are only **proposed**.
xa: ⚠ **Padur** = in both **Phase I** and **Phase II**.
Phase I total: **5.33 MMT**.
Proposed **41 MT** strategic fuel programme = **28 MT crude + 9 MT LNG + 4 MT LPG**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. HELP provides a single licence for all hydrocarbons.
2. OALP is associated with upstream exploration and production.
3. ONGC Videsh is the overseas arm of ONGC.
4. Overseas acreages can augment India’s oil and gas supply.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: HELP provides a unified licence for hydrocarbons; OALP concerns upstream exploration; ONGC Videsh is ONGC’s overseas arm; and overseas acreages help augment supply.
54.tq: Test the institutional roles together, while avoiding the trap of treating overseas acquisition as domestic production.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**HELP** = single licence for all hydrocarbons; **OALP** = upstream exploration.
**ONGC Videsh (OVL)** = overseas arm of **ONGC**; **acquiring overseas acreages** augments supply.
xa: **One Nation One Gas Grid** is part of the upstream push.
Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 sought **equity oil abroad**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about the Krishna-Godavari Basin:
1. It is an offshore hydrocarbon zone on India’s East Coast.
2. It is one of India’s most prolific hydrocarbon zones.
3. Andhra Pradesh produces gas and crude oil in the Godavari Basin.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: The KG Basin is an offshore East Coast zone, is among India’s most prolific hydrocarbon zones, and Andhra Pradesh produces gas and crude oil in the Godavari Basin.
54.tq: Verify location, significance and production together before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
The **KG Basin** is **offshore** on the **East Coast** and one of India's **most prolific hydrocarbon zones**.
**AP** produces **gas + crude** in the **Godavari** basin.
xa: **IIPE Visakhapatnam** (est. **2016**, **INI 2017**) has a **shale**-modelling pact with **OIL India** for the KG basin.
**Visakhapatnam** hosts the **SPR**, **HPCL** refinery and **IIPE**.
Only **7** of **26** sedimentary basins produce.

54.s:
Which of the following are identified as import-substitution tools in the energy sector?
1. The target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030
2. The Green Hydrogen Mission
3. The proposed 41 MT strategic fuel system
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: The 500 GW non-fossil target and the Green Hydrogen Mission are identified as import-substitution tools. The 41 MT strategic fuel system is a response to energy disruption, not the stated pair of import-substitution tools.
54.tq: Separate long-term import substitution from emergency strategic-storage responses.
xs: The **500 GW non-fossil target by 2030** and the **Green Hydrogen Mission** are the import-substitution tools — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
The **41 MT** strategic fuel system is a **storage** response to the **2026 Hormuz** disruption, not import substitution.
xa: The 41 MT plan gives ~two months crude, **56 days** LNG and six weeks LPG cover.
Criticism: RE build-out is not yet cutting fossil imports.
Other substitution fuels: **methanol** (M15), **DME**, **ethanol** (E20) and **compressed biogas**.

54.s: Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 was adopted by the Government of India in
54.x: Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 was adopted by the Government of India in 2000.
54.tq: Distinguish the adoption year from the policy’s horizon year in its title.
xs: **Hydrocarbon Vision 2025** was adopted by GoI in **2000** — option **(2)**.
It is a **long-term hydrocarbon sector plan**, linked in exams with **storage of petroleum products** (UPPSC **2000**).
xa: Focus: energy security via domestic output + **equity oil abroad**; **strategic and buffer stocks**.
Also: appraisal of all sedimentary basins, globally competitive refining, **free market**, better fuel quality.
⚠ "**2025**" is the vision's horizon, not its year of adoption.

54.s: Which one of the following is NOT a focus area associated with Hydrocarbon Vision 2025?
o: Complete prohibition of private participation in hydrocarbons
54.x: Hydrocarbon Vision 2025 promotes a free market and competition; it does not seek complete prohibition of private participation. The other three are stated focus areas.
54.tq: Find the option that reverses the policy’s market-oriented approach.
xs: **Complete prohibition of private participation** is not a focus — option **(1)**; the vision backs a **free market + competition**.
Stated focus areas include **appraisal of all sedimentary basins**, **globally competitive refining** and **free market**.
xa: Other focus areas: **strategic and buffer stocks**, **equity oil abroad**, **better fuel quality**.
Adopted in **2000**.
Upstream follow-ups: **HELP**, **OALP**, **One Nation One Gas Grid**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP):
1. The E20 target was advanced to ESY 2025-26 from 2030.
2. E20 with a minimum 91 RON was mandated from 1 April 2026.
3. Pilots began in 2001, and 5% EBP was resolved from 1 January 2003 in 9 States and 4 UTs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
54.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct (blending was only ~1.53% in 2013-14; E20 was reached ahead of schedule). Statement 2 is wrong: E20 with a minimum 95 RON is mandated from 1 Apr 2026. So '1 and 3 only'.
54.tq: E20 advanced to 2025-26; 95 RON from April 2026.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **E20** was advanced to **ESY 2025-26** from **2030**.
Statement 2 is wrong: E20 with **min 95 RON** is mandated from **1 Apr 2026**.
Statement 3 is correct: pilots in **2001**; **5% EBP from 1 Jan 2003** in **9** States + **4** UTs.
xa: Blending was only ~**1.53%** in **2013-14**.
Farmer payments over **₹1,29,032 crore**.

54.s: The Compressed Biogas Obligation as a proportion of CNG-PNG is correctly represented by which sequence?
54.x: The obligation is 1% in FY26, 3% in FY27, 4% in FY28 and 5% from FY 2028–29.
54.tq: Track the year-wise progression instead of assuming a uniform annual increase.
xs: Option (1) reverses the order; option (3) has wrong steps.
xa: CBO applies to **CNG/PNG** consumption in **CGD**.
Aim: substitute **LNG** imports.
Gas / LNG import share is **~47-51%**.

54.s:
Consider the following statements about Di-Methyl Ether (DME):
1. It is obtained by adding one water molecule to two methanol molecules.
2. It can substitute propane in LPG.
3. It can substitute diesel in slow-RPM engines.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
54.x: Statement 1 is wrong: DME is two methanol molecules minus (not plus) one water molecule. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: DME can substitute propane in LPG and diesel in slow-RPM engines. So '2 and 3 only' is right; '1 and 2 only', '1 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' all include the false statement 1.
54.tq: DME = methanol dehydration: water is removed, not added.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **DME** = **two methanol molecules minus one water molecule**, not plus.
Statement 2 is correct: DME can **substitute propane in LPG**.
Statement 3 is correct: DME can replace **diesel in slow-RPM engines**.
xa: **20% DME in LPG** saves **₹6,000 crore/yr** — **₹50-100 per cylinder**.
**Methanol** = low-carbon **hydrogen-carrier fuel**.

54.s:
Consider the following aims of NITI Aayog's 'Methanol Economy' programme:
1. Reducing India's oil import bill
2. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions
3. Converting coal reserves and municipal solid waste into methanol
Which of the above are aims of the programme?
54.x: All three are aims of the Methanol Economy programme (APPSC-G1 2024 key: all three). Each of the other options leaves out a correct aim.
54.tq: Methanol Economy: import bill + GHG + coal/MSW to methanol - all three.
xs: All three are aims — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (APPSC-G1 **2024** key: all three).
NITI's **Methanol Economy**: cut the **oil import bill**, cut **GHG** emissions, turn **coal reserves + municipal solid waste** into methanol.
xa: **M15** benefit: at least **15%** cut in imports; **20%** cut in PM, NOx, SOx.
**20% DME in LPG**: **₹6,000 crore/yr** savings.
Methanol sources: biomass, **high-ash coal**, agri-residue, **CO2**, natural gas.

54.s: India’s LPG supply depends mainly on which of the following?
o: Underground storage maintained by state governments alone
54.x: India’s LPG supply depends mainly on stocks held by oil marketing companies. Semi-strategic underground LPG storage is only about 0.14 MT.
54.tq: Identify the principal operational source rather than the limited reserve arrangement.
xs: LPG supply depends mainly on **oil marketing company (OMC) stocks** — option **(4)**.
Semi-strategic underground LPG storage is only ~**0.14 MT**.
xa: **2026**: **LPG shortage** after the Hormuz shock; refineries ordered under the **LPG control order** raised output **35 to 54 TMT/day** in five days.
**PNGRB** authorised **~1,800 km** of LPG pipelines in **six States**.
The proposed **41 MT** strategic fuel programme includes **4 MT LPG** (six weeks' cover).

54.s: Which of the following is identified as the core challenge affecting India’s oil consumption and energy security?
o: Only the shortage of coal in inland regions
Declining use of renewable energy and falling global prices
Excess domestic crude production and stable prices
Supply-chain disruptions and fluctuating global oil prices
54.x: India’s core oil-related challenge is the combination of supply-chain disruptions and fluctuating global oil prices.
54.tq: Select the option that combines the two linked causes rather than an isolated factor.
xs: The core challenge is **supply-chain disruptions and fluctuating global oil prices** — option **(4)** (APPSC-G2 **2025** key).
India is the **3rd largest energy consumer** and **3rd largest oil consumer**.
xa: **Price** volatility feeds domestic inflation; **fiscal** pressure through subsidies and excise.
Oil is the biggest driver of the **trade deficit/CAD**; managed by **SPR, ethanol, EVs, RE**.
Chokepoint risk: the **Strait of Hormuz**.

54.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Indian Institute of Petroleum and Energy (IIPE), Visakhapatnam, is correct?
o: It was established in 2020 and signed a lithium-mining pact with KABIL in 2025.
It was established in 2015 and signed a pipeline-construction pact with PNGRB in 2026.
It was established in 2016, declared an Institution of National Importance in 2017, and signed a shale-modelling research pact with OIL India in April 2026.
It was established in 2017, declared an Institution of National Importance in 2016, and signed a coal-mining pact with Coal India.
54.x: IIPE Visakhapatnam was established in 2016, became an Institution of National Importance in 2017, and signed the stated shale-modelling pact with OIL India in April 2026.
54.tq: Keep establishment year, status year, partner and research subject distinct.
xs: **IIPE Visakhapatnam** was established in **2016**, became an **Institution of National Importance** in **2017**, and signed a **shale**-modelling pact with **OIL India** in **April 2026** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) swaps the two years; the pact is with OIL India, not KABIL, PNGRB or Coal India.
xa: The shale-modelling pact is for the **KG basin**.
**KG Basin** (offshore, East Coast) is one of India's most prolific hydrocarbon zones; AP produces gas + crude in the **Godavari** basin.
**Visakhapatnam** also hosts the **HPCL** refinery and the Phase I **SPR**.

54.s:
Assertion (A): Renewable-energy expansion has not yet eliminated India’s dependence on fossil-fuel imports.
Reason (R): Renewable energy can take years to become firm power, whereas external supply shocks can affect the system at once.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
54.x: Both statements are true, and the time required for renewable capacity to become firm power helps explain why it has not immediately displaced fossil-fuel imports during sudden shocks.
54.tq: Test whether the reason explains the time-scale mismatch stated in the assertion.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
A: the **renewable build-out** is **not yet cutting fossil imports**.
R explains why: **RE takes years to become firm power**, while **shocks hit at once**.
xa: Import-substitution tools: **RE target 500 GW non-fossil by 2030** + **Green Hydrogen Mission**.
Crude import dependence is still **88.5%** (**PPAC**, **July 2026**).
Oil is the **biggest driver** of the trade deficit/CAD.

55.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Ministry of Coal allots mines under the CMSP Act 2015 and the MMDR Act 1957.
2. BEE, set up under the Energy Conservation Act 2001, runs the NMEEE under NAPCC.
3. PNGRB is the regulator of the electricity sector.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
55.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: PNGRB (Act 2006) regulates petroleum and natural gas under MoPNG. So '1 and 2 only'.
55.tq: PNGRB = oil and gas; BEE = efficiency.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **Ministry of Coal** allots mines under the **CMSP Act 2015** and **MMDR Act 1957**.
Statement 2 is correct: **BEE** (**Energy Conservation Act 2001**) runs **NMEEE** under **NAPCC**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **PNGRB** regulates petroleum and natural gas under **MoPNG**, not electricity.
xa: **Department of Atomic Energy** is directly under the **Prime Minister**.
OIL India is a **Navratna** under MoPNG.
MNRE mission (APPSC-G2 2025): energy security, clean power, access, affordability, equity.

55.s:
Consider the following pairs (document : drafting body):
1. Draft National Energy Policy (2017) : Ministry of Power
2. National Electricity Policy (2005) : Ministry of Power
3. India Energy Security Scenarios 2047 : NITI Aayog
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
55.x: Pairs 2 and 3 are correct. Pair 1 is wrong: the Draft National Energy Policy (2017) was prepared by NITI Aayog. Note the trap: National Energy Policy = NITI; National Electricity Policy = Ministry of Power. So '2 and 3 only'.
55.tq: Energy Policy = NITI; Electricity Policy = Ministry of Power.
xs: Pairs **2 and 3** are correctly matched — option **(3)**.
Pair 1 is wrong: the **Draft National Energy Policy (2017)** is by **NITI Aayog**.
Pair 2 is correct: **National Electricity Policy (2005)** = **Ministry of Power**.
Pair 3 is correct: **IESS 2047** = **NITI Aayog**.
xa: ⚠ **National Energy Policy** = NITI; **National Electricity Policy** = Ministry of Power.
**Integrated Energy Policy** (**2006**, approved 2008) was by an expert committee under **Kirit Parikh**.
