Statement 2 is wrong: since FY 2021-22 States must pay the full subsidy and also clear legacy subsidy dues. So 1 only; 'both' and '2 only' include the wrong statement, and 'neither' rejects a true one.
59.tq: The reform is full payment plus clearing old dues, not half.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: States spend ~**₹2.4 lakh crore/yr** on farm + domestic power subsidies (12 Apr 2026).
Statement 2 is wrong: since **FY 2021-22** States pay the **full subsidy** and **clear legacy dues**.
xa: AP gives **20.79 lakh** BPL SC/ST households free power up to **200 units a month**.
AP aqua farmers pay **₹1.50/unit**.

59.s:
Consider the following statements about DISCOM loss metrics:
1. AT&C loss covers technical and commercial losses, including theft and inefficiency in billing and collection.
2. The ACS-ARR gap is the average revenue realised minus the average cost of supply per unit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
59.x: Statement 1 is correct: AT&C loss means technical plus commercial losses (theft, billing and collection inefficiency). Statement 2 is wrong because the order is reversed: the ACS-ARR gap is the average cost of supply minus the average revenue realised per unit. So 1 only.
59.tq: ACS-ARR is read in order: cost minus revenue, and a positive gap means a loss per unit.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **AT&C loss** = technical + commercial loss (**theft, billing and collection inefficiency**).
Statement 2 is reversed: **ACS-ARR gap** = **average cost of supply minus average revenue realised** per unit.
xa: ACS-ARR gap: **₹0.06/kWh** (FY25) = **6 paise** — ⚠ "**0.06 paise**" is wrong.

59.s:
Consider the following statements about the finances of DISCOMs in India:
1. DISCOMs posted a profit of Rs 2,701 crore in FY 2024-25 after a loss of Rs 67,962 crore in 2013-14.
2. AT&C losses rose from 15.04% in FY 2013-14 to 22.62% in FY 2024-25.
3. The ACS-ARR gap fell to Rs 0.06 per kWh (6 paise per unit) in FY 2024-25.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
59.x: Statement 2 is wrong: AT&C losses fell, from 22.62% (FY14) to 15.04% (FY 2024-25); the figures are reversed. Statement 3 is correct: the ACS-ARR gap fell from Rs 0.78 to Rs 0.06/kWh, i.e. 6 paise (not 0.06 paise). Statement 1 is correct: a profit of Rs 2,701 crore in FY25 against a loss of Rs 67,962 crore in 2013-14. So '1 and 3 only'.
59.tq: Every DISCOM metric improved: AT&C down to 15.04%, gap down to 6 paise, loss turned into profit.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **profit of ₹2,701 crore** in FY 2024-25 vs loss of **₹67,962 crore** in 2013-14.
Statement 2 is wrong: **AT&C losses fell** from **22.62%** (FY14) to **15.04%** (FY25).
Statement 3 is correct: **ACS-ARR gap** = **₹0.06/kWh** = **6 paise** per unit.
xa: ⚠ "**0.06 paise**" is a trap.
ACS-ARR gap was **₹0.78** in FY14.
**LPS Rules 2022** cut dues to gencos by **96%**.

59.s:
Consider the following components of DDUGJY:
1. Separation of agricultural and non-agricultural feeders
2. Strengthening of sub-transmission and distribution systems
3. Development of micro-grids and off-grid systems
4. Metering of distribution transformers, feeders and consumers
Which of the statements given above are correct?
59.x: All four are components of DDUGJY. The scheme also includes rural electrification as a major component.
59.tq: Test the completeness of a scheme by checking whether each listed component belongs to its design.
xs: All four — **feeder separation**, **sub-transmission/distribution strengthening**, **micro-grid + off-grid**, **metering** — are DDUGJY components, so option **(4)** is correct.
**Rural electrification** is a further component of DDUGJY.
xa: Goal: **24x7 power in rural India**; nodal **REC**; subsumed **RGGVY**.
Funding: **60%** grant + up to **15%** on milestones (**85%** + **5%** for special category States).
**Feeder separation** continues under **RDSS**; separated agricultural feeders are **solarised under PM-KUSUM**.

59.s: Repayment associated with the SPVs created to warehouse discom debt would qualify for
o: the Special Incentive Scheme for Capital Investment
59.x: Repayment of the warehoused discom debt qualifies for the Special Incentive Scheme for Capital Investment.
59.tq: Distinguish the incentive linked to debt repayment from the names of other electricity schemes.
xs: Repayment of **SPVs warehousing DISCOM debt** qualifies for the **Special Incentive Scheme for Capital Investment** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is part of the **16th Finance Commission's** Reform 2 (power sector).
xa: The **16th FC** recommends States **privatise DISCOMs** actively.
**Delhi** DISCOMs were privatised in **2002** (Tata Power-DDL, BSES).
⚠ **UDAY** (2015) was a debt-takeover scheme — different from the 16th FC's SPV route.

59.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Delhi DISCOMs — Privatised in 2002
2. Odisha DISCOMs — Taken over by Tata Power in 2020-21
3. Bhiwandi input-based franchise model — Torrent, 2007
4. Sixteenth Finance Commission — Recommendation for active DISCOM privatisation by States

Select the correct answer using the code below.
59.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Delhi’s DISCOMs were privatised in 2002, Odisha’s were taken over by Tata Power in 2020-21, Bhiwandi pioneered the cited franchise model in 2007, and the Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended active State-led privatisation.
59.tq: Start with the sure historical pair and verify the remaining institutional associations.
xs: All four pairs are correctly matched — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Delhi** DISCOMs privatised **2002** (Tata Power-DDL, BSES); **Odisha** DISCOMs taken over by **Tata Power** in **2020-21**.
**Bhiwandi** input-based franchisee — **Torrent, 2007**; **16th FC** recommends active DISCOM privatisation by States.
xa: The 16th FC also asks States to create **SPVs to warehouse DISCOM debt**.
Repayment qualifies for the **Special Incentive Scheme for Capital Investment**.

59.s:
Which of the following publications are associated with NITI Aayog?
1. India Energy Security Scenarios 2047
2. Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero
3. National Electricity Plan
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
59.x: NITI Aayog is associated with India Energy Security Scenarios 2047 and the 2026 Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero. The National Electricity Plan is a CEA report.
59.tq: Reject the statement that assigns a CEA publication to NITI Aayog.
xs: **NITI Aayog** produced **India Energy Security Scenarios 2047** and **Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero** (Feb 2026) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **National Electricity Plan** is a **CEA** report, so statement 3 is wrong.
xa: CEA also produces **NGAP 2026-27 to 2035-36** (**1,121 GW**, **70%** non-fossil).
NITI projects coal's generation share falling from about **74%** to **6-10% by 2070**.
**Energy Statistics (India)** is by **NSO, MoSPI**.

59.s: India’s peak power shortage declined from approximately 4.2% in 2014 to what level in 2025?
59.x: The peak shortage fell sharply from 4.2% in 2014 to 0.03% in 2025.
59.tq: Pay attention to the decimal placement in a near-zero deficit figure.
xs: Peak shortage fell from **4.2% (2014)** to **0.03% (2025)** — option **(1)**.
The demand-supply gap became **zero by Nov 2025** (ES).
xa: Record peak demand **270.82 GW** on **21 May 2026**.
NGAP projects peak demand of **459 GW** by **2035-36**.

59.s: The Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules, 2022 enable discoms to
o: fix tariffs without approval of the regulator
obtain free power from renewable generators
clear old dues in instalments and face restriction of power-exchange access for defaulting entities
59.x: The 2022 Rules permit discoms to clear old dues in instalments and provide for cutting power-exchange access for defaulters.
59.tq: Apply the rule to a defaulting discom rather than confuse it with tariff regulation.
xs: The **LPS Rules 2022** let DISCOMs clear **old (legacy) dues** in **interest-free EMIs**, with **power-exchange access cut** for defaulters — option **(3)**.
Result: dues to gencos fell from ~**₹1.35-1.39 lakh crore** (2022) to **₹4,927 crore** (Jan 2026) — a **96%** cut.
xa: Earlier figure: **₹6,576 crore** (Nov 2025).
Payment cycle: **178 days (FY21)** → **113 days (FY25)**.

59.s: Under the Rights of Consumers Rules, a new electricity connection is to be provided within which maximum periods in metropolitan, municipal and rural areas respectively?
59.x: The prescribed periods are 3 days in metropolitan areas, 7 days in municipal areas and 15 days in rural areas.
59.tq: Retain the geographical order while matching each area with its time limit.
xs: New connection within **3 days** (metro), **7 days** (municipal), **15 days** (rural) — option **(1)**.
Option (3) reverses the order.
xa: The **Rights of Consumers Rules 2020** also set **service standards**.
Adopted by all **36** States/UTs.

59.s: Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana (UDAY), launched in November 2015, was primarily intended for which of the following purposes?
o: Financial turnaround and revival of DISCOMs
Universal installation of nuclear power plants
Privatisation of all State Electricity Boards
59.x: UDAY was launched in November 2015 to achieve the financial turnaround and revival of distribution companies.
59.tq: Directly identify the purpose associated with the named scheme.
xs: **UDAY** (Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, **Nov 2015**) aimed at the **financial turnaround and revival of DISCOMs** — so option **(1)** is correct (UPSC 2016).
It is a DISCOM scheme, not a transmission-corridor, nuclear or privatisation scheme.
xa: ⚠ **UDAY** = debt takeover (financial) vs **RDSS** = results-linked infrastructure + reform grant.
UDAY had **operational** interventions (feeder/DT metering, smart meters, AT&C loss reduction) and **demand-side** ones (**LED bulbs**).
The **Green Energy Corridor** handles RE transmission — begun with a **PGCIL** study in **2012**.

59.s:
Consider the following statements about rural electrification schemes:
1. Saubhagya, launched in 2017, provides last-mile household connections with REC as its nodal agency.
2. The nodal agency for DDUGJY is the Power Finance Corporation.
3. DDUGJY, conveyed in December 2014, subsumed RGGVY and aims at 24x7 power in rural areas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
59.x: Statement 3 is correct: DDUGJY (3 Dec 2014) subsumed RGGVY and targets 24x7 rural power. Statement 2 is wrong: the nodal agency of DDUGJY is REC, not PFC. Statement 1 is correct: Saubhagya (2017) is for last-mile household connections, nodal agency REC. So '1 and 3 only'.
59.tq: DDUGJY = villages/feeders (2014); Saubhagya = households (2017); both nodal REC.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **Saubhagya** (**2017**) = last-mile household connections; nodal **REC**.
Statement 2 is wrong: DDUGJY's nodal agency is **REC**, not PFC.
Statement 3 is correct: **DDUGJY** (**3 Dec 2014**) subsumed **RGGVY**; aims at 24x7 rural power.
xa: All inhabited census villages electrified on **28 April 2018**; last: **Leisang (Manipur)**.
Saubhagya electrified ~**2.86 crore** households.
**RDSS** (2021) outlay **₹3.03 lakh crore**; nodal **REC and PFC**.

59.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the relationship between feeder separation, RDSS and PM-KUSUM?
o: Feeder separation ended with DDUGJY and has no connection with later schemes.
Feeder separation continues under RDSS, and separated agricultural feeders are subsequently solarised under PM-KUSUM.
PM-KUSUM separates urban commercial feeders under RDSS.
RDSS replaced feeder separation with only off-grid micro-grids.
59.x: Feeder separation continues under RDSS, while separated agricultural feeders can subsequently be solarised under PM-KUSUM.
59.tq: Trace the policy sequence from an infrastructure intervention to its later application.
xs: **Feeder separation continues under RDSS**, and separated agricultural feeders are **solarised under PM-KUSUM** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Feeder separation did not end with DDUGJY, and PM-KUSUM concerns **agricultural** feeders, not urban commercial ones.
xa: **Separation of agricultural and non-agricultural feeders** was a core **DDUGJY** component.
**PM-KUSUM in AP:** solarise **2.93 lakh** farm pump sets.
**APSPDCL** segregated **312 of 3,015** agricultural feeders (2024-25).

59.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

xs: **(a)–28 April 2018**, **(b)–18,374**, **(c)–Leisang**, **(d)–Manipur** — so option **(1)** is correct.
On **28 April 2018** all inhabited census villages were electrified; the last was **Leisang (Manipur)**.
xa: The **IEA** called it one of the world's greatest success stories.

59.s:
Which of the following features characterises RDSS?
1. It is reform-based.
2. It is results-linked.
3. It has been extended by two years up to FY 2027-28.
4. REC and PFC are its nodal agencies.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
59.x: All four statements are correct. RDSS is reform-based and results-linked, has been extended to FY 2027-28, and uses REC and PFC as nodal agencies.
59.tq: Use a four-part scheme profile rather than relying on its name alone.
xs: All four statements are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
RDSS is **reform-based** and **results-linked**; **extended by 2 years to FY 2027-28**; nodal **REC and PFC**.
xa: Outlay **₹3.03 lakh crore** (2021 scheme).
Smart metering under RDSS uses the **TOTEX (PPP)** model; **~4.7 crore installed, 20.34 crore sanctioned**.
**100% Indian HES/MDMS** is mandated for smart metering.

59.s:
Consider the following statements about Energy Efficiency Services Limited (EESL):
1. It undertakes demand aggregation for large smart-metering programmes.
2. It signed an MoU with PNGRB for smart domestic PNG meters.
3. It has replaced REC as the nodal agency of the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
59.x: Statement 1 is correct: EESL aggregates demand for large smart-metering programmes. Statement 2 is correct: it signed an MoU with PNGRB for smart domestic piped natural gas meters. Statement 3 is wrong: the nodal agencies of RDSS are REC and PFC, not EESL. So 1 and 2 only.
59.tq: RDSS nodal agencies = REC + PFC; EESL only aggregates demand.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **EESL** does **demand aggregation** for large smart-metering programmes.
Statement 2 is correct: EESL signed an **MoU with PNGRB** for smart domestic **PNG meters** (7 Sept 2026).
Statement 3 is wrong: RDSS nodal agencies are **REC and PFC** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: RDSS smart meters: **~4.7 crore installed, 20.34 crore sanctioned**; **TOTEX (PPP)** model.
RDSS is **reform-based, results-linked**, extended to **FY 2027-28**.

59.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Initiative/feature)
 a. UDAY
 b. RDSS
 c. ICEP-2024 in Andhra Pradesh
 d. PM JANMAN through AP DISCOMs

List-II (Description)

AP's **ICEP-2024** targets **160 GW** of RE; **PM JANMAN** electrified **24,691** tribal households via AP DISCOMs.
xa: UDAY was launched in **Nov 2015** for the **financial turnaround of DISCOMs**.
RDSS (**2021**): outlay **₹3.03 lakh crore**, nodal **REC and PFC**, extended to **FY 2027-28**.
RDSS sanction for AP: **₹15,083.14 crore** (2025-26).
AP's **T&D losses** are **9.25%**.

59.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Andhra Pradesh’s coal supply:
1. Andhra Pradesh has no coal of its own.
2. It depends on coal from Singareni and MCL.
3. Its thermal power plants therefore depend entirely on imported coal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
59.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Andhra Pradesh has no coal of its own and draws coal from Singareni and MCL. Statement 3 is wrong: because its supply comes from these domestic sources (Singareni and MCL), its plants do not depend entirely on imported coal. So 1 and 2 only.
59.tq: Reject the extreme word “entirely” and distinguish domestic external sources from imports.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **AP has no coal of its own**.
Statement 2 is correct: it depends on **Singareni** and **MCL** coal.
Statement 3 is wrong: the supply comes from these sources, not entirely imports — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: AP coal plants: **Simhadri (NTPC, 2,000 MW)**, **Dr NTTPS**, **RTPP**, **Krishnapatnam**, **Hinduja**.
**APERC** approved buying **1,600 MW** coal power under **Section 63** (Aug 2026).
**CEA** plan: **5,588 MW** thermal additions in AP by **2035-36**.

59.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

a. Simhadri STPP
b. Dr NTTPS
c. Dr M.V.R. RTPP
 d. Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah TPS

**Dr M.V.R. RTPP** — Muddanur, Kadapa; **Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah TPS** — Krishnapatnam, Nellore.

**Hinduja National Power** (private) is also at **Visakhapatnam**.
AP coal comes from **Singareni** and **MCL**.

59.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Dr M.V.R. RTPP — APGENCO — 600 MW unit
Dr NTTPS — APGENCO — 500 MW and 800 MW units
59.x: Hinduja National Power in Visakhapatnam is owned by the Hinduja group, not APGENCO. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
59.tq: Find the swapped owner in a plant–location–capacity association.
xs: **Hinduja National Power** is owned by the **Hinduja group** (private), not APGENCO — so option **(4)** is the wrong pair.
**RTPP** — APGENCO, **600 MW** unit; **Simhadri** — NTPC, **2,000 MW** (APPSC 2025 key); **NTTPS** — APGENCO, **500 MW and 800 MW** units.
xa: Hinduja plant is in **Visakhapatnam**; **Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah TPS** belongs to **APPDCL**.
**RTPP** is at **Muddanur, Kadapa**; **NTTPS** at **Ibrahimpatnam**.

59.s: The transmission and distribution (T&D) losses of Andhra Pradesh's power system are reported at about
59.x: AP's T&D losses are 9.25%, with 376 EHT substations and 33,379.72 ckm of transmission lines. 15.04% and 22.62% are the national AT&C losses for FY25 and FY14, and 4.2% was India's peak power shortage in 2014.
59.tq: AP T&D 9.25% vs national AT&C 15.04%.
xs: AP's **T&D losses** are **9.25%** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**15.04%** and **22.62%** are national **AT&C losses** (FY25, FY14); **4.2%** was India's power **shortage in 2014**.
xa: AP has **376 EHT substations** and **33,379.72 ckm** of transmission lines.
National shortage fell to **0.03% (2025)**.
AP's RDSS sanction: **₹15,083.14 crore**.

59.s: Who introduced free electricity for farmers in Andhra Pradesh after becoming Chief Minister on 14 May 2004?
59.x: Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy introduced free electricity for farmers after becoming Chief Minister on 14 May 2004.
59.tq: Match the policy decision with the correct office-holder and date.
xs: **Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy** gave **free electricity to farmers** after becoming CM on **14 May 2004** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This is the AP free farm power policy; the notes link it to no other CM.
xa: **Aqua farmers** pay a concessional **₹1.50/unit**.
**20.79 lakh** BPL SC/ST households get free power up to **200 units a month**.
States spend ~**₹2.4 lakh crore/yr** subsidising farm and domestic power.

59.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched regarding Andhra Pradesh DISCOMs?
o: APSPDCL — Headquartered at Hyderabad after its 2020 re-formation
59.x: APSPDCL is headquartered at Tirupati. APCPDCL was re-formed in 2020 at Vijayawada; the older pre-2014 APCPDCL was associated with Hyderabad.
59.tq: Find the single location and organisational-history mismatch.
xs: **APSPDCL** is headquartered at **Tirupati**, not Hyderabad — so option **(3)** is the wrong pair.
**APEPDCL** — **Visakhapatnam**; **APCPDCL** — re-formed **2020** at **Vijayawada**.
xa: The pre-2014 **APCPDCL** was at **Hyderabad**.
At bifurcation, APSPDCL took over **Anantapur and Kurnool** from APCPDCL.
AP discoms began **Phase-2 smart meters** for industrial consumers (Jan 2026).

59.s: In Andhra Pradesh, BPL SC/ST households receive free electricity up to how many units a month?
59.x: About 20.79 lakh BPL SC/ST households get free power up to 200 units a month. 100, 150 and 300 units are not the stated limit. Aqua farmers, by contrast, get a concessional tariff of Rs 1.50 per unit.
59.tq: SC/ST BPL: 200 units free; aqua: Rs 1.50/unit.
xs: **BPL SC/ST households** in AP get free power up to **200 units a month** — so option **(3)** is correct.
About **20.79 lakh** such households benefit.
xa: **Aqua farmers:** concessional **₹1.50/unit**.
**Free farm power** began under **Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy** (CM from **14 May 2004**).
**PM JANMAN** electrified **24,691** tribal households via AP DISCOMs.

59.s: Which one of the following was NOT identified as a cause of the financial sickness of State Electricity Boards?
o: Autonomy of State Governments over power generation and distribution
Sale of electricity to agricultural and domestic consumers below cost
59.x: State autonomy over power generation and distribution was identified as not being a problem. Below-cost sales, high T&D losses and poor cost recovery were causes of financial sickness.
59.tq: Find the exception by separating a governance feature from genuine financial problems.
xs: States' **autonomy over power generation and distribution** is **not** a problem — option **(1)** (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
Real causes (BPSC 2011 key): **sale below cost** to farm/domestic users, high **T&D losses**, **poor cost recovery**, **commercial losses (theft)**.
xa: Other real problems: **rising commercial losses of SEBs**, **delays in commissioning projects**.
States spend ~**₹2.4 lakh crore/yr** on farm + domestic power subsidy.

59.s: Which one of the following is a demand-side intervention under UDAY?
59.x: The use of energy-efficient LED bulbs is a demand-side intervention. Coal swapping, transformer upgrades and feeder metering are operational interventions.
59.tq: Separate operational measures from measures that reduce consumer-side energy demand.
xs: **Energy-efficient LED bulbs** are a **demand-side intervention** under UDAY — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2017).
**Feeder/DT metering**, **transformer upgrading** and **coal swapping** are **operational interventions**.
xa: Other demand-side items: energy-efficient **agricultural pumps, fans and ACs**; LED bulbs came via **UJALA**.
Other operational items: **consumer indexing**, **smart meters**, reducing **AT&C loss**.
UDAY was launched in **Nov 2015** for the **financial turnaround of DISCOMs**.

59.s: Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are particularly relevant to the electricity system for:
o: Replacing all transmission and distribution networks
Meeting the evening peak in demand
Eliminating the need for power-purchase agreements
59.x: BESS is highlighted as a means of managing the evening peak in electricity demand, especially alongside variable renewable generation.
59.tq: Scenario application: identify the system role naturally associated with storage.
xs: **BESS** is relevant for meeting the **evening peak** in demand — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does not raise coal's share, replace networks or remove the need for PPAs.
xa: The **NGAP** plans storage of **174 GW/888 GWh**: **94 GW** pumped storage + **80 GW BESS**.
AP plans BESS for the evening peak while buying **1,600 MW** of thermal power.
Record peak demand: **270.82 GW** on **21 May 2026**.

60.s: In a hydroelectric power plant, which sequence correctly represents the conversion of energy?
o: Electrical energy → potential energy → kinetic energy → mechanical energy
Potential energy → kinetic energy → mechanical energy of turbine → electrical energy
Kinetic energy → chemical energy → mechanical energy → electrical energy
Mechanical energy → potential energy → thermal energy → electrical energy
60.x: Stored water has potential energy; falling water gains kinetic energy, turns the turbine through mechanical energy, and the generator produces electricity by electromagnetic induction.
60.tq: Follow the physical sequence from stored water to turbine motion and then generation.
xs: The sequence is **potential → kinetic → mechanical (turbine) → electrical** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Stored water = **potential energy**; falling water → **kinetic**; it spins the turbine → **mechanical**; the generator gives **electrical energy** by **electromagnetic induction**.
Options (1), (3) and (4) bring in wrong starting forms or **chemical/thermal** energy, which play no part.
xa: Net transformation: **Potential → Electrical** (APPSC 2023; APPSC-GS 2023 key).
**Pumped storage** reverses the cycle: surplus power pumps water uphill, released at peak.
**Run-of-the-river** plants use natural flow with little or no storage.

60.s: Which APGENCO thermal plant commissioned a Stage V 1x800 MW unit in December 2023?
60.x: Dr NTTPS near Vijayawada commissioned its Stage V 800 MW unit in December 2023 (total 2,560 MW). RTPP at Muddanur is 1,650 MW, Simhadri belongs to NTPC, and Hinduja National Power is a private plant.
60.tq: NTTPS Stage V 800 MW = Dec 2023.
xs: **Dr NTTPS, Vijayawada** commissioned **Stage V 1x800 MW** in **Dec 2023** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**RTPP Muddanur** is **1,650 MW**; **Simhadri** is NTPC's; **Hinduja** is private.
xa: Dr NTTPS total = **2,560 MW** (APGENCO).
**Krishnapatnam (SDSTPS)** Stage I = **2x800 MW**.
APGenco plans two **3,200 MW** plants.

60.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy.
II. Thermal energy is internal energy due to molecular motion.
III. Kinetic energy includes translational and rotational forms.
IV. Potential energy includes gravitational and elastic forms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
60.x: All four are correct: mechanical energy is KE + PE, thermal energy comes from molecular motion, KE can be translational or rotational, and PE can be gravitational or elastic.
60.tq: Recall the classification of energy forms.
n: Kinetic energy can be translational. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Kinetic energy can be rotational. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Potential energy can be gravitational. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Potential energy can be elastic or spring energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Mechanical energy equals kinetic energy plus potential energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Thermal or heat energy is internal energy due to molecular motion. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
xs: **All four — I, II, III and IV** — are correct — option **(3)**.
I: **mechanical energy = kinetic + potential**; II: **thermal energy** = internal energy from **molecular motion**.
III: kinetic energy is **translational** or **rotational**; IV: potential energy includes **gravitational** and **elastic**.
xa: Other forms of potential energy: **electric**, **chemical**, **nuclear**.
In a hydro plant, **potential → electrical** (APPSC 2023).
**Friction in brakes** converts **kinetic → heat**.

60.s:
How many of the following energy conversions are correctly matched?
1. Mechanical → Electrical: Generator
2. Electrical → Mechanical: Electric motor
3. Chemical → Electrical: Battery
4. Light → Electrical: Solar cell
60.x: All four are correct: a generator turns mechanical into electrical, a motor electrical into mechanical, a battery chemical into electrical and a solar cell light into electrical energy.
60.tq: Check each device's input and output energy.
n: A generator or dynamo converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A battery or cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A solar cell converts light energy into electrical energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
xs: **All four** are correctly matched — option **(4)**.
**Generator**: **mechanical → electrical**; **electric motor**: **electrical → mechanical**.
**Battery**: **chemical → electrical**; **solar cell**: **light → electrical**.
xa: **LED / bulb**: **electrical → light**.
**Nuclear power plant**: **nuclear → heat → electrical**.
In a hydro plant, the generator works by **electromagnetic induction**.

60.s:
How many of the following are examples of potential energy being converted into kinetic energy?
1. Free fall
2. A pendulum
3. A roller coaster
60.x: All three convert potential into kinetic energy: a falling body, a swinging pendulum and a roller coaster going down.
60.tq: Recall examples of PE turning into KE.
n: Free fall demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A pendulum demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A roller coaster demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
xs: **All three** convert potential to kinetic energy — option **(3)**.
**Free fall**, a **pendulum** and a **roller coaster** all turn **potential → kinetic** energy.
xa: Hydro plant: stored water (**potential**) → falling water (**kinetic**) → turbine (**mechanical**) → **electrical**.
**Friction in brakes**: **kinetic → heat**.
**Mechanical energy** = kinetic + potential.

60.s:
Consider the following statements about types of hydroelectric plants:
1. A storage (reservoir) plant uses a dam to store water and regulate output.
2. A run-of-the-river plant needs a large reservoir that substantially alters the watercourse.
3. A pumped-storage plant acts as a 'grid battery', pumping water uphill with surplus power and releasing it at peak demand.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
60.x: Statement 2 is wrong: a run-of-the-river plant has little or no storage and uses the natural flow without much altering the watercourse. Statement 1 is correct: a storage plant's dam stores water and regulates output. Statement 3 is correct: pumped storage is a grid battery and the fastest large-scale storage. So '1 and 3 only'.
60.tq: Run-of-river = no big dam; storage = dam regulates; pumped storage = grid battery.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: a **storage (reservoir)** plant's dam stores water and **regulates output**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **run-of-the-river** has **little or no storage** and uses natural flow.
Statement 3 is correct: **pumped storage** is a "**grid battery**".
xa: ⚠ **Small hydro (≤25 MW) = MNRE**; **large hydro (>25 MW) = Ministry of Power**.
Large hydro was declared **renewable** in **March 2019**.
India's hydro potential is **>145 GW**, only ~**36%** developed.

60.s: According to the classification specified for hydro projects, which statement is correct?
o: Small hydro means projects above 25 MW, while large hydro means projects up to 3 MW.
Small hydro means projects up to 25 MW, while large hydro means projects above 25 MW.
Large hydro is defined as projects between 3 MW and 25 MW only.
Both small and large hydro are limited to projects below 3 MW.
60.x: MNRE treats projects up to 25 MW as small hydro, while the Ministry of Power treats projects above 25 MW as large hydro.
60.tq: Discriminate between adjacent threshold categories using the exact numerical cutoff.
xs: **Small hydro = up to 25 MW** (**MNRE**); **large hydro = above 25 MW** (**Ministry of Power**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**3 MW** was only the older threshold transferred to MNRE in **1989**.
xa: The ceiling was raised to **25 MW** in **November 1999**.
⚠ Large hydro, though under the Ministry of Power, is counted as **renewable** since **March 2019**.
Installed: large hydro **51.96 GW**; small hydro **5.18 GW**.

60.s: Which sequence correctly represents the change in the small-hydro threshold mentioned in the policy history?
o: Up to 25 MW in 1989 and up to 3 MW in November 1999
Up to 3 MW in 1989 and up to 25 MW in November 1999
Up to 3 MW in 1999 and up to 25 MW in 2005
Up to 25 MW in 1989 and above 25 MW in November 1999
60.x: Small hydro plants up to 3 MW were transferred to MNRE in 1989, and the ceiling was raised to 25 MW in November 1999; today small hydro means up to 25 MW (MNRE) and large hydro above 25 MW (Ministry of Power). Options that reverse the two thresholds or dates are wrong.
60.tq: Arrange policy changes by date and verify the associated numerical threshold.
xs: Plants **up to 3 MW** went to MNRE in **1989**; the limit became **up to 25 MW** in **November 1999** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the thresholds; options (3) and (4) have wrong years or limits.
xa: Today small hydro (**≤25 MW**) = **MNRE**; large hydro (**>25 MW**) = **Ministry of Power**.
**Small hydro potential:** **21,133 MW from 7,133 sites** (IIT Roorkee HRED, July 2016).

60.s: Which geographical observation regarding peninsular rivers and hydropower is correct?
o: Waterfalls in peninsular rivers can aid hydropower, while east-flowing rivers are generally more suited to irrigation than power generation
Peninsular rivers have no waterfalls useful for hydropower
East-flowing rivers are unsuitable for irrigation but ideal for hydropower
All peninsular rivers are primarily used for pumped storage
60.x: Waterfalls support hydropower generation in peninsular rivers, whereas east-flowing rivers are generally more suitable for irrigation than power generation.
60.tq: Use the comparison between river gradient and preferred use.
xs: **Waterfalls** on peninsular rivers aid hydropower, while **east-flowing rivers** suit **irrigation more than power** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other options reverse or overstate this.
xa: Peninsular example: **Koyna** (Maharashtra, **Western Ghats**) = **1,960 MW**.
**Srisailam** and **Nagarjuna Sagar** are on the **Krishna**.
Main hydro potential lies in the **Himalayan/Northeast** belt.

60.s: Which characteristic makes pumped-storage hydropower especially useful for balancing a power grid?
o: It is the fastest-responding large-scale storage option
It functions only when solar generation is absent throughout the year
It is the slowest form of large-scale electricity storage
It eliminates the need for transmission networks
60.x: Pumped storage is described as the fastest-responding large-scale storage, making it useful for balancing variable renewable generation and peak demand.
60.tq: Identify the precise functional advantage rather than the general description.
xs: **Pumped storage** is the **fastest-responding large-scale storage** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is used at peak, needs transmission, and is not the slowest option.
xa: It is called a "**giant water battery**".
It lets solar and wind stand in for coal at **peak hours** — needed for **500 GW** non-fossil.
ISTS charges are waived for **BESS and PSP till 2028**.

60.s: Which category of pumped-storage projects is exempted from concurrence of the Central Electricity Authority?
o: Only projects owned by State governments

60.s:

60.tq: Arrange the operational stages from charging to discharging.
xs: Order: **pump with surplus power (2) → store (3) → release at peak (1)** — so option **(2)**, **2–3–1**.

xa: PSP = "**giant water battery**", fastest large-scale storage.

NGAP storage: **94 GW PSP + 80 GW BESS**.

n: Potential energy can be electric. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Potential energy can be chemical. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Potential energy can be nuclear. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
xs: **Only three** are forms of potential energy — option **(3)**: **electric**, **chemical** and **nuclear**.
**Thermal energy** is **internal energy** due to **molecular motion**, not potential energy.
xa: Potential energy also includes **gravitational** and **elastic / spring**.
**Kinetic energy** is **translational** or **rotational**.

The AP power plan lists **Polavaram hydro + Upper Sileru PSP** (Aug 2026).
**Upper Sileru** hydro = **240 MW (4 x 60 MW)**.

60.s:
With reference to hydroelectric projects in Andhra Pradesh, consider the following pairs:
1. Upper Sileru — 240 MW
2. Lower Sileru — 460 MW
3. Machkund — 114.75 MW
4. Polavaram — 815.6 MW
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
60.x: Upper Sileru has 240 MW, Lower Sileru 460 MW and Machkund 114.75 MW. Polavaram has 960 MW, not 815.6 MW.
60.tq: Check each numerical pairing against the project capacity before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct: **Upper Sileru 240 MW**, **Lower Sileru 460 MW**, **Machkund 114.75 MW** — so option **(1)**.
Pair 4 is wrong: **Polavaram** is **960 MW**; **815.6 MW** is **Nagarjuna Sagar** main PH.
xa: **Lower Sileru** is adding **2 more 115 MW units** for peak demand.
**Machkund** is an **AP-Odisha joint project**.
⚠ **Upper Sileru PSP** = **1,350 MW** — different from the 240 MW hydro.

60.s: Which multipurpose project on the Krishna is one of the largest masonry dams in the world?
60.x: Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna is one of the world's largest masonry dams and serves irrigation, power and drinking water. Srisailam is also on the Krishna but is not the cited masonry dam, Polavaram is on the Godavari, and Machkund is an AP-Odisha project on the Machkund river.
60.tq: Nagarjuna Sagar = largest masonry dam; Polavaram = 960 MW.
xs: **Nagarjuna Sagar** on the Krishna is one of the **largest masonry dams** in the world — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Srisailam** is also on the Krishna but not the cited masonry dam; **Polavaram** is on the **Godavari**; **Machkund** is AP-Odisha.
xa: Nagarjuna Sagar is **multipurpose**: irrigation, power, drinking water.
Main PH **815.6 MW** (Telangana); Right Canal PH **90 MW** (AP).
Srisailam: Right Bank **770 MW** (AP), Left Bank **900 MW** (Telangana).

60.s: An Ultra Mega Power Project (UMPP) is best described as a
o: 4,000 MW gas plant established through administrative allocation
5,000 MW renewable-energy park awarded through viability-gap funding
3,000 MW subcritical hydro plant awarded through reverse auction
4,000 MW supercritical coal plant awarded through tariff-based bidding
60.x: A UMPP is a 4,000 MW supercritical coal plant awarded through tariff-based bidding.
60.tq: Break the definition into its capacity, technology, fuel and bidding method.
xs: A **UMPP** is a **4,000 MW supercritical coal plant** awarded by **tariff-based bidding** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is coal-based, not gas, renewable or hydro, and is not given by allocation or reverse auction.
xa: UMPPs: **Sasan** (MP), **Mundra** (Gujarat), **Krishnapatnam** (AP, stalled), **Tilaiya** (Jharkhand, given up).
**Mundra UMPP** = **Tata Power**; the others = **Reliance Power**.
APGenco plans two **3,200 MW ultra mega supercritical** plants.

60.s:
Which of the following are measures associated with flexible operation of the power system?
1. Pumped storage
2. Batteries
3. Cyclical operation of gas plants
4. Hydro optimisation alongside coal
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
60.x: Flexible operation includes pumped storage, batteries, cyclical operation of gas plants and optimisation of hydro generation alongside coal.
60.tq: Treat the listed flexibility measures as a combined system-management toolkit.
xs: All four — **pumped storage, batteries, cyclical operation of gas plants, hydro optimisation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
These provide **flexible operation** alongside coal.
xa: Heatwave 2026: peak **256 GW**, **18-21 GW** coal units out, ~**150 GW** solar off after sunset.
NGAP storage: **94 GW PSP + 80 GW BESS**.
PSP = the **grid battery** for the **500 GW non-fossil** target.

60.s: APGenco's proposed two 3,200 MW ultra mega supercritical plants are planned at
o: Srikakulam and a pithead site at Talcher (Odisha)
60.x: APGenco plans two 3,200 MW ultra mega supercritical plants: one at Srikakulam and one at a pithead site at Talcher (Odisha), likely as a JV with Coal India. Krishnapatnam, Muddanur and Ibrahimpatnam host existing plants (SDSTPS, RTPP, Dr NTTPS). Polavaram is a hydro project and Singareni is a coal company.
60.tq: APGenco 2 x 3,200 MW: Srikakulam + Talcher pithead.
xs: APGenco's two **3,200 MW ultra mega supercritical** plants are at **Srikakulam** and a **pithead site at Talcher (Odisha)** — option **(1)**.
**Krishnapatnam**, **Muddanur** and **Ibrahimpatnam** host existing plants; **Polavaram** is hydro.
xa: Talcher plant is likely a **JV with Coal India** (Mar 2026).
APERC resource plan: **11,544 MW** extra capacity in **five years**.
**Krishnapatnam UMPP** (Reliance Power) is **stalled**.

60.s: Which State is identified as having the largest hydropower potential in India?
60.x: Arunachal Pradesh is identified as having the largest State-level hydropower potential.
60.tq: Select the largest-potential State from the Himalayan and Northeast group.
xs: **Arunachal Pradesh** has the **largest state hydro potential** — so option **(4)** is correct.
AP has only about **4 GW** hydro/reverse-pumped potential; Maharashtra leads in **number of dams**, not potential.
xa: NE flagship: **Subansiri Lower (2,000 MW)**; **Tato-II** **700 MW**.
Other major hydro states: **Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, J&K**.
Only about **36%** of the **>145 GW** potential is developed.

60.s: Which factor represents a major weakness of hydropower despite its renewable and low-operating-emission characteristics?
o: Permanent depletion of the water cycle
Dependence on drought and snowpack variability
Inability to respond flexibly to demand
60.x: Hydropower is renewable, clean in operation and flexible, but its output can be affected by drought and variability in snowpack.
60.tq: Balance the stated advantages against the specific environmental vulnerability.
xs: Hydropower's key weakness is **drought and snowpack variability** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It uses a renewable water cycle, needs no uranium and is **flexible**, so options (1), (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Strengths: clean (**near-zero operating emissions**), renewable, flexible.
El Niño years hurt hydro output.
Major projects take **10-20 years** to build.

60.s: The Subansiri Lower hydroelectric project is located across which States?
60.x: The Subansiri Lower project is associated with Arunachal Pradesh and Assam and has a capacity of 2,000 MW.
60.tq: Distinguish the two-State location from projects located wholly within one State.
xs: **Subansiri Lower** lies in **Arunachal Pradesh-Assam** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It has a capacity of **2,000 MW** on the Subansiri river.
xa: Arunachal has the **largest state hydro potential**.
**Tato-II** (Arunachal): **700 MW**, **2,738 MU/yr**.
**Teesta** projects — **Sikkim**.

60.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Srisailam — Krishna — Andhra Pradesh/Telangana — 770 MW right bank
60.x: Nathpa Jhakri is in Himachal Pradesh, not Uttarakhand. Its river and capacity are Satluj and 1,500 MW respectively.
60.tq: Find the single incorrect location in an otherwise familiar project profile.
xs: **Nathpa Jhakri** is in **Himachal Pradesh**, not Uttarakhand — so option **(3)** is the wrong pair.
**Koyna** (Maharashtra, **1,960 MW**), **Srisailam** right bank (**770 MW**) and **Tehri** (Bhagirathi, Uttarakhand, **1,000 MW**) are correct.
xa: Nathpa Jhakri is on the **Satluj**, **1,500 MW**.
**Parbati** project — Himachal Pradesh.
Srisailam **Left Bank PH** = **900 MW** (Telangana).

60.s:
Consider the following statements regarding renewable energy in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Renewable energy currently accounts for about 30% of the State's share.
2. Andhra Pradesh targets a renewable-energy share of more than 75% by 2047.
3. The target is associated with the Swarna Andhra Vision.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
60.x: Andhra Pradesh has about 30% renewable-energy share currently and targets more than 75% by 2047 under the Swarna Andhra Vision.
60.tq: Test present status, future target and policy association together.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
AP's renewable share is about **30%** now, with a target of **>75% by 2047** under the **Swarna Andhra Vision** (2024-25).
xa: AP has about **4 GW** of hydro/reverse-pumped potential.
RE allocated in AP = **112.45 GW** (June 2026).
AP PSP policy (**2022**): **29 locations = 33,240 MW** potential.

60.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Srisailam hydroelectric project is correct?
o: Its Right Bank Power House has 770 MW in Andhra Pradesh and its Left Bank Power House has 900 MW in Telangana.
Its Right Bank Power House has 900 MW in Andhra Pradesh and its Left Bank Power House has 770 MW in Telangana.
It is situated on the Godavari River and has a total capacity of 960 MW.
Both its Right Bank and Left Bank Power Houses are located in Andhra Pradesh.
60.x: Srisailam is on the Krishna River. Its Right Bank Power House in Andhra Pradesh has 770 MW and its Left Bank Power House in Telangana has 900 MW.
60.tq: Use the bank-wise and State-wise capacity distinction to avoid reversing the two power houses.
xs: **Srisailam** (Krishna): **Right Bank PH 770 MW (AP)** and **Left Bank PH 900 MW (Telangana)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps the figures; it is on the **Krishna**, not Godavari; the Left Bank PH is in **Telangana**.
xa: **Nagarjuna Sagar** (Krishna): main PH **815.6 MW** (Telangana); Right Canal PH **90 MW** (AP).
**Polavaram** (Godavari) = **960 MW**.
**Koyna 1,960 MW** is far larger than Srisailam right bank.

60.s: Which of the following was the correct order of States by installed thermal capacity in the ranking cited for the past ranking?
o: Maharashtra, Gujarat, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal
West Bengal, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh
Maharashtra, West Bengal, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh
60.x: The cited past ranking placed Maharashtra first, Gujarat second, West Bengal third and Uttar Pradesh fourth.
60.tq: Preserve the first-to-fourth order and reject options that swap neighbouring States.
xs: The past ranking (UPPSC 2008 key): **Maharashtra 1st, Gujarat 2nd, West Bengal 3rd, Uttar Pradesh 4th** — option **(1)**.
The other options shuffle this order.
xa: All-India thermal capacity: **246.90 GW (48.45%)** of **509.64 GW** (**30 Nov 2025**).
Now (Aug 2026) total **~552 GW**, non-fossil **>54%**.
**Tiroda** (Maharashtra) = **3,300 MW**; **Mundra** (Gujarat) = **4,620 MW**.

60.s: Pumped-storage projects are significant for India’s energy transition because they function as
o: the grid battery for the 500 GW non-fossil target
a source of fossil fuel for thermal stations
a replacement for all coal generation immediately
60.x: Pumped storage is described as the grid battery supporting India’s 500 GW non-fossil target by providing storage and flexibility.
60.tq: Apply the grid-balancing function of storage to the non-fossil-capacity target.
xs: PSP is the **grid battery** for India's **500 GW non-fossil** target — so option **(2)** is correct.
It lets **solar and wind** stand in for coal at **peak hours**; it does not replace networks or all coal at once.
xa: NGAP storage: **174 GW/888 GWh** = **94 GW PSP + 80 GW BESS**.
APGENCO is building **Upper Sileru PSP (1,350 MW)**.
**Pinnapuram** (**1,680 MW**) is commissioned.

60.s: Why is hydro-electricity identified as a source suitable for sustainable development in the cited comparison?
o: It has no land or ecological impacts during construction.
It requires no water storage or river flow.
It is cheap and clean once built.
It produces electricity only during floods.
60.x: Hydroelectricity is regarded as cheap and clean once the project has been built, although large projects can still involve displacement and ecological trade-offs.
60.tq: Select the precise benefit while rejecting absolute claims about environmental impacts.
xs: **Hydro-electricity** is **cheap and clean once built** (UPSC) — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does have land/ecological impacts, needs water flow, and does not run only in floods.
xa: **Hydro is the best source for sustainable development** (UPPSC 2012).
Weakness: **drought/snowpack variability**.
Trade-offs: displacement, **sedimentation**, **seismic risk**, gestation of **10-20 years**.

60.s: In the UPSC 2024 context, pumped-storage hydropower was discussed under which category of energy storage?
60.x: Pumped-storage hydropower is long-duration energy storage: it stores surplus solar and wind power as water in an upper reservoir and releases it over the peak hours. It is mechanical (water) storage, not electrochemical batteries, thermal molten-salt storage or short-duration flywheels.
60.tq: PSP = giant water battery = long-duration storage.
xs: UPSC 2024 discussed pumped-storage hydropower under **long-duration energy storage** — so option **(1)** is correct.
PSP stores surplus solar/wind as water in an **upper reservoir** and releases it at **peak** — water storage, not electrochemical, molten-salt or flywheel.
xa: PSP = "**giant water battery**", the **fastest-responding large-scale storage**.
NGAP storage need by **2035-36**: **174 GW / 888 GWh** (**94 GW PSP + 80 GW BESS**).
ISTS charges are **waived for BESS and PSP till 2028**.

61.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Light Water Reactors is correct?
o: They use only natural uranium and heavy water.
They account for more than 85% of world nuclear power capacity and use light water as moderator and coolant.
They use liquid sodium and have no moderator.
They are restricted to India's Stage III thorium programme.
61.x: LWRs account for more than 85% of global nuclear capacity and use light water for both moderation and cooling. India is prioritising them for rapid capacity addition.
61.tq: Combine the global share with the defining reactor characteristics.
xs: **LWRs** are **>85%** of world capacity and use **light water** as moderator and coolant — so option **(2)** is correct.
Natural uranium + heavy water = **PHWR**; sodium, no moderator = **FBR**; Stage III = **AHWR**.
xa: India now **prioritises LWRs** for fast capacity addition.
**Tarapur = BWR**; **Kudankulam = VVER**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the sequence of India's three-stage nuclear power programme?
61.x: India's programme begins with PHWRs using natural uranium, proceeds to FBRs using plutonium-based fuel, and culminates in thorium-based AHWRs or other thorium reactors.
61.tq: Use the fuel-cycle sequence to identify the correct order.
xs: **PHWR → FBR → AHWR/thorium reactors** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Stage I **PHWR** (natural uranium) → Stage II **FBR** (MOX) → Stage III **AHWR** (Th-232 + U-233).
xa: Conceived by **Homi J. Bhabha** in the **1950s**.
Aim: **self-reliance through a closed fuel cycle**.
⚠ AHWR is a **bridge from Stage I to Stage III** without Stage II.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about Stage II of India's three-stage nuclear programme:
1. Its reactors use liquid sodium as coolant and no moderator.
2. Its Fast Breeder Reactors use MOX fuel made of Pu-239 and U-238.
3. The thorium-232 blanket in its reactors is meant to produce Pu-239.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 2 is correct: Stage II FBRs burn MOX (Pu-239 + U-238). Statement 1 is correct: FBRs use liquid sodium coolant and no moderator, since fast neutrons are needed. Statement 3 is wrong: the Th-232 blanket breeds U-233 (Pu-239 is bred from U-238). So '1 and 2 only'.
61.tq: U-238 breeds Pu-239; Th-232 breeds U-233.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: FBRs use **liquid sodium coolant** and **no moderator**.
Statement 2 is correct: FBRs burn **MOX: Pu-239 + U-238**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **Th-232 blanket** makes **U-233**; Pu-239 is bred from **U-238**.
xa: **PFBR, Kalpakkam**: **500 MWe**, first criticality **6 April 2026**.
PFBR designed by **IGCAR**, built by **BHAVINI**.
⚠ **Stage I PHWR = natural uranium**; **Stage III AHWR = Th-232 + U-233**.

61.s:
Assertion (A): Homi Bhabha's three-stage nuclear programme was designed to achieve self-reliance through a closed fuel cycle.
Reason (R): The programme was intended to overcome India's scarcity of uranium by making use of its abundant thorium resources.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
61.x: Both the assertion and reason are true. The need to overcome scarce uranium through abundant thorium underlies the programme's objective of self-reliance and a closed fuel cycle.
61.tq: Check whether the resource constraint directly explains the programme's strategic objective.
xs: **Both A and R are true** and R is the **correct explanation** of A — so option **(1)** is correct.
Bhabha designed the plan in the **1950s** to get round **scarce uranium** using **abundant thorium**, aiming at **self-reliance through a closed fuel cycle**.
xa: India has ~**2%** of world uranium vs ~**25%** of thorium.
Stage III **AHWR** = large-scale **thorium** use.
PFBR criticality (**6 Apr 2026**) = entry into **Stage II**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly compares fuel use and burn-up in PHWRs and fast breeder reactors?
o: PHWRs use about 1% fuel and FBRs about 10% or more; burn-up can rise from about 8,000 to about 1,00,000 units
PHWRs use about 1% fuel and FBRs about 10% or more; burn-up falls from about 1,00,000 to about 8,000 units
PHWRs use about 10% fuel and FBRs about 1%; burn-up falls to about 8,000 units
Both PHWRs and FBRs use about 1% fuel; burn-up remains around 8,000 units
61.x: Fuel use is about 1% in PHWRs and about 10% or more in FBRs. Burn-up is expected to increase from approximately 8,000 to 1,00,000 units.
61.tq: Check both sides of the comparison and watch for reversed figures and trends.
xs: PHWRs use ~**1%** of fuel, FBRs ~**10%**+; burn-up rises from ~**8,000** to ~**1,00,000** units — option **(1)**.
Options (2) and (3) reverse the direction or the percentages.
xa: FBR fuel: **MOX** from reprocessed **Stage-I spent fuel**.
FBRs breed **more Pu-239 than they burn**.
FBRs use **fast neutrons**, **no moderator**, **liquid sodium** coolant.

61.s: The 2005 milestone associated with IGCAR and the Fast Breeder Test Reactor was:
61.x: IGCAR’s 2005 milestone was the reprocessing of the mixed-carbide fuel used in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor.
61.tq: Match the institution and year with the specific technological achievement.
xs: IGCAR's **2005 milestone** was **reprocessing FBTR's mixed carbide fuel** (UPSC 2006) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**KAMINI** uses U-233 but was not this milestone; **PFBR** is not yet commercial.
xa: **FBTR** runs on a unique **uranium-plutonium mixed carbide** fuel.
**IGCAR** (Kalpakkam) handles **FBR technology and fuel cycle**.
IGCAR designed the **PFBR**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about a fast breeder reactor:
1. Its core is surrounded by a U-238 blanket that fast neutrons convert into Pu-239.
2. It produces more fissile fuel than it consumes.
3. It uses heavy water as moderator to slow down the neutrons.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: fast neutrons turn the U-238 blanket into Pu-239. Statement 2 is correct: hence it breeds more fuel than it consumes. Statement 3 is wrong: an FBR has no moderator (it needs fast neutrons) and uses liquid sodium as coolant. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' omits statement 2, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
61.tq: Fast breeder = fast neutrons = no moderator; sodium coolant.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: fast neutrons turn the **U-238 blanket** into **Pu-239**.
Statement 2 is correct: it makes **more fuel than consumed** (APPSC-G1 2022).
Statement 3 is wrong: an FBR has **no moderator** and uses **liquid sodium** coolant — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: A **Th-232 blanket** makes **U-233**.
Fuel: **MOX (U-Pu oxide)**.

61.s: Which statement best explains the position of the AHWR in India's nuclear programme?
o: It constitutes the first stage based on natural uranium mining.
It replaces the first stage based on PHWRs.
It acts as a bridge from Stage I to Stage III and advances thorium use without passing through Stage II.
It is exclusively a research reactor unrelated to the three-stage programme.
61.x: The AHWR is intended to bridge Stage I and Stage III by advancing thorium utilisation without requiring the conventional passage through Stage II.
61.tq: Test the programme sequence by identifying the reactor's transitional role.
xs: AHWR is a **bridge from Stage I to Stage III**, advancing thorium **without passing through Stage II** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does not replace Stage I PHWRs and is part of the three-stage programme.
xa: Stage I **PHWR** = natural uranium; Stage II **FBR** = MOX; Stage III **AHWR** = Th-232 + U-233.
**ANEEL** fuel could also hasten Stage III by running in **existing PHWRs**.
Bottleneck: **thin fissile inventory** for Stage III.

61.s: The Bharat Small Reactors proposed by NPCIL are based on which of the following reactor types?
o: Fast Breeder Reactor using only thorium
61.x: NPCIL floated a request for proposals for 220 MW PHWR-based Bharat Small Reactors to be used as captive plants for industry.
61.tq: Match the programme with its distinctive capacity and reactor technology.
xs: NPCIL floated an RFP for **220 MW PHWR-based** (**Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor**) **Bharat Small Reactors** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They are captive plants for **industry**; **300 MW AHWR** and **55 MWe SMR-55** are different designs.
xa: Budget **2024-25** announced **private partnership** for BSRs.
**₹20,000 crore** for SMRs/BSRs (Budget 2025-26).
**BSR-200** = **200 MWe** BARC design.

61.s: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is significant because it is:
o: India's first indigenous Fast Breeder Reactor
61.x: PFBR is described as India's first indigenous Fast Breeder Reactor.
61.tq: Separate the national-first associated with PFBR from the firsts associated with Apsara and KAMINI.
xs: **PFBR** is **India's first indigenous FBR** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Apsara** = Asia's first research reactor; **KAMINI** = only U-233 reactor; **Jaduguda** = first uranium mine.
xa: PFBR = **500 MWe**, designed by **IGCAR**, built by **BHAVINI**.
Core loading on **4 March 2024**.
Next: **2 x 500 MWe** FBR 1&2 at Kalpakkam.

61.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. ³H and ⁴He are isotones.
II. ³H and ⁴He each have two neutrons.
III. ¹⁴C, ¹⁵N and ¹⁶O are isotones.
IV. ¹⁴C, ¹⁵N and ¹⁶O each have eight neutrons.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: All four are correct: ³H and ⁴He both have 2 neutrons, and ¹⁴C, ¹⁵N and ¹⁶O all have 8 neutrons, so each set is isotonic.
61.tq: Compute neutrons as A − Z.
n: ³H and ⁴He are isotones. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
³H and ⁴He each have two neutrons. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
¹⁴C, ¹⁵N, and ¹⁶O are isotones. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
¹⁴C, ¹⁵N, and ¹⁶O each have eight neutrons. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xs: **All four — I, II, III and IV** — are correct — option **(2)**.
**³H** and **⁴He** are **isotones** with **two neutrons** each.
**¹⁴C, ¹⁵N** and **¹⁶O** are **isotones** with **eight neutrons** each.
xa: Isotones are also called **isoneutronic species**.
Isotones differ in **atomic numbers** and **mass numbers**.
**Tritium** = 1 proton + 2 neutrons; half-life **12.3 years**.

61.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Isotope)
a. U-235
b. U-238
c. Pu-239
d. U-233

List-II (Characteristic)
i. Fertile isotope converted into Pu-239
ii. Fissile fuel of Stage III and KAMINI
iii. Fissile isotope present in natural uranium
iv. Fissile isotope produced from U-238 by neutron absorption

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
61.x: U-235 is the naturally occurring fissile isotope, U-238 is fertile, Pu-239 is bred from U-238, and U-233 is used as the Stage III and KAMINI fuel.
61.tq: Start with the sure pair U-235–fissile isotope and eliminate codes containing conflicting matches.
xs: U-235 is the **natural fissile** isotope; U-238 is **fertile**; Pu-239 is **bred** from U-238; U-233 fuels **Stage III and KAMINI**.
xa: **Th-232** (fertile) → **U-233** in FBR blankets.
**KAMINI** = world's only operating **U-233** reactor.

61.s: Enrichment of uranium refers to:
o: Removing all radioactive isotopes from natural uranium
Increasing the proportion of U-238 through chemical separation
Increasing the proportion of U-235 through isotope separation
61.x: Enrichment raises the share of U-235, the fissile isotope, by isotope separation; it does not increase U-238.
61.tq: Discriminate between the fissile isotope U-235 and the fertile isotope U-238.
xs: **Enrichment** = raising the share of **U-235** by **isotope separation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It does not raise **U-238** or convert U-235 into thorium.
xa: ⚠ APPSC-G1 2022 trap: the answer was "**Neither I nor II**" (both statements false).
**LWRs** use **low-enriched uranium (3-5% U-235)**; weapons-grade ≈ **90%**.
Natural uranium has only **0.72%** U-235.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about hydrogen isotopes:
1. Deuterium contains one proton and one neutron.
2. Tritium is produced by bombarding lithium with neutrons.
3. Tritium is a stable isotope and does not emit beta particles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: deuterium (heavy hydrogen, stable) has 1 proton and 1 neutron. Statement 2 is correct: tritium (1 proton + 2 neutrons) is made by bombarding lithium with neutrons. Statement 3 is wrong: tritium is radioactive, a beta emitter with a half-life of 12.3 years. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '2 and 3 only', '1 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' all wrongly include statement 3.
61.tq: Deuterium is stable; tritium is radioactive (beta, 12.3 years) and bred from lithium.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **deuterium** = **1 proton + 1 neutron** (heavy hydrogen, stable).
Statement 2 is correct: **tritium** is made by bombarding **lithium** with neutrons.
Statement 3 is wrong: tritium is a **beta emitter**, half-life **12.3 years** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Tritium has **1 proton + 2 neutrons** and is a **fusion fuel**.
Fusion joins **two light nuclei** — as in the **Sun and stars**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes nuclear fission from nuclear fusion?
o: Fission joins light nuclei, whereas fusion splits heavy nuclei.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus, whereas fusion joins two light nuclei.
Both fission and fusion involve only chemical changes.
Both processes require the same temperature and pressure conditions.
61.x: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus, while fusion is the joining of two light nuclei.
61.tq: Use the reversed-process trap to distinguish splitting from joining.
xs: **Fission splits a heavy nucleus**; **fusion joins two light nuclei** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses them; both are nuclear (not chemical) changes, and fusion needs **extremely high temperature and pressure**.
xa: ⚠ "Breaking apart of a nucleus is called fusion" is the **incorrect** statement (APPSC 2019).
All present-day nuclear electricity is from **fission**; fusion is still **R&D**.
**Atom bomb** = fission; **hydrogen bomb** = fusion.

61.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Nuclear fission occurs in present-day nuclear power reactors.
2. Fusion occurs naturally in the Sun and stars.
3. Fusion-based electricity generation is already the source of all present nuclear electricity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. All present-day nuclear electricity is generated through fission; fusion power remains at the research-and-development stage.
61.tq: Check the present status of technology before accepting the broad claim about fusion electricity.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **fission** powers all present-day reactors.
Statement 2 is correct: **fusion** occurs in the **Sun and stars**.
Statement 3 is wrong: fusion power is still at the **R&D stage** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: **ITER** (Cadarache, France) is a **tokamak** fusion experiment.
**NIF** (USA) achieved the first fusion **ignition** in **Dec 2022** by laser.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about nuclear reactor terms:
1. Xenon-135 is called a 'nuclear poison' because it absorbs neutrons.
2. Critical mass is the maximum mass of fissile material that can be stored safely without a chain reaction.
3. Criticality refers to a self-sustaining chain reaction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 2 is wrong: critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material that sustains a chain reaction. Statement 3 is correct: criticality means a self-sustaining chain reaction. Statement 1 is correct: Xenon-135 absorbs neutrons and is a nuclear poison. So '1 and 3 only'.
61.tq: Critical MASS = minimum mass; CRITICALITY = self-sustaining state.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **Xenon-135** is a "**nuclear poison**" absorbing neutrons.
Statement 2 is wrong: **critical mass** is the **minimum** mass that sustains a chain reaction.
Statement 3 is correct: **criticality** = **self-sustaining chain reaction**.
xa: **Fission**: U-235 + neutron → **barium + krypton** + **2-3** neutrons.
**Half-life** = time for half the nuclei to decay.
⚠ "Breaking apart of a nucleus is called fusion" is wrong — that is **fission** (APPSC 2019).

61.s:
Consider the following statements comparing nuclear fission and nuclear fusion:
1. Fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure.
2. Fission releases more energy per unit mass than fusion.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: fusion needs extremely high temperature and pressure, whereas fission needs a neutron hit and critical mass. Statement 2 is wrong: fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission. Hence '1 only' is right; '2 only' and 'Both 1 and 2' accept the false statement 2, and 'Neither 1 nor 2' rejects the true statement 1.
61.tq: Fusion: harder conditions, bigger energy per unit mass.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **fusion** needs **extremely high temperature and pressure**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **fusion** gives **more energy per unit mass** than fission — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Fission needs a **neutron hit** and **critical mass**.
Fusion examples: **Sun and stars**, **hydrogen bomb**.
ITER is designed for **500 MW** output from **50 MW** input.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes an atomic bomb from a hydrogen bomb?
o: An atomic bomb uses thorium fusion, whereas a hydrogen bomb uses uranium moderation.
An atomic bomb involves uncontrolled fission, whereas a hydrogen bomb involves fusion initiated by a fission bomb.
An atomic bomb uses controlled fusion, whereas a hydrogen bomb uses controlled fission.
Both are based exclusively on chemical explosions.
61.x: An atomic bomb is based on an uncontrolled fission reaction. A hydrogen bomb uses fusion, with a fission explosion serving as the trigger.
61.tq: Separate the primary reaction from the triggering mechanism.
xs: **Atom bomb = uncontrolled fission**; **hydrogen bomb = fusion triggered by a fission bomb** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Neither is a chemical explosion, and the atom bomb does not use thorium fusion.
xa: **Hiroshima** (Little Boy) = **U-235**; **Nagasaki** (Fat Man) = **Pu-239**.
Fusion naturally powers the **Sun and stars**.
**Atomic Energy Act 1948** limited atomic energy to **peaceful uses**.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
61.x: The Hiroshima bomb, Little Boy, used U-235. The Nagasaki bomb, Fat Man, used Pu-239.
61.tq: Match the city, bomb name and fissile material as a three-part pair.
xs: **Hiroshima — Little Boy — U-235** is correct — so option **(3)**.
**Nagasaki** was **Fat Man** with **Pu-239**; options (1), (2), (4) mix these.
xa: Atom bomb = uncontrolled **fission**.
**Pu-239** is not natural — bred from **U-238**.
⚠ **Hiroshima = U-235**; **Nagasaki = Pu-239**.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly matches radiation with its usual shielding requirement?
o: Beta — a few millimetres of aluminium
Gamma — a thin layer of aluminium only
61.x: Beta radiation can generally be stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, whereas gamma requires dense shielding such as lead or concrete.
61.tq: Use penetration order to reject swapped shielding materials.
xs: **Beta** is stopped by **a few mm of aluminium** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Alpha** is stopped by **paper/skin**, not lead; **gamma** needs **lead/concrete**, not paper or thin aluminium.
xa: Alpha = **helium-4 nucleus**; beta = **fast electrons/positrons**.
Gamma = **electromagnetic waves**.
Tritium is a **beta emitter**.

61.s: The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time required for:
o: Its atomic mass to become zero
Its radiation to lose half its penetrating power
Half of its radioactive nuclei to decay
61.x: Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to undergo decay.
61.tq: Choose the definition involving nuclei, not the intensity or mass of the sample.
xs: **Half-life** = time for **half the nuclei to decay** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not the time for all nuclei to decay or for mass/penetration to change.
xa: **Tritium** half-life = **12.3 years**.
Uranium series: **U-238 → Pb-206**.
Thorium series: **Th-232 → Pb-208**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements regarding radioactive series:
1. The uranium series begins with U-238 and ends with Pb-206.
2. The thorium series begins with Th-232 and ends with Pb-208.
3. The actinium series begins with U-235 and ends with Pb-207.
4. The neptunium series is a natural radioactive series.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the neptunium series is artificial.
61.tq: Find the exception in an otherwise standard list of natural decay series.
xs: Statements 1, 2, 3 are correct: **U-238 → Pb-206**, **Th-232 → Pb-208**, **U-235 → Pb-207** (actinium).
Statement 4 is wrong: the **neptunium series is artificial** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Radioactivity discovered by **Henri Becquerel (1896)**.
**Half-life** = time for half the nuclei to decay.
Emissions: **alpha, beta, gamma**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Stage I of India's three-stage nuclear programme:
1. It uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors.
2. Natural uranium is used as fuel.
3. Plutonium-239 is obtained from the spent fuel.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Stage I uses PHWRs with natural uranium. Its spent fuel yields Pu-239, which is required for the subsequent stage.
61.tq: Match each statement with the defining features of the first stage.
xs: All three are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
Stage I uses **PHWRs** (heavy water moderator + coolant), fuelled by **natural uranium**; spent fuel gives **Pu-239**.
xa: Stage II **FBR** uses **MOX (Pu-239 + U-238)**.
FBR uses ~**10%**+ of fuel vs ~**1%** in PHWR.
**NPCIL fleet:** **25 reactors, 8,880 MW**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about ANEEL fuel:
1. It combines thorium with HALEU and was developed by the US firm Clean Core Thorium Energy.
2. It can be used only in new fast breeder reactors, not in existing PHWRs.
3. It could hasten India's move to Stage III of the nuclear programme.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: ANEEL is thorium + HALEU, from Clean Core Thorium Energy (USA). Statement 2 is wrong: it works in existing PHWRs (high-burnup tests done at Idaho National Laboratory). Statement 3 is correct: because it runs in PHWRs it could hasten Stage III. So '1 and 3 only' is right; '1 only' omits statement 3, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 2.
61.tq: ANEEL = thorium + HALEU in existing PHWRs: a shortcut to Stage III.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **ANEEL** = **thorium + HALEU**, from US firm **Clean Core Thorium Energy**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it **works in existing PHWRs** (high-burnup tests at **Idaho National Laboratory**).
Statement 3 is correct: it could **hasten Stage III** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(4)**.
xa: BARC cautions: shutdown rods **~26% less effective**; stabilisation **7-10 years**.
**NTPC** has a tie-up for ANEEL.

61.s:
With reference to the AHWR, consider the following statements:
1. It is a conceptual prototype designed at BARC.
2. It is regarded as the flagship thorium reactor of India.
3. It forms the core of the third stage of India's nuclear programme.
4. It is designed for large-scale use of plutonium-bearing spent fuel.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because AHWR is intended for large-scale thorium use, not large-scale utilisation of plutonium-bearing spent fuel.
61.tq: Identify the wrong-fuel trap in the final statement.
xs: Statements 1, 2, 3 are correct: **BARC conceptual prototype**, **flagship thorium reactor**, **core of Stage III**.
Statement 4 is wrong: it is for large-scale **thorium**, not plutonium-bearing spent fuel — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: APPSC-G2 2025 used this trap in an A/R item.
AHWR design: **heavy-water moderated**, **boiling light-water coolant**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about ITER:
1. It is a tokamak, the world's largest magnetic confinement fusion experiment.
2. It is designed to give about 500 MW of output from 50 MW of input.
3. It aims to demonstrate fission as a large-scale, carbon-free source of power.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: ITER (Cadarache, southern France) is a tokamak fusion device, the world's largest magnetic confinement experiment. Statement 2 is correct: it is designed for 500 MW output from 50 MW input, about ten times more out than in. Statement 3 is wrong: ITER aims to demonstrate fusion, not fission, as a large-scale carbon-free source. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' omits the true statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
61.tq: ITER = tokamak = fusion; 50 MW in, 500 MW out.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: ITER is a **tokamak**, the world's **largest magnetic confinement** experiment.
Statement 2 is correct: designed for **500 MW** output from **50 MW** input.
Statement 3 is wrong: it demonstrates **fusion**, not fission — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: Members: **EU, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, USA**.
APPSC-G1 2022 had all four ITER statements correct.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about India's fusion research:
1. Aditya was India's first tokamak.
2. SST-1 stands for Steady State Superconducting Tokamak.
3. Aditya and SST-1 are located at BARC, Trombay.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: Aditya was the first Indian tokamak. Statement 2 is correct: SST-1 is the Steady State Superconducting Tokamak. Statement 3 is wrong: both are at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, not BARC. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' omits statement 2, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
61.tq: Indian tokamaks (Aditya, SST-1) = IPR Gandhinagar.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Aditya** = first Indian tokamak.
Statement 2 is correct: **SST-1** = **Steady State Superconducting Tokamak**.
Statement 3 is wrong: both are at **Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar**, not BARC — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **ITER** is also a **tokamak** (Cadarache, France).
First fusion ignition: **NIF**, USA, **Dec 2022**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's nuclear power sector:
1. Nuclear power accounted for 3.1% of electricity in 2024–25.
2. NPCIL operates 25 reactors.
3. NPCIL's operating capacity is stated as 8,880 MW.
4. The target is 22.38 GW by 2031–32.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: All four figures describe India's nuclear electricity share, NPCIL's reactor fleet and capacity, and the stated capacity target for 2031–32.
61.tq: Retain the complete set of capacity and target figures together.
xs: All four are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Nuclear = **3.1%** of electricity (2024-25); **NPCIL** has **25 reactors, 8,880 MW**; target **22.38 GW by 2031-32**.
xa: Long-term target: **100 GW by 2047**; NPCIL share **54 GW**.
Nuclear gives about **3%** of generation.
SHANTI Act allows **private companies and JVs** under licence.

61.s:
With reference to Small Modular Reactors, consider the following statements:
1. They are generally factory-built.
2. Their refuelling interval is about 3–7 years.
3. Their refuelling interval is shorter than that of conventional reactors, which is generally 1–2 years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because SMRs generally have a longer, not shorter, refuelling interval than conventional reactors.
61.tq: Find the reversed comparison in the statement about refuelling intervals.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: SMRs are **factory-built**.
Statement 2 is correct: refuelling every **3-7 years**.
Statement 3 is wrong: that is **longer**, not shorter, than **1-2 years** for conventional reactors — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: SMR = up to **300 MWe** per unit.
BARC also has a gas-cooled reactor up to **5 MW** for **hydrogen**.

61.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. IGCAR — Kalpakkam — FBR technology and associated fuel cycle
2. AMD — Hyderabad — exploration of uranium and thorium
3. NPCIL — Mumbai — design, construction and operation of nuclear power reactors
4. BHAVINI — Kalpakkam — construction and operation of FBRs
61.x: All four institutional-role pairs are correct. BHAVINI is the PSU associated with building and running fast breeder reactors, with NPCIL holding equity.
61.tq: Start with the sure headquarters-role pairs and verify the complete combination.
xs: All four pairs are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**IGCAR** (Kalpakkam) — FBR tech; **AMD** (Hyderabad) — uranium/thorium exploration; **NPCIL** (Mumbai) — power reactors; **BHAVINI** (Kalpakkam) — FBRs.
xa: **NPCIL** holds equity in **BHAVINI**.
**NFC** (Hyderabad) — fuel fabrication.
**UCIL** (Jaduguda) — uranium mining and milling.

61.s: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The neutron is a neutral particle.
61.x: Option A is incorrect: radioactivity is a nuclear process, unaffected by chemical bonding, and it emits alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
61.tq: Discriminate nuclear from chemical processes.
n: The neutron is a neutral particle. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
Radioactivity is not a chemical phenomenon. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
Radioactivity emits alpha particles. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Radioactivity is a chemical phenomenon**" — option **(1)**.
Radioactivity is a **nuclear phenomenon**, ⚠ **not** chemical.
It **emits** **alpha particles**, **beta particles** and **gamma radiation**.
xa: Discovered by **Henri Becquerel (1896)**.
**Alpha** = **helium nucleus**, charge **+2**, stopped by paper.
