**Gamma** rays have **zero** charge and **zero** mass; highest penetration.

61.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Alpha particle
(b) Beta particle as a negative particle
(c) Beta particle as a positive particle
(d) Gamma radiation

List-II
(i) Electron
(ii) Electromagnetic radiation
(iii) Helium nucleus with a +2 charge
(iv) Positron
61.x: An alpha particle is a +2 helium nucleus, negative beta is an electron, positive beta is a positron and gamma is electromagnetic radiation, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
61.tq: Recall the nature of each radiation.
n: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with a +2 charge. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
A beta particle is an electron or positron. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
Gamma radiation is electromagnetic radiation. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Alpha** = **helium nucleus** (**+2**); negative **beta** = **electron**.
Positive beta = **positron**; **gamma** = **electromagnetic radiation**.
xa: Alpha mass: about **4 atomic mass units**.
Beta penetrates a few mm of **aluminium**; gamma needs **lead/concrete**.

61.s: Which one of the following is NOT a nuclear fuel but may serve as a moderator, coolant or absorber in a reactor?
61.x: Graphite is a reactor moderator, not a nuclear fuel. U-235, Pu-239 and U-233 are fissile fuels.
61.tq: Find the non-fuel by separating reactor-support materials from fissile isotopes.
xs: **Graphite** is a **moderator**, not a nuclear fuel — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Pu-239**, **U-235** and **U-233** are all **fissile fuels**.
xa: Other non-fuels: **heavy water, sodium, boron, cadmium, zirconium**.
**Control rods** (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons.
**Liquid sodium** is the **FBR** coolant.

61.s:
Match List-I (reactor component) with List-II (function):
List-I: a. Moderator  b. Coolant  c. Control rods
List-II: i. Absorb neutrons and control the rate of the chain reaction  ii. Slow neutrons so that U-235 can undergo fission  iii. Carry heat from the core to make steam
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
61.x: Moderator (heavy water, light water, graphite) slows neutrons (ii); coolant (heavy water, light water, liquid sodium) carries heat to make steam (iii); control rods (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons and control the rate (i). So a-ii, b-iii, c-i. 'a-iii, b-ii, c-i' swaps moderator and coolant; 'a-i, b-iii, c-ii' swaps moderator and control rods; 'a-ii, b-i, c-iii' swaps coolant and control rods.
61.tq: Moderator slows, coolant carries heat, control rods absorb.
xs: **Moderator – slows neutrons (ii)**, **coolant – carries heat (iii)**, **control rods – absorb neutrons (i)**: **a-ii, b-iii, c-i**, option **(3)**.
Moderators: **heavy water, light water, graphite**; coolants include **liquid sodium** (FBR); control rods: **boron, cadmium**.
xa: Without **control rods** the reaction runs away (meltdown risk).
Without a **moderator** a thermal reactor stops.
**FBRs** use **no moderator**.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: BWR — light water as moderator and coolant
AHWR — no moderator and no coolant
61.x: A BWR uses light water both as moderator and coolant, with the water boiling in the core. PHWRs use heavy water, while FBRs use sodium and no moderator.
61.tq: Compare the moderator-coolant combinations across reactor types.
xs: **BWR** uses **light water** as moderator and coolant (it **boils in core**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**PHWR** uses **heavy water**, not sodium; **FBR** has **no moderator**; **AHWR** has a heavy-water moderator and **boiling light-water coolant**.
xa: **Tarapur = BWR**.
**PWR/VVER**: **low-enriched uranium**, pressurised light water coolant.
**SMR**: up to **300 MWe** per unit.

61.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the AHWR?
o: A 500 MWe sodium-cooled fast breeder reactor using only plutonium
A 300 MW thorium reactor with heavy-water moderator and boiling light-water coolant
A 30 kW U-233 reactor used for neutron radiography
A 40 MW natural-uranium reactor moderated by heavy water and shut down in 2010
61.x: The AHWR is a 300 MW thorium reactor designed by BARC, using a heavy-water moderator, boiling light-water coolant and a Th-232 plus U-233 fuel combination.
61.tq: Match the reactor’s capacity, fuel strategy, moderator and coolant together.
xs: **AHWR** = **300 MW thorium** reactor, **heavy-water moderated**, **boiling light-water coolant** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**500 MWe sodium-cooled** = **PFBR**; **30 kW U-233** = **KAMINI**; **40 MW** natural uranium, shut **2010** = **CIRUS**.
xa: AHWR fuel: **Th-232 + U-233**.
Designed at **BARC**; core of **Stage III**.
It is a **bridge from Stage I to Stage III**.

61.s: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam was built and commissioned by which organisation?
o: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited
61.x: BHAVINI built and commissioned the 500 MWe PFBR at Kalpakkam. The reactor was designed by IGCAR.
61.tq: Identify the organisation directly associated with construction and commissioning.
xs: **BHAVINI** built and commissioned the **PFBR** (APPSC-G1 2024 answer) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**IGCAR** designed it; **NPCIL** builds and operates power reactors; **BARC** is the R&D centre.
xa: ⚠ **PFBR designed by IGCAR**, **built by BHAVINI** — the exam answer is **BHAVINI**.
BHAVINI was set up in **2003** under **DAE**; **NPCIL** holds equity.
PFBR: **500 MWe (1,250 MWt)**, sodium-cooled, **pool type**.

61.s:
With reference to the PFBR at Kalpakkam, consider the following statements:
1. It is a sodium-cooled reactor.
2. It is of the pool type.
3. Its rated electrical capacity is 500 MWe and thermal capacity is 1,250 MWt.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: The PFBR is sodium-cooled and pool-type, with a capacity of 500 MWe and 1,250 MWt. Therefore, all three statements are correct.
61.tq: Split the options by checking the reactor’s coolant, design and capacity.
xs: All three are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
PFBR, Kalpakkam is **liquid-sodium-cooled**, **pool type**, **500 MWe (1,250 MWt)**.
xa: Final cost **₹8,181 crore** — more than double the sanction.
Criticality came **16+ years late**.
Next: **2 x 500 MWe FBR 1&2** at Kalpakkam after a year's performance review.

61.s: Once the PFBR operates commercially, India is expected to become the second country after which country to operate a commercial-scale fast breeder reactor?
61.x: India is expected to become the second country after Russia to operate a commercial-scale fast breeder reactor.
61.tq: Use the country comparison and identify the stated predecessor.
xs: India becomes the **2nd country after Russia** to operate a commercial-scale FBR — so option **(4)** is correct.
The notes name **Russia** only, not the USA, France or Canada.
xa: PFBR = **India's first indigenous FBR**.
Criticality = entry into **Stage II**.
PFBR fuel: **MOX (Pu-239 + U-238)**.

61.s:
With reference to APSARA, consider the following statements:
1. It is located at BARC, Trombay.
2. It became critical in 1956.
3. It was the first research reactor of India and Asia.
4. It is a swimming-pool or pool-type reactor.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: APSARA is a pool-type reactor at Trombay that became critical in 1956 and was India’s and Asia’s first research reactor. All four statements are correct.
61.tq: Verify each statement against the reactor’s location, date, status and design.
xs: All four are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Apsara** (BARC, **Trombay**) is **pool-type**, critical **1956**, the **first research reactor of India and Asia**.
xa: It was designed and built by **Indian scientists**.
**APSARA-U** is its upgraded version.
⚠ **Apsara = first**; **Dhruva = largest**; **KAMINI = only U-233**.

61.s: Which one of the following best describes a Small Modular Reactor (SMR)?
o: A reactor having a minimum capacity of 3000 MWe per unit
A reactor that must be constructed entirely at the site
A reactor that can operate only with fusion fuel
A reactor with a capacity of up to 300 MWe per unit
61.x: An SMR has a capacity of up to 300 MWe per unit and is generally about one-third the size of a conventional reactor.
61.tq: Use the precise numerical definition rather than the broad size description.
xs: An **SMR** has capacity of **up to 300 MWe per unit** — so option **(4)** is correct.
SMRs are **factory-built**, not fully site-built, and are **fission** reactors.
xa: SMR size is about **one-third** of conventional reactors.
Refuelling every **3-7 years** vs **1-2**.

61.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: BHAVINI — Mumbai — uranium mining and milling
BARC — Trombay — research and development in nuclear technologies
UCIL — Jaduguda — uranium mining and milling
61.x: BHAVINI is located at Kalpakkam and is associated with fast breeder reactors. Uranium mining and milling is the role of UCIL at Jaduguda.
61.tq: Use the specialised function to expose the swapped organisation and location.
xs: **BHAVINI** is at **Kalpakkam** and builds/runs **FBRs**, not uranium mining — so option **(1)** is the wrong pair.
**BARC – Trombay – R&D**, **UCIL – Jaduguda – mining**, **NFC – Hyderabad – fuel fabrication** are correct.
xa: BHAVINI built the **PFBR** (**500 MWe**).
**UCIL** also runs **Tummalapalle** (YSR Kadapa).
**AMD** is in **Hyderabad**.

61.s: The criticality of the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor in April 2026 signified entry into which stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme?
61.x: PFBR criticality in April 2026 marked India's entry into Stage II of the three-stage programme.
61.tq: Distinguish the programme stage from the reactor type instead of treating all stages as interchangeable.
xs: PFBR criticality (**6 Apr 2026**) marks entry into **Stage II** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Stage I = **PHWR**; Stage III = **AHWR/thorium**.
xa: Stage II FBR fuel = **MOX (Pu-239 + U-238)**.
India = **2nd country after Russia** to run a commercial-scale FBR.
PFBR ran **16** years late and its cost doubled.

61.s: The PFBR project has been reported as facing which combination of cost and schedule difficulties?
o: Its cost was halved and it finished 5 years early.
Its cost doubled and it ran 16 years late.
Its cost tripled and it ran 30 years late.
Its cost remained unchanged and it ran 2 years late.
61.x: The PFBR's cost was reported to have doubled, while the project ran 16 years late.
61.tq: Pair the two quantitative project indicators and avoid mixing the reported cost and delay figures.
xs: PFBR's **cost doubled** and it ran **16 years late** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Parliamentary Standing Committee put the final cost at **₹8,181 crore**, more than double the sanction, with criticality **16+ years late**.
xa: Work began in **2004**; first criticality on **6 April 2026**.
The **fast-reactor fuel cycle facility** is due **2029**.
Next: **2 x 500 MWe FBR 1&2** at Kalpakkam after a year's performance review.
Other bottlenecks: **10-12-year builds**, thin fissile inventory, local protests.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about the CIRUS research reactor at Trombay:
1. It was built with Canada, following a decision taken in 1956.
2. It was fuelled by enriched uranium and moderated by light water.
3. It was used for research and Pu-239 production and was shut down in 2010.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: CIRUS was built with Canada (decided 1956). Statement 2 is wrong: CIRUS was a 40 MW natural-uranium, heavy-water-moderated reactor. Statement 3 is correct: it served research and Pu-239 production and was shut down in 2010. So '1 and 3 only' is right; '1 and 2 only', '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' all include the false statement 2.
61.tq: CIRUS: Canada, natural uranium, heavy water, closed 2010.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **CIRUS** was built with **Canada** (decided **1956**).
Statement 2 is wrong: it was **40 MW**, **natural uranium**, **heavy-water moderated**.
Statement 3 is correct: research + **Pu-239 production**; **shut down 2010** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: **Dhruva** (**100 MW**) is India's largest research reactor, also natural uranium.
Both are at **Trombay**.

61.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: AHWR — reactor already built and operating at Trombay
61.x: AHWR is a BARC design for a 300 MW thorium reactor; it is not described as an already built and operating reactor at Trombay. The other pairs are correct.
61.tq: Reject the option that changes a design-stage reactor into an operating facility.
xs: **AHWR** is a **conceptual prototype** designed at **BARC**, not an operating reactor at Trombay — so option **(2)** is the wrong pair.
**CIRUS** — shut down **2010**; **Purnima** — thorium/U-233 research reactors; **APSARA-U** — upgraded Apsara.
xa: AHWR = **300 MW**, **thorium-based** (Th-232 + U-233).
AHWR is the core of **Stage III**.
Purnima reactors are now **shut down**.

61.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Reactor)
 a. APSARA
 b. CIRUS
 c. KAMINI
 d. Dhruva

List-II (Characteristic)
 i. 30 kW U-233-fuelled reactor
 ii. India’s largest research reactor
 iii. Asia’s first research reactor
 iv. Natural uranium and heavy-water moderation

Select the correct code.
61.x: APSARA was Asia’s first research reactor; CIRUS used natural uranium and heavy-water moderation; KAMINI is the 30 kW U-233 reactor; Dhruva is India’s largest research reactor.
61.tq: Start from the distinctive KAMINI and Dhruva pairs, then complete the remaining matches.
xs: **Apsara – Asia's first**, **CIRUS – natural uranium + heavy water**, **KAMINI – 30 kW U-233**, **Dhruva – largest**: option **(1)**.
So **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii**.
xa: **Dhruva** = **100 MW**, natural uranium (some notes wrongly say "enriched").
APPSC-G2 2025: "Dhruva is India's largest research reactor" is **TRUE**.
**CIRUS** (**40 MW**) was built with **Canada**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about India's nuclear-mineral resource position:
1. India possesses about 2% of the world's uranium.
2. India possesses about 25% of the world's thorium.
3. India is described as having the world's third-largest thorium reserves.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: India has approximately 2% of global uranium and about 25% of global thorium, and is described as having the third-largest thorium reserves.
61.tq: Retain the numerical shares together with the ranking.
xs: All three are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
India has ~**2%** of world uranium, ~**25%** of thorium, and the **world's 3rd-largest** thorium reserve.
xa: Thorium **~3,60,000 tonnes** vs natural uranium **~70,000 t**.
Older 2025 notes give the thorium share as **21%**.
Thorium source: **monazite** beach sands.

61.s:
With reference to monazite in India, consider the following statements:
1. It occurs along the entire Indian coast without exception.
2. It is found in beach sands of Kerala and Odisha.
3. Only government bodies such as IREL may process and export monazite.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false because monazite occurs only in specified coastal regions, not along the entire coast.
61.tq: Spot the absolute geographical claim and retain the regulatory statement.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: monazite is **not along the entire coast**.
Statement 2 is correct: it occurs in beach sands of **Kerala** and **Odisha** (also TN, AP, Maharashtra, WB).
Statement 3 is correct: only **government bodies (IREL)** may process and export it — so **2 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: UPSC 2022 had statements **1, 2 and 4** correct on monazite.
Monazite yields **thorium**, **rare earths**, phosphate and a little uranium.

61.s: Jaduguda, India's first uranium mine, is located in which district and State?
61.x: Jaduguda is located in East Singhbhum district of Jharkhand and is India's first uranium mine.
61.tq: Use the location-based direct-recall method and distinguish Jaduguda from Tummalapalle.
xs: **Jaduguda** is in **East Singhbhum, Jharkhand** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**YSR Kadapa** (AP) hosts **Tummalapalle**, not Jaduguda.
xa: Jaduguda = **India's first uranium mine** and **UCIL's seat**.
Domestic reserves: mainly **Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh**.
**AMD** (Hyderabad) explores atomic minerals.

61.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Tummalapalle:
1. It is located in YSR Kadapa district of Andhra Pradesh.
2. It is a uranium mine of the Uranium Corporation of India Limited.
3. It has an associated processing plant.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Tummalapalle is located in YSR Kadapa district, is operated as a UCIL uranium mine and has a processing plant.
61.tq: Identify the option containing all three precise location, ownership and facility details.
xs: All three are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
**Tummalapalle** is in **YSR Kadapa** (AP) and is a **UCIL uranium mine + processing plant**.
xa: **Jaduguda** (East Singhbhum, Jharkhand) = India's **first uranium mine**, UCIL's seat.
Domestic uranium reserves are mainly in **Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh**.
AP angle: **NFC** and **AMD** are in **Hyderabad**; **CODENE** at **IIT Hyderabad**.

61.s: Approximately what proportion of India's imported uranium comes from Kazakhstan?
61.x: About 80 percent of imported uranium is stated to come from Kazakhstan.
61.tq: Anchor the quantitative fact to the highest listed percentage without reversing the comparison.
xs: About **80%** of India's imported uranium comes from **Kazakhstan** (Dec 2025) — about **80 percent**, so option **(3)** is correct.
20%, 40% and 60% are not the notes' figure.
xa: India has only ~**2%** of world uranium vs ~**25%** of thorium.
Domestic uranium: **Jharkhand and Andhra Pradesh**.
The thorium strategy is meant to get round **scarce uranium**.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a bottleneck affecting the progression towards Stage III?
o: Absence of any thorium resources in India
61.x: The identified bottlenecks include a thin fissile inventory for Stage III, 10–12-year construction periods and local protests. Absence of thorium resources is not identified as a bottleneck; the programme is based on India's abundant thorium.
61.tq: Reject the broad contradiction and identify the item not belonging to the stated bottleneck list.
xs: **Absence of thorium** is **not** a bottleneck — India has abundant thorium — so option **(1)** is correct.
Real bottlenecks: **thin fissile inventory** for Stage III, **10-12-year builds**, **local protests**.
xa: PFBR's cost doubled and it ran **16** years late.
**ANEEL** could run in PHWRs and skip slow FBR rollout, but experts clash on it.
BARC: HALEU-thorium stabilisation takes **7-10 years**.

61.s: The Atomic Energy Act of 1948 primarily limited atomic energy in India to:
61.x: The Atomic Energy Act, 1948, limited the use of atomic energy to peaceful purposes.
61.tq: Identify the stated policy purpose without importing later legal changes.
xs: The **Atomic Energy Act 1948** limited atomic energy to **peaceful uses** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It did not limit it to space, military or private ownership.
xa: **SHANTI Act 2025** (assent **20 Dec 2025**) repealed the **Atomic Energy Act 1962** and **CLNDA 2010**.
It allows **private companies and JVs** to build, own and operate plants under licence.
⚠ SHANTI repealed the **1962** Act — not the **1948** Act.

61.s: Thorium is considered advantageous over uranium because it:
o: Can be used directly in every reactor without conversion
Is more abundant, yields more energy per unit mass of mined mineral and produces less harmful waste
Requires no reactor or fuel-cycle technology
Is less abundant but produces no energy waste
61.x: Thorium is more abundant, provides greater energy per unit mass of mined mineral and leaves less harmful waste compared with uranium.
61.tq: Choose the option containing all three comparative advantages.
xs: **Thorium** is **more abundant**, gives **more energy per unit mass of mined mineral** and **less harmful waste** — so option **(2)** is correct (UPSC 2012).
It is fertile — **Th-232 must become U-233** first — so it cannot be used directly in every reactor.
xa: India has ~**25%** of world thorium.
Stage III **AHWR** (**300 MW**) is thorium-based.
**ANEEL** fuel = thorium + **HALEU**.

61.s: The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) is being constructed at:
o: Lawrence Livermore in the United Kingdom
61.x: ITER is located at Cadarache in southern France. Gandhinagar is associated with India's Institute for Plasma Research.
61.tq: Use the location trap by distinguishing ITER's site from Indian fusion facilities.
xs: **ITER** is at **Cadarache, southern France** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Gandhinagar** hosts the **Institute for Plasma Research**; **Lawrence Livermore** is in the **USA** (NIF).
xa: ITER = **tokamak**, the world's largest **magnetic confinement** experiment (APPSC 2018).
India joined in **2005** and supplies the **cryostat**.
⚠ **ITER = magnetic confinement, France**; **NIF ignition = laser, USA**.

61.s: The SHANTI Act 2025 is associated with which of the following developments?
o: It restricts nuclear power generation exclusively to government companies.
It transfers all nuclear research from BARC to IIT Hyderabad.
It abolishes the Nuclear Energy Mission and the three-stage programme.
It repeals the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010, enabling licensed private participation.
61.x: The SHANTI Act 2025 repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010, allowing licensed private companies and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear plants.
61.tq: Identify the legal change by focusing on the authority and participation it enables.
xs: **SHANTI Act 2025** repealed the **Atomic Energy Act 1962** and **CLNDA 2010**, allowing **licensed private** players and JVs — option **(4)**.
It opens, not restricts, the sector; it does not abolish the mission or move BARC research.
xa: Assent: **20 Dec 2025**.
⚠ It repealed the **1962** Act, not the **1948** Act (which limited atomic energy to **peaceful uses**).
The programme is now framed as "thorium-led, private-participation, **100 GW by 2047**".

61.s:
With reference to the Nuclear Energy Mission announced in the Union Budget 2025-26, consider the following statements:
1. It targets 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.
2. It provides an outlay of Rs 20,000 crore for Small Modular Reactors.
3. NPCIL alone is expected to provide the entire 100 GW.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: the target is 100 GW by 2047. Statement 2 is correct: Rs 20,000 crore is earmarked for Small Modular Reactors/Bharat Small Reactors. Statement 3 is wrong: NPCIL's share is 54 GW, with private players enabled by the SHANTI Act. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' omits statement 2, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
61.tq: 100 GW by 2047; NPCIL 54 GW; Rs 20,000 crore SMRs.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: target **100 GW by 2047**.
Statement 2 is correct: **₹20,000 crore** for **SMRs / Bharat Small Reactors**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **NPCIL's share is 54 GW** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: NPCIL's 54 GW = **PHWRs + foreign-assisted LWRs**.
**SHANTI Act** lets private companies and JVs build plants.

61.s:
Consider the following statements about India's nuclear institutions:
1. The Department of Atomic Energy was set up in 1954 and is responsible for all nuclear activities.
2. BARC began in 1954 as AEET and was renamed in 1967 after Homi Bhabha.
3. NPCIL is the PSU that mines and mills uranium at Jaduguda.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: DAE (Mumbai) was set up in 1954 for all nuclear activities. Statement 2 is correct: BARC began in 1954 as AEET and was renamed in 1967 after Bhabha. Statement 3 is wrong: uranium mining and milling at Jaduguda is UCIL's role; NPCIL designs, builds and operates power reactors. So '1 and 2 only' is right; '1 only' omits statement 2, and '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' include the false statement 3.
61.tq: DAE and AEET both 1954; BARC name 1967; mining = UCIL, reactors = NPCIL.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **DAE** set up **1954**, for all nuclear activities.
Statement 2 is correct: **BARC** began **1954** as **AEET**, renamed **1967** after Bhabha.
Statement 3 is wrong: Jaduguda mining is **UCIL**'s; NPCIL runs power reactors — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **AEE Trombay** is sometimes dated **1957**, the year of its formal inauguration.
**NPCIL** became a PSU in **1987**.

61.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Statement B: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
61.x: Both are true: isotopes share Z but differ in A, and isobars share A but differ in Z.
61.tq: Discriminate isotopes (same Z) from isobars (same A).
n: An isotope has the same atomic number and different mass numbers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
An isobar has the same mass number and different atomic numbers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: **isotopes** share the **atomic number** but differ in **mass numbers**.
B: **isobars** share the **mass number** but differ in **atomic numbers**.
xa: Isotope example: **¹H, ²H, ³H** — ²H = **deuterium**, ³H = **tritium**.
Isobar example: **³H** and **³He**.
**Isotones** share the **number of neutrons**.

61.s: The first successful fusion ignition and net energy gain announced in December 2022 was achieved at the:
o: National Ignition Facility of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, USA
61.x: The National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States achieved fusion ignition and net energy gain in December 2022 using lasers.
61.tq: Use the institution-location pair to distinguish the ignition experiment from tokamak projects.
xs: The first fusion **ignition / net energy gain** (**Dec 2022**) was at the **National Ignition Facility**, **Lawrence Livermore**, USA — option **(3)**.
It was achieved by **laser**, not by ITER's magnetic tokamak or at IPR/KAMINI.
xa: ⚠ **ITER = magnetic confinement (tokamak), France**; **NIF = laser, USA**.
ITER is designed for about **10 times** more power out than in.
Fusion is still at the **R&D stage**.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
61.x: Tarapur is associated with BWR technology, whereas Kudankulam uses VVER reactors.
61.tq: Use the reactor-technology pair to distinguish the two well-known sites.
xs: **Tarapur — BWR** is correct — so option **(3)**.
**Kudankulam** uses **VVER** reactors, not BWR or PHWR.
xa: **VVER** = PWR type: **low-enriched uranium**, pressurised light water.
**BWR**: light water boils in the core.
Stage I of India's programme uses **PHWRs**.

62.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Kalpakkam nuclear power station?
o: It is a proposed AP1000 station in Andhra Pradesh.
It has India’s first fully indigenous PHWRs and is also associated with a PFBR.
It uses only VVER reactors supplied by Russia.
It is India’s first BWR station, located in Maharashtra.
62.x: Kalpakkam’s MAPS units are PHWRs representing the first fully indigenous PHWR design, and the site is also associated with a Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR).
62.tq: Use a combined description to separate a plant from similar nuclear stations.
xs: **Kalpakkam (MAPS)** has India's **first fully indigenous PHWRs** and also the **PFBR** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**AP1000** is proposed at **Kovvada** (AP); **VVER** is **Kudankulam**; the first **BWR** station is **Tarapur** (Maharashtra).
xa: MAPS 1-2 = **2 units, 440 MW**, in **Tamil Nadu**.
⚠ **Kalpakkam (MAPS) and Kudankulam = both Tamil Nadu**.
PFBR (**500 MWe**) was developed by **BHAVINI**.

62.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
62.x: Narora uses PHWRs, not VVER reactors. Gorakhpur is in Haryana, Kudankulam is in Tamil Nadu, and Kovvada is proposed in Andhra Pradesh.
62.tq: Find the swapped reactor type in an otherwise familiar plant-state pair.
xs: **Narora** uses **PHWRs**, not VVER — so option **(3)** is the wrong pair.
**Kudankulam – TN – VVER**, **Kovvada – AP – AP1000**, **Gorakhpur – Haryana – 700 MW PHWRs** are correct.
xa: Narora: **2 x 220 MW** in **Uttar Pradesh**.
Gorakhpur (GHAVP): **2 x 700 MW** under construction.
Kovvada is in **Srikakulam** district.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about firsts in India's nuclear power programme:
1. Tarapur, India's first nuclear power plant, began operation in 1960 with two PHWRs.
2. Rajasthan-1, India's first PHWR, was built with AECL of Canada and started in 1972.
3. Jaitapur, with a planned 9,900 MW, is the largest planned nuclear power project.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Tarapur went into operation in 1969 with two BWRs (boiling water reactors), not in 1960 with PHWRs. Statement 2 is correct: Rajasthan-1 (RAPS-1), the first PHWR, was built with AECL, Canada, and started in 1972. Statement 3 is correct: Jaitapur (9,900 MW) is the largest planned project. So '2 and 3 only'.
62.tq: Tarapur 1969 = BWR; RAPS-1 1972 = first PHWR; Jaitapur 9,900 MW = largest planned.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **Tarapur** went into operation in **1969** with **2 BWRs**, not in 1960 with PHWRs.
Statement 2 is correct: **Rajasthan-1**, the **first PHWR**, was built with **AECL, Canada** and started in **1972**.
Statement 3 is correct: **Jaitapur** (**9,900 MW**) is the **largest planned** project.
xa: **Largest operating** plant: **Kudankulam, 2,000 MW**; next **Kakrapar, 1,840 MW**.
**KAPP-3** = first indigenous **700 MW** PHWR (commercial operation **30 June 2023**).
**MAPS** (Kalpakkam) = **first fully indigenous PHWR**.
⚠ **Gorakhpur NPP** is in **Haryana**, not UP; **Narora** is in UP.

62.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
62.x: Kakrapar is stated to be the second-largest operating plant, with 1,840 MW. Jaitapur, at 9,900 MW, is the largest planned plant.
62.tq: Check both the status label and the capacity before accepting a plant-capacity pair.
xs: **Kakrapar – 1,840 MW** is the **second-largest operating** plant — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Kudankulam** is the largest operating (**2,000 MW**); **Jaitapur** is the largest planned (**9,900 MW**).
xa: Kakrapar (Gujarat): **4 units**; India's first **700 MW PHWRs**.
**Kashiwazaki-Kariwa** (Japan) = world's largest NPP by capacity.
Tarapur is the **first**, not the largest, plant.

62.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. KAPP-3 is located at Kakrapar in Gujarat.
2. It is the first indigenous 700 MW PHWR.
3. It began commercial operation on 30 June 2023.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: All three statements correctly describe KAPP-3, India's first indigenous 700 MW PHWR.
62.tq: Confirm a plant by combining location, technology, capacity and date.
xs: All three are correct — so option **(4)**, **1, 2 and 3**.
**KAPP-3** at **Kakrapar (Gujarat)** = **first indigenous 700 MW PHWR**, commercial operation **30 June 2023** (APPSC 2022).
xa: Kakrapar has **4 units, 1,840 MW**.
**KAPP-4** is also listed under construction.
700 MW PHWR costs ~**$2 million/MW** — among the lowest in the world.

62.s: The Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP) atomic power station, India's oldest PHWR site, is located in which State?
62.x: Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP) is in Rajasthan; its Canada-assisted RAPS-1 began in 1972 and RAPP-7 (700 MW) now operates. Kakrapar is in Gujarat, Chutka (planned) in Madhya Pradesh and Narora in Uttar Pradesh.
62.tq: Rawatbhata = Rajasthan (APPSC-GS 2018); Kakrapar = Gujarat.
xs: **Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP)** is in **Rajasthan** (APPSC-GS 2018) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Kakrapar** is in Gujarat, **Chutka** in MP, **Narora** in UP.
xa: RAPS-1 (**Canada, AECL**) started **1972**.
RAPS 1-6 = **1,180 MW**; **RAPP-7 (700 MW)** running, RAPP-8 next.
**Kota (Rawatbhata)** heavy water plant was commissioned in **1985**.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Project)
A. Kaiga 5–6
B. Chutka 1–2
C. Mahi Banswara 1–4
D. Gorakhpur 3–4

List-II (State)
1. Haryana
2. Karnataka
3. Madhya Pradesh
4. Rajasthan

Select the correct answer using the code below:
62.x: Kaiga is in Karnataka, Chutka in Madhya Pradesh, Mahi Banswara in Rajasthan and Gorakhpur in Haryana.
62.tq: Start from the sure Kaiga–Karnataka pair and complete the elimination.
xs: **Kaiga – Karnataka**, **Chutka – MP**, **Mahi Banswara – Rajasthan**, **Gorakhpur – Haryana**: **A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1**, option **(1)**.
These are the **ten 700 MW PHWRs** sanctioned in **fleet mode (2017)**.
xa: **Mahi Banswara 1-4** = **2,800 MW**, built by **ASHVINI**.
⚠ **Gorakhpur = Haryana**, not UP.
The PM laid Mahi Banswara's foundation stone.

62.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Nangal — Punjab
2. Tuticorin — Tamil Nadu
3. Talcher — Odisha
4. Thal — Gujarat
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
62.x: Nangal is in Punjab, Tuticorin in Tamil Nadu and Talcher in Odisha. Thal is in Maharashtra, not Gujarat.
62.tq: Find the location swapped with a nearby plant before selecting the code.
xs: **Nangal – Punjab**, **Tuticorin – Tamil Nadu**, **Talcher – Odisha** are correct — so option **(2)**, **1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Thal** is in **Maharashtra**, not Gujarat (Gujarat has **Baroda** and **Hazira**).
xa: Thal was commissioned in **1987**.
**Hazira** (Gujarat) and **Manuguru** both came in **1991**.
Manuguru, now **Telangana**, is the largest.

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding delays in the Kudankulam project:
1. The disintegration of the USSR delayed the project.
2. Civil-society protests contributed to the delay.
3. The economic crisis of 1991 is counted as a reason for the delay.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: The breakup of the USSR and civil-society protests are counted among the delays. The 1991 economic crisis is not included in the stated explanation.
62.tq: Reject the plausible but specifically excluded cause in the list of delays.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the **USSR broke up** and **civil-society protests** delayed Kudankulam.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **1991 economic crisis** is not counted — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** (APPSC-G1 2022 "I and III only" trap).
xa: Kudankulam came from the **1988** USSR accord.
Units: **2 x 1,000 MW VVER** operating (2013, 2016).
Kudankulam faced a ransomware leak of **19,000+** files (Jul 2026).

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Nuclear Suppliers Group:
1. It has 48 members.
2. Its decisions are taken by consensus.
3. It has a permanent secretariat.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: The NSG has 48 members and works by consensus. It does not have a permanent secretariat.
62.tq: Find the statement containing the institutional exception.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the NSG has **48 members**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: it works by **consensus**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: the NSG has **no permanent secretariat** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Formed in **1975** (the **"London Club"**) in response to India's **1974 Pokhran-I** test.
India applied in **2016**; blocked mainly by **China** (India is not an NPT party).
Benefits of membership: **access to latest technology** and a **say in rule-making**.
**Australia** reaffirmed support for India's NSG bid (Jul 2026).

62.s:
Which of the following functions continues to be retained by the Government under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
1. Enrichment
2. Spent-fuel reprocessing
3. Heavy-water production
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The Government retains control over enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy water under the SHANTI Act.
62.tq: Recognize the complete list when all three strategic functions belong to the same category.
xs: Under SHANTI, the Government keeps **enrichment**, **spent-fuel reprocessing** and **heavy water** — all three, option **(4)**.
Heavy-water production stays with the Government under SHANTI (Dec 2025), as noted for **Trombay**.
xa: Private firms and JVs may **build, own, operate** plants — NPCIL's monopoly ends.
All heavy water plants are under the **Heavy Water Board, Mumbai** (DAE).
**Manuguru** (now Telangana) is India's **largest** HWP; **Nangal** the **first**.

62.s:
Consider the following functions of the AERB:
1. Licensing nuclear power plants and fuel-cycle facilities.
2. Regulating radiation safety in medical and industrial applications.
3. Inspecting facilities and suspending or revoking licences.
4. Regulating the management and transport of radioactive waste.
Which of the above are functions of the AERB?
62.x: The AERB performs all the listed functions, including licensing, radiation regulation, inspection, licence action, and control of radioactive waste and transport.
62.tq: Recognise the complete regulatory mandate instead of selecting only licensing functions.
xs: AERB **licenses plants and fuel-cycle facilities**, regulates **radiation safety in medicine/industry**, **inspects and suspends/revokes licences**, and handles **waste management and transport** — all four, option **(4)**.
It also reviews **design, construction, operation and decommissioning**.
xa: Set up **15 Nov 1983** by **executive order**; made **statutory** by the **SHANTI Act 2025**.
Zones: **exclusion 1.6 km**, **sterilised 5 km**, **emergency planning 16 km**.
Waste rules: **Safe Disposal of Radioactive Wastes Rules 1987**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Nuclear power plants must have both on-site and off-site emergency plans.
2. The Convention on Nuclear Safety was adopted in 1994 and entered into force in 1996.
3. India is not a party to the Convention on Nuclear Safety.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is correct: emergency preparedness needs both on-site and off-site plans. Statement 2 is correct: the Convention was adopted in 1994 and came into force in 1996. Statement 3 is wrong: India is a party to it. So (a) leaves out statement 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
62.tq: CNS: 1994 adopted, 1996 in force, India a party; it requires on-site + off-site plans.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: emergency preparedness needs **on-site + off-site plans**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: the **Convention on Nuclear Safety** was adopted **1994**, in force **1996**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **India is a party** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: The **emergency planning zone** extends to **16 km**.
**Exclusion zone 1.6 km**; **sterilised zone 5 km**.
AERB can **suspend or revoke licences**.

62.s: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa is notable because it is:
o: the first nuclear plant in India
the world's oldest nuclear power plant
the world's largest nuclear power plant by capacity
the only Level 7 nuclear accident site
62.x: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa in Japan is the world's largest nuclear power plant by capacity.
62.tq: Separate a capacity distinction from accident-severity distinctions.
xs: **Kashiwazaki-Kariwa** (Japan) is the **world's largest nuclear power plant by capacity** — so option **(3)** is correct.
India's first plant is **Tarapur** (**1969**); the only level 7 sites are **Chernobyl** and **Fukushima**.
xa: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa had a **2007** earthquake: fire and a small radioactive leak (a **minor event**).
India's largest operating plant: **Kudankulam, 2,000 MW**; next **Kakrapar, 1,840 MW**.
Largest planned in India: **Jaitapur, 9,900 MW**.

62.s:
Which of the following radioactive materials are mentioned as typical sources for a dirty bomb?
1. Caesium-137
2. Cobalt-60
3. Uranium-235 used in a reactor core
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: Caesium-137 and Cobalt-60, commonly associated with medical or industrial sources, are mentioned as typical materials. Uranium-235 in a reactor core is not included in that description.
62.tq: Identify the two stated source materials and reject an unrelated fissile-material option.
xs: Typical dirty-bomb sources are **medical or industrial** — **Cs-137 (Caesium-137)** and **Co-60 (Cobalt-60)** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
**Uranium-235 in a reactor core** is not listed among the typical sources — statement 3 is wrong.
xa: A dirty bomb uses a **conventional explosive**; there is **no nuclear chain reaction**.
Its damage = **contamination and panic**.
**ICONS** is the IAEA's ministerial **International Conference on Nuclear Security**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the Nuclear Security Summits:
1. At the 2010 summit, India announced the Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership.
2. The Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership is now located at Bahadurgarh.
3. The summit series, started by US President Obama, held five summits and ended at Seoul.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: India announced the GCNEP at the 2010 summit and it is now at Bahadurgarh. Statement 3 is wrong: Obama's series had four summits (Washington 2010, Seoul 2012, The Hague 2014, Washington 2016), ending at Washington. So (a) leaves out statement 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
62.tq: Four summits: Washington - Seoul - The Hague - Washington; GCNEP at Bahadurgarh.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: at the **2010** summit India announced the **Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: it is now at **Bahadurgarh**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **four** summits were held, ending at **Washington (2016)**, not Seoul (**2012**) — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: The summit series was started by US President **Obama**.
Order: **Washington 2010 → Seoul 2012 → The Hague 2014 → Washington 2016**.
**ICONS** is the IAEA's ministerial nuclear-security conference (**2013, 2016, 2020, 2024**).

62.s: The proposed Kovvada nuclear power project is located in:
62.x: Kovvada is located in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh.
62.tq: Test the project location directly while using other nuclear-site locations as distractors.
xs: **Kovvada** is in **Srikakulam district** of **Andhra Pradesh** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Kakrapar** is in **Gujarat**, **Rawatbhata** in **Rajasthan**, and **Kudankulam** in **Tamil Nadu** — separate plants.
xa: Kovvada will use **AP1000 (PWR)** reactors from the **USA** — proposed.
Capacity and unit details are **still to be finalised**.
Other AP angle: **Manuguru HWP** (**1991**) was in undivided AP, now **Telangana**.

62.s: The reactor technology proposed for the Kovvada nuclear project is:
o: AP1000 reactors from the United States
62.x: Kovvada is proposed to use AP1000 reactors from the United States; its capacity and unit details remain to be finalised.
62.tq: Match the project with its specific foreign reactor technology.
xs: Kovvada will use **AP1000** reactors from the **United States** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **Kudankulam = Russia (VVER)**; **Jaitapur = France (EPR)**; **Kovvada = USA (AP1000)**.
**PFBR** is a **BHAVINI** fast-breeder at **Kalpakkam**, and **Canada** assisted the **PHWR** RAPS-1 — not Kovvada.
xa: The **USA** link comes through the **123 Agreement (2008)**.
Kovvada is in **Srikakulam district**, AP; capacity and units still to be finalised.
**AP DISCOMs** sought **100 MW** from BHAVINI's plant.

62.s:
Which of the following concerns has been raised regarding the nuclear liability framework in relation to supplier accountability?
1. Supplier indemnity may weaken accountability.
2. Clause 46 of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act has been omitted in the criticised framework.
3. Victims may lose other-law remedies.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The criticisms concern supplier indemnity and the omission of CLNDA Clause 46, which relates to remedies under other laws and therefore affects accountability and victims’ compensation.
62.tq: Treat the accountability concerns as a connected set and check the omitted legal provision.
xs: Critics say **supplier indemnity** and the **omission of CLNDA Clause 46** (other-law remedies) weaken accountability, hurting **victims' compensation** — all three, option **(4)**.
CLNDA's **Sec 46** had kept other civil laws open; SHANTI **removed supplier liability**.
xa: CLNDA **Sec 17(b)** gave recourse against **suppliers** for defective equipment.
SHANTI total liability is capped at **300 million SDR (~₹3,900 crore)**.
The Supreme Court issued notice on SHANTI's **liability caps** (Aug 2026).

62.s:
Consider the following statements regarding milestones in India’s nuclear power programme:
1. RAPS-1 was the first PHWR in India.
2. MAPS was the first fully indigenous PHWR.
3. KAPP-3 was the first 700 MW nuclear power unit in India.
4. Nangal housed the first Heavy Water Plant.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: All four statements are correct: RAPS-1 was the first PHWR, MAPS the first fully indigenous PHWR, KAPP-3 the first 700 MW unit, and Nangal the site of the first Heavy Water Plant.
62.tq: Check each milestone independently before selecting the complete combination.
xs: **RAPS-1** (**1972**) was the **first PHWR**; **MAPS** the **first fully indigenous PHWR** — statements 1 and 2 correct.
**KAPP-3** (**2023**) was the **first indigenous 700 MW** unit; **Nangal** the **first HWP** — so **all four**, option **(4)**.
xa: First NPP: **Tarapur** (**1969**, **BWR**).
Largest station: **Kudankulam** (**2,000 MW**); first post-waiver partner: **France**.
⚠ **Nangal = first HWP**; **Manuguru = largest**.
KAPP-3 began commercial operation on **30 June 2023**.

62.s: Mahi Banswara nuclear power project is being built by:
o: AERB and the Department of Space jointly
62.x: Mahi Banswara is being developed by Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Limited (ASHVINI), an NPCIL–NTPC joint venture.
62.tq: Identify the implementing body through the joint-venture relationship.
xs: **Mahi Banswara** is built by **ASHVINI (Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Ltd)**, an **NPCIL-NTPC JV** — option **(4)**.
**BHAVINI** builds FBRs (PFBR); **AERB** is the regulator.
xa: ⚠ **Mahi Banswara = ASHVINI**; **PFBR = BHAVINI**.
**AERB approved excavation** for units 1-2.
Mahi Banswara 1-4 = **2,800 MW** in **Rajasthan**.

62.s: The principal objective of adopting fleet-mode construction for nuclear reactors is to reduce the construction period from approximately:
62.x: Fleet-mode construction aims to reduce the build time from 13 years to 8 years.
62.tq: Test the paired before-and-after numerical targets.
xs: **Fleet mode** aims to cut build time from **13 to 8 years** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The other pairs are not the notes' figures.
xa: **2017** fleet-mode sanction: **ten 700 MW PHWRs**.
Projects: **Kaiga 5-6, Gorakhpur 3-4, Chutka 1-2, Mahi Banswara 1-4**.
Builds otherwise take **10-12 years** — a known bottleneck.

62.s: In 2017 the Government of India sanctioned in 'fleet mode':
62.x: The 2017 fleet-mode sanction covered ten 700 MW PHWRs (Kaiga 5-6, Gorakhpur 3-4, Chutka 1-2 and Mahi Banswara 1-4). Six EPRs are the French-assisted Jaitapur plan, VVERs are the Russian units at Kudankulam, and the 2 x 500 MWe FBRs are the follow-on to PFBR at Kalpakkam.
62.tq: Fleet mode 2017 = 10 x 700 MW PHWR.
xs: In **2017** India sanctioned **ten 700 MW PHWRs** in fleet mode — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Six EPRs** are the French **Jaitapur** plan; **VVERs** are Russian **Kudankulam**; FBRs are the PFBR follow-on.
xa: Units: **Kaiga 5-6, Gorakhpur 3-4, Chutka 1-2 (MP), Mahi Banswara 1-4 (Rajasthan)**.
Aim: build time **13 → 8 years**.
700 MW PHWR ≈ **$2 million/MW**.

62.s: What was the share of nuclear power in India's total electricity generation in 2024–25?
62.x: Nuclear power accounted for 3.1% of electricity generation in 2024–25. The 1.62% figure refers to its share of installed capacity.
62.tq: Distinguish the share of generation from the share of installed capacity.
xs: Nuclear gave **3.1%** of electricity generation in **2024-25** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1.62%** is its share of **installed capacity**; **8.78** is the capacity in GW.
xa: ⚠ **~3%** = share of generation; **1.62%** = share of capacity.
Record **56.681 BU** in FY2024-25 — first time NPCIL crossed **50 BU**.

62.s: The Nuclear Energy Mission envisages India's nuclear power capacity reaching approximately what level by 2047?
62.x: The Nuclear Energy Mission targets 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047.
62.tq: Match the long-term target with its terminal year.
xs: The **Nuclear Energy Mission** targets **100 GW by 2047** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**22.38 GW** is the **2031-32** target; **54 GW** is NPCIL's share.
xa: **SHANTI Act 2025** lets **private companies and JVs** enter.
Present capacity **8.78 GW**.
The **100 GW** goal is part of the current debate on SHANTI.

62.s: Under the 2047 nuclear power target, NPCIL is expected to add approximately:
62.x: NPCIL is expected to add 54 GW as part of the effort to reach the 100 GW target by 2047.
62.tq: Distinguish the institutional contribution from the national target.
xs: NPCIL is to add **54 GW** of the **100 GW** goal — so option **(4)** is correct.
**22.38 GW** is the 2031-32 target; **13.1** (13,100 MW) is capacity under implementation.
xa: The remainder is to come with **private players** under the **SHANTI Act**.
NPCIL: PSE under **DAE**, registered **1987**.
Current fleet: **24 reactors**, **8,780 MW**.

62.s: India's installed nuclear power capacity in 2026 is approximately:
62.x: Installed nuclear capacity is about 8.78 GW (8,780 MW) from 24 NPCIL reactors. 1.62 is the percentage share of installed power capacity, 22.38 GW is the 2031-32 target, and 54 GW is NPCIL's share of the 100 GW 2047 goal.
xs: Installed nuclear capacity is about **8.78 GW (8,780 MW)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1.62** is the % share of capacity; **22.38 GW** is the 2031-32 target; **54 GW** is NPCIL's 2047 share.
xa: **24 reactors** run by NPCIL after one Rawatbhata unit shut (Apr 2026).
IYB 2026 gave **25 reactors, 7 sites, 8,880 MW** incl. RAPP-7.

62.s: The VVER units being added at Kudankulam are significant because they will increase India’s capacity of which type of reactors?
62.x: The VVER units at Kudankulam add imported light-water reactor capacity to India’s nuclear fleet.
62.tq: Decode the reactor category without confusing imported technology with indigenous PHWRs.
xs: Kudankulam's **VVER** units add **imported light-water reactor (LWR)** capacity — so option **(1)** is correct.
**VVER** is a **PWR** design from **Russia** — not heavy-water, boiling-water or fast-breeder.
xa: Kudankulam: **2 x 1,000 MW VVER** operating; **Units 3-6 (4,000 MW)** under construction.
India's **largest operating station** (**2,000 MW**).
A ransomware group leaked **19,000+** KKNPP files (Jul 2026).

62.s: Which one of the following heavy water plants was commissioned in 1962?
62.x: Nangal in Punjab was the first heavy water plant and was commissioned in 1962.
62.tq: Use the commissioning year to distinguish the earliest plant from later facilities.
xs: **Nangal** (Punjab) was commissioned in **1962** — India's **first** heavy water plant — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Tuticorin** came in **1978**, **Baroda** in **1980**, **Talcher** in **1985**.
xa: ⚠ **Nangal = first HWP**; **Manuguru = largest**.
All HWPs are under the **Heavy Water Board, Mumbai** (DAE).
**Kota** and **Talcher** both came in **1985**.

62.s: Manuguru heavy water plant is presently located in which State?
62.x: Manuguru was in undivided Andhra Pradesh when established, but it is presently in Telangana.
62.tq: Separate the historical administrative reference from the present State location.
xs: **Manuguru** HWP is now in **Telangana** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was in **undivided AP** when set up (**1991**), hence the AP trap.
xa: Manuguru = **India's largest** HWP (APPSC 2021).
All HWPs are under the **Heavy Water Board, Mumbai**.
AP angle: **Kovvada** (US AP1000) is AP's planned NPP.

62.s: Which one of the following is the largest heavy water plant in India?
62.x: Manuguru is identified as India's largest heavy water plant.
62.tq: Use the size claim carefully; do not confuse the largest plant with the first plant.
xs: **Manuguru** is India's **largest** heavy water plant — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Nangal** is the **first** (**1962**); **Kota** and **Hazira** are other HWPs.
xa: Manuguru: commissioned **1991**, then undivided AP, now **Telangana**.
⚠ **Nangal = first**; **Manuguru = largest**.
**Trombay** hosts BARC's early heavy-water work.

62.s: Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant uses which reactor technology and foreign collaboration?
62.x: Kudankulam uses Russian VVER pressurised water reactors (PWRs).
62.tq: Discriminate between reactor technology and collaborating country.
xs: **Kudankulam** uses **VVER (PWR)** reactors from **Russia** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**PFBR** is indigenous; **BWR** came from the USA at Tarapur; **AP1000** (USA) is for **Kovvada**.
xa: Russia link: **USSR accord 1988**; **DAE-Rosatom "Strategic Vision" (Dec 2014)**.
Operating: **2 x 1,000 MW** (2013, 2016); units **3-6** under construction.
⚠ **Kudankulam = Russia (VVER)**; **Jaitapur = France (EPR)**; **Kovvada = USA (AP1000)**.

62.s: Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project is associated with which combination?
o: Maharashtra, France, EDF and six EPR units
Andhra Pradesh, USA, Westinghouse and six AP1000 units
Tamil Nadu, Russia, Rosatom and six VVER units
Gujarat, Canada, AECL and six PHWR units
62.x: Jaitapur is located in Maharashtra and is associated with France's EDF and six EPR units.
62.tq: Match the project by combining location, partner company and reactor design.
xs: **Jaitapur** = **Maharashtra**, **France (EDF)**, **6 EPR** units — so option **(1)** is correct.
**AP1000** (USA) is **Kovvada** (AP); **VVER** (Russia) is **Kudankulam** (TN); AECL PHWR was **RAPS-1**.
xa: Jaitapur = **9,900 MW**, planned world's largest NPP.
Industrial Way Forward Agreement: **March 2018**.
**France** = **first post-waiver** deal (**30 September 2008**).

62.s: The Industrial Way Forward Agreement relating to Jaitapur was signed between NPCIL and EDF in:
62.x: NPCIL and France's EDF signed the Industrial Way Forward Agreement for Jaitapur in March 2018.
62.tq: Separate the project-specific agreement year from the broader civil nuclear agreement year.
xs: NPCIL-EDF signed the **Industrial Way Forward Agreement** for **Jaitapur** in **March 2018** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**September 2008** is the India-France civil nuclear deal; **December 2014** is the DAE-Rosatom Strategic Vision.
xa: Jaitapur: **6 EPR** units, **9,900 MW**.
France gave a **lifetime fuel-supply guarantee**.
⚠ **Jaitapur = France (EPR)**; **Kovvada = USA (AP1000)**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about India's Additional Protocol with the IAEA:
1. India signed it in 2009 and it came into force in 2014.
2. It gives the IAEA wider inspection access to all Indian nuclear facilities, including military ones.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is correct: signed 2009, in force 2014. Statement 2 is wrong: the wider inspection access is limited to India's declared civilian facilities. So (b), (c) and (d) are wrong.
62.tq: Additional Protocol = wider access, but only to declared civilian facilities.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: India's **Additional Protocol** was signed **2009**, in force **2014**.
Statement 2 is wrong: wider access is **limited to India's declared civilian facilities** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **India-Specific Safeguards Agreement** came after the **2008** India-US deal.
**Imported fuel** goes only to **safeguarded** reactors.
Military facilities stayed **outside safeguards** under the 2006 plan.

62.s: Under the 2006 separation plan linked to the Indo-US nuclear deal, India:
o: Placed all its nuclear facilities, including military ones, under IAEA safeguards
Separated civil and military facilities and placed civil reactors under IAEA safeguards
Signed the NPT as a non-nuclear-weapon state
Shut down all its research reactors at Trombay
62.x: In 2006 India separated civil and military facilities and put its civil reactors under IAEA safeguards so that NSG members could supply fuel. Military facilities stayed outside safeguards, India has never signed the NPT, and the research reactors were not all shut by this plan.
62.tq: Separation plan: civil only under safeguards; imported fuel only to safeguarded reactors.
xs: The **2006 separation plan** split **civil and military** facilities and put **civil reactors under IAEA safeguards** — option **(2)**.
Military sites stayed out; India **never signed the NPT**; research reactors were not all shut.
xa: Purpose: let **NSG members supply fuel**.
**NSG waiver (September 2008)** ended **34 years** of exclusion.
**123 Agreement** (2008): PM **Manmohan Singh** + President **Bush**.

62.s: Which one of the following statements regarding India’s nuclear doctrine is correct?
o: India is legally bound by the TPNW to renounce nuclear weapons.
India has formally abandoned the No First Use policy.
India follows a policy of First Use only against non-nuclear states.
India follows a policy of No First Use.
62.x: India follows the No First Use policy. India is not a party to the TPNW.
62.tq: Separate a stated national doctrine from obligations under treaties India has not joined.
xs: India follows a policy of **No First Use** — so option **(4)** is correct.
India has **not signed the TPNW**, so it is not legally bound by it — option (1) is wrong.
The notes give **No First Use** as India's doctrine, so "abandoned NFU" or "First Use against non-nuclear states" (options 2 and 3) do not fit.
xa: India has **not signed** the **NPT**, which it calls **discriminatory** (only the **P5** are nuclear-weapon states).
India has not signed the **CTBT** (**1996**): no time-bound disarmament; subcritical tests still allowed.
The **TPNW** entered into force in **2021**; India says it adds nothing to customary law.
India **signed and ratified** the **PTBT** (**1963**).

62.s: The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), popularly known as the ‘London Club’, was formed in response to which event?
o: The signing of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
62.x: The NSG was formed in 1975, in response to India’s 1974 Pokhran-I nuclear test.
62.tq: Link the organisation with the event that led to its formation.
xs: The **NSG** ("**London Club**") was formed in **1975** in response to **India's 1974 Pokhran-I test** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It predates both **Pokhran-II (1998)** and **Chernobyl (1986)**, so options (1) and (4) are impossible.
xa: The NSG has **48 members**, works by **consensus** and has **no permanent secretariat**.
India **applied in 2016**; its entry is blocked mainly by **China** on NPT grounds.
The **NSG waiver (September 2008)** ended **34 years** of India's exclusion from nuclear trade.
⚠ NSG membership does **not** make a country an **NPT** member.

62.s: Which country supplies approximately 80 per cent of India's uranium imports?
62.x: Kazakhstan supplies approximately 80 per cent of India's uranium imports.
62.tq: Use the supplier-share association rather than a general nuclear cooperation association.
xs: **Kazakhstan** supplies about **80%** of India's uranium imports — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Russia**, **Uzbekistan**, **Canada** and **Australia** are the other suppliers, with smaller shares.
xa: **Canada**: **10,000 t** uranium for **2027-2035**, for **safeguarded PHWRs** (Jun 2026).
**Australia**: agreement signed **2014**, in force **2015**; uranium under **IAEA safeguards**.
Imported fuel goes **only to safeguarded reactors**.

62.s: The agreement associated with the Kudankulam project was signed in:
62.x: The India-USSR agreement associated with Kudankulam was signed in 1988.
62.tq: Distinguish the project agreement year from later commissioning and civil nuclear agreement years.
xs: The **India-USSR accord** for **Kudankulam** was signed in **1988** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Kudankulam has **2 x 1,000 MW VVER** units operating (**2013, 2016**); **units 3-6** are being built.
**2008** is the year of the **NSG waiver** and the **123 Agreement**, not Kudankulam.
xa: Delays came from the **disintegration of the USSR** and **civil-society protests** (APPSC-G1 2022 key).
**DAE-Rosatom "Strategic Vision" (Dec 2014)**: **12+ units**.
Kudankulam (**2,000 MW**) is India's **largest operating station**.
⚠ **Kudankulam = Russia (VVER)**; **Jaitapur = France (EPR)**; **Kovvada = USA (AP1000)**.

62.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. France — Civil nuclear agreement of 30 September 2008
2. Japan — Civil nuclear agreement of 2016
3. Australia — Nuclear agreement of 2014
4. Canada — Agreement for 10,000 tonnes of uranium during 2027–2035
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
62.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. France's agreement included a lifetime fuel-supply guarantee, while the Canada arrangement concerns 10,000 tonnes of uranium for 2027–2035.
62.tq: Verify each partner-year or partner-quantity pair before choosing the comprehensive code.
xs: **France**: civil nuclear agreement **30 September 2008** — correct.
**Japan**: agreement **2016**; **Australia**: signed **2014** (in force **2015**) — both correct.
**Canada**: **10,000 t uranium, 2027-2035** — correct; so **all four**, option **(4)**.
xa: France was the **first post-waiver** partner, with a **lifetime fuel-supply guarantee** (Jaitapur).
**USA**: **123 Agreement** (2008); Kovvada (**AP1000**).
**Russia**: **1988** accord; **DAE-Rosatom Strategic Vision (Dec 2014)**.
Australia's **Administrative Arrangement** was finalised at the **3rd Annual Summit** (Jul 2026).

62.s: Which country was the first to conclude a civil nuclear agreement with India after the NSG waiver of 2008?
62.x: France was the first country to conclude a post-waiver civil nuclear agreement with India, on 30 September 2008.
62.tq: Use the word FIRST to distinguish the earliest post-waiver agreement from later famous agreements.
xs: **France** signed the **first** post-waiver civil nuclear deal, on **30 September 2008** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Japan**'s agreement came only in **2016**; **Russia**'s ties go back to the **1988** Kudankulam accord.
xa: The France deal included a **lifetime fuel-supply guarantee** and the **Jaitapur** project.
**Jaitapur**: **6 EPR** units, **9,900 MW**; NPCIL-EDF "Industrial Way Forward Agreement" in **March 2018**.
The **NSG waiver (September 2008)** ended **34 years** of exclusion from nuclear trade.

62.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 123 Agreement was signed under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush.
2. The NSG waiver of September 2008 made India a full member of the Nuclear Suppliers Group.
3. The India-US 123 Agreement is named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the 2008 NSG waiver allowed civil nuclear trade and ended 34 years of exclusion, but India is still not an NSG member. Statement 3 is correct: the name comes from Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954. Statement 1 is correct: it was signed under Manmohan Singh and Bush. So '1 and 3 only'.
62.tq: Waiver is not membership: India applied for NSG membership in 2016 and is still blocked.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: the **123 Agreement** was signed under PM **Manmohan Singh** and President **Bush**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **NSG waiver** (**September 2008**) allowed civil nuclear trade; India is **not yet an NSG member**.
Statement 3 is correct: named after **Sec 123** of the **US Atomic Energy Act 1954**.
xa: The waiver ended **34 years** of exclusion from nuclear trade.
**France** signed the **first** post-waiver deal on **30 September 2008**.
India applied to the NSG in **2016**; blocked mainly by **China**.

62.s: Which of the following represents the occupational dose limits stated for radiation workers?
o: 30 mSv per year averaged over five years, 20 mSv maximum in one year, and 100 mSv cumulative
5 mSv per year averaged over five years, 20 mSv maximum in one year, and 30 mSv cumulative
20 mSv per year averaged over five years, 30 mSv maximum in one year, and 100 mSv cumulative
20 mSv maximum in one year, 30 mSv cumulative, and 100 mSv averaged over five years
62.x: The stated limits are 20 mSv per year averaged over five years, a maximum of 30 mSv in a year, and 100 mSv cumulative.
62.tq: Keep the average, annual maximum and cumulative limits in their correct order.
xs: Limits: **20 mSv/yr** averaged over **5 years**, **30 mSv** max in a year, **100 mSv** cumulative — option **(3)**.
Options (1) and (4) swap the **20** and **30** figures; option (2) is wrong on all counts.
xa: Safety principles: **Defence in Depth** and **ALARA**.
Waste rules: **Safe Disposal of Radioactive Wastes Rules 1987**.
**700 MW PHWRs** carry **advanced safety features** post-Fukushima.

62.s: The design approach that uses multiple successive layers of protection in nuclear safety is known as:
62.x: Defence in Depth is the nuclear-safety design approach based on multiple successive and independent protective layers.
62.tq: Identify the exact technical term from its functional description.
xs: **Defence in Depth** is AERB's layered safety-design approach — so option **(2)** is correct.
It goes with the **ALARA** principle for radiation exposure.
xa: Dose limits: **20 mSv/yr** (5-year average), **30 mSv** max, **100 mSv** cumulative.
Post-Fukushima, **700 MW PHWRs** have **advanced safety features**; releases kept **<1% of AERB limits**.
Emergency preparedness needs **on-site + off-site** plans (**Convention on Nuclear Safety**).

62.s: The International Conference on Nuclear Security (ICONS) is a ministerial conference organised by the:
62.x: ICONS is the IAEA's ministerial International Conference on Nuclear Security.
62.tq: Identify the correct international body rather than a neighbouring nuclear or environmental organisation.
xs: **ICONS** is the **IAEA**'s (International Atomic Energy Agency) ministerial **International Conference on Nuclear Security** — option **(1)**.
xa: **IAEA**: founded **1957**, HQ **Vienna, Austria** (APPSC 2021); India a **founding member**.
IAEA functions: **safeguards and verification**, safety standards, **nuclear security (ITDB)**, technical cooperation.
The **NSG** is a separate export-control group (**48 members**, **1975**).

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA):
1. It was founded in 1957 and is headquartered in Vienna, Austria.
2. It is an autonomous body in the UN system with about 180 members.
3. India joined the IAEA only after the 2008 India-US civil nuclear deal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is correct: the IAEA was founded in 1957 with its HQ at Vienna. Statement 2 is correct: it is an autonomous body in the UN system with about 180 members. Statement 3 is wrong: India is a founding member and joined in 1957. So (a) leaves out statement 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
62.tq: India is a founding member (1957); Vienna is the HQ (APPSC 2021).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **IAEA** founded **1957**, HQ **Vienna, Austria**.
Statement 2 is correct: autonomous body in the **UN system**, ~**180** members.
Statement 3 is wrong: India is a **founding member** (joined **1957**) — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: APPSC 2021 asked IAEA HQ: **Vienna**.
IAEA's **INES** scale runs **0-7**.

62.s: When the IAEA detects non-compliance with safeguards obligations, it may report the matter to the:
62.x: The IAEA can report safeguards non-compliance to the United Nations Security Council.
62.tq: Identify the correct international authority linked to safeguards violations.
xs: The IAEA reports safeguards non-compliance to the **UN Security Council** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The notes link it to no WTO, ICJ or Human Rights Council role.
xa: India placed **civil reactors under IAEA safeguards** (2006 separation plan).
**Additional Protocol**: signed **2009**, in force **2014**.
IAEA is an **autonomous** body in the UN system.

62.s: Which statement regarding the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) is correct?
o: It was created through the 2008 India–US civil nuclear agreement.
It was signed in 1957 and entered into force in 1968.
It was signed in 1970 and India joined it in 2005.
It was signed in 1968, entered into force in 1970, and India has never signed it.
62.x: The NPT dates from 1968, entered into force in 1970, and India has never signed it.
62.tq: Separate the treaty dates from the dates of IAEA agreements.
xs: The **NPT** dates from **1968**, in force **1970**, and **India has never signed it** — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ Claims that India "signed the NPT in **2005**" are **WRONG**; **1957** is the IAEA's founding year.
xa: India calls the NPT **discriminatory** — only the **P5** are weapon states.
**NSG** membership does **not** make a country an NPT member (UPSC 2018).
China blocks India's NSG bid on **NPT grounds**.

62.s: India has not signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) mainly because it objects to which of the following features?
o: The absence of any reference to nuclear disarmament
The absence of time-bound nuclear disarmament and the continued possibility of subcritical tests
The recognition of only five nuclear-weapon states
The treaty’s restriction of only atmospheric tests
62.x: India has not signed the CTBT because it does not provide for time-bound nuclear disarmament and still permits subcritical tests.
62.tq: Test the treaty-specific objection rather than the general purpose of the treaty.
xs: India has not signed the **CTBT** because it has **no time-bound nuclear disarmament** and still allows **subcritical tests** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **CTBT** (**1996**) bans all nuclear test explosions, not just atmospheric ones — so option (4) is wrong.
Recognising **only five** (the **P5**) nuclear-weapon states is India's objection to the **NPT**, not the CTBT — option (3).
xa: **PTBT** (**1963**) bans tests in **air, space and underwater**; India **signed and ratified** it.
**TPNW** (in force **2021**): first binding treaty banning nuclear weapons; India stays out as it **adds nothing to customary law**.
**NPT** (1968; in force **1970**): India **never signed**, calling it **discriminatory**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about India's stand on nuclear treaties:
1. India has signed and ratified the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963).
2. India has not signed the TPNW, holding that it adds nothing to customary law.
3. The TPNW entered into force in 2017.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is correct: India signed and ratified the PTBT, which bans tests in air, space and underwater. Statement 2 is correct: India stays out of the TPNW because it adds nothing to customary law. Statement 3 is wrong: the TPNW entered into force in 2021. So (a) leaves out statement 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
62.tq: India: PTBT yes; NPT, CTBT, TPNW no. TPNW in force 2021.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: India **signed and ratified** the **PTBT** (**1963**), which bans tests in **air, space and underwater**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: India has **not signed the TPNW**, holding that it **adds nothing to customary law**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: the **TPNW** entered into force in **2021**, not 2017 — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: The **TPNW** is the **first binding treaty** banning nuclear weapons.
**CTBT** (**1996**) bans all nuclear test explosions; India has **not signed** it (no time-bound disarmament; subcritical tests still allowed).
**NPT** (1968; in force **1970**): only the **P5** are nuclear-weapon states; India calls it **discriminatory**.
India's doctrine: **No First Use**.

62.s: India’s application for membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group was made in which year, and which country has mainly blocked its entry?
62.x: India applied for NSG membership in 2016. China has mainly blocked India’s entry, particularly because India is not a party to the NPT.
62.tq: Pair the year of application with the country associated with the opposition.
xs: India applied for NSG membership in **2016**, and **China** has mainly blocked it — so option **(2)** is correct.
China objects on **NPT grounds**: India is **not an NPT party**.
xa: India is still **not a member**; **Australia** reaffirmed support for the bid (Jul 2026).
India's other regimes: **MTCR (2016)**, **Wassenaar Arrangement (2017)**, **Australia Group (2018)**.
The NSG (**1975**, "**London Club**") has **48 members** and works by **consensus**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLNDA), 2010:
1. Section 17(b) gave the operator a right of recourse against suppliers for defective equipment.
2. The Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool was created to cover supplier-related liability.
3. It made operator liability fault-based and placed no cap on it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 3 is wrong: CLNDA made operator liability no-fault and capped it at Rs 1,500 crore, with the Centre paying beyond the cap. Statement 1 is correct: Section 17(b) gave recourse against suppliers. Statement 2 is correct: the Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool was created to cover suppliers. So '1 and 2 only'.
62.tq: CLNDA = no-fault, capped Rs 1,500 crore, Sec 17(b) supplier recourse; SHANTI removed supplier liability.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **Section 17(b)** gave a right of **recourse against suppliers** for defective equipment.
Statement 2 is correct: the **Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool** was created to cover suppliers.
Statement 3 is wrong: CLNDA made operator liability **no-fault**, **capped at ₹1,500 crore**; the Centre pays beyond.
xa: The **SHANTI Act 2025** repealed **CLNDA 2010** and the **Atomic Energy Act 1962**.
SHANTI caps: **₹3,000 crore** (large) / **₹1,500 crore** (medium) / **₹100 crore** (SMRs); **supplier liability removed**.
SHANTI got Presidential assent on **20 Dec 2025**.

62.s:
The SHANTI Act, 2025 repealed which of the following enactments?
1. Atomic Energy Act, 1962
2. Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010
3. Patents Act, 1970 in its entirety
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
62.x: The SHANTI Act repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010. It amended Section 4 of the Patents Act rather than repealing the Patents Act in its entirety.
62.tq: Reject the extreme claim that an entire neighbouring law was repealed.
xs: The **SHANTI Act 2025** repealed the **Atomic Energy Act 1962** and **CLNDA 2010** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)**.
The Patents Act was only **amended** (s.4, to allow **peaceful nuclear patents**), not repealed — statement 3 is wrong.
xa: Timeline: introduced in Lok Sabha **15 Dec 2025**; passed LS/RS **17 / 18 Dec 2025**; assent **20 Dec 2025**.
It **ends NPCIL's monopoly**: Indian private firms and JVs can build, own, operate.
It made the **AERB statutory**, answerable to Parliament.

62.s: Which of the following combinations correctly matches the category of nuclear facility with the liability cap under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
o: Large facility—₹100 crore; Medium facility—₹1,500 crore; SMR—₹3,000 crore
Large facility—₹1,500 crore; Medium facility—₹100 crore; SMR—₹3,000 crore
Large facility—₹3,000 crore; Medium facility—₹1,500 crore; SMR—₹100 crore
Large facility—₹3,900 crore; Medium facility—₹3,000 crore; SMR—₹1,500 crore
62.x: The graded caps are ₹3,000 crore for large facilities, ₹1,500 crore for medium facilities and ₹100 crore for small modular reactors.
62.tq: Start from the distinctive SMR figure and then match the two larger categories.
xs: SHANTI's graded caps: **Large ₹3,000 crore**, **Medium ₹1,500 crore**, **SMR ₹100 crore** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**₹3,900 crore** is the **total** cap (**300 million SDR**), not the large-facility cap — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Liability beyond the cap is met by a **Nuclear Liability Fund**.
**Supplier liability removed** (unlike CLNDA's **Sec 17(b)**).
CLNDA's old operator cap was **₹1,500 crore**.

62.s:
With reference to liability under the SHANTI Act, 2025, consider the following statements:
1. Total liability is capped at 300 million SDR (about Rs 3,900 crore).
2. Liability in excess of the cap is met through a Nuclear Liability Fund.
3. The operator's right of recourse against suppliers under CLNDA Section 17(b) is retained.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
62.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the SHANTI Act caps total liability at 300 million SDR (~Rs 3,900 crore) and meets the excess through a Nuclear Liability Fund. Statement 3 is wrong: the Act removed supplier liability, the CLNDA provision that had deterred foreign vendors. So (b), (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
62.tq: SHANTI: 300 m SDR cap, Liability Fund, no supplier liability.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: total liability capped at **300 million SDR (~₹3,900 crore)**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: the excess is met by a **Nuclear Liability Fund**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: SHANTI **removed supplier liability** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **CLNDA Sec 17(b)** = supplier recourse; **SHANTI** = supplier liability removed.
Graded caps: **₹3,000 crore** (large), **₹1,500 crore** (medium), **₹100 crore** (SMRs).
Critics: removing supplier liability and capping damages hurts **victims' compensation**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB):
1. It was set up on 15 November 1983 by an executive order under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962.
2. The Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill was enacted to give it statutory status.
3. The SHANTI Act, 2025 made it a statutory body answerable to Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: Statement 1 is correct: the AERB was set up on 15 Nov 1983 by executive order under the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and worked under the DAE. Statement 2 is wrong: the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill was never enacted. Statement 3 is correct: the SHANTI Act 2025 made the AERB statutory and answerable to Parliament. So (a), (c) and (d) are wrong because they include statement 2.
62.tq: AERB: executive order 1983 -> statutory only through SHANTI 2025; the NSRA Bill lapsed.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: AERB was set up on **15 Nov 1983** by **executive order** under the **Atomic Energy Act 1962**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: the **Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill** was **never enacted**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: the **SHANTI Act 2025** made AERB **statutory**, **answerable to Parliament** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: AERB earlier worked **under the DAE**, the promoter — hence the independence debate.
It can **suspend or revoke licences** after inspections.
