Supreme Court issued notice to the Union and **AERB** on SHANTI's liability caps (Aug 2026).

62.s: In August 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice to the Union and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board in connection with a petition challenging which aspect of the SHANTI framework?
o: Its target of 100 GW nuclear capacity by 2047
62.x: A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant issued notice in a petition challenging the liability caps under SHANTI.
62.tq: Match the current judicial development with the precise legal issue.
xs: The Supreme Court (CJI **Surya Kant**, **3-judge Bench**) issued notice on a petition challenging SHANTI's **liability caps** — option **(1)**.
SHANTI **lets private companies and JVs enter**, so "prohibition on private participation" (option 2) is wrong.
xa: SHANTI caps: **₹3,000 crore** (large), **₹1,500 crore** (medium), **₹100 crore** (SMRs); total **300 million SDR**.
**Supplier liability removed**; excess via a **Nuclear Liability Fund**.
The **100 GW by 2047** target is the Nuclear Energy Mission, not the subject of the case.

62.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its INES rating?
62.x: Three Mile Island was rated Level 5. Chernobyl and Fukushima Daiichi were Level 7, while Kashiwazaki-Kariwa was classified as a minor event.
62.tq: Eliminate the options by comparing the event with its scale rating.
xs: **Three Mile Island** is rated **INES level 5** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Fukushima** and **Chernobyl** are **level 7**, not 5; **Kashiwazaki-Kariwa** was only a **minor event**.
xa: ⚠ **Three Mile Island = level 5**; **Chernobyl and Fukushima = level 7**.
Three Mile Island: **USA** (Pennsylvania), **1979** (APPSC 2019).
INES runs **0-7**.

62.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Three Mile Island accident occurred in 1979 in the USA.
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster occurred in 2010 in Japan.
The Mayapuri incident involved an orphan Cobalt-60 source.
The Chernobyl disaster occurred on 26 April 1986.
62.x: Option B is incorrect: the Fukushima Daiichi disaster, set off by a tsunami, happened in 2011, not 2010, and was rated INES Level 7. Chernobyl was on 26 April 1986.
62.tq: Match each nuclear accident to its year.
n: The Three Mile Island accident occurred in 1979. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Three Mile Island accident occurred in the USA. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Chernobyl disaster occurred on 26 April 1986. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster occurred in 2011. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster occurred in Japan. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Mayapuri incident involved an orphan Cobalt-60 source. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**Fukushima Daiichi occurred in 2010**" — option **(2)**: it happened in **2011**.
**Three Mile Island** was in **1979** (USA); **Chernobyl** on **26 April 1986**; **Mayapuri** involved an **orphan Cobalt-60 source** — all correct.
xa: Fukushima was **tsunami-triggered** and rated **Level 7** on INES.
**Mayapuri** (**Delhi**, **2010**) was a **radiological emergency**.
⚠ **Three Mile Island = level 5**; **Chernobyl and Fukushima = level 7**.

62.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. Chernobyl and Fukushima Daiichi were both rated Level 7 INES.
2. The Mayapuri incident occurred in Delhi in 2010.
3. The Three Mile Island accident involved a partial core meltdown with no major release.
4. A nuclear explosion is a natural disaster.
62.x: Three are correct: Chernobyl and Fukushima were both INES Level 7, Mayapuri happened in Delhi in 2010, and Three Mile Island was a partial meltdown with no major release. A nuclear explosion is not a natural disaster.
62.tq: Find the false classification.
n: A nuclear explosion is not a natural disaster. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Three Mile Island accident caused a partial core meltdown. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Three Mile Island accident caused no major release. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Chernobyl disaster was rated Level 7 on the INES scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster was rated Level 7 on the INES scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Mayapuri incident occurred in 2010. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Mayapuri incident occurred in Delhi, India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: **Only three** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **Chernobyl** and **Fukushima Daiichi** were both **Level 7** on **INES**.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: **Mayapuri** (**Delhi**, **2010**); **Three Mile Island** = **partial core meltdown**, **no major release**.
Statement 4 is keyed false: a **nuclear explosion** is not a natural disaster.
xa: INES runs **0-7**; only Chernobyl and Fukushima are at level 7.
Chernobyl (**Ukraine**, formerly USSR) is the **worst nuclear accident**.
**Kashiwazaki-Kariwa** (Japan, **2007**): earthquake caused a fire and small leak.

62.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Chernobyl disaster
(b) Fukushima Daiichi disaster
(c) Three Mile Island accident
(d) Mayapuri Incident

List-II
(i) 1979, USA; partial core meltdown with no major release
(ii) 1986, Ukraine (formerly USSR); worst nuclear accident
(iii) 2010, Delhi, India; orphan Cobalt-60 source and radiological emergency
(iv) 2011, Japan; tsunami-triggered disaster

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
62.x: Chernobyl was in 1986 (Ukraine, the worst accident), Fukushima in 2011 (tsunami), Three Mile Island in 1979 (USA, partial meltdown), and Mayapuri in 2010 (Delhi, Cobalt-60). The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
62.tq: Match each accident to its year and place.
n: The Chernobyl disaster occurred in Ukraine, formerly the USSR. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Chernobyl disaster was the worst nuclear accident. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster was tsunami-triggered. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(3)**.
**Chernobyl** = **1986**, **Ukraine**, worst accident; **Fukushima** = **2011**, **Japan**, **tsunami-triggered**.
**Three Mile Island** = **1979**, **USA**, partial core meltdown; **Mayapuri** = **2010**, **Delhi**, orphan **Cobalt-60**.
xa: Three Mile Island was rated INES **5**.
**SL-1** was an accident in the USA (Idaho), **1961**.
A **dirty bomb** uses a conventional explosive to spread sources like **Cs-137** or **Co-60**.

62.s:
Consider the following statements about the zones around a nuclear reactor in India:
1. The exclusion zone, with no habitation, extends to 1.6 km from the reactor.
2. The sterilised zone extends up to 5 km and population growth is curbed in it.
3. The emergency planning zone extends up to 5 km.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x:
Statement 1 is correct: the exclusion zone is 1.6 km, under NPCIL/AERB control. Statement 2 is correct: the sterilised zone goes up to 5 km and population growth is curbed. Statement 3 is wrong: the emergency planning zone is 16 km. So (a) leaves out statement 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include statement 3.
⚠ Sources differ: AERB monograph: at least 1.5 km; AERB safety guide and Bulletin 2019: 1.6 km; APPSC 2022 key: 1 km. This key follows the notes (1.6 km).
62.tq: 1.6 - 5 - 16 km. (APPSC-GS 2022 keyed the exclusion zone as 1 km.)
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **exclusion zone** — no habitation within **1.6 km**, under NPCIL/AERB control.
Statement 2 is **correct**: **sterilised zone** up to **5 km**, population growth curbed.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: the **emergency planning zone** is **16 km** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-GS 2022** key gave the exclusion zone as **1 km** (options 1/1.5/2/2.5 km).
Safety design: **Defence in Depth** and the **ALARA** principle.
AERB licenses plants and can **suspend or revoke licences**.

62.s: What does the Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) consist of?
o: A single exclusion area of 1–1.5 km around a reactor
A network of specialised centres for detection and response
A district-level command structure led by the District Collector
62.x: The Emergency Planning Zone is a set of concentric zones around a plant for planning protective actions. The 1–1.5 km exclusion area is only its inner part.
62.tq: Discriminate the EPZ from the exclusion zone.
n: The Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) consists of concentric zones for protective actions. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: The **EPZ** consists of **concentric zones for protective actions** — option **(1)**, extending to **16 km**.
The **1–1.5 km** area is the **exclusion zone**, where **public habitation is prohibited** — not the EPZ.
xa: The **sterilised zone** extends up to **5 km**, curbing population growth.
⚠ APPSC-GS 2022 keyed the exclusion zone as **1 km**.
**AERB** was set up on **15 Nov 1983** and made **statutory** by the **SHANTI Act 2025**.

62.s: The 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam has been developed by:
o: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre's Dhruva unit
62.x: PFBR is developed by BHAVINI (APPSC-G1 2024 key) and designed by IGCAR; NPCIL holds equity in BHAVINI. ASHVINI is the NPCIL-NTPC joint venture building Mahi Banswara, AERB is the regulator, and Dhruva is a BARC research reactor.
62.tq: PFBR: built by BHAVINI, designed by IGCAR.
xs: The **PFBR (500 MWe, Kalpakkam)** was developed by **BHAVINI** (APPSC-G1 2024 key) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**ASHVINI** builds **Mahi Banswara**; **AERB** is the regulator; **Dhruva** is a research reactor.
xa: PFBR was designed by **IGCAR**.
NPCIL holds **equity in BHAVINI**.
AP DISCOMs sought **100 MW** from BHAVINI's plant (2024-25).

62.s: Which one of the following is a benefit that India would obtain from NSG membership, but which would NOT by itself follow from such membership?
o: Participation in the export-control decision process
Access to the latest nuclear technology
62.x: NSG membership could provide access to advanced technology and a say in rule-making, but it would not make India an NPT member.
62.tq: Separate membership of an export-control regime from membership of a treaty.
xs: **Automatic membership of the NPT** would **not** follow from NSG membership — so option **(2)** is correct.
NSG membership gives **access to the latest technology** and a **say in rule-making** (export rules) — options (1), (3) and (4) are genuine benefits.
⚠ **UPSC 2018** trap: NSG membership does **not** make a country an **NPT** member.
xa: The NSG was formed in **1975** in response to India's **1974 Pokhran-I** test.
India **applied in 2016**; blocked mainly by **China** on NPT grounds.
The NSG has **48 members** and **no permanent secretariat**.

62.s:
Arrange the following Indian memberships of international export-control regimes in chronological order:
A. Australia Group
B. Missile Technology Control Regime
C. Wassenaar Arrangement
62.x: India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018.
62.tq: Place the memberships by their stated years before comparing the sequences.
xs: India joined the **MTCR** in **2016**, the **Wassenaar Arrangement** in **2017** and the **Australia Group** in **2018** — so the order is **B, C, A**, option **(1)**.
Options starting with the **Australia Group** or **Wassenaar** put a later membership first.
xa: India's **NSG** bid (applied **2016**) is still **pending**.
The NSG (**1975**) was formed in response to India's **Pokhran-I** test of **1974**.
⚠ Memory aid: **MTCR 2016 → Wassenaar 2017 → Australia Group 2018**.

62.s: Which principle requires exposure to ionising radiation to be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable?
62.x: ALARA is the radiation-protection principle requiring exposure to be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable.
62.tq: Expand the acronym and distinguish a safety principle from an institution or reactor type.
xs: **ALARA** = **As Low As Reasonably Achievable** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**PHWR** is a reactor type, **INES** is the accident scale (**0-7**), and **DAE** is the department — none is a principle.
xa: AERB's design approach pairs ALARA with **Defence in Depth**.
Occupational dose: **20 mSv/yr** averaged over **5 years**, **30 mSv** max in a year, **100 mSv** cumulative.
Post-Fukushima, releases are kept **<1% of AERB limits** (2026).

62.s: A dirty bomb is best described as:
o: A reactor meltdown caused by loss of coolant
A missile carrying a thermonuclear warhead
A conventional explosive that disperses radioactive material
A nuclear weapon producing a sustained chain reaction
62.x: A dirty bomb, or radiological dispersal device, uses a conventional explosion to spread radioactive material.
62.tq: Discriminate between radioactive contamination and a nuclear chain-reaction explosion.
xs: A **dirty bomb** (radiological dispersal device) is a **conventional explosive that disperses radioactive material** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has **no nuclear chain reaction** and no city-flattening blast — so it is not a nuclear weapon or thermonuclear warhead (options 2 and 4).
xa: Typical sources are **medical or industrial**, e.g. **Cs-137** and **Co-60**.
Its damage is **contamination and panic**.
The IAEA's nuclear-security work includes the **ITDB** database.

63.s: Which one of the following radioisotopes is supplied by BRIT as sodium iodide for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disorders?
63.x: Iodine-131 emits beta and gamma radiation and is supplied by BRIT as sodium iodide for thyroid diagnosis and treatment.
63.tq: Match the isotope with its characteristic organ-related application.
xs: **Iodine-131** (beta + gamma) is supplied by BRIT as **sodium iodide** for **thyroid** diagnosis and treatment — option **(2)**.
**Iron-59** = iron metabolism/anaemia; **Phosphorus-32** = leukaemia; **Tc-99m** = imaging heart, brain, bones, lungs.
xa: ⚠ **I-131 = thyroid**; **Na-24 = blood flow**; **As-74 = brain tumour**; **P-32 or Co-60 = leukaemia**.
**Tc-99m** is the **most widely used diagnostic imaging isotope**.
**I-131** is also exported, with Co-60, to **40+ countries**.

63.s: Sodium-24 is particularly useful for studying:
63.x: Sodium-24 emits gamma radiation and is used in blood-flow and circulation studies; it can also help detect pipeline leaks.
63.tq: Identify the isotope from its specific diagnostic application.
xs: **Sodium-24** (gamma) is used to study **speed of blood flow** and **circulation blocks** — option **(1)**.
**Thyroid** = **I-131**; **iron metabolism/anaemia** = **Iron-59** — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: UPPSC 2012 key: blood-flow speed = **radio-sodium**.
Na-24 is also used for **pipeline leak detection**.
**As-74** locates **brain tumours**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about Technetium-99m:
1. It is the most widely used diagnostic isotope.
2. It is used for imaging the heart, brain, bones and lungs.
3. It is a principal isotope used in radioimmunoassay to measure hormones in blood.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Technetium-99m is the most widely used diagnostic isotope and is used in imaging the heart, brain, bones and lungs. Radioimmunoassay is a technique, not the principal stated use of Technetium-99m.
63.tq: Separate the isotope’s established imaging uses from the broader radioimmunoassay technique.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **Tc-99m** is the **most widely used diagnostic imaging isotope**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: it images the **heart, brain, bones, lungs**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **radioimmunoassay (RIA)** is a technique measuring **hormones, enzymes and drugs** in blood, not Tc-99m's stated use — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Tc-99m is a **gamma** emitter used in **SPECT**.
BRIT supplies **Tc-99m** among its radiopharmaceuticals.
⚠ **PET = positron (F-18 FDG)**; **SPECT = single gamma (Tc-99m)**.

63.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
63.x: Arsenic-74 emits positrons and is used for locating brain tumours. Iron-59 concerns iron metabolism, Sodium-24 concerns blood flow, and Carbon-14 is used for dating organic material.
63.tq: Start with the sure isotope–use pair and eliminate swapped applications.
xs: **Arsenic-74** (positron) locates **brain tumours** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Iron-59** = **iron metabolism**; **Sodium-24** = **blood flow**; **Carbon-14** = **dating organic material** — options (2)-(4) are mismatched.
xa: **I-131** = **thyroid** disorders.
**P-32** or **Co-60** = **leukaemia** (UPPSC 2012 accepted either).
Exam angle: match isotope with **organ/disease**.

63.s: Radioimmunoassay is a technique used to measure minute quantities of which of the following in blood?
o: Only red blood cells and platelets
63.x: Radioimmunoassay uses radioisotopes to measure minute quantities of hormones, enzymes and drugs in blood.
63.tq: Recognise the exact analytes associated with a specialised diagnostic technique.
xs: **Radioimmunoassay (RIA)** uses radioisotopes to measure minute amounts of **hormones, enzymes and drugs** in blood — option **(1)**.
It is not limited to minerals, blood cells or gases — it targets **minute amounts** of biomolecules and drugs.
xa: **BRIT** supplies **RIA kits**.
**Teletherapy** = external beam (**Co-60** unit); **brachytherapy** = source inside/next to the tumour.
**Tc-99m** is the most widely used diagnostic imaging isotope.

63.s: Which one of the following radioisotopes is used in the treatment of blood cancer (leukaemia)?
63.x: Phosphorus-32, a beta emitter, treats leukaemia and polycythaemia; exam keys (UPPSC 2012) also accept Cobalt-60. Sodium-24 is used to study blood-flow speed, Arsenic-74 to locate brain tumours, and Carbon-14 to date organic material.
63.tq: Blood cancer = P-32 (or Co-60); blood flow = Na-24.
xs: **Phosphorus-32** (beta) treats **blood cancer (leukaemia)** and polycythaemia — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Sodium-24** = **blood-flow speed**; **Arsenic-74** = **brain tumours**; **Carbon-14** = **dating** organic material.
xa: ⚠ Keys accept both **P-32 and Co-60** for leukaemia (UPPSC 2012: either; BPSC 2016: "more than one").
P-32 also traces **plant phosphorus uptake**.
**Radon** is the radioactive **noble gas** used to treat cancer (APPSC-G1 2018).

63.s: SPECT imaging generally uses:
o: Ultrasound waves from a medical cyclotron
Single gamma emitters such as Technetium-99m
Only positron emitters such as F-18 FDG
63.x: SPECT uses single gamma emitters, particularly Technetium-99m. PET, in contrast, mainly uses positron emitters such as F-18 FDG.
63.tq: Compare the radiation emitted in PET and SPECT rather than memorising the names alone.
xs: **SPECT** uses **single gamma emitters** such as **Technetium-99m** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Positron emitters** like **F-18 FDG** are for **PET** — option (4) is wrong.
xa: **Tc-99m** images the **heart, brain, bones, lungs**.
⚠ **PET = positron (F-18 FDG)**; **SPECT = single gamma (Tc-99m)**.
**P-32** is a **beta** emitter used for leukaemia, not imaging.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about food irradiation:
1. It works by radiolysis of water in the food.
2. Only Cobalt-60 gamma rays can be used as its source.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: food irradiation works by radiolysis of water. Statement 2 is wrong: the sources can be gamma rays (Co-60), X-rays or electron beams. So (b), (c) and (d) are wrong.
63.tq: Radiolysis of water; three sources: gamma (Co-60), X-rays, electron beams.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: food irradiation works by **radiolysis** of water.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: sources are **gamma (Co-60)**, **X-rays** and **electron beams** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: It applies controlled radiant energy to **packed or bulk** food.
India has **28** commercial food-irradiation facilities.
Irradiated food carries the green **Radura** logo.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Quantity)
A. Activity
B. Absorbed dose
C. Biological effect

List-II (Unit)
1. Gray
2. Sievert
3. Becquerel

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: Activity is measured in Becquerel, absorbed dose in Gray, and biological effect in Sievert.
63.tq: Start from the sure pair and distinguish activity, absorbed dose and biological effect.
xs: **Activity → Becquerel**, **absorbed dose → Gray**, **biological effect → Sievert** — so **A-3, B-1, C-2**, option **(2)**.
**Becquerel** = **1 decay/second**; **Gray** = **1 J/kg**; mSv measures the **effect on the body**.
xa: AERB occupational limits: **20 mSv/yr** (5-year average), **30 mSv** max in a year, **100 mSv** cumulative.
⚠ Do not swap **Gray** (absorbed dose) with **Sievert** (biological effect).

63.s: Brachytherapy differs from teletherapy in that brachytherapy involves:
o: Detecting positrons emitted from injected glucose
Using only an external Co-60 beam from a distant unit
Using gamma emitters only for blood-flow studies
Placing a sealed radiation source inside or next to the tumour
63.x: Brachytherapy places a sealed source, such as Ir-192 or I-125 seeds, inside or adjacent to the tumour. Teletherapy is external-beam treatment, commonly using a Co-60 unit.
63.tq: Discriminate between two similar radiation-treatment modalities by their source location.
xs: **Brachytherapy** places a **sealed source inside or next to the tumour** (e.g. **Ir-192**, **I-125 seeds**) — option **(4)**.
**Teletherapy** is the **external beam** (**Co-60** unit) — option (2) describes teletherapy, not brachytherapy.
Detecting **positrons** from injected glucose (**F-18 FDG**) is **PET** imaging — option (1).
xa: Radiotherapy may use **gamma rays**, X-rays or beta emitters.
New therapy: **177Lu-DOTA-FAPI-2286** (Lutetium-177), targeted radionuclide therapy (2026).
**Ir-192** is also used in **gamma radiography** of welds.

63.s: Which of the following is primarily used as a positron emitter in PET imaging?
63.x: PET mainly uses the positron emitter F-18 FDG. Tc-99m is commonly associated with SPECT, while Co-60 is used in teletherapy.
63.tq: Separate PET positron emitters from SPECT and therapy sources.
xs: **PET** detects **positron** emitters, mainly **F-18 FDG** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Tc-99m** is a single-gamma **SPECT** isotope; **Co-60** is for **teletherapy**; **I-125 seeds** are for **brachytherapy**.
xa: The **30 MeV Medical Cyclotron, Kolkata** produces **FDG** commercially.
**Gamma rays** underpin **PET**, radiotherapy and nuclear medicine (UPSC GS).
**As-74**, another **positron** emitter, locates brain tumours.

63.s: The 30 MeV Medical Cyclotron located at Kolkata is associated with the commercial production of:
63.x: The 30 MeV Medical Cyclotron at Kolkata produces F-18 FDG commercially for PET applications and delivers doses to hospitals.
63.tq: Link a specialised facility with its distinctive product.
xs: The **30 MeV Medical Cyclotron, Kolkata** produces **FDG** (**F-18 FDG**) commercially — option **(1)**.
It has delivered **371 Ci** of doses to hospitals.
xa: **F-18 FDG** is the main **positron** emitter for **PET**.
The **Kolkata accelerator** is one of India's isotope production sites.
**Co-60** teletherapy units and **I-131** come from reactors/BRIT, not the cyclotron.

63.s: Which radioactive noble gas is used in the treatment of cancer?
63.x: Radon is the radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer (APPSC-G1 2018). Argon, neon and xenon are noble gases too, but none is the cancer-therapy gas in question.
63.tq: Radioactive noble gas for cancer = Radon.
xs: **Radon** is the radioactive **noble gas used to treat cancer** (APPSC-G1 2018) — option **(1)**.
**Argon**, **neon** and **xenon** are noble gases, but the notes link only **radon** to cancer therapy.
xa: Radiotherapy rays: **gamma rays** (Co-60 teletherapy), X-rays or beta emitters.
**Brachytherapy** uses **Ir-192** or **I-125** seeds next to the tumour.
**P-32 or Co-60** treat **leukaemia**.

63.s: Which one of the following is identified as a new therapy in the stated nuclear-medicine context?
63.x: Lu-177 therapy is identified as the new therapy in the stated current-affairs context. Tc-99m is primarily identified as a diagnostic isotope.
63.tq: Use the diagnostic-versus-therapy distinction to avoid confusing isotope applications.
xs: The new therapy is **Lu-177** — **177Lu-DOTA-FAPI-2286**, a targeted radionuclide therapy (2026) — option **(1)**.
**Tc-99m** is a **diagnostic** isotope; **K-40** is used for **dating** volcanic rocks.
xa: It entered **routine clinical practice** in 2026.
Radiotherapy otherwise uses **gamma rays** (Co-60), X-rays or beta emitters.
**Radon** is the noble gas used to treat cancer (APPSC-G1 2018).

63.s:
Consider the following statements about radiometric dating:
1. Uranium-238 to Lead-206 dating is used for the oldest rocks and the age of the Earth.
2. Carbon-14 dating is used mainly for volcanic rocks older than a billion years.
3. Potassium-40 to Argon-40 dating is used for volcanic rocks and fossil-bearing layers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
63.x: Statement 2 is wrong: Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) dates once-living organic remains up to about 50,000 years. Statement 1 is correct: U-238 to Pb-206 dates the oldest rocks and the Earth. Statement 3 is correct: K-40 to Ar-40 dates volcanic rocks and fossil-bearing layers. So '1 and 3 only'.
63.tq: C-14 only for once-living material and only up to ~50,000 years.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 is correct: **U-238 → Pb-206** dates the **oldest rocks** and the **age of the Earth**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Carbon-14** (half-life ~**5,730 years**) dates **once-living organic remains** up to ~**50,000 years**.
Statement 3 is correct: **K-40 → Ar-40** dates **volcanic rocks** and **fossil-bearing layers**.
xa: **RTG** fuel is **Plutonium-238**; it turns **decay heat** into electricity via **thermocouples**.
⚠ RTG = **Pu-238** (not Pu-239); **C-14** only for once-living remains.
RTGs power deep-space missions: **Voyager**, **Cassini**, **Curiosity**, **Perseverance**.

63.s:
Which of the following industrial applications are associated with radiotracers?
1. Detecting leaks in buried oil and gas pipelines
2. Studying seepage from dams
3. Tracking sediment transport at ports
4. Measuring flow
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: Radiotracers are used for pipeline leak detection, dam seepage studies, port sediment transport, and flow measurement. Sediment tracking can help reduce the frequency of desilting campaigns.
63.tq: Recognise the common tracer principle across several industrial monitoring applications.
xs: Radiotracers detect **leaks in buried oil/gas pipes**, study **dam seepage**, track **port sediment transport** and measure **flow** — all four, option **(4)**.
BARC is **Asia-Pacific's leading** radiotracer centre.
xa: Sediment tracking means **longer gaps between desilting** campaigns.
**Sodium-24** is used for **pipeline leak detection**.
**Gamma radiography** tests welds and castings non-destructively.

63.s: The Tata Memorial Centre serves as the Anchor Centre for the IAEA initiative known as:
63.x: Tata Memorial Centre is the Anchor Centre for the International Atomic Energy Agency’s ‘Rays of Hope’ initiative.
63.tq: Match the institution with the exact international initiative.
xs: **Tata Memorial Centre** is the **Anchor Centre** for the IAEA's **'Rays of Hope'** — option **(3)**.
'Rays of Hope' is an **IAEA** cancer-care initiative; Tata Memorial anchors it in India.
xa: **National Cancer Grid (2012)**: treats **7.5 lakh+** new patients a year = **>60%** of India's cancer burden.
The **30 MeV Medical Cyclotron, Kolkata** supplies **FDG** to hospitals.
New therapy: **Lutetium-177** targeted radionuclide therapy in routine practice (2026).

63.s: Who first demonstrated mutation breeding using X-rays in 1930?
63.x: L. J. Stadler first demonstrated mutation breeding using X-rays in 1930. Gamma and neutron radiation are also used subsequently for inducing mutations.
63.tq: Use the person-year association to identify the scientific contribution.
xs: **L.J. Stadler** first showed mutation breeding in **1930** using **X-rays** — option **(3)**.
Today **gamma** and **neutron** radiation are also used.
xa: Mutation breeding: radiation changes seeds **at the genetic level** so desired traits can be chosen.
BARC has released **72** Trombay varieties (2026) — **non-GMO**, climate-resilient.
Newest: banana **TBM-9**, sorghum **RTS-43**.

63.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the newer BARC Trombay variety information?
63.x: TBM-9 is the newer banana variety developed with NRCB, Trichy. RTS-43 is a sorghum variety reported to have 15–20% higher yield.
63.tq: Start with the sure crop-variety pair and eliminate the swapped associations.
xs: **Banana — TBM-9** (with **NRCB Trichy**) is correct — option **(1)**.
**RTS-43** is **sorghum** (**15-20%** higher yield); **TG** series is **groundnut** — options (2)-(4) are swapped.
xa: ⚠ **TBM-9 = banana**; **RTS-43 = sorghum**.
BARC Trombay varieties: **72** now vs older count **23**.
The older **23**: **10 pulses**, **9 groundnut**, **2 mustard**, **1 rice**, **1 jute**.

63.s: In the sterile insect technique, the release of radiation-sterilised male insects is intended to
o: increase the number of fertile pest males
increase the fertility of wild females
cause wild pests to fail to produce viable offspring
63.x: Gamma-sterilised males are released so that mating with wild females reduces successful reproduction and causes pest populations to decline.
63.tq: Infer the population effect from the reproductive consequence of sterility.
xs: In the **sterile insect technique**, radiation-sterilised males are released so **wild pests fail to breed** — option **(4)**.
Pest numbers then **crash** — the aim is fewer fertile males, not more.
xa: BARC also makes cheap **pheromones** for **sweet-potato** and **cotton moths**.
**Food irradiation** also **kills insects, parasites and pathogens**.
Mutation breeding uses **gamma** and **neutron** radiation.

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated effect or use of food irradiation?
o: Increasing the genetic diversity of crop seeds in the field
63.x: Food irradiation can stop sprouting, delay ripening and kill insects, parasites and pathogens. Increasing genetic diversity of field crops is associated with mutation breeding, not food irradiation.
63.tq: Find the option belonging to a neighbouring technology rather than food irradiation.
xs: **Increasing the genetic diversity of crop seeds** is not food irradiation — option **(1)** is the answer; that is **mutation breeding**.
Food irradiation **stops sprouting**, **delays ripening** and **kills insects, parasites and pathogens** — options (2)-(4).
xa: These effects **extend shelf life**.
Works by **radiolysis** of water; sources **Co-60 gamma**, **X-rays**, **electron beams**.
**KRUSHAK** at **Lasalgaon** irradiates **onions**.

63.s: The 'Radura' logo is an international symbol used to indicate:
63.x: Radura is the international green symbol marking irradiated food. Organic, GM and fortified foods carry their own separate labels; Radura says only that the food was treated with radiation.
63.tq: Radura = irradiated food.
xs: The **Radura logo** is the international green symbol marking **irradiated food** — option **(1)**.
It does not denote **organic**, **GM** or **fortified** food.
xa: Food irradiation sources: **Co-60 gamma**, **X-rays**, **electron beams**.
India has **28** commercial food-irradiation facilities.
Irradiation **stops sprouting** and **delays ripening**.

63.s: In the context of nuclear applications in agriculture, the number of crop varieties developed using Trombay (BARC) technology is
63.x: 72 crop varieties have been developed by Trombay (BARC), a non-power use of nuclear technology that supports food security.
63.tq: Trombay 72 - reverse of 27.
xs: BARC has released **72** Trombay crop varieties (2026) — option **(2)**.
They are **non-GMO** and **climate-resilient**, made by **mutation breeding**.
xa: ⚠ Older notes count only **23** BARC varieties (**10 pulses**, **9 groundnut**, **2 mustard**, **1 rice**, **1 jute**).
Newest: banana **TBM-9** (with NRCB Trichy), sorghum **RTS-43** (**15-20%** higher yield).
Mutation breeding was first shown by **L.J. Stadler** (**1930**, X-rays).

63.s: BRIT is best described as:
o: An international agency regulating PET scans
An industrial unit of the Department of Atomic Energy dealing with radioisotopes and related technology
A private organisation responsible only for cancer treatment
A research reactor situated at Trombay
63.x: BRIT, or the Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology, is an industrial unit of the Department of Atomic Energy involved in radioisotopes, radiopharmaceuticals and isotope technology.
63.tq: Identify the correct institutional identity and controlling department.
xs: **BRIT (Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology)** is an **industrial unit of the DAE** dealing with **isotope technology** — option **(2)**.
It is not a regulator, not private, and not a reactor — **Dhruva**, **Apsara** and **KAMINI** are BARC's reactors at **Trombay**.
xa: APPSC-GS 2012 key: BRIT works in **isotope technology**.
Products: radioisotopes, **radiopharmaceuticals** (Tc-99m, **I-131 as sodium iodide**), **RIA kits**, **radiography cameras**, **gamma chambers**.
Serves **1,470+** user organisations plus exports.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about BARC:
1. It was established in 1954 as the Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay.
2. It was renamed BARC in 1967.
3. It is India’s leading producer of radioisotopes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All three statements are correct. The institution was set up as AEET in 1954, renamed BARC in 1967 and became India’s leading producer of radioisotopes.
63.tq: Check each institutional-history statement before selecting the combined code.
xs: **BARC, Trombay** was set up in **1954** as **AEET**, renamed **1967**, and is **India's leading producer of radioisotopes** — all three, option **(4)**.
AEET = **Atomic Energy Establishment, Trombay**; it took the name **BARC** in **1967**.
xa: BARC's research reactors: **Dhruva** (largest), **Apsara** (Asia's first), **KAMINI** (only **U-233** fuelled).
Isotope production: **Trombay research reactors**, **Kolkata accelerator**, **NPCIL power plants**.
Radioisotopes (**Co-60**, **I-131**) are exported to **40+ countries**.

63.s:
Consider the following pairs of BARC research reactors:
1. Dhruva — largest research reactor
2. Apsara — Asia's first research reactor
3. KAMINI — largest research reactor
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
63.x: Pair 1 is correct: Dhruva is the largest. Pair 2 is correct: Apsara was Asia's first research reactor. Pair 3 is wrong: KAMINI is the only U-233-fuelled reactor, not the largest. So (a) leaves out pair 2, and (c) and (d) wrongly include pair 3.
63.tq: Dhruva = largest, Apsara = Asia's first, KAMINI = only U-233 fuel.
xs: **Dhruva = largest** and **Apsara = Asia's first** research reactor are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
**KAMINI** is the **only U-233 fuelled** reactor, not the largest — pair 3 is wrong.
xa: All three are at **BARC, Trombay** (set up **1954**, renamed **1967**).
BARC is **India's leading producer of radioisotopes**.
BARC also runs **KRUSHAK** (onion irradiation, **Lasalgaon**).

63.s:
Isotopes used in India are produced at which of the following locations or types of facilities?
1. Trombay research reactors
2. The Kolkata accelerator
3. NPCIL power plants
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: India produces isotopes in Trombay research reactors, at the Kolkata accelerator and in NPCIL power plants.
63.tq: Test whether all listed production locations belong to the same supply chain.
xs: Isotopes are produced at **Trombay research reactors**, the **Kolkata accelerator** and **NPCIL power plants** — all three, option **(4)**.
So isotopes come from **research reactors**, an **accelerator** and **power reactors** alike.
xa: **Co-60** and **I-131** are exported to **40+ countries**.
The **30 MeV Medical Cyclotron, Kolkata** produces **FDG** commercially (**371 Ci** delivered).
**BRIT** processes and supplies the isotopes to **1,470+** users.

63.s:
Which of the following applications is correctly matched with its radioisotope or nuclear technique?
1. Phosphorus-32 — tracing nutrient uptake from fertiliser
2. Nuclear moisture gauge — assisting irrigation decisions
3. Tissue culture — propagation of banana and pineapple
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: P-32-labelled fertiliser traces nutrient uptake, nuclear moisture gauges help determine irrigation requirements, and BARC applies tissue culture to banana and pineapple.
63.tq: Match each agricultural technology with its specific practical use.
xs: **P-32** labelled fertiliser tracks **nutrient uptake**; **nuclear moisture gauges** time **irrigation**; BARC's **tissue culture** propagates **banana and pineapple** — all three, option **(4)**.
Each pair matches the **BARC** farm-tool list in the notes.
xa: P-32 tracing is the basis of **"optimised fertiliser use"**.
BARC's newest banana: **TBM-9** (with NRCB Trichy).
BARC pheromones target **sweet-potato** and **cotton moths**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about food irradiation in India:
1. There are 28 commercial food-irradiation facilities.
2. Irradiated mangoes have been exported to the United States, Australia, Malaysia and South Africa.
3. Food irradiation is restricted to unpacked food and cannot be applied to bulk food.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: India has 28 commercial food-irradiation facilities, and irradiated mangoes have been exported to the four listed countries. Irradiation can be carried out on packed or bulk food, so statement 3 is false.
63.tq: Spot the restrictive false statement against the broader application of the technology.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: India has **28** commercial food-irradiation facilities.
Statement 2 is **correct**: irradiated **mangoes** go to the **USA, Australia, Malaysia, South Africa**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: irradiation works on **packed or bulk** food — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: **KRUSHAK** (BARC) at **Lasalgaon (Nashik)** irradiates onions.
The **Radura** logo marks irradiated food.
Gamma processing plants: **17 MoUs**, **40** now operating.

63.s: The KRUSHAK facility at Lasalgaon is associated with the irradiation of
63.x: KRUSHAK at Lasalgaon in Nashik, Maharashtra, is an onion irradiation facility. Food irradiation helps control sprouting and extend shelf life.
63.tq: Use the facility-location-commodity association.
xs: **KRUSHAK** at **Lasalgaon (Nashik)**, Maharashtra, is BARC's irradiation facility for **Onions** — option **(2)**.
Irradiation **stops sprouting** and extends shelf life.
xa: ⚠ **KRUSHAK = Lasalgaon (onions)**; **e-beam plant = Indore**; **cyclotron = Kolkata**.
**Mangoes** irradiated in India are exported to the **USA, Australia, Malaysia, South Africa**.
**ISOMED 2.0** (May **2025**) sterilises **healthcare products**.

63.s: ISOMED 2.0 is correctly described as:
o: A 30 MeV accelerator for producing FDG
A centre for radioimmunoassay blood testing only
A high-intensity gamma irradiator for sterilising healthcare products
63.x: ISOMED 2.0 is a high-intensity gamma irradiator for sterilising healthcare products and was completed in May 2025.
63.tq: Identify a facility from its technology and purpose.
xs: **ISOMED 2.0** is a **high-intensity gamma irradiator for sterilising healthcare products** — option **(3)**.
The **30 MeV** accelerator making FDG is the **Kolkata cyclotron**; the **U-233** reactor is **KAMINI**.
xa: Completed **May 2025**; the **only land-based stationary** one of its kind in the world.
Gamma processing plants: **17 MoUs**, **40** now operating; **BRIT supplies Co-60**.
**Electron-beam plant, Indore**: **1.53 crore** medical devices sterilised by Sept 2025.

63.s:
With reference to a radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG), consider the following statements:
1. It converts heat from natural radioactive decay into electricity.
2. It operates through thermocouples based on the Seebeck effect.
3. It is a fission reactor with moving mechanical parts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: An RTG converts radioactive decay heat into electricity through thermocouples using the Seebeck effect. It is not a fission reactor and has no moving parts.
63.tq: Reject the wrong-category statement by distinguishing an RTG from a fission reactor.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: an RTG turns **heat of natural radioactive decay** into electricity.
Statement 2 is **correct**: it uses **thermocouples** (**Seebeck effect**).
Statement 3 is **wrong**: an RTG is **not a fission reactor** and has **no moving parts** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: RTG fuel: **Plutonium-238**, a by-product of weapons programmes.
Uses: **spacecraft power** for deep-space missions — **Voyager**, **Cassini**, **Curiosity**, **Perseverance**.
UPSC 2024 key: statements **2 and 3 only** correct.

63.s: The isotope generally used as fuel in radioisotope thermoelectric generators is
63.x: Plutonium-238 is the fuel commonly associated with RTGs. It has been described as a by-product of weapons-development programmes.
63.tq: Identify the fuel isotope rather than the isotope used for dating or detection.
xs: RTGs run on **Plutonium-238** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ RTG fuel is **Pu-238**, not Pu-239; **Americium-241** is the alpha emitter in **smoke detectors**; **K-40** and **C-14** are dating isotopes.
xa: Pu-238 is a **by-product of weapons programmes**.
RTGs turn **decay heat** into electricity through **thermocouples** — **no fission**, no moving parts.
Used where **sunlight is weak**: **Voyager**, **Cassini**, **Curiosity**, **Perseverance**.

63.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of spacecraft or planetary missions associated with the use of RTG power sources?
63.x: Voyager, Cassini and Curiosity are examples of missions using RTG power where sunlight is weak. Perseverance is another such example.
63.tq: Recognise the mission group linked to RTG use.
xs: **Voyager**, **Cassini** and **Curiosity** used **RTG** power — option **(1)**.
**Perseverance** is another RTG-powered rover.
xa: RTGs suit **deep-space missions** where **sunlight is weak**.
Fuel: **Plutonium-238**; principle: **Seebeck effect** thermocouples.
RTGs are **not reactors** — no fission.

63.s: Gamma radiography for non-destructive testing of welds and castings commonly uses sources such as
63.x: Gamma radiography of welds and castings uses radiography cameras with sources such as Iridium-192 and Cobalt-60.
63.tq: Distinguish industrial radiography sources from dating and tracer isotopes.
xs: Gamma radiography of welds and castings uses **radiography cameras** with **Ir-192** (Iridium-192) and **Co-60** (Cobalt-60) — option **(1)**.
**C-14** and **K-40** are **dating** isotopes; **P-32** is for leukaemia and tracers; **Am-241** is in **smoke detectors**.
xa: It is a **non-destructive testing** method.
**BRIT** makes the **radiography cameras**.
**Ir-192** is also a **brachytherapy** source.

63.s: The alpha emitter commonly used in smoke detectors is
63.x: Smoke detectors use an alpha emitter, commonly Americium-241. The other listed isotopes are associated with RTGs or industrial and medical radiation applications.
63.tq: Separate the smoke-detector isotope from gamma-radiography and RTG isotopes.
xs: **Smoke detectors** use the alpha emitter **Americium-241** (UPSC GS) — option **(4)**.
**Plutonium-238** fuels **RTGs**; **Cobalt-60** and **Iridium-192** are **gamma radiography** and radiotherapy sources.
xa: Other gauging uses: **thickness gauges** for plates and pipes, **fill levels**, automotive sensors.
**Radiotracers** detect **leaks in buried oil/gas pipes** and **dam seepage**.
BARC is **Asia-Pacific's leading** radiotracer centre.

64.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Energy source)
A. Conventional source
B. Non-conventional source
C. Renewable source
D. Non-renewable source

List-II (Example)
1. Coal
2. Solar energy
3. Firewood
4. Wind energy

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
64.x: Firewood is conventional, solar energy is non-conventional, wind energy is renewable and coal is non-renewable.
64.tq: Start from the sure pairs—firewood with conventional and coal with non-renewable.
xs: **Firewood → conventional**, **solar → non-conventional**, **wind → renewable**, **coal → non-renewable** — so **A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1**, option **(1)**.
**Firewood** sits in the **conventional** list; **solar** is the typical **non-conventional** source.
xa: Conventional list: **coal, petroleum, natural gas, hydel, firewood, cattle-dung cake**.
Non-conventional = by definition **renewable** (UPPSC 2023).
⚠ **Hydel** is conventional yet renewable.

64.s: Non-conventional sources of energy are, by definition:
64.x: Non-conventional sources (solar, wind, etc.) are by definition renewable (UPPSC 2023 key). Non-renewable and fossil-based describe coal, oil and gas, which are conventional; 'imported' is not a classification of energy sources.
64.tq: Non-conventional = renewable.
xs: Non-conventional sources are by definition **Renewable** (UPPSC 2023 key) — option **(1)**.
**Non-renewable**/**fossil** sources — coal, oil, natural gas — fall under **conventional**.
xa: Conventional also includes **hydel**, **firewood** and **cattle-dung cake**.
⚠ **Hydel** is conventional yet renewable.
**Natural gas is NOT green energy** (APPSC 2019).

64.s: Which one of the following energy sources is NOT derived from the Sun?
64.x: Geothermal energy comes from the Earth's internal heat, so it is not solar-derived (like nuclear and tidal). Wind, hydro and biomass are stored solar energy: the Sun drives winds and the water cycle and powers photosynthesis.
64.tq: Not from the Sun: nuclear, geothermal, tidal.
xs: **Geothermal energy** comes from the **Earth's internal heat**, not the Sun — option **(1)**.
**Wind**, **hydro** and **biomass** are **stored solar energy**.
xa: Also NOT from the Sun: **nuclear** (fission) and **tidal** (Moon's pull).
UPPSC 2022 key accepted both **nuclear** and **geothermal**.
Fossil fuels too are **stored solar energy**.

64.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding India's energy-capacity profile as stated for 2026?
o: Nuclear capacity was 8.78 GW and formed about 1.6–1.7% of total capacity.
Non-fossil capacity was below 40% of total installed capacity.
Solar capacity was below 100 GW in August 2026.
Coal formed over 54% of total installed capacity.
64.x: Nuclear capacity was 8.78 GW, accounting for about 1.6–1.7% of capacity. Non-fossil sources exceeded 54%, coal was about 42%, and solar reached 164.59 GW.
64.tq: Use percentage and magnitude comparisons to reject reversed or understated claims.
xs: **Nuclear** was **8.78 GW**, about **1.6-1.7%** of capacity — option **(1)**.
Non-fossil was **>54%** (not below 40%); **solar** was **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026); **coal** was only ~**42%**.
xa: Nuclear is **non-fossil but not RE**.
**Wind 58.14 GW**; **bio-power 11.75 GW** (Aug 2026).
Total capacity ~**552 GW** (Aug 2026).

64.s: As of August 2026, which source formed the largest component of India's installed renewable-energy capacity?
64.x: Solar, at 164.59 GW (Aug 2026), is the largest RE component. Wind (58.14 GW) is second, large hydro is about 52 GW, and bio-power about 11.75 GW. In 2014 wind was the largest, but solar has overtaken it.
64.tq: Now solar > wind > large hydro; in 2014 wind led.
xs: **Solar** is the **largest RE component** — **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026) — option **(1)**.
**Wind** is 2nd (**58.14 GW**); **large hydro** ~**51.96 GW**; **bio-power** **11.75 GW**.
xa: In **2014** wind (**21 GW**) was the largest; solar was **2.8 GW**.
Bio-power = biomass/bagasse **10.87 GW** + waste-to-energy **0.88 GW**.
**Small hydro**: **5.18 GW**.

64.s: India's global rank in installed wind-power capacity is:
64.x: India ranks 4th in the world in wind power, while it is 3rd in total renewable capacity after China and the USA. China ranks first; India is neither second nor as low as tenth.
64.tq: RE overall 3rd; wind 4th.
xs: India is **4th in wind** — option **(1)** (Fourth).
In total RE capacity India is **3rd**, after **China** and the **USA**.
xa: Wind capacity: **58.14 GW** (Aug 2026), 2nd-largest RE source.
Wind **crossed 50 GW** in **Mar 2025**.
**Gujarat** leads wind with **12,314 MW**.

64.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Coal — non-renewable resource
2. Wind — renewable resource
3. Nuclear fuel — non-renewable resource
4. Geothermal energy — renewable resource
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
64.x: Coal and nuclear fuels are finite resources, while wind and geothermal energy are renewable sources. Hence all four pairs are correctly matched.
64.tq: Check each pair independently before selecting the complete combination.
xs: **Coal** and **nuclear fuel** are **non-renewable** (finite); **wind** and **geothermal** are **renewable** — all four pairs correct, option **(4)**.
Renewable = **naturally replenished**; non-renewable = **finite on a human timescale**.
xa: Renewable list: **solar, wind, hydro (incl. tidal/wave), geothermal, biomass**.
**Nuclear is NOT renewable** (APPSC 2024), though it is **non-fossil**.
**Geothermal** is **not derived from the Sun** — it is Earth's internal heat.

64.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with cumulative installed capacity in 2014?
64.x: In 2014, cumulative solar capacity was 2.8 GW and wind capacity was 21 GW. Wind was then the largest renewable source.
64.tq: Anchor the comparison to the historical base year before judging later milestones.
xs: **Wind** was then the **largest RE source** (CGPSC 2015 key); solar overtook it later.
xa: Wind **crossed 50 GW** in **Mar 2025**; **58.14 GW** in Aug 2026.

64.s: Which one of the following correctly gives India's cumulative solar capacity on 31 December 2022?
64.x: Cumulative solar capacity stood at 63.30 GW on 31 December 2022.
64.tq: Distinguish the dated milestone from the later 2025 and 2026 figures.
xs: Solar stood at **63.30 GW** on **31 Dec 2022** (APPSC 2023 key) — option **(4)**.
**127.33 GW** was Oct-Nov 2025; **150.26 GW** was 31 Mar 2026; **53.12 GW** is a **wind** figure.
xa: Solar in **2014**: only **2.8 GW**.
FY 2025-26: record **44.6 GW** solar added.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India’s renewable-energy position in 2024–25:
1. Renewable energy accounted for about 50% of installed capacity.
2. Renewable energy contributed about 22% of electricity generation.
3. Coal and thermal sources contributed about 75% of electricity generation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All three statements are correct. In 2024–25, renewable energy represented about half of capacity but supplied only 22% of generation, while coal and thermal sources supplied about 75%.
64.tq: Compare capacity shares with generation shares instead of assuming that installed capacity equals actual output.
xs: In **2024-25**, RE was **~50% of capacity** but gave only **22%** of **1,824 TWh**; coal/thermal gave **75%** — all three, option **(4)**.
The point: **capacity is not generation**.
xa: ~**40 GW** RE projects **lack PPAs**.
**8,133 GWh** solar curtailed in Apr-Jun 2026 (transmission mismatch).
Coal is ~**42%** of capacity (Jul 2026).

64.s: The original target of 175 GW renewable-energy capacity by 2022 consisted of which combination?
o: 75 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 30 GW bio-power and 10 GW small hydro
60 GW solar, 100 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
100 GW solar, 50 GW wind, 20 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
64.x: The 175 GW target comprised 100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro. The target was not achieved on time and was later superseded.
64.tq: Break the aggregate target into its source-wise components.
xs: **175 GW by 2022** = **100 GW solar**, **60 GW wind**, **10 GW bio-power**, **5 GW small hydro** — option **(4)**.
It was **missed on time** and is now **superseded**.
xa: New target: **500 GW** non-fossil capacity by **2030** (~**292 GW** solar).
**Net Zero by 2070**.
Small hydro has used only ~**24.6%** of its **21 GW** potential.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's non-fossil capacity targets:
1. The 2015 NDC set a target of 40% non-fossil capacity by 2030.
2. The updated NDC and COP26 Panchamrit raised the target to 50% by 2030.
3. The 50% target was achieved in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
4. Non-fossil capacity stood at 51.93% in December 2025.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All four statements are correct: the 2015 target was 40%, the updated target was 50%, it was achieved in June 2025, and the December 2025 level was 51.93%.
64.tq: Track the progression from the original target to the revised target and achievement.
xs: **NDC 2015**: **40%** non-fossil by **2030** — correct; **updated NDC / Panchamrit**: **50%** by 2030 — correct.
**50%** was **achieved June 2025**, five years early; **51.93%** in **Dec 2025** — all four, option **(4)**.
xa: ⚠ **40%** = NDC 2015; **50%** = updated NDC / Panchamrit — both by 2030.
Non-fossil share was **>54%** by Aug 2026.
Long-term goal: **Net Zero by 2070**.

64.s: Which one of the following pairs correctly states India's 2030 and 2070 energy commitments?
o: 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2050
300 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070
500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2060
500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070
64.x: India's stated commitments include 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and achieving Net Zero by 2070.
64.tq: Separate the capacity milestone from the long-term emissions target.
xs: **500 GW non-fossil** by **2030** and **Net Zero by 2070** — option **(4)**.
It is **non-fossil**, not just renewable; and the Net Zero year is **2070** — not 2050 or 2060.
xa: The 500 GW includes ~**292 GW** solar.
**50%** non-fossil share achieved **June 2025**.

64.s: Which of the following correctly describes India's solar-energy potential and its utilisation?
o: 748 GW potential, of which about 54.5% had been utilised
748 GW potential, of which about 24.5% had been utilised
748 GW potential, of which about 4.5% had been utilised
248 GW potential, of which about 4.5% had been utilised
64.x: India's solar potential was estimated at 748 GW, while only about 4.5% had been utilised.
64.tq: Keep the potential figure separate from the percentage already utilised.
xs: Solar potential is **748 GW**, of which only ~**4.5%** is used — option **(3)**.
**248 GW** is not the potential, and **54.5%** / **24.5%** overstate the use.
xa: Top RE-potential states: **Rajasthan (23.70%)** … **Andhra Pradesh (9.10%)**.
⚠ **24.6%** is the share of **small hydro** potential (**21 GW**) used, not solar.
Solar capacity reached **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026), ~**58x** of 2014.

64.s: According to IRENA 2026 rankings, India stood at which position globally in renewable-energy capacity?
64.x: India ranked third in renewable-energy capacity after China and the United States. The stated capacities were China 2,258 GW, the USA 468 GW and India 250.5 GW.
64.tq: Rank the countries using the capacity figures rather than the order of mention alone.
xs: India is **3rd** in RE capacity after **China** and the **USA** (IRENA 2026) — option **(3)** (Third).
China **2,258 GW**; USA **468 GW**; **India 250.5 GW**; Brazil **228 GW**.
xa: India is **4th in wind** and **3rd in solar** (2025-26).
Top RE state: **Gujarat** (**42.58 GW**).

64.s: Which State was the leading renewable-energy State, with 42.58 GW and 16.5% of India's renewable capacity in June 2026?
64.x: Gujarat was the leading renewable-energy State in June 2026, with 42.58 GW and 16.5% of India's renewable capacity.
64.tq: Link the State ranking to both its capacity and percentage figures.
xs: **Gujarat** led with **42.58 GW**, **16.5%** of India's RE (Jun 2026) — option **(2)**.
**Rajasthan** leads RE **potential** (**23.70%**), not installed capacity.
xa: Gujarat also leads **wind** (**12,314 MW**).
⚠ **Top RE potential = Rajasthan**; **top installed RE = Gujarat**.
**Andhra Pradesh** has **9.10%** of RE potential.

64.s: Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) requires which entities to purchase a prescribed share of electricity from renewable sources?
o: DISCOMs and large or designated consumers
64.x: RPO requires DISCOMs and large or designated consumers to procure a prescribed share of their power from renewable sources.
64.tq: Identify the obligated party rather than the agency that regulates the obligation.
xs: **RPO**: **DISCOMs and large/designated consumers** must buy a set share of power from renewables — option **(4)**.
It is not limited to households, regulators or generators.
xa: **Solar RPO** raised to **8% by March 2022** (2017).
A **wind RPO trajectory up to 2030** was declared.
The obligation was recast as **RCO** under the **Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022**.

64.s: The Solar Renewable Purchase Obligation was raised to what level by March 2022?
64.x: The Solar RPO trajectory raised the solar obligation to 8% by March 2022.
64.tq: Recall the specific percentage and date attached to the Solar RPO trajectory.
xs: **Solar RPO** was raised to **8%** by **March 2022** (in **2017**) — option **(3)**.
The **8%** figure belongs to the **solar** RPO trajectory.
xa: RPO binds **DISCOMs** and **large/designated consumers**.
**Wind RPO trajectory up to 2030** declared.
**RCO** recast RPO as an obligation to **consume** renewable energy.

64.s: What is the principal distinction between RPO and RCO?
o: RPO applies only to households, whereas RCO applies only to generators.
RPO concerns nuclear power, whereas RCO concerns coal consumption.
RPO is a tax, whereas RCO is a capital subsidy.
RPO concerns renewable purchase, whereas RCO recasts it as an obligation to consume renewable energy.
64.x: RPO requires procurement of renewable power, while RCO recasts the obligation as consumption of renewable energy under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022.
64.tq: Discriminate between the paired terms by focusing on purchase versus consumption.
xs: **RPO** is about **purchasing** renewable power; **RCO** recasts it as an obligation to **consume renewable energy** — option **(4)**.
RCO comes under the **Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022**.
xa: RPO applies to **DISCOMs** and **large/designated consumers**, not just households.
**Solar RPO**: **8% by March 2022**.

64.s: Inter-State Green Energy Corridor lines are built by which agency, and what is their principal purpose?
o: MNRE; transporting coal from mines to power stations
IREDA; supplying renewable energy only to rural households
KfW; connecting only intra-State distribution networks
PGCIL; evacuating renewable energy from renewable-rich zones to load centres
64.x: Inter-State GEC lines are built by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL) to evacuate renewable energy from renewable-rich zones to load centres.
64.tq: Ask who performs the infrastructure function and where the power is moved.
xs: Inter-state GEC lines are built by **PGCIL**, to **evacuate RE from RE-rich zones to load centres** — option **(4)**.
**MNRE** and **KfW** are funders of intra-state GEC-I; **IREDA** is an RE financier.
xa: GEC-I funding: **MNRE 40% : KfW 40% : state utility 20%**.
The **PGCIL study 2012** triggered the GEC.
Curtailment of **8,133 GWh** solar (Apr-Jun 2026) shows the transmission gap.

64.s: Which of the following States was NOT included among the eight States covered by Intra-State GEC-I?
64.x: GEC-I included Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. Telangana was not included in the listed eight-State group.
64.tq: Find the outsider by comparing each option with the complete membership list.
xs: **Telangana** is not among GEC-I's states — option **(1)**.
GEC-I: **Andhra Pradesh**, **Gujarat**, HP, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, **Tamil Nadu**.
xa: GEC-I: ~**9,700 ckm** lines, ~**24 GW** RE.
Funding: **MNRE 40% : KfW (Germany) 40% : state utility 20%**.
AP has **9.10%** of India's RE potential.

64.s: The financing pattern for Intra-State GEC-I was:
o: MNRE 50%, KfW loan 25% and State utility 25%
MNRE 20%, KfW loan 40% and State utility 40%
MNRE 40%, KfW loan 20% and State utility 40%
MNRE 40%, KfW loan 40% and State utility 20%
64.x: The cost-sharing pattern was MNRE 40%, KfW of Germany loan 40% and State utility contribution 20%.
64.tq: Match each percentage with the correct financing institution or agency.
xs: GEC-I funding: **MNRE 40%**, **KfW loan 40%**, **state utility 20%** — option **(4)**.
Total cost **₹10,141.68 cr**; **KfW** is from **Germany**.
xa: ⚠ Memory aid: **40 : 40 : 20** = **MNRE : KfW : state utility**.
GEC-II approved **2022** for **7** states.
Inter-state lines are built by **PGCIL**.

64.s: The Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA) is best described as:
o: A commercial bank under the Ministry of Finance
An NBFC under the administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
A statutory regulator under the Ministry of Power
A non-governmental organisation under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
64.x: IREDA is an NBFC under the administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).
64.tq: Identify the institution by both its category and controlling ministry.
xs: **IREDA** is an **NBFC** under the administrative control of **MNRE** (Ministry of New and Renewable Energy) — option **(2)**.
It is a lender to RE projects — not a commercial bank, regulator or NGO.
xa: Set up **1987**; listed via IPO in **November 2023**.
It gives term loans for **renewable energy** and **energy-efficiency** projects.
Funds come from **Govt**, **multilateral agencies** and the **capital market**.

64.s: Which of the following is NOT a function of IREDA?
o: Determining statutory electricity tariffs for all States
Providing term, bridge and working-capital loans
64.x: IREDA undertakes project financing, appraisal, consultancy and provides term, bridge and working-capital loans. Determination of statutory tariffs for all States is not its function.
64.tq: Find the activity that belongs to a regulator rather than a project-financing agency.
xs: **Determining statutory electricity tariffs** is not IREDA's job — option **(2)** is the answer.
IREDA does **project financing**, **appraisal**, **consultancy**, and **term, bridge and working-capital loans**.
xa: IREDA is an **NBFC** under **MNRE**.
Set up **1987**; IPO **November 2023**.
Funds: Govt, multilateral agencies, capital market.

64.s: Which one of the following is NOT generally classified as a source of green energy in the given classification?
64.x: Natural gas is a fossil fuel and is not classified as green energy in this comparison; sunlight, wind and algae-based sources are treated as green sources.
64.tq: Apply the exact category distinction rather than assuming every low-emission fuel is green.
xs: **Natural gas is NOT green energy** — **algae** and **sunlight** are (APPSC 2019) — option **(3)**.
Natural gas is a finite **non-renewable** fossil fuel, unlike **wind**.
xa: Exam pattern: "NOT renewable / NOT green / NOT from the Sun" → **nuclear**, **natural gas**, **geothermal**.
**Nuclear is NOT renewable** (APPSC 2024).
**Solar energy** is the most important for India (APPSC-G2 2017).

64.s: For India, which of the following is regarded as the most important non-conventional source of energy?
64.x: Solar energy is regarded as the most important non-conventional source of energy for India.
64.tq: Direct recall of the leading source in the national context.
xs: **Solar energy** is the most important for India (APPSC-G2 2017) — option **(1)**.
Solar is now the **largest RE component** — **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026).
xa: Solar potential: **748 GW**, only ~**4.5%** used.
India ranks **3rd** in solar (2025-26).
The **500 GW** non-fossil target for 2030 includes ~**292 GW** solar.

65.s: Which one of the following statements about the National Institute of Solar Energy is correct?
o: It is a State government agency responsible only for rooftop solar in Andhra Pradesh.
It is a commercial power-generating company headquartered at Khandwa.
It is an international treaty body headquartered in Kutch.
It is an autonomous body of MNRE located at Gurugram and serves as a technical focal point for solar R&D.
65.x: NISE is an autonomous body of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy located at Gurugram and acts as a technical focal point for solar research and development.
65.tq: Use the institution’s status, location and function together to identify it.
xs: **NISE** is an **autonomous body of MNRE** at **Gurugram**, the **technical focal point for solar R&D** — option **(4)**.
It is not a state agency, a company in **Khandwa** (that is Omkareshwar floating plant's district) or a treaty body.
xa: The **ISA** HQ foundation stone was laid at the **NISE campus, Gwal Pahari, Gurugram** (**25 Jan 2016**).
NISE made the first national floating-solar assessment: **102.18 GW**.
NISE estimated ground potential at **748 GW**.

65.s: Which one of the following solar-cell technologies is correctly matched with its characteristic?
o: Crystalline silicon — dominant market technology based on the photovoltaic effect
Thin-film — higher efficiency than all crystalline silicon cells
Bifacial — absorbs sunlight only through its front face
Perovskite — technology incapable of being combined with silicon
65.x: Crystalline silicon cells, including mono- and polycrystalline types, use the photovoltaic effect and remain dominant in the market. Thin-film cells are generally cheaper and flexible but have lower efficiency, while bifacial cells absorb light on both faces.
65.tq: Use precise principle–technology matching and reject reversed characteristics.
xs: **Crystalline silicon** (mono, poly) uses the **photovoltaic effect** and dominates the market — option **(1)**.
**Thin-film** is cheaper and flexible but **lower efficiency**; **bifacial** absorbs light on **both faces**.
**Perovskite** combines with silicon in a **tandem** that reached **30.2%**.
xa: IIT Bombay (MNRE) perovskite cell: **26%**, world's **2nd highest**.
Thin-film types: **CdTe, CIGS, a-Si**.
PV gives **DC**; an **inverter** converts it to AC.

65.s:
Which of the following correctly describes solar thermal or concentrated solar power technology?
1. Mirrors may concentrate sunlight to heat a fluid.
2. The heat can be used to produce steam for a turbine.
3. Flat-plate collectors and solar power towers are associated with solar thermal applications.
4. Heat storage is possible in such systems.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
65.x: All four statements are correct. Solar thermal systems collect or concentrate solar heat, use it for water, steam and power generation, and can store heat.
65.tq: Recognise the complete set of applications and features of one technology.
xs: CSP **mirrors concentrate sunlight to heat a fluid** → **steam turbine**; uses **flat-plate collectors** and **solar power towers**; can **store heat** — all four, option **(4)**.
⚠ Only **CSP** can store heat; **PV** turns light directly into electricity (**DC**).
xa: Solar thermal heat serves **water, steam and power**.
**Agrivoltaics** = crops + panels on the same land.
Solar PV CUF is only ~**21%**.

65.s: In a solar photovoltaic system, the photovoltaic effect directly produces which kind of electricity, and which device makes it usable on the grid?
o: Alternating current; a transformer converts it to direct current
Direct current; an inverter converts it to alternating current
Alternating current; a steam turbine stabilises it
Direct current; a concentrator converts it to heat
65.x: In PV cells the photovoltaic effect frees electrons and produces direct current (DC); an inverter converts it to alternating current (AC). A transformer only changes voltage, steam turbines belong to solar thermal (CSP), and concentrators focus sunlight in CSP plants.
65.tq: PV gives DC; inverter makes AC. Steam turbine means CSP, not PV.
xs: The photovoltaic effect frees electrons → **direct current (DC)**; an **inverter** converts it to **alternating current (AC)** — option **(2)**.
**Steam turbines** and **concentrators** belong to **solar thermal / CSP**, not PV.
xa: PV cells: **monocrystalline**, **polycrystalline silicon**, **thin-film**.
⚠ **PV** = light → electricity directly; **CSP** = heat → steam turbine.
**Bifacial** modules absorb light on **both faces**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's solar resource:
1. Most parts of India receive 4–7 kWh per square metre per day of solar irradiation.
2. India has approximately 250–300 clear sunny days in a year.
3. The estimated annual incident solar energy is about 5,000 trillion kWh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: All three statements describe the stated solar-resource conditions in India: 4–7 kWh/m²/day irradiation, 250–300 clear sunny days and about 5,000 trillion kWh of annual incident energy.
65.tq: Combine multiple quantitative indicators of the same resource potential.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: insolation is **4-7 kWh/sq m/day** over most of India.
Statement 2 is **correct**: India has **250-300 clear sunny days** a year.
Statement 3 is **correct**: incident energy is about **5,000 trillion kWh** a year — so **all three**, option **(4)**.
xa: APPSC-G1 2024: "both statements true, II explains I" on sunny days and potential.
Ground potential: **748 GW** (NISE; **3%** of wasteland); only ~**4.5%** used.
Installed solar: **157.05 GW** (2026), **29%** of total capacity.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about India's ground-based solar potential:
1. NISE has estimated it at about 748 GW, assuming use of 3% of wasteland.
2. About 45% of this estimated potential has already been used.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct: NISE estimates about 748 GW, assuming 3% of wasteland. Statement 2 is wrong: only about 4.5% has been used, not 45%. So '1 only'; '2 only' and 'Both' accept the wrong figure, and 'Neither' rejects the correct NISE estimate.
65.tq: 748 GW potential, only ~4.5% used - watch for a decimal shifted to 45%.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **NISE** estimates **748 GW**, assuming **3% of wasteland**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: only ~**4.5%** is used, not 45% — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Floating solar potential: **102.18 GW** on reservoirs (NISE, Jun 2026).
RE-potential leader: **Rajasthan 23.70%**; **AP 9.10%**.
⚠ **748 GW** = ground potential; **63.30 GW** = installed on **31 Dec 2022**.

65.s: Which of the following correctly compares the stated capacity-utilisation factors?
65.x: The stated capacity-utilisation factors are 36–40% for wind, about 21% for solar and about 85% for coal.
65.tq: Compare all three values together to avoid swapping the technologies.
xs: Options (2) and (4) swap the solar, wind and coal figures.
xa: Low CUF explains why RE's **capacity** share exceeds its **generation** share.
Installed solar: **157.05 GW** (2026), **29%** of capacity.
Solar pumps under **PM-KUSUM B, C**.

65.s: Which one of the following correctly states the reported installed solar capacity and its share of total capacity?
65.x: The reported installed solar capacity was 157.05 GW, constituting about 29 per cent of total capacity.
65.tq: Pair the capacity figure with its percentage instead of mixing figures from different reporting dates.
xs: Installed solar was **157.05 GW** (2026), approximately **29 per cent** of total capacity — option **(1)**.
xa: Solar in **2014**: only **2.82 GW**.

65.s: India added a record solar capacity of approximately how much in financial year 2025-26?
65.x: A record 44.61 GW of solar capacity was added in FY 2025-26. The 2.82 GW figure relates to the earlier 2014 level, while about 38 GW refers to the 2025 addition in another comparison.
65.tq: Distinguish annual additions from historic benchmark and cross-country comparison figures.
xs: A record **44.61 GW** solar was added in **FY2025-26** — option **(3)**.
**2.82 GW** was the **2014** level; ~**38 GW** was the calendar-**2025** addition.
xa: The 2025 addition (~**38 GW**) **beat the US for the first time** (Ember).
India was the **2nd-largest solar growth market** in 2025.

65.s: The Energy Survey 2025-26 places India at which position globally in solar energy and total renewable energy?
65.x: The Energy Survey 2025-26 places India third globally in solar energy and total renewable energy. Other publications cited different rankings for solar, so the source-specific wording is important.
65.tq: Follow the named source when rankings differ across publications.
xs: The 2025-26 energy chapter places India **3rd** (Third) in solar and total RE — option **(3)**.
⚠ The Survey's climate chapter and some notes say **4th**, others **5th** in solar — quote the source the question follows.
xa: **China** is the world's largest solar producer.
India was the **2nd-largest solar growth market** in 2025.
Solar capacity: **164.59 GW** (Aug 2026).

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's solar-sector growth:
1. India was the second-largest solar growth market in 2025.
2. India's approximately 38 GW addition in 2025 exceeded that of the United States for the first time.
3. India had added only 2.82 GW of solar capacity in 2014.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: All three statements are correct. India was the 2nd-largest solar growth market in 2025, and its ~38 GW addition in 2025 beat the US for the first time (Ember). Statement 3 is also true: in 2014 India's solar capacity stood at only 2.82 GW (a cumulative level, against 157 GW+ now).
65.tq: Combine a ranking, a comparison and a historical numerical benchmark.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: India was the **2nd-largest solar growth market** in 2025.
Statement 2 is **correct**: the ~**38 GW** 2025 addition **beat the US for the first time** (Ember).
Statement 3 is **correct**: solar stood at only **2.82 GW** in **2014** — so **all three**, option **(4)**.
xa: Record **44.61 GW** added in FY2025-26.
**63.30 GW** on **31 Dec 2022** (APPSC key).
Module imports fell **65%** (**$2,152 M** in FY25 → **$758 M**).

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission:
1. It was launched in June 2015.
2. It is one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008).
3. Its brand name is 'Solar India'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 3 is correct: the mission's brand name is 'Solar India'. Statement 1 is wrong: it was launched in January 2010; June 2015 is when its target was revised to 100 GW. Statement 2 is correct: it is one of the 8 missions of NAPCC (2008). So '2 and 3 only'.
65.tq: Jan 2010 = launch; June 2015 = target raised from 20 GW to 100 GW.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is wrong: the mission was launched in **January 2010**; **June 2015** is when its target was revised to **100 GW**.
Statement 2 is correct: one of the **8 missions** of **NAPCC (2008)**.
Statement 3 is correct: its brand name is **"Solar India"**.
xa: ⚠ **20 GW** = original target; **100 GW** = revised (**40 GW rooftop + 60 GW** grid).
Off-grid targets: **200 MW** (Phase I), **1,000 MW** (II), **2,000 MW** (III).
Successor goal: **500 GW non-fossil by 2030**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements about the grid-connected solar targets of the National Solar Mission:
1. The original target was 20 GW of grid-connected solar capacity by 2022.
2. In June 2015 the target was revised to 100 GW by 2022.
3. The revised 100 GW target comprised 60 GW of rooftop solar and 40 GW of large/medium grid-connected projects.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct: the original target was 20 GW (20,000 MW) by 2022. Statement 2 is correct: it was revised in June 2015 to 100 GW by 2022. Statement 3 is wrong: the split was 40 GW rooftop and 60 GW large/medium grid-connected, not the reverse. Hence '1 and 2 only'; options with statement 3 are wrong, and '1 only' misses the correct revision.
65.tq: Remember 40 rooftop + 60 ground-mounted = 100 GW; the swapped split is the trap.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: original target **20 GW** (**20,000 MW**) by **2022**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: revised in **June 2015** to **100 GW by 2022**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: the split was **40 GW rooftop + 60 GW large/medium grid** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **20 GW** = original; **100 GW** = revised (**40 rooftop + 60 grid**).
"NSM target" without a year = **100 GW by 2022**; live goal = **500 GW** non-fossil by **2030** (~**292 GW** solar).
Rooftop solar today: **27.88 GW** grid-connected (2026).

65.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Phase)
a. Phase I
b. Phase II
c. Phase III

List-II (Period)
i. 2017–2022
ii. 2010–2013
iii. 2014–2017

Codes:
65.x: Phase I covered 2010–2013, Phase II covered 2014–2017, and Phase III covered 2017–2022.
65.tq: Start with the first phase and eliminate codes with a misplaced period.
xs: Off-grid PV targets rose with each phase: **200 → 1,000 → 2,000 MW**.
xa: Solar thermal collector area: **15 million sq m (2017)** / **20 million (2022)**.
**20 million** solar lights for rural areas by **2022**.
JNNSM launched **January 2010**.

65.s:
With reference to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX), consider the following statements:
1. It was established in 2008.
2. It is regulated by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission.
3. It trades in Day Ahead Market, Term Ahead Market, renewable energy and ESCerts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: IEX was established in 2008, is regulated by CERC, and trades DAM, TAM, renewable energy and ESCerts.
65.tq: Combine institutional identity, regulatory authority and functions in one statement set.
xs: **IEX** was set up in **2008**, is **CERC**-regulated, and trades **DAM, TAM, RE and ESCerts** — all three, option **(4)**.
Its **GTAM** segment (launched **2020**) is RE-only.
xa: **Green Energy Open Access Rules, 2022**: **Ministry of Power**; threshold **1 MW → 100 kW**.
RPO obliges DISCOMs to buy a share of renewable power.

65.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Solar Park Scheme:
1. It was launched on 12 December 2014.
2. Its initial objective was to develop more than 25 solar parks with an aggregate capacity of 20 GW in five years.
3. The target was enhanced to 40 GW on 21 March 2017.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
65.x: All three statements are correct. The scheme was launched on 12 December 2014, initially envisaged over 25 parks and 20 GW, and was raised to 40 GW on 21 March 2017.
65.tq: Use the date and revised target to verify all three statements.
