xa: Other limitations: high **cultivation and harvesting cost**, **contamination** and scale-up problems, heavy **water and nutrient** needs.
**CSIR-NIIST** and **DBT-ICT Centre** research algal biofuel.
**3G** biofuels = **algae** (PYQ **2023**).

67.s:
With reference to biodiesel in India, consider the following statements:
1. Its blending in diesel remains below 0.5%.
2. India has set a target of 5% biodiesel blending by 2030.
3. Biodiesel feedstock is entirely domestically sourced.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because biodiesel is mostly dependent on imported feedstock.
67.tq: Find the false absolute claim in a policy-status question.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: biodiesel blend is still **below 0.5%**; target **5% by 2030** (NPB 2018).
Statement 3 wrong: **palm stearin**, the feedstock for about **94%** of biodiesel, is **mostly imported**.
xa: OMC biodiesel procurement rose from **1.1 crore L (FY16)** to **36.7 crore L (FY25)**.
Belgian firm **VITO** launched a biodiesel project at **Ayodhya** (**April 2023**).
The original NPB 2018 targets were **E20 + B5** by **2030**.

67.s: Which one of the following is NOT an objective of the National Policy on Biofuels?
o: Discouraging the production of advanced biofuels
67.x: The National Policy on Biofuels aims to reduce import dependence, promote domestic feedstock, strengthen energy security and generate employment. It does not discourage advanced biofuels.
67.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated policy objectives.
xs: **Discouraging advanced biofuels** is NOT an objective — option **(4)**; the policy actually boosts **2G/advanced fuels**.
NPB aims: cut **import dependence**, promote **domestic feedstock**, **energy security**, **jobs**.
xa: **Advanced biofuels** = 2G ethanol, drop-in fuels from MSW, 3G biofuels, **bio-CNG**.
Original targets: **20%** ethanol and **5%** biodiesel by **2030**.
VGF, tax credits and **differential pricing** support advanced biofuels.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Policy on Biofuels:
1. The 2018 policy set targets of 20% ethanol in petrol and 5% biodiesel in diesel by 2030.
2. The 2022 amendment advanced the E20 target to Ethanol Supply Year 2025-26.
3. The original 2018 policy targeted 30% ethanol blending by 2030.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: E20 + B5 by 2030. Statement 2 is correct: the 2022 amendment advanced E20 to ESY 2025-26. Statement 3 is wrong: the original target was 20%, not 30%; E30 by 2030 is the later goal. So '1 and 2 only'.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: NPB 2018 set **20% ethanol** in petrol and **5% biodiesel** in diesel by **2030** (**E20 + B5**).
Statement 2: the **2022 amendment** advanced **E20** to **ESY 2025-26**.
Statement 3 wrong: **E30 by 2030** is a later goal (**May 2026**), not the original 2018 target.
xa: Blends in 2018 were only ~**2%** and **<0.1%**.
**E20** achieved; **mandatory E20** petrol from **1 Apr 2026**, minimum **RON 95**.
**BIS IS 19850:2026** covers **E22, E25, E27, E30** petrol.

67.s:
Which of the following changes was introduced through the 2022 amendment to the National Policy on Biofuels?
1. More feedstocks were permitted.
2. Biofuel units in SEZs and EOUs were permitted under the Make in India provision.
3. Exports were permitted in specific cases.
4. New members could not be added to the NBCC.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The amendment allowed more feedstocks, covered biofuel units in SEZs and EOUs, and permitted exports in specific cases. It also allowed new members to be added to the NBCC, so statement 4 is false.
67.tq: Identify the single reversed statement in a list of amendment provisions.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2)**.
The **2022 amendment**: **more feedstocks**, biofuel units in **SEZs / EOUs** (Make in India), **exports** in specific cases.
Statement 4 wrong: **new members may be added** to the **NBCC**.
xa: It also advanced **E20** to **ESY 2025-26** from **2030**.
It gave a **boost to 2G/advanced fuels**.
**PM JI-VAN** now says "**advanced biofuels**" in place of "2G ethanol".

67.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes basic biofuels from advanced biofuels under the National Policy on Biofuels?
o: Basic biofuels include 1G bioethanol and biodiesel, whereas advanced biofuels include 2G ethanol, drop-in fuels, 3G biofuels and bio-CNG.
Basic biofuels and advanced biofuels have identical categories and feedstocks.
Basic biofuels include 2G ethanol and bio-CNG, whereas advanced biofuels include only biodiesel.
Basic biofuels are produced only from municipal solid waste, whereas advanced biofuels are produced only from sugarcane.
67.x: Basic biofuels comprise 1G bioethanol and biodiesel. Advanced biofuels include 2G ethanol, drop-in fuels from MSW, 3G biofuels and bio-CNG.
67.tq: Use the category boundary to eliminate options that swap basic and advanced fuels.
xs: **Basic** = **1G bioethanol, biodiesel**; **advanced** = **2G ethanol, drop-in fuels from MSW, 3G biofuels, bio-CNG** — option **(1)**.
2G ethanol and bio-CNG are not basic, and biodiesel is not advanced — so options (2)-(4) are wrong.
xa: **1G** uses food crops; **3G** uses **algae**.
Differential pricing, **VGF** and tax credits support advanced biofuels.
**PM JI-VAN Yojana**: **12 commercial ABPs**, outlay **₹1,969.50 crore**, extended to **2028-29**.

67.s:
Which of the following statements regarding enabling provisions for biofuels is correct?
1. Section 52 of the Motor Vehicles Act permits engine conversion to biofuels.
2. Automatic-route 100% FDI is permitted for biofuel technology when intended for domestic use.
3. FDI is permitted for plantations connected with biofuel production.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Plantations are barred from FDI, making statement 3 false.
67.tq: Watch for the reversed exception concerning FDI in plantations.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **MV Act s.52** allows **engine conversion** to biofuels.
Statement 2: **100% FDI (automatic)** for biofuel technology if for **domestic use**.
Statement 3 wrong: **plantations are barred** to FDI.
xa: Other enablers: **VGF**, **tax credits**, **differential pricing** for advanced biofuels.
The **2022 amendment** allowed biofuel units in **SEZs / EOUs**.

67.s:
Which of the following correctly describes the revised PM JI-VAN Yojana?
1. It supports advanced biofuels.
2. Its implementation timeline extends to 2028–29.
3. It covers bolt-on and brownfield projects.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: The revised scheme replaces the narrower expression '2G ethanol' with 'advanced biofuels', extends the timeline to 2028–29 and covers bolt-on and brownfield projects.
67.tq: Track the changes introduced by the revised scheme rather than its original title alone.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
The revised **PM JI-VAN** replaces "2G ethanol" with **advanced biofuels** and is extended to **2028-29**.
It now covers **bolt-on / brownfield** plants.
xa: Launched in **2019** to support **2G ethanol**.
**12 commercial ABPs**, outlay **₹1,969.50 crore**, ~**10** demo units.
The **Ethanol Interest Subvention Scheme** separately funds **distillery capacity**.

67.s: The PM JI-VAN Yojana was launched in:
67.x: PM JI-VAN Yojana was launched in 2019 to support 2G ethanol and subsequently expanded to advanced biofuels.
67.tq: Use the launch year, not the later revision period, as the deciding fact.
xs: **PM JI-VAN Yojana** was launched in **2019** — option **(3)**.
It began as support for **2G ethanol**; now revised to **advanced biofuels**.
xa: Extended to **2028-29**, covering **bolt-on / brownfield** plants.
⚠ **NPB** and **SATAT** are from **2018**; **National Bioenergy Programme** from **2021**.
First commercial 2G plant: **IOCL Panipat (2022)**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) targets for international flights:
1. The target is 1% by 2027.
2. The target is 2% by 2028.
3. The target is 5% by 2030.
4. The roadmap is linked to ICAO’s net-zero 2050 objective.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: All four statements are correct. The SAF roadmap specifies 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030, in line with ICAO’s net-zero 2050 objective.
67.tq: Read the targets as a progression and connect them with the stated international objective.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
SAF in ATF for international flights: **1% (2027)** → **2% (2028)** → **5% (2030)**.
Aligned with ICAO **net zero for international aviation by 2050**.
xa: **BioE3 Policy 2024** backs bio-jet fuel.
SAF uses **drop-in synthesised hydrocarbons**, not direct ethanol.
**IOCL Panipat** = first Indian ISCC **CORSIA**-certified SAF producer (**Aug 2025**).

67.s:
Small hydro projects are commonly developed using which of the following site conditions?
1. Hill streams
2. Canal falls
3. Toes of dams
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Run-of-river small hydro projects may use hill streams, canal falls and water released at dam toes.
67.tq: Recognise the application-based list and avoid treating run-of-river projects as dam-only projects.
xs: All three — **hill streams**, **canal falls**, **dam toes** — option **(4)**.
Small hydro is **run-of-river** on such sites.
xa: Small hydro = up to **25 MW**.
Installed **5.18 GW** (~**25%** of potential).
**Small Hydro Power Development Scheme** was in the news.

67.s: Which institution is India's lead ocean-energy research body?
o: CSIR-NIIST, Golaghat, under the Ministry of Petroleum
IOCL, Panipat, under the Ministry of Agriculture
NIOT, Chennai, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences
67.x: The National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is India's lead ocean-energy research body.
67.tq: Identify the correct institutional authority by matching body, location and ministry.
xs: **NIOT, Chennai**, under the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)**, is India's lead ocean-energy research body — option **(4)**.
**CSIR-NIIST** does **algal biofuel** research; **FSSAI** runs **RUCO**; **IOCL Panipat** is a **2G ethanol** plant.
xa: First wave plant: **Vizhinjam, Kerala (1991)**.
**IIT Roorkee** supports small hydro; **Kapurthala** institute inspects bioenergy projects.
OTEC sites: **Lakshadweep**, **Andaman and Nicobar**.

67.s:
Which of the following locations in Andhra Pradesh are associated with Jindal waste-to-energy plants?
1. Guntur
2. Naidupalem
3. Kapuluppada, Visakhapatnam
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Jindal waste-to-energy plants are associated with Guntur, Naidupalem and Kapuluppada in Visakhapatnam.
67.tq: Use location-based recall and include all listed plant sites.
xs: All three — option **(4)**: Jindal (**JITF**) WtE plants are at **Naidupalem, Guntur** and **Kapuluppada, Visakhapatnam**.
So **Guntur** (district), **Naidupalem** and **Kapuluppada** all fit.
xa: AP WtE capacity = **MSW power 36.15 MW** + **industrial waste 40.96 MW**.
Delhi WtE plants: **Okhla**, Ghazipur, Narela-Bawana.
National WtE capacity: **0.88 GW**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the food-versus-fuel debate:
1. Maize-ethanol pricing has been associated with diversion of land from pulses and oilseeds.
2. An increase in maize area has been accompanied by a decline in pulse area.
3. The debate includes concern over rising sugar prices.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: The debate covers diversion of land from pulses and oilseeds, rising maize area with declining pulse area, and concerns regarding rising sugar prices.
67.tq: Group related consequences under the food-versus-fuel comparison and test all three dimensions.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Maize-ethanol pricing pulled land from **pulses and oilseeds** (**maize area up, pulses down**).
The **food vs fuel** debate includes **rising sugar prices** (**Sep 2026**).
xa: EBP pricing: **maize highest**, rice lowest, molasses in between.
**Surplus food grains** need **NBCC** approval.
**2G** biofuels avoid the food-fuel conflict.

67.s: Inspection under MNRE's National Bioenergy Programme is entrusted to the Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy located at:
67.x: SSS-NIBE is at Kapurthala, Punjab. Chennai hosts NIWE and NIOT, Gurugram hosts NISE, and Dehradun hosts CSIR-IIP - none is the bioenergy inspection body.
67.tq: Bio-energy institute = Kapurthala (SSS-NIBE).
xs: The **Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy** is at **Kapurthala, Punjab** — option **(1)**.
It handles **inspection** under MNRE's **National Bioenergy Programme**.
xa: **NIOT, Chennai** (MoES) is India's lead **ocean-energy** research body.
**IIT Roorkee**'s Dept. of Hydro and Renewable Energy gives **small hydro** technical support.
**CSIR-NIIST** and the **DBT-ICT Centre** do **algal biofuel** research.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the Numaligarh bamboo bioethanol plant:
1. It was dedicated on 14 September 2025.
2. It is described as India's first commercial-scale bamboo bioethanol plant.
3. It is a first-generation plant based mainly on corn.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because bamboo is a non-food lignocellulosic feedstock associated with second-generation bioethanol.
67.tq: Reject the generation mismatch by checking the plant's non-food feedstock.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
**Numaligarh Refinery** (**Golaghat, Assam**) was dedicated on **14 Sep 2025** as India's first commercial-scale **bamboo** bioethanol plant.
Statement 3 wrong: it is a **2G** plant using **bamboo**, not a 1G corn plant.
xa: **IOCL Panipat (2022)** = first commercial **2G** plant (rice straw, bagasse).
⚠ First 2G **bamboo** plant = **Numaligarh**; first commercial 2G = **Panipat**.
**Corn** and **sugarcane** are **1G** food-crop feedstocks.

67.s:
Match the following 2G ethanol plants with their locations or feedstocks:

List-I (Plant)
a. IOCL Panipat
b. Numaligarh Refinery
c. HPCL Bathinda
d. BPCL Bargarh

List-II (Location or feedstock)
i. Odisha
ii. Haryana; rice straw and bagasse
iii. Golaghat, Assam; bamboo
iv. Punjab

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: IOCL Panipat is in Haryana and uses rice straw and bagasse; Numaligarh is in Golaghat, Assam and uses bamboo; HPCL Bathinda is in Punjab; BPCL Bargarh is in Odisha.
67.tq: Begin with the distinctive bamboo–Numaligarh pair and then complete the remaining matches.
xs: **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**IOCL Panipat** = **Haryana** (rice straw, bagasse); **Numaligarh** = **Golaghat, Assam** (**bamboo**).
**HPCL Bathinda** = **Punjab**; **BPCL Bargarh** = **Odisha**.
xa: **IOCL Panipat (2022)** was India's first commercial 2G plant.
Numaligarh was dedicated on **14 Sep 2025**.
**PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019)** supports these: **12 commercial ABPs**, outlay **₹1,969.50 crore**.

67.s: Which policy specifically supports bio-jet fuel among the following?
67.x: The BioE3 Policy 2024 supports bio-jet fuel.
67.tq: Match the policy name with its stated fuel application.
xs: **BioE3 Policy 2024** backs **bio-jet fuel** — option **(4)**.
The policy name to remember: **BioE3** (**2024**) is the biotechnology-led policy that backs aviation biofuel.
xa: SAF feedstock: **agri residues, corn grain, wastewater sludge, wood-mill waste** (UPSC **2024**).
First biojet-fuelled flight: **SpiceJet**, **Dehradun-Delhi**, **27 Aug 2018**.

67.s: Technical support for the small hydro programme is provided by the Department of Hydro and Renewable Energy, IIT Roorkee. Which statement is correct regarding this department?
o: It provides technical support but is not under MNRE control.
It is an autonomous body of the United Nations.
It functions directly under the control of MNRE.
It functions under the Ministry of Power alone.
67.x: The Department of Hydro and Renewable Energy at IIT Roorkee provides technical support and is not under the control of MNRE.
67.tq: Apply the authority-versus-technical-support distinction.
xs: The Dept. of Hydro and Renewable Energy, **IIT Roorkee**, gives **small hydro technical support** but is **not under MNRE control** — option **(1)**.
So option (3), "under MNRE control", is the trap.
xa: **NIOT, Chennai** (MoES) leads **ocean-energy** research.
**Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy, Kapurthala** inspects under the National Bioenergy Programme.
Small hydro = up to **25 MW**.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about geothermal energy firsts:
1. India's first geothermal power project is at Puga Valley in Ladakh.
2. The Puga project is being led by ONGC.
3. The world's first geothermal power was generated in Iceland.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: India's first geothermal project is at Puga Valley, Ladakh. Statement 2 is correct: ONGC leads it (Ladakh extended the ONGC MoU by 5 years in May 2026). Statement 3 is wrong: the world's first geothermal power was at Larderello, Italy (1904). So '1 and 2 only'.
67.tq: Larderello (Italy, 1904) = world first; Puga (Ladakh, ONGC) = India first.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 is correct: India's **first geothermal power project** is at **Puga Valley, Ladakh**.
Statement 2 is correct: it is by **ONGC**; Ladakh extended the MoU by **5 years**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the world's first geothermal power was at **Larderello, Italy (1904)**.
xa: **National Policy on Geothermal Energy** was notified on **15 Sep 2025**.
Geothermal potential: **~10,600 MW** from **381** hot springs (GSI).
India's first wave plant: **Vizhinjam, Kerala** (**1991**).

67.s: Which of the following is NOT a listed geothermal province or region of India?
67.x: The listed geothermal regions include the Himalaya, Godavari Valley, Cambay, SONATA, Mahanadi, West Coast and Andaman-Nicobar. The Indo-Gangetic Plain is not included in that list.
67.tq: Find the option outside the stated geographical classification.
xs: The **Indo-Gangetic Plain** is NOT a listed geothermal province — option **(4)**.
Listed: Himalaya, **Godavari valley**, **Cambay**, **Son-Narmada-Tapi (SONATA)**, Mahanadi, West Coast, Andaman-Nicobar.
xa: Some notes count **7** provinces; others say **10**.
**Cambay graben** is in Gujarat; Godavari valley site is **Manuguru** (Telangana).
**Puga Valley** (Ladakh) has the highest potential.

67.s: Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) are designed to:
o: Prevent all water movement in geothermal fields
Convert solar radiation directly into electricity
Replace radioactive decay with chemical combustion
67.x: EGS technology artificially stimulates geothermal reservoirs to improve access to underground heat.
67.tq: Match the technology with its functional purpose.
xs: **Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS)** **artificially stimulate** geothermal reservoirs — option **(2)**.
EGS works on the reservoirs that hold **Earth's internal heat** — it does not stop water movement or use solar radiation.
xa: Geothermal heat comes from **Earth's interior** (radioactive decay).
Geothermal gives **24x7 baseload** power.
**National Policy on Geothermal Energy (2025)** focuses on research, technology and ecosystem development.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Policy on Geothermal Energy:
1. It was notified by MNRE on 15 September 2025 as India's first such policy.
2. It provides for ten pilot projects.
3. It supports India's Net Zero 2070 goal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: MNRE notified it on 15 Sep 2025, India's first geothermal policy. Statement 2 is wrong: it has five pilot projects, not ten. Statement 3 is correct: it supports Net Zero 2070. So '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses 3, options with 2 are wrong.
67.tq: Geothermal policy: 15 Sep 2025, MNRE, five pilots, Net Zero 2070.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: notified by **MNRE** on **15 Sep 2025** as **India's first** geothermal policy.
Statement 2 wrong: it provides **five** pilot projects, not ten.
Statement 3: it supports **Net Zero 2070**.
xa: Focus: **research, technology, ecosystem and capacity development**.
First geothermal project: **Puga, Ladakh** (**ONGC**).
World's first geothermal power: **Larderello (1904)**.

67.s: India's first wave-energy plant was established at:
67.x: India's first wave-power pilot was established at Vizhinjam, Kerala, in 1991.
67.tq: Combine the distinctive site with the associated year and technology.
xs: India's first wave-energy plant was at **Vizhinjam, Kerala** (**1991**) — option **(2)**.
**Sundarbans**, **Durgaduani creek** and **Gulf of Khambhat** are **tidal** sites, not wave.
xa: **NIOT, Chennai** (MoES) is India's lead ocean-energy research body.
**OTEC** sites: **Lakshadweep**, **Andaman and Nicobar**.
Ocean sources (**tidal**, **OTEC**) are still **under development** in MNRE's classification.

67.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Site or plant)
a. Larderello
b. Puga
c. Panipat
 d. Numaligarh

List-II (Description)
i. First commercial 2G plant
 ii. World geothermal first
 iii. India geothermal first
 iv. First 2G bamboo plant

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
67.x: Larderello is associated with the world geothermal first, Puga with the Indian geothermal first, Panipat with the first commercial 2G plant, and Numaligarh with the first 2G bamboo plant.
67.tq: Start from the sure site–achievement pairs and eliminate codes containing a mismatched first.
xs: **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**Larderello** = world geothermal first (**1904**); **Puga** = India geothermal first.
**Panipat** = first commercial **2G** plant (**2022**); **Numaligarh (Golaghat)** = first 2G **bamboo** plant.
xa: Numaligarh was dedicated on **14 Sep 2025**.
Puga is by **ONGC** — world's highest at ~**14,000 ft**.
IOCL Panipat is also the first **CORSIA**-certified SAF producer (**Aug 2025**).

67.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The first airline biofuel flight was operated by SpiceJet.
II. The first biofuel flight was on the Dehradun–Delhi route.
III. The date of the first biofuel flight was 27 August 2018.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
67.x: All three are correct: SpiceJet flew India's first biofuel flight, from Dehradun to Delhi, on 27 August 2018.
67.tq: Recall the first biofuel flight.
n: SpiceJet was the first airline associated with biofuel ATF. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
The first biofuel flight operated between Dehradun and Delhi. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
The first biofuel flight occurred on 27 August 2018. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
xs: **All three — I, II and III** — are correct — option **(2)**.
**SpiceJet** was the **first airline** with **biofuel ATF**, flying **Dehradun to Delhi** on **27 August 2018**.
The biojet fuel was **Jatropha-based**, from **CSIR-IIP**.
xa: **IOCL Panipat** is India's first **CORSIA**-certified **SAF** producer (**Aug 2025**).
SAF targets: **1%** by **2027**, **2%** by **2028**, **5%** by **2030** (international flights).
**Numaligarh** (Golaghat, Assam) runs a **bamboo** bioethanol plant.

67.s:
Consider the following statements regarding small hydro classification:
1. Micro hydro refers to plants up to 100 kW.
2. Mini hydro refers to plants from 101 kW to 2 MW.
3. Small hydro refers to plants above 2 MW and up to 25 MW.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: All three statements correctly describe the micro, mini and small hydro capacity ranges.
67.tq: Check each numerical range separately before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Micro** up to **100 kW**; **mini** **101 kW-2 MW**; **small** **2-25 MW**.
xa: Small hydro sites: **hill streams**, **canal falls**, **dam toes** (run-of-river).
**Arunachal, Himachal, J&K, Uttarakhand** hold ~half of small hydro potential.
AP small hydro: **10.5 MW** (2024-25).

67.s: The Geological Survey of India has estimated India's geothermal potential at approximately:
67.x: India's estimated geothermal potential is about 10,600 MW from 381 hot springs, according to the stated GSI estimate.
67.tq: Match the capacity figure with the corresponding number of sites.
xs: GSI puts India's geothermal potential at ~**10,600 MW** from **381 hot springs** — option **(1)**.
The estimate is by the **Geological Survey of India (GSI)**.
xa: First geothermal project: **Puga Valley, Ladakh** (**ONGC**).
**National Policy on Geothermal Energy** notified **15 Sep 2025**.
Challenges: uneven reservoirs, **high drilling cost**, **subsidence**, water pollution.

67.s:
Which of the following is a surface expression of geothermal energy?

1. Hot springs
2. Geysers
3. Volcanoes

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Hot springs, geysers and volcanoes are all surface expressions of heat originating within the Earth.
67.tq: Recognise the common underlying process behind different surface manifestations.
xs: **Hot springs**, **geysers** and **volcanoes** are all surface expressions — option **(4)** (APPSC **2018** key: "volcanoes").
Geothermal heat from the **Earth's interior** reaches the surface as **steam**, **hot springs**, **geysers** and **volcanoes**.
xa: Others: steam and **hot dry rock**.
Heat source: **Earth's interior**, largely **radioactive decay**.
**Tattapani** springs are **45-90 °C**.

67.s: Which of the following sites has the greatest tidal-energy potential among the listed Indian sites?
67.x: The Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat is identified as India's best tidal-energy site, with an estimated potential of about 7,000 MW.
67.tq: Distinguish the best tidal site from an offshore-wind site and other ocean-energy locations.
xs: The **Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay)**, Gujarat, is the best tidal site — tidal range **5-10 m**, ~**7,000 MW** potential — option **(2)** (PYQ **2025**).
**Gulf of Kutch** has a smaller range (**5-8 m**); **Lakshadweep** is an **OTEC** site.
⚠ **Gulf of Mannar** is an offshore **wind** zone, not the tidal answer.
xa: Tidal criterion: large tidal range (roughly **5 m** or more) in a **narrow gulf/estuary**.
**Sundarbans** (Gangetic delta, West Bengal) has a range of ~**5 m**.
Proposed pilots — **Durgaduani creek** and a **Gulf of Kutch** plant — neither commissioned.

67.s:
Consider the following statements about Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC):
1. It needs a temperature difference of about 20 deg C between surface and deep water.
2. It is viable mainly between 30N and 30S.
3. It produces only electricity and cannot help in desalination.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
67.x: Statement 1 is correct: about 20 deg C difference is needed. Statement 2 is correct: it is viable in the tropics, 30N-30S. Statement 3 is wrong: OTEC gives power plus desalination, useful for islands. So '1 and 2 only'.
67.tq: OTEC: ~20 deg C, tropics, power + desalination (Lakshadweep, A&N).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **OTEC** needs ~**20 deg C** difference and is viable in the tropics (**30N-30S**).
Statement 3 wrong: OTEC gives **power + desalination** for islands.
xa: Principle: temperature difference between **warm surface** and **cold deep water** runs a turbine.
OTEC sites: **Lakshadweep**, **Andaman and Nicobar**.
⚠ **Tidal** energy instead needs a large **tidal range** (~**5 m**+).

67.s:
Which of the following locations are associated with OTEC potential in India?
1. Lakshadweep
2. Andaman and Nicobar Islands
3. Gulf of Khambhat
4. Gulf of Kutch
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
67.x: Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are identified as Indian OTEC locations. The Gulfs of Khambhat and Kutch are discussed as tidal-energy sites.
67.tq: Separate OTEC island locations from tidal-energy gulfs.
xs: **Lakshadweep** and **Andaman and Nicobar** are the OTEC sites — option **(1)**.
**Gulf of Khambhat** and **Gulf of Kutch** are **tidal** sites in Gujarat.
xa: OTEC needs ~**20 deg C** difference; viable in **30N-30S**.
OTEC can also supply **desalination** for islands.
Gulf of Khambhat tidal potential: ~**7,000 MW**.

67.s:
Assertion (A): Geothermal energy can provide 24×7 baseload power.
Reason (R): Geothermal energy is derived from heat available beneath the Earth's surface and is not dependent on daily solar radiation or wind movement.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
67.x: Both statements are true, and the availability of underground geothermal heat explains why geothermal power can provide continuous baseload generation.
67.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains the continuity claimed in the assertion.
xs: Both A and R are **true**, and R is the **correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
Geothermal heat comes from the **Earth's interior** (largely **radioactive decay**), so it gives **24x7 baseload** power.
xa: Surface expressions: **hot springs**, **geysers**, **volcanoes**.
Challenges: **uneven reservoirs**, **high drilling cost**, **subsidence**, water pollution.
**National Policy on Geothermal Energy** (**15 Sep 2025**): **five** pilot projects, supports **Net Zero 2070**.

67.s: Since 2019, which additional source has been included in MNRE's renewable-energy classification?
o: Tidal power as the dominant renewable source
Geothermal power as a fully developed source
67.x: Large hydro has been included in MNRE's renewable-energy classification since 2019. Nuclear remains non-fossil but not renewable, while geothermal, tidal and OTEC are under development.
67.tq: Use the date-linked classification change and reject sources described only as under development.
xs: **Large hydropower** has been part of MNRE's RE classification **since 2019** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Nuclear** is non-fossil but **not renewable**; **geothermal** and **tidal** are still **under development**, not fully developed sources.
xa: Core MNRE RE: **solar**, **wind**, **bio-power**, **small hydro**.
**Small hydro cut-off: 25 MW** — micro up to **100 kW**, mini **101 kW-2 MW**, small **2-25 MW**.
⚠ Geothermal, tidal and **OTEC** are listed as sources **under development**.

67.s: Biomass energy is best understood as:
o: Solar energy stored by plants through photosynthesis
Energy obtained from tidal currents alone
Heat stored only in the Earth's mantle
67.x: Biomass energy represents solar energy captured and stored by plants through photosynthesis. It may be burned directly or converted into biogas and biofuels.
67.tq: Trace the energy source through the biological conversion chain.
xs: **Biomass energy** is **solar energy stored by plants** through **photosynthesis** — option **(1)**.
It is burned directly or converted to **biogas/biofuels**.
Earth's internal heat is **geothermal**; tidal currents are **ocean energy** — not biomass.
xa: **Gobar gas** is biomass energy (**APPSC 2019**).
Agricultural waste: **crop residue** (stubble, paddy-husk), **manure**, **cattle dung**, **dairy waste** — all biodegradable.
**Biomass gasification**: biomass heated with **controlled oxygen** → **syngas** (CO + H2 + CO2).

67.s: Which one of the following is an example of biomass energy?
67.x: Gobar gas is a form of biomass energy because it is produced from organic biological material, especially cattle dung.
67.tq: Classify the example according to its biological feedstock.
xs: **Gobar gas** is an example of **biomass energy** (**APPSC 2019**) — option **(3)**.
Biomass energy = solar energy stored by plants in **photosynthesis**; geothermal steam comes from **Earth's internal heat**.
xa: **Nuclear** is non-fossil but **not renewable**.
Biogas is produced by **anaerobic digestion**; methane ~**50-75%**.
The **"Gramalakshmi"** floating-drum gobar gas plant was by **Jashbhai Patel** (**1950s**).

67.s: The biodiesel project launched by the Belgian firm VITO in April 2023 was located at:
67.x: VITO launched a two-year biodiesel project at Ayodhya in April 2023.
67.tq: Match the foreign partner with the correct project location and date.
xs: Belgian firm **VITO** launched a **2-year biodiesel project** at **Ayodhya** in **April 2023** — option **(2)** (PYQ **2023**).
**Golaghat** hosts the Numaligarh bamboo plant; **Panipat** the IOCL 2G plant; **Vizhinjam** the first wave plant.
xa: Biodiesel blend is still **below 0.5%**; target **5% by 2030**.
Biodiesel is made by **transesterification**.

67.s: The primary source of geothermal energy is:
o: Heat from the Earth's interior, largely associated with radioactive decay
Chemical energy released by surface oxidation
67.x: Geothermal energy originates from the internal heat of the Earth, much of which is generated by radioactive decay in its interior.
67.tq: Identify the source-process relationship rather than a surface manifestation.
xs: Geothermal energy comes from **heat of the Earth's interior**, largely from **radioactive decay** — option **(2)**.
Solar energy stored by plants is **biomass**, not geothermal.
xa: Surface expressions: **hot springs**, steam, **geysers**, hot dry rock, **volcanoes** (APPSC **2018**).
Geothermal gives **24x7 baseload** power.
**Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS)** artificially stimulate reservoirs.

67.s: Which of the following is NOT a major challenge associated with geothermal energy?
o: Subsidence and water pollution from geothermal fluids
67.x: The stated challenges are uneven reservoir distribution, high drilling costs, subsidence and water pollution from geothermal fluids. Geothermal energy necessarily depends on underground heat.
67.tq: Reject the absolute statement that contradicts the basic principle of the resource.
xs: **Complete absence of underground heat** is NOT a challenge — option **(2)**; Earth's **internal heat** is the very source.
Real challenges: **uneven distribution of reservoirs**, **high drilling cost**, **subsidence**, **water pollution** from geothermal fluids.
xa: Potential: ~**10,600 MW** from **381** hot springs.
**EGS** artificially stimulate reservoirs.
Geothermal advantage: **24x7 baseload**.

67.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Durgaduani Creek — pilot tidal project — Sundarbans
Vizhinjam — first Indian wave-energy plant — Gujarat
Gulf of Mannar — best tidal site — Gujarat
Lakshadweep — first wave-energy plant — West Bengal
67.x: The Durgaduani Creek tidal project is a pilot project in the Sundarbans. Vizhinjam is in Kerala, Gulf of Mannar is associated here with offshore wind, and Lakshadweep is an OTEC location.
67.tq: Use the project–technology–location combination to expose swapped sites.
xs: **Durgaduani creek** (**Sundarbans**) is a proposed **pilot tidal project** — option **(1)**.
**Vizhinjam** is in **Kerala**, not Gujarat; the best tidal site is the **Gulf of Khambhat**, not Mannar; **Lakshadweep** is an **OTEC** site.
xa: Neither Durgaduani nor the Gulf of Kutch tidal plant has been **commissioned**.
Sundarbans tidal range: ~**5 m**.
India's coastline: ~**7,517 km**.

67.s: Which policy of Andhra Pradesh supports biofuels as part of its clean-energy approach?
67.x: The AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024 supports biofuels.
67.tq: Use the exact policy title and year to distinguish it from related sectoral policies.
xs: The **AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024** supports production and export of **green hydrogen and biofuels** — option **(1)**.
It is cited in **APSES 2024-25**.
xa: AP (**2024-25**): **10.5 MW** small hydro; **119.6 MW** from biomass, bagasse, municipal and industrial waste.
AP (APSES **2025-26**): bagasse cogeneration **206.95 MW**, biomass **171.25 MW**, small hydro **106.80 MW**.
AP WtE plants at **Naidupalem, Guntur** and **Kapuluppada, Visakhapatnam**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements regarding hydrogen colour codes:
1. Grey hydrogen is produced by steam methane reforming of natural gas, releasing carbon dioxide.
2. Blue hydrogen is produced through a fossil route combined with carbon capture and storage.
3. White hydrogen occurs naturally through geological processes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: All three statements are correct. Grey hydrogen releases carbon dioxide during steam methane reforming, blue hydrogen uses carbon capture and storage, and white hydrogen is naturally occurring geological hydrogen.
68.tq: Use the production-route distinctions to test all three colour codes together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Grey** = steam methane reforming of natural gas, CO2 released; **Blue** = fossil route + **carbon capture and storage**.
**White** = naturally occurring (**geological**) hydrogen.
xa: **Green** = electrolysis of water using **renewable power** — the only **zero-carbon** type.
⚠ **Pink** = nuclear electrolysis; **Turquoise** = methane pyrolysis.
Cost: grey **$1.5-2/kg** vs green ~**$4/kg** (**Jul 2026**).

68.s:
With reference to the different forms of hydrogen, consider the following statements:
1. Pink hydrogen is produced by electrolysis using nuclear power.
2. Turquoise hydrogen has solid carbon as a by-product.
3. White hydrogen is produced by steam methane reforming of natural gas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. White hydrogen is naturally occurring geological hydrogen, not hydrogen produced by steam methane reforming.
68.tq: Find the wrong production route by separating natural hydrogen from manufactured hydrogen.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Pink** = electrolysis powered by **nuclear** energy. Statement 2: **Turquoise** = methane pyrolysis, giving **solid carbon**.
Statement 3 wrong: steam methane reforming makes **grey** hydrogen; **white** is naturally occurring.
xa: **Blue** = fossil route + **CCS**.
**Brown / Black** = **coal gasification**.
**Green** = electrolysis using renewable power (PYQ **2023**); also biomass gasification.

68.s: Green hydrogen is produced mainly by:
o: Steam methane reforming of natural gas
Electrolysis of water using renewable power
Electrolysis of water using nuclear power
68.x: Green hydrogen comes from electrolysis of water using renewable power (PYQ 2023) and is the only zero-carbon colour. Steam methane reforming gives grey, methane pyrolysis gives turquoise, and nuclear-powered electrolysis gives pink hydrogen.
68.tq: Green = RE electrolysis; pink = nuclear; turquoise = pyrolysis.
xs: **Green hydrogen** is made by **electrolysis of water using renewable power** — option **(2)** (PYQ **2023**).
Reforming of natural gas = **grey**; methane pyrolysis = **turquoise**; nuclear electrolysis = **pink**.
xa: Green hydrogen can also come from **biomass gasification**.
**Green Hydrogen Standard** (MNRE, **Aug 2023**): well-to-gate emissions **not more than 2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2**.
An **electrolyser** splits water into hydrogen + oxygen using electricity.

68.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated method for storing or carrying hydrogen for vehicle use?
o: Storage only as carbon dioxide in insulated tanks
68.x: Hydrogen may be stored as compressed gas, cryogenic liquid hydrogen, or solid metal hydrides, and may also be carried as ammonia or methanol. Carbon dioxide is not a stated hydrogen-storage method.
68.tq: Identify the option that is not a hydrogen-storage form or carrier.
xs: **Storage as carbon dioxide** is NOT a hydrogen storage method — option **(1)**.
Real methods: **compressed gas** (Type-IV tanks), **liquid hydrogen at -253 °C**, **metal hydrides**, chemical carriers.
xa: Liquid hydrogen has very low density, **0.071 g/ml** → bulky tanks.
**Metal hydrides** absorb hydrogen in alloys and release it on heating.
Chemical carriers: **ammonia**, **methanol**, **LOHC**.

68.s: Green ammonia is produced by combining:
68.x: Green ammonia is produced from nitrogen and green hydrogen. It is important for fertiliser production and can also serve as a fuel and marine fuel.
68.tq: Distinguish the feedstocks of ammonia from those of other hydrogen derivatives.
xs: **Green ammonia** = **nitrogen (N2)** + **green hydrogen** — option **(4)**.
Green ammonia leads green-hydrogen adoption (**fertiliser**, fuel, **marine fuel**).
xa: **7,24,000 TPA** green ammonia at weighted average **₹53.27/kg** (SECI) — among the world's lowest.
**AM Green** is building a green-ammonia plant at **Kakinada** (AP).
Green ammonia/methanol standards: **Mar 2026**.

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding hydrogen types and carbon dioxide emissions.

List-I
(a) Grey hydrogen
(b) Blue hydrogen
(c) Green hydrogen
(d) Brown/Black hydrogen

List-II
(i) Zero emissions
(ii) High emissions, with carbon dioxide released
(iii) Low emissions, with carbon dioxide captured
(iv) Very high emissions
68.x: Grey hydrogen (from natural gas) releases high CO₂, blue captures it for low emissions, green (renewable electrolysis) has zero, and brown/black (coal) very high, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
68.tq: Recall the emissions of each hydrogen colour.
n: Grey hydrogen has high carbon dioxide emissions, which are released. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Blue hydrogen has low carbon dioxide emissions because the emissions are captured. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen has zero carbon dioxide emissions. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Brown or black hydrogen has very high carbon dioxide emissions. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Blue hydrogen is transitional and is not fully zero-carbon. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is described as the cleanest hydrogen type. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Brown or black hydrogen is the dirtiest hydrogen type. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — option **(3)**.
**Grey** = **high** emissions, CO₂ **released**; **blue** = **low**, CO₂ **captured**.
**Green** = **zero** emissions; **brown/black** = **very high**.
xa: Grey hydrogen is about **95%** of current global production — the **cheapest**.
**Pink** = nuclear electrolysis; **turquoise** = **methane pyrolysis**.
Green Hydrogen Standard: not more than **2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements regarding green hydrogen:
I. It can be used for green steel by replacing coking coal.
II. Green ammonia and green methanol can serve as energy carriers for export.
III. It is produced from natural gas with carbon capture and storage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
68.x: I and II are correct: green hydrogen can replace coking coal in steelmaking, and green ammonia and methanol can carry its energy for export. III is false because hydrogen from natural gas with carbon capture is blue hydrogen; green hydrogen comes from electrolysis using renewable power.
68.tq: Distinguish green from blue hydrogen by production route.
n: Green hydrogen is used to produce green steel by replacing coking coal. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen can be exported as green ammonia or green methanol energy carriers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used in aviation through synthetic fuels. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen is used in steel production through the direct reduced iron (DRI) process. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used in hard-to-abate industries. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used to produce fertiliser through green ammonia. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used to produce green methanol. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen decarbonises steel. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen decarbonises aviation. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used to produce other chemical derivatives. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(1)**.
I is correct: green hydrogen makes **green steel** by **replacing coking coal** (DRI).
II is correct: **green ammonia** and **green methanol** are **energy carriers** for export.
III is wrong: natural gas with **CCS** gives **blue** hydrogen; green comes from **electrolysis** with **renewable electricity**.
xa: Green ammonia = **nitrogen** + green hydrogen.
India signed green ammonia/methanol **export deals** with **Japanese** firms (Jul 2026).
Green ammonia discovered at **₹53.27/kg** (SECI).

68.s:
Match the hydrogen production method with its source or process and resulting type.

List-I
(a) Steam Methane Reforming
(b) Coal/Biomass Gasification
(c) Water Electrolysis
(d) Methane Pyrolysis

List-II
(i) Water and renewable electricity — Green
(ii) Natural gas and steam — Grey/Blue with CCS
(iii) Natural gas at high temperature without oxygen — Turquoise
(iv) Coal or biomass — Grey/Brown
68.x: Steam reforming of natural gas gives grey or blue hydrogen, coal or biomass gasification gives grey or brown, renewable electrolysis gives green, and methane pyrolysis gives turquoise, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
68.tq: Recall the source and colour of each method.
n: Steam methane reforming uses natural gas and steam as its source or process. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Steam methane reforming produces grey hydrogen or blue hydrogen when CCS is used. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Coal or biomass gasification uses coal or biomass as its source. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Coal or biomass gasification produces grey hydrogen or brown hydrogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Water electrolysis uses water and electricity as its source or process. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Water electrolysis using renewable electricity produces green hydrogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Methane pyrolysis uses natural gas at high temperature without oxygen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Methane pyrolysis produces turquoise hydrogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Grey hydrogen is produced by steam methane reforming (SMR) of natural gas or by coal gasification. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Blue hydrogen is produced by steam methane reforming with carbon capture and storage (CCS). [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen can use solar, wind, or hydroelectricity as its renewable electricity source. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Turquoise hydrogen is produced by methane pyrolysis. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Brown or black hydrogen is produced by coal gasification without carbon capture and storage. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**SMR** = **natural gas and steam** → **grey** (or **blue** with CCS); **gasification** = **coal or biomass** → **grey or brown**.
**Water electrolysis** with **renewable electricity** → **green**; **methane pyrolysis** without oxygen → **turquoise**.
xa: Methane pyrolysis produces **solid carbon** as a by-product.
**Nuclear-powered electrolysis** gives **pink** hydrogen.
**Biological / photobiological** routes (microbes, algae) are emerging green routes.

68.s:
Assertion (A): Most of current global hydrogen production is grey hydrogen.
Reason (R): Grey hydrogen is produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
68.x: A is true: about 95% of hydrogen today is grey, made from fossil fuels. R is false because grey hydrogen comes from steam reforming of natural gas with CO₂ released; electrolysis with renewable power gives green hydrogen.
68.tq: Recall the production route behind each hydrogen colour.
n: Approximately 95% of current global hydrogen production is grey hydrogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Grey hydrogen is the cheapest hydrogen type. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: **A is true, but R is false** — option **(3)**.
A: about **95%** of current global hydrogen is **grey**.
R is wrong: grey hydrogen comes from **steam methane reforming** of **natural gas** (or **coal gasification**); **electrolysis** with **renewable electricity** gives **green**.
xa: Grey costs **$1.5-2/kg** vs green ~**$4/kg**.
**Blue** = SMR + **CCS** — transitional, not fully zero-carbon.
**Brown / black** = coal gasification **without CCS** — the dirtiest.

68.s:
How many of the following are listed applications of hydrogen in power or domestic use?

1. Backup power
2. Grid balancing by storing excess renewable energy
3. Heating in the future
4. Production of methanol
68.x: Three are power or domestic uses: backup power, grid balancing and future heating. Methanol production is an industrial use.
68.tq: Discriminate power uses from industrial uses.
n: Hydrogen is used for backup power. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen is used for grid balancing by storing excess renewable energy. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen may be used for heating in the future. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: **Only three** are power/domestic uses — option **(3)**: **backup power**, **grid balancing** and **heating in the future**.
**Methanol** production is an **industry** use.
xa: Fuel cells **generate electricity** for the power sector.
Hydrogen enables **long-duration energy storage** and **peak power**.
Industry uses also include **ammonia** for **fertilisers**.

68.s: Hydrogen is particularly useful for which of the following situations?
o: Sectors where direct electrification is difficult
Only sectors where direct electrification is already complete
68.x: Hydrogen suits hard-to-abate sectors such as steel, shipping and fertilisers, where direct electrification is difficult.
68.tq: Recall why hydrogen targets hard-to-abate sectors.
n: Hydrogen is useful for hard-to-abate sectors where direct electrification is difficult. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: Hydrogen is useful where **direct electrification is difficult** — option **(2)**.
These **hard-to-abate sectors** include **steel**, **cement**, **fertilisers**, **heavy transport**, **shipping** and **aviation**.
xa: Green hydrogen **produces only water** and **reduces dependence** on imported fossil fuels.
It is **critical** for India's **2070** net-zero target.
**National Green Hydrogen Mission** (**4 January 2023**) targets **5 MMT/year** by 2030.

68.s: The total outlay approved for the National Green Hydrogen Mission up to 2029-30 is:
68.x: The Mission has a total outlay of ₹19,744 crore up to financial year 2029-30.
68.tq: Use the exact headline figure rather than a component amount.
xs: The **National Green Hydrogen Mission** outlay is **₹19,744 crore** up to FY **2029-30** — option **(2)**.
**₹17,490 crore** is only the **SIGHT** component.
xa: Pilot projects **₹1,466 cr**; **SHIP** (R&D) **₹400 cr**; other components **₹388 cr**.
Approved by the Union Cabinet on **4 January 2023**; nodal ministry **MNRE**.
Target: **5 MMT/year** green hydrogen by **2030**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Green Hydrogen Mission:
1. SIGHT gives incentives for electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production.
2. SHIP is a public-private partnership for research and development.
3. Green Hydrogen Hubs are centres meant only for importing liquefied hydrogen.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: Statement 1 is correct: SIGHT has two incentives, electrolyser manufacturing and green H2 production. Statement 2 is correct: SHIP (Strategic Hydrogen Innovation Partnership) is a PPP for R&D. Statement 3 is wrong: hubs are integrated production-use-export clusters. So '1 and 2 only'.
68.tq: SIGHT = incentives, SHIP = R&D PPP, Hubs = production-use-export clusters.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: **SIGHT** gives **2 incentives** — electrolyser manufacturing + green H2 production. Statement 2: **SHIP** = **PPP for R&D**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Green Hydrogen Hubs** are integrated **production-use-export** clusters.
xa: ⚠ **SIGHT** = incentives (**₹17,490 cr**); **SHIP** = R&D partnership (**₹400 cr**).
**Hydrogen Valley Innovation Clusters**: **four** sanctioned, **₹170 crore**.
**National Centre for Hydrogen Safety** is also a mission component.

68.s:
Consider the following statements about the National Green Hydrogen Mission:
1. It was approved by the Union Cabinet on 4 January 2023.
2. Its nodal ministry is the Ministry of Power.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
68.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Cabinet approved the Mission on 4 January 2023. Statement 2 is wrong: MNRE is the nodal ministry (BEE under the Ministry of Power handles only certification). So '1 only'.
68.tq: NGHM: 4 Jan 2023, MNRE, Rs 19,744 cr.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1)**: the Cabinet approved the mission on **4 January 2023** (APPSC **2022** key).
Statement 2 wrong: the nodal ministry is **MNRE**, not the Ministry of Power.
xa: ⚠ The **Bureau of Energy Efficiency** (under the **Ministry of Power**) is the nodal authority for **certification**.
**GHCI** launched **April 2025**.

68.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated 2030 target of the National Green Hydrogen Mission?
o: Production of 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen annually
Addition of 125 GW of renewable energy capacity
68.x: The Mission targets 60-100 GW of electrolyser capacity, not 200 GW. The other three figures are stated 2030 targets.
68.tq: Find the altered numerical target among closely related figures.
xs: **200 GW of electrolysers** is NOT a target — option **(1)**; the target is **60-100 GW** electrolysers.
Stated 2030 targets: **5 MMT/year** green H2, **125 GW** added RE, **6 lakh jobs**.
xa: Also: **50 MMT/yr** GHG cut, **₹1 lakh crore+** lower fossil imports, **₹8 lakh crore+** investment.
Production could reach **10 MMT** with exports.
Progress (**Aug 2026**): **15 companies** awarded **3,000 MW** electrolyser manufacturing capacity.

68.s: Which institution is the nodal authority for certification under the National Green Hydrogen Mission?
68.x: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency, under the Ministry of Power, is the nodal authority for certification.
68.tq: Distinguish the nodal ministry from the certification authority.
xs: The **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)**, under the **Ministry of Power**, is the nodal authority for certification — option **(1)**.
This is under the **Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India (GHCI)**, launched **April 2025**.
xa: **Green Hydrogen Standard** (MNRE, **Aug 2023**): not more than **2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2**.
Standards for **green ammonia and green methanol**: **Mar 2026**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements regarding applications of green hydrogen in India:

3. Hydrogen blending in city-gas networks is being evaluated as H-CNG.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: All four statements describe identified applications of green hydrogen, including industrial decarbonisation, heavy mobility, H-CNG and long-duration storage.
68.tq: Use the sector list to test whether all applications are covered.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4)**.
Uses: **fertilisers, refineries, steel**; heavy mobility — **fuel-cell trucks, buses, ships**.

68.s:
With reference to the green hydrogen initiative at V.O. Chidambaranar Port, consider the following statements:

68.s: Which of the following correctly represents the 2030 production target and the possible level including exports under the National Green Hydrogen Mission?
o: 2 MMT per year, potentially up to 5 MMT with exports
5 MMT per year, potentially up to 10 MMT with exports
5 MMT per year, with no provision for export-linked expansion
10 MMT per year, potentially up to 15 MMT with exports
68.x: The Mission targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen annually by 2030, with production potentially reaching 10 MMT when exports are included.
68.tq: Keep the base target distinct from the export-linked upper level.
xs: Target: **5 MMT per year** green hydrogen by **2030**, up to **10 MMT** with exports — option **(2)**.
**Exports** are part of the plan — long-term **green ammonia and green methanol** deals with **Japanese firms** (**Jul 2026**).
xa: Commissioned so far: ~**8,000 TPA** at **₹387-397/kg**.

68.s:
Consider the following as expected outcomes or targets of the National Green Hydrogen Mission by 2030:
1. Reduction of greenhouse-gas emissions by about 50 MMT annually.
2. Reduction in fossil-fuel imports by more than ₹1 lakh crore.
3. Mobilisation of investment exceeding ₹8 lakh crore.
4. Creation of about 6 lakh jobs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: All four are stated Mission outcomes: about 50 MMT annual GHG reduction, more than ₹1 lakh crore lower fossil imports, over ₹8 lakh crore investment and 6 lakh jobs.
68.tq: Group related target figures and verify each numerical statement.
xs: All four are mission outcomes by **2030** — option **(4)**.
**50 MMT/yr** GHG cut; **₹1 lakh crore+** lower fossil imports; **₹8 lakh crore+** investment; **6 lakh jobs**.
xa: Also **125 GW** added RE and **60-100 GW** electrolysers.
Production target: **5 MMT/year** (up to **10 MMT** with exports).
Outlay: **₹19,744 crore**.

68.s: Under the Green Hydrogen Standard notified by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy in August 2023, hydrogen is classified as green when well-to-gate emissions do not exceed:
o: 3 kg CO2-eq per kg H2, calculated quarterly
5 kg CO2-eq per kg H2, calculated as a 12-month average
1 kg CO2-eq per kg H2, calculated annually
2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2, calculated as a 12-month average
68.x: The Green Hydrogen Standard permits well-to-gate emissions of not more than 2 kg CO2-equivalent per kg of hydrogen, measured as a 12-month average.
68.tq: Discriminate between closely related numerical thresholds and averaging periods.
xs: Hydrogen is "green" if well-to-gate emissions are **not more than 2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2**, as a **12-month average** — option **(4)**.
The standard was notified by **MNRE** in **Aug 2023**.
xa: **GHCI** launched **April 2025**; certification by **BEE**.
Green ammonia and green methanol standards: **Mar 2026**.
Only **green** hydrogen is zero-carbon.

68.s: The Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India (GHCI) was launched in:
68.x: The Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India was launched in April 2025.
68.tq: Use the date as the distinguishing clue among related policy milestones.
xs: **GHCI** was launched in **April 2025** — option **(1)**.
**Aug 2023** is the **Green Hydrogen Standard**; **Mar 2026** is the green ammonia/methanol standards.
xa: Nodal certifying authority: **Bureau of Energy Efficiency**.
Threshold: **2 kg CO2-eq per kg H2** (12-month average).
Mission approved **4 January 2023**.

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

68.s:
Consider the following statements:

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Electrolyser type)
a. Alkaline
b. PEM
c. Solid oxide
d. AEM

xs: **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.

**Solid oxide** = high-temperature steam electrolysis; **AEM** = anion exchange membrane, avoids precious metals.

**SIGHT Component-I** gives performance-linked incentives for domestic **electrolyser** manufacturing.
Concern: **Chinese dominance** of electrolyser supply.

68.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or challenge associated with green hydrogen?
o: Costly cryogenic transport and water stress
Mature domestic electrolyser industry with no import dependence
High production cost compared with grey hydrogen
68.x: Import dependence on electrolysers is identified as a challenge; a mature domestic industry with no import dependence is not. High cost, cryogenic transport and water stress are also recognised concerns.
68.tq: Identify the option that reverses a stated criticism rather than merely changing its wording.
xs: A **mature domestic electrolyser industry with no import dependence** is NOT a criticism — option **(3)**; the industry is **nascent** and **import-dependent**.
Real criticisms: **high cost** (~**$4/kg** vs grey **$1.5-2/kg**), **costly cryogenic transport**, **water stress**.
xa: **Chinese dominance** of electrolyser supply is a concern.
US credits up to **$3/kg** compete for exports.
~**9 litres** of purified water per kg of hydrogen.

68.s: An electrolyser is a device that:
o: Combines nitrogen and hydrogen to produce electricity
Splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity
Converts hydrogen directly into crude oil
68.x: An electrolyser uses electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
68.tq: Use the basic input-process-output relationship to identify the device.
xs: An **electrolyser** **splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity** — option **(2)**.
With **renewable power** this gives **green hydrogen**; with nuclear power, **pink**.
xa: Types: **Alkaline**, **PEM**, **Solid oxide**, **AEM**.
Water need: ~**9 litres** of purified water per kg of hydrogen.
**15 companies** awarded **3,000 MW** electrolyser manufacturing capacity (**Aug 2026**).

68.s:
Consider the following statements about a PEM fuel cell:
1. Hydrogen is split into protons and electrons at the anode.
2. Electrons pass through an external circuit and thereby produce electricity.
3. Protons cross the membrane towards the cathode.
4. Hydrogen is burnt inside the fuel cell to release electrical energy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
68.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Hydrogen is not burnt in a PEM fuel cell; its chemical energy is converted into electricity through electrochemical reactions.
68.tq: Reject the combustion trap and trace the movement of electrons and protons.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1)**.
Anode: **H2 → 2H+ + 2e-**; electrons flow in the **external circuit** → **electricity**; **protons cross the membrane**.
Statement 4 wrong: hydrogen is **not burnt** — chemical energy becomes electricity.
xa: Cathode: **1/2 O2 + 2H+ + 2e- → H2O** + heat.
Exhaust: **only water vapour and warm air** — zero tailpipe emissions.
Cochin ferry uses an indigenous **LT-PEM** fuel cell.

68.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A fuel cell produces electricity and water through an electrochemical process involving hydrogen and oxygen.
Statement B: A fuel cell has zero emissions at the point of use.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
68.x: Both are true: a fuel cell turns hydrogen and oxygen into electricity and water, so nothing harmful comes out at the point of use.
68.tq: Recall how a fuel cell works.
n: A fuel cell is an electrochemical device. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
A fuel cell converts H₂ and O₂ into electricity and H₂O. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Fuel cells have zero emissions at the point of use. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: a **fuel cell** is an **electrochemical device** converting **H₂ and O₂** into **electricity and H₂O**.
B: it has **zero emissions** at the **point of use**.
xa: At the anode, **H2 → 2H+ + 2e-**; at the cathode oxygen forms **H2O**.
Hydrogen is **not burnt**; exhaust is **only water vapour and warm air**.
First indigenous **hydrogen fuel-cell ferry**: **Cochin Shipyard** (LT-PEM).

68.s: The first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell ferry in India was built by which organisation?
68.x: The first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell ferry was built by Cochin Shipyard Limited. It was a fully indigenous LT-PEM fuel-cell ferry.
68.tq: Match the transport type with its specific builder rather than with a testing site.
xs: **Cochin Shipyard Ltd** built India's first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell **ferry** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2024**).
It uses a fully indigenous **LT-PEM** fuel cell and was flagged off by the PM.
**KPIT with CSIR-NCL** made the **bus**; **ICF Chennai** the tested **train coach**; **IOCL** the H-CNG buses.
xa: VOC port (**Tuticorin**) pilot: bunkering and refuelling, **₹35 crore**.
Mission **shipping** pilot: **₹115 cr**.

68.s: The hydrogen-powered coach tested by the Railways was associated with which location and organisation?
68.x: The first hydrogen-powered train coach tested by the Railways was associated with Chennai’s Integral Coach Factory (ICF). This is distinct from the hydrogen train in service associated with Jind-Sonipat.
68.tq: Separate the coach-testing site from the locations of the ferry, bus and train.
xs: The first hydrogen-powered **train coach tested** by Railways was at **Chennai (ICF – Integral Coach Factory)** — option **(2)** (APPSC **2025**).
**Jind-Sonipat** is where the train runs **in service**, not where the coach was tested.
xa: ⚠ Train coach **tested** = **Chennai**; train **in service** = **Jind-Sonipat**.
The Jind-Sonipat train has **10 coaches**, **89 km** route, from **July 2026**.
Hydrogen is stored in roof-mounted **Type-IV** cylinders.

68.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell bus mentioned in the context of India?
o: It was developed by Veera Vahana at Chennai in 2025.
It was developed by Cochin Shipyard Limited at Kochi in 2024.
It was developed by KPIT with CSIR-NCL at Pune in 2022.
It was developed by IOCL at Delhi in 2020.
68.x: The first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell bus was developed by KPIT with CSIR-NCL, Pune, in 2022. “Veera Vahana” is not the correct identification for this bus.
68.tq: Use the builder-year-place combination to reject the look-alike name trap.
xs: India's first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell bus was by **KPIT with CSIR-NCL, Pune (2022)** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
"**Veera Vahana**" is the wrong answer; **Cochin Shipyard** built the **ferry**; **IOCL Delhi (2020)** = **H-CNG** buses.
xa: Hydrogen shuttle bus: **Central Vista, Delhi**.
Mission **mobility** pilot outlay: **₹496 cr**.
Fuel-cell exhaust: only **water vapour and warm air**.

68.s: The first hydrogen fuel-cell train in service is associated with which of the following descriptions?
o: A shuttle bus operating at Central Vista, Delhi, from 2022
A ferry launched from Cochin Shipyard Limited in 2024
A 10-coach train operating on the Jind-Sonipat route in Haryana from July 2026
A single coach tested at Chennai’s ICF in 2025
68.x: The first hydrogen fuel-cell train in service is described as a 10-coach train on the 89-km Jind-Sonipat route in Haryana from July 2026. It is identified as the world’s longest and most powerful broad-gauge hydrogen train.
68.tq: Distinguish the train in service from the earlier coach-testing milestone.
xs: The first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell **train in service** is a **10-coach** train on **Jind-Sonipat** (**89 km**), **Haryana**, from **July 2026** — option **(3)**.
It is the world's **longest and most powerful broad-gauge** hydrogen train.
xa: ⚠ Single coach **tested** at **Chennai (ICF)**.
Hydrogen stored in roof-mounted **Type-IV** composite cylinders.
**Central Vista** = shuttle bus; **Cochin Shipyard** = ferry.

68.s: The world's first hydrogen fuel-cell car to reach Sydney (27 December 2003) was built and driven by students of:
68.x: It was built and driven by students of Tamagawa University, Tokyo (PYQ 2004). The other institutions are not linked to this run.
68.tq: Sydney H2 car 2003 = Tamagawa (Japan).
xs: Students of **Tamagawa University (Tokyo)** built and drove the first hydrogen fuel-cell car to reach **Sydney** (**27 Dec 2003**) — option **(1)** (PYQ **2004**).
It is a world FIRST, not an Indian or Australian university project.
xa: India's first indigenous fuel-cell bus: **KPIT with CSIR-NCL, Pune (2022)**.
Fuel cells emit **only water vapour and warm air**.
PEM anode: **H2 → 2H+ + 2e-**.

68.s: About how much purified water is required to produce one kilogram of hydrogen through electrolysis?
68.x: Approximately 9 litres of purified water are required per kilogram of hydrogen, which can constrain projects in arid solar regions.
68.tq: Retain the order of magnitude and connect it with the stated regional constraint.
xs: About **9 litres** of purified water is needed per kg of hydrogen — option **(3)**.
This is a **constraint in arid solar states**.
xa: Other constraints: **Chinese dominance** of electrolysers, high cost (~**$4/kg**), costly **cryogenic** transport.
**NTPC Simhadri** began trials with a **seawater-to-hydrogen** plant (**Jan 2026**).
US credits up to **$3/kg** compete for exports.

68.s: Which one of the following correctly describes liquid hydrogen storage?
o: Hydrogen remains liquid at about -253°C and has very low density, requiring large tanks.
Hydrogen remains liquid at 0°C and can be stored in ordinary water tanks.
Hydrogen is liquefied by mixing it with ammonia at ambient pressure.
Hydrogen becomes liquid at about 253°C and requires no specialised insulation.
68.x: Liquid hydrogen is maintained at approximately -253°C. Its very low density, about 0.071 g/ml, necessitates large storage tanks.
68.tq: Combine the temperature, density and storage implication instead of accepting a single altered detail.
xs: Liquid hydrogen is kept at **-253 °C** (cryogenic) and has very **low density** (**0.071 g/ml**) → **large, bulky tanks** — option **(1)**.
It is **not** liquid at 0 °C, and needs **cryogenic** handling.
xa: Criticism: **costly cryogenic transport**.
Alternatives: **compressed gas** (Type-IV), **metal hydrides**, chemical carriers.

68.s: Which of the following group contains only chemical carriers that can transport hydrogen for export?
68.x: Ammonia, methanol and liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHC) are chemical carriers for transporting hydrogen, including for export.
68.tq: Eliminate groups that are gases, raw materials or non-carrier substances.
xs: **Ammonia, methanol and LOHC** are chemical carriers for hydrogen **export** — option **(4)**.
They are used because liquid hydrogen needs **-253 °C** and has very low density.
xa: Long-term **green ammonia and green methanol** export deals with **Japanese firms** (**Jul 2026**).
**Green ammonia** = **nitrogen + green hydrogen**.
Hydrogen hub ports: **Deendayal (Kandla)**, **V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin)**, **Paradip**.

68.s:
Consider the following statements about green hydrogen in Andhra Pradesh:
1. The Green Hydrogen Valley Declaration was made at Amaravati on 19 July 2025 to make AP India's green hydrogen capital.

xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Green Hydrogen Valley Declaration**, **Amaravati**, **19 Jul 2025** — to make AP India's green hydrogen capital.
Statement 2: **1.5 MMTPA** green hydrogen by **2030**.
Statement 3 wrong: the electrolyser target is **5 GW**, not 1.5 GW.
xa: Aim to cut cost from **₹460/kg** to **₹160-170/kg**.
**SRM University-AP** = nodal agency; CoE with **JK Srivastava Hynfra** (**Feb 2026**).
Projects: **NTPC Green** hub at **Pudimadaka (Anakapalli)**; **AM Green** at **Kakinada**.

68.s: Which institution is the state nodal agency for the Andhra Pradesh Green Hydrogen Valley?
68.x: SRM University-AP is the state nodal agency for the Andhra Pradesh Green Hydrogen Valley.
68.tq: Identify the designated institutional agency rather than a nearby higher-education institution.

xa: **Green Hydrogen Valley Declaration**, **Amaravati**, **19 Jul 2025** — to make AP India's green hydrogen capital.
AP **2030** goal: **1.5 MMTPA** green hydrogen + **5 GW** electrolyser manufacturing.
Aim: cut cost from **₹460/kg** to **₹160-170/kg** (APSES **2025-26**).

68.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Pudimadaka — NTPC Green Energy green hydrogen hub
Simhadri — Seawater-to-hydrogen plant and blending trials
Amaravati — Paradip green ammonia export terminal
68.x: Amaravati is associated with the Green Hydrogen Valley Declaration, not a Paradip green ammonia export terminal. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
68.tq: Find the invented project-location pair by comparing each option with the known AP projects.

Correct: **Pudimadaka** = **NTPC Green Energy** hub; **Simhadri** = **seawater-to-hydrogen** blending trials; **Kakinada** = **AM Green** green ammonia.
xa: Declaration at Amaravati: **19 Jul 2025**.
**NTPC Simhadri** is a **2,400 MW** coal plant near **Visakhapatnam**.
Hub ports: **Deendayal (Kandla)**, **V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin)**, **Paradip**.

68.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding sectors decarbonised by hydrogen.

List-I
(a) Steel
(b) Fertilisers
(c) Petroleum refining
(d) Heavy transport

(i) Direct reduced iron replacing coking coal

68.tq: Link each sector to the way hydrogen is used in it.
n: Hydrogen decarbonises cement. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen decarbonises fertilisers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen decarbonises heavy transport. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen decarbonises shipping. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]

Hydrogen hub ports: **Deendayal (Kandla)**, **V.O. Chidambaranar**, **Paradip**.

68.s: The approximate cost comparison between green and grey hydrogen is:
o: Green hydrogen: about $4 per kg; grey hydrogen: $1.5–2 per kg

Green hydrogen: $1.5–2 per kg; grey hydrogen: about $4 per kg
Both green and grey hydrogen: $4 per kg
68.x: Green hydrogen is estimated at about $4 per kg, whereas grey hydrogen costs approximately $1.5–2 per kg.

xs: Green hydrogen costs ~**$4 per kg**; grey **$1.5-2 per kg** — option **(1)** (**Jul 2026**).

68.s:

1. Fuel-cell vehicles
2. Rocket fuel
3. Blending in CNG
4. Ammonia for fertilisers

68.tq: Discriminate transport uses from industrial uses.
n: Hydrogen is used as fuel for fuel-cell vehicles. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen is used as rocket fuel. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen can be blended in compressed natural gas (CNG). [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen is used to produce ammonia for fertilisers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles include buses, trucks, trains, and ships. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
Green hydrogen is used to produce fertiliser through green ammonia. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 36-39]
xs: **Only three** are fuel/transport uses — option **(3)**: **fuel-cell vehicles**, **rocket fuel** and **blending in CNG**.
**Ammonia for fertilisers** is an **industry** use.
xa: Industry uses: **petroleum refining** (desulphurisation), **methanol**, **steel** via **DRI**.

Jind-Sonipat (**89 km**) runs India's first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell train.

69.s: During the discharge of an electrochemical cell, which one of the following correctly describes the functions of the electrodes?
o: Anode undergoes reduction and cathode undergoes oxidation
Anode undergoes oxidation and cathode undergoes reduction
Both anode and cathode undergo oxidation
Both anode and cathode undergo reduction
69.x: During discharge, oxidation involving loss of electrons occurs at the anode, while reduction involving gain of electrons occurs at the cathode.
69.tq: Use the standard oxidation-at-anode and reduction-at-cathode rule.
xs: During discharge the **anode undergoes oxidation** (loses electrons) and the **cathode undergoes reduction** (gains electrons) — option **(2)**.
Options (1), (3) and (4) reverse or merge the two roles.
xa: The **electrolyte** lets ions flow and keeps the electrodes apart.
⚠ Anode = **oxidation**; cathode = **reduction** (during discharge).
Li-ion: **graphite anode**, **lithium metal-oxide cathode**.

69.s:
Consider the following statements regarding an electrolyte in a battery:
1. It permits the movement of ions between the electrodes.
2. It prevents direct contact between the electrodes.
3. It necessarily conducts electrons between the electrodes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
69.x: An electrolyte allows ions to flow and keeps the electrodes apart. It does not provide a direct electronic path between the electrodes.
69.tq: Separate ionic conduction through the electrolyte from electronic conduction through the external circuit.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1)**.
The **electrolyte** **lets ions flow** and **keeps the electrodes apart** (prevents direct contact).
Statement 3 wrong: it carries **ions**, not electrons.
xa: **Solid-state** batteries use a **solid electrolyte** — better safety, higher energy density.
**Lead-acid** uses a **sulphuric acid** electrolyte.
**Flow** batteries keep liquid electrolytes in tanks.

69.s:
Consider the following statements regarding lithium-ion battery cathodes:
1. Lithium, nickel and cobalt are usually used in the cathode.
2. Graphite is generally the anode material.
3. All four materials—lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite—usually form the cathode.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
69.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: lithium, nickel and cobalt (with manganese) usually make the cathode, while graphite is the anode. Statement 3 is wrong because only three of the four make the cathode, not graphite (the UPSC 2025 'only three' trap).
69.tq: Watch for the ‘all four’ trap when one listed material belongs to the anode.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2)**.
EV cathodes usually use **lithium, nickel, cobalt** (and manganese); **graphite** is the **anode**.
Statement 3 wrong: ⚠ only **three** of the four make **cathodes** (UPSC **2025** key).
xa: **NMC** = nickel-manganese-cobalt cathode.
**LFP** = **LiFePO4** cathode chemistry.
**Sodium-ion** avoids cobalt, nickel and copper.

69.s: Which one of the following correctly expresses the concern regarding global critical-mineral supply chains?
o: More than 70% of lithium processing and most cobalt refining are concentrated in a few countries.
Only graphite processing is concentrated, while lithium and cobalt are geographically dispersed.
Lithium processing and cobalt refining are evenly distributed across all countries.
No significant concentration exists in the processing or refining of battery minerals.
69.x: More than 70% of lithium processing and most cobalt refining are concentrated in a few countries, creating a supply-chain risk for battery manufacturing.
69.tq: Reject absolute reversals of the stated concentration and identify the precise supply-chain risk.
xs: **Over 70%** of **lithium processing** and most **cobalt refining** are concentrated in a few countries — option **(1)**.
Upstream minerals are concentrated in **China and Africa**.
xa: Lithium, cobalt, nickel and **REEs** are largely imported by India.
**NCMM**: **₹16,300 crore**; **₹1,500 crore** recycling scheme.
**Sodium-ion** is pitched as a **mineral-light** alternative.

69.s:
With reference to nickel-cadmium batteries, consider the following statements:
1. They are rechargeable.
2. They contain nickel and cadmium electrodes.
