o: 40% of the cost is covered for 2 kW and 60% for additional capacity up to 3 kW.
100% of the cost is covered up to 3 kW.
30% of the cost is covered for 2 kW and 30% for additional capacity up to 3 kW.
60% of the cost is covered for 2 kW and 40% for additional capacity up to 3 kW.
71.x: CFA covers 60% of the cost for 2 kW and 40% for the additional capacity up to 3 kW.
71.tq: Avoid reversing the two subsidy percentages and their capacity limits.
xs: CFA = **60%** of cost for **2 kW** and **40%** for extra capacity up to **3 kW** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the rates; **30%** shares belong to **PM-KUSUM**.
xa: Free power up to **300 units per month**.
Target: **1 crore households**; **30 GW** RTS.
AP SC/ST households get **free rooftop solar** via **Virtual Net Metering**.

71.s: How many willing households were electrified under Saubhagya according to the latest reported figure?
71.x: Saubhagya electrified 2.86 crore willing households. An older figure cited 2.82 crore households as of March 2021.
71.tq: Distinguish the updated figure from the older reference figure.
xs: **Saubhagya** electrified **2.86 crore** willing households — option **(3)**.
**2.82 crore** is the older figure (as of **Mar 2021**, UPSC), not the latest.
xa: Saubhagya (**2017**) aimed at **universal household electrification** and claimed **100%**.
Leftovers: **₹6,521 crore** under **RDSS** for **13.65 lakh** households.
**Leisang (Manipur)** was the last village electrified, **28 Apr 2018**.

71.s: What was the Phase I target of PMUY by 2019?
71.x: Phase I of PMUY targeted 8 crore deposit-free LPG connections by 2019; the reported number of connections later exceeded 9.5 crore.
71.tq: Distinguish the original target from the later cumulative achievement.
xs: PMUY Phase I targeted **8 crore** connections by **2019** — option **(2)**.
**9.5 crore+** is the later total of connections, not the Phase I target.
xa: **Ujjwala 2.0**: free first refill and stove; **migrants via self-declaration**.
Cash assistance: **₹1,600** per **14.2 kg** connection.
**Grameen Vitrak Yojana (2009)** raised rural LPG distributors from **18%** to **60%**.

71.s: Since October 2023, the targeted subsidy for PMUY beneficiaries has been:
o: ₹200 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 12 refills a year
₹300 per 5 kg refill without an annual limit
₹1,600 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 5 refills a year
₹300 per 14.2 kg refill for up to 9 refills a year
71.x: Since October 2023, the targeted subsidy has been ₹300 per 14.2 kg refill for up to nine refills a year. Older provisions cited ₹200 and up to 12 refills.
71.tq: Give priority to the latest figure while distinguishing it from the older subsidy arrangement.
xs: Since **Oct 2023**: **₹300** per **14.2 kg** refill, up to **9** refills a year — option **(4)**.
**₹200 × 12** was the older provision; **₹1,600** is cash assistance per **connection**, not per refill.
xa: Ujjwala 2.0 gives a **free first refill and stove**.
PMUY has **9.5 crore+** connections.
Refill problem: households want clean fuel but face **cost and habit** barriers (CEEW's **IRES** survey).

71.s: Which village in Manipur was identified as the last village to be electrified?
71.x: Leisang in Manipur was identified as the last village to be electrified.
71.tq: Use the distinctive place-name association to distinguish the first/last fact from nearby locations.
xs: **Leisang (Manipur)** was the last village electrified, on **28 Apr 2018** — option **(1)**.
Imphal, Thoubal and Churachandpur are not mentioned as last villages.
xa: **Saubhagya (2017)** later claimed **100%** household electrification.
Saubhagya electrified **2.86 crore** willing households.
Connections came first via **DDUGJY** and **Saubhagya**.

71.s: In Andhra Pradesh, free power up to how many units per month is provided to BPL SC/ST households?
71.x: Free power is provided up to 200 units per month to eligible BPL SC/ST households in Andhra Pradesh.
71.tq: Use the exact numerical limit and eliminate nearby but altered figures.
xs: AP gives free power **up to 200 units/month** to **20.26 lakh** BPL SC/ST households — option **(3)**.
**300 units** is the PM Surya Ghar free-power limit.
xa: AP power subsidy (**FY 2024-25**): **₹10,449.92 crore**.
Concessional tariffs: **BC/MBC professionals, dhobi ghats, handlooms, saloons**.
SC/ST households get **free rooftop solar** via **Virtual Net Metering**.

71.s: Free rooftop solar power for SC/ST households in Andhra Pradesh is proposed through:
71.x: The provision of free rooftop solar for SC/ST households is associated with Virtual Net Metering.
71.tq: Discriminate between closely related electricity-metering concepts.
xs: AP's SC/ST households get **free rooftop solar** via **Virtual Net Metering** — option **(2)**.
**Prepaid** smart metering is an **RDSS** component, not this.
xa: AP PM Surya Ghar: **2,27,549** installations.
Discom progress (**Aug 2026**): **SPDCL 47%, CPDCL 35%, EPDCL 32%**.
**APCPDCL**: **50,114** rooftop units, **180 MW**.

71.s: The installed renewable-energy capacity of Andhra Pradesh is 10,639.75 MW. Which component-wise distribution is correct?
71.x: Andhra Pradesh had 10,639.75 MW of renewable-energy capacity, comprising 5,614.52 MW of solar and 4,397.67 MW of wind capacity.
71.tq: Match the component figures with their correct labels before checking the total.
xs: Options (1) and (2) swap solar and wind; option (4) gives wind as the whole total.
xa: PM-KUSUM in AP: solarisation of **2.93 lakh** pump sets.
India's installed capacity **509.74 GW**, RE **49.83%** (Nov **2025**).
⚠ Solar exceeds wind in AP's RE mix.

71.s: For Components B and C of PM-KUSUM, the subsidy-sharing pattern is:
71.x: For Components B and C, the Centre contributes 30%, the State 30% and the farmer 40%; a bank loan may also be used by the farmer.
71.tq: Check the three-way percentage split without confusing it with rooftop-solar CFA.
xs: For Components **B and C**: **30% Centre, 30% State, 40% farmer** — option **(3)**.
The farmer's share can come from a **bank loan**.
xa: **B** progress: **9.42 lakh** pumps; **C**: **10.99 lakh** pumps.
AP: solarisation of **2.93 lakh** agricultural pump sets under PM-KUSUM.
⚠ PM Surya Ghar CFA is **60%** for 2 kW, **40%** for extra up to **3 kW**.

72.s: An Ultra Mega Solar Park is defined as a solar park having a capacity of at least:
72.x: An Ultra Mega Solar Park has a capacity of 500 MW or more at one location.
72.tq: Discriminate the official threshold from the higher 1,000 MW figure.
xs: An **Ultra Mega Solar Park** is **500 MW or more** at one location — option **(3)**.
⚠ "**1,000 MW**" is the trap — it is WRONG (**APPSC 2019**).
xa: **Kurnool UMSP (1,000 MW)**, Gani-Sakunala, was once the **world's largest** single-location solar park.
**Ananthapuram-I** (**1,500 MW**) is at **NP Kunta**.
Solar Park Scheme target: **40,000 MW** (raised **21 Mar 2017**).

72.s:
Consider the following statements about floating solar power in India:
1. India has an estimated floating-solar potential of about 102 GW.
2. The existing floating-solar capacity is approximately 0.7 GW.
3. Omkareshwar in Madhya Pradesh is associated with a 278 MW floating solar project.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
72.x: India has about 0.7 GW of floating solar capacity against an estimated 102 GW potential, and the 278 MW Omkareshwar project in Madhya Pradesh is the largest identified project.
72.tq: Compare existing capacity, potential and the largest project without reversing units.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: floating solar potential ~**102 GW** — correct.
Statement 2: installed ~**0.7 GW** — correct.
Statement 3: largest = **Omkareshwar** (**278 MW**, Narmada, MP) — correct.
xa: AP: NTPC's **25 MW** floating solar at **Simhadri, Visakhapatnam** (**APPSC 2021**).
⚠ **Simhadri** = floating solar; **Ramagiri** = hybrid park; **Talaricheruvu** = UMSP-II.

72.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Kadapa Ultra Mega Solar Park — Galiveedu
72.x: Ananthapuram-I Solar Park is located at NP Kunta, not Galiveedu. Galiveedu is the location of Kadapa Ultra Mega Solar Park.
72.tq: Find the swapped location among closely related projects.
xs: **Ananthapuram-I — Galiveedu** is wrong — option **(4)**; Ananthapuram-I is at **NP Kunta**.
**Galiveedu** is the **Kadapa** UMSP; **Ramagiri** (hybrid) and **Talaricheruvu** (UMSP-II) are correct pairs.
xa: ⚠ **Talaricheruvu** = UMSP-II; **Ramagiri** = hybrid; **Simhadri** = floating solar.
Kurnool UMSP was once the **world's largest** single-location solar park (**APPSC 2019**).

72.s: The 1,000 MW Ultra Mega Solar Park at Gani-Sakunala in Panyam mandal, once the world's largest single-location solar park, is in which district of Andhra Pradesh?
72.x: The Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park (1,000 MW) is at Gani-Sakunala, Panyam mandal, Kurnool (APPSC 2019). Ananthapuramu hosts NP Kunta, Talaricheruvu and Ramagiri; YSR Kadapa hosts the Galiveedu park; Nellore is not linked to these parks.
72.tq: Gani-Sakunala/Panyam = Kurnool UMSP, once world's largest
xs: The **Gani-Sakunala** (Panyam mandal) UMSP is in **Kurnool** — option **(2)**.
**Ananthapuramu** hosts **NP Kunta**, **Talaricheruvu**, **Ramagiri**; **YSR Kadapa** hosts **Galiveedu**.
xa: It was once the **world's largest** single-location solar park (**APPSC 2019**).
Krishnapatnam (**Nellore**) has APPDCL's **2,400 MW** thermal plant.

72.s: NTPC's 25 MW floating solar plant in Andhra Pradesh, operational by July 2022, is at:
72.x: The 25 MW floating solar plant is at NTPC Simhadri in Visakhapatnam (APPSC 2021). Omkareshwar (MP) is India's largest floating solar project (278 MW); Krishnapatnam has an APPDCL thermal plant; Ramagiri has the hybrid solar-wind park.
xs: NTPC's **25 MW** floating solar plant is at **Simhadri, Visakhapatnam** (**APPSC 2021**) — option **(3)**.
**Omkareshwar** (MP, **278 MW**) is India's largest floating plant; **Krishnapatnam** is thermal; **Ramagiri** is the hybrid park.
xa: **Simhadri STPS** (NTPC) is a **2,000 MW** thermal plant.
Floating solar: ~**0.7 GW** installed vs **102 GW** potential.

72.s: Which of the following correctly describes the Tata Renewable hybrid project in Andhra Pradesh?
o: 800 MW wind at Kanekallu and no solar component
400 MW solar at Pathikonda and 400 MW wind at Kanekallu
400 MW wind at Pathikonda and 400 MW solar at Kanekallu
800 MW solar at Pathikonda and no wind component
72.x: The project comprises 400 MW of solar capacity at Pathikonda in Kurnool and 400 MW of wind capacity at Kanekallu in Anantapur.
72.tq: Separate the two equal capacities by their technology and location.
xs: **Tata Renewable 800 MW hybrid**: **400 MW solar at Pathikonda** (Kurnool) + **400 MW wind at Kanekallu** (Anantapur) — option **(2)**.
Option (3) swaps solar and wind locations.
xa: Investment **₹5,750 crore**; ~**4,000** construction jobs.
Some notes place both parts in **Anantapur** district.
It is under **ICEP-2024** (Jul **2026**).

72.s: The 600 MW Kadapa renewable-energy project associated with SAEL is a current-relevance development under which policy framework?
o: Andhra Pradesh Green Hydrogen and Green Ammonia Policy, 2023
72.x: The 600 MW SAEL project in Kadapa is identified as a development under the Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024 (ICEP-2024).
72.tq: Use the project-to-policy association and distinguish the State’s recent policy from older solar and green-hydrogen policies.
xs: The **SAEL 600 MW** Kadapa project is the first commissioned under **ICEP-2024** (**Integrated Clean Energy Policy, 2024**) — option **(4)**.
It was done in **11** months (May **2026**).
xa: Cost **₹3,000 crore**; land **2,400 acres**.
The **Tata 800 MW** hybrid (Jul **2026**) is also under ICEP-2024.
**Kadapa UMSP** (**1,000 MW**) is at **Galiveedu**.

72.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Srisailam Right Bank hydel — APPDCL — Kurnool
72.x: Simhadri STPS at Visakhapatnam is operated by NTPC and has a capacity of 2,000 MW. Krishnapatnam is operated by APPDCL, while Dr NTTPS and Srisailam Right Bank hydel are associated with APGENCO.
72.tq: Match plant, operator and capacity while detecting swapped authorities.
xs: **Simhadri STPS — NTPC — 2,000 MW** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Krishnapatnam SDSTPS** is **APPDCL** (**2,400 MW**), not APGENCO.
**Dr NTTPS** and **Srisailam Right Bank hydel** are **APGENCO** plants.
xa: **Rayalaseema TPP** is at **Muddanur (Kadapa)**, under APGENCO.
APGENCO thermal: NTTPS + RTPP = **4,210 MW**.

72.s: Which agency functions as the State nodal agency for renewable energy in Andhra Pradesh and handles land, clearances and single-window facilitation?
72.x: NREDCAP is the State nodal agency for renewable energy and facilitates land, clearances and single-window services.
72.tq: Identify the agency by its functional responsibility.
xs: **NREDCAP** is AP's **state nodal agency for RE** — land, clearances, single window — option **(1)**.
**APPDCL** = generation; **APSECM** = conservation; **APTRANSCO** = transmission.
xa: APTRANSCO has **13** ongoing **400 kV** works worth **₹3,698 crore**.
AP opened **50,000 acres** barren land for solar leases.

72.s: The agency primarily associated with energy conservation in Andhra Pradesh is:
72.x: APSECM is the agency associated with energy conservation.
72.tq: Direct agency-role recall with closely related energy bodies as distractors.
xs: **APSECM** is AP's energy-conservation agency — option **(1)**.
**APGENCO** = generation; **NREDCAP** = RE nodal agency; **APTRANSCO** = transmission.
xa: APGENCO also runs the **Srisailam Right Bank** hydel plant.
APGENCO thermal: **4,210 MW**.

72.s: Andhra Pradesh opened 50,000 acres of barren land for solar leases primarily to:
o: replace all wind projects with nuclear projects
restrict private participation in solar generation
72.x: The barren land was opened for solar leases to avoid diversion of farmland for renewable-energy projects.
72.tq: Identify the policy rationale behind land-use decisions.
xs: AP opened **50,000 acres** of barren land for solar leases to **avoid farmland diversion** (Apr **2026**) — option **(1)**.
It is a response to **food-vs-fuel** land conflicts.
xa: **NREDCAP** handles land, clearances and single window for RE.
SAEL **600 MW** Kadapa used **2,400 acres**.
PM-KUSUM in AP targets **2.93 lakh** farm pumps.

72.s: According to the Andhra Pradesh renewable-energy mix of 10,639.75 MW, which one of the following correctly represents the approximate shares of solar and wind energy, respectively?
72.x: Solar energy accounts for approximately 53% and wind energy for approximately 41% of Andhra Pradesh’s renewable-energy mix of 10,639.75 MW.
72.tq: Split the options by comparing the order and approximate shares of the two energy sources.
xs: AP RE mix: **solar ~53%** and **wind ~41%** of **10,639.75 MW** — option **(2)**.
Option (4) reverses them.
xa: AP's solar is ~**5.6 GW** vs India's **162.15 GW** (Jun **2026**) — a small share.
Major **2025** wind partnership in **Anantapur** (**APPSC 2025**).
Tata **800 MW** hybrid: **400 MW** wind at **Kanekallu**.

72.s: After the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, which factor contributed to increased coal-related difficulty in power generation?
o: Abolition of transmission charges for coal-based power
Excess availability of high-quality coal within Andhra Pradesh
Replacement of all thermal plants by nuclear plants
Loss of coal mines, resulting in long-distance coal haulage and poor coal quality
72.x: Andhra Pradesh lost its coal mines after bifurcation, causing long coal haulage and exposure to poor coal quality.
72.tq: Apply the stated cause-and-effect chain to an energy-sector situation.
xs: AP **lost its coal mines** after bifurcation, leading to **long coal haulage** and **poor coal quality** — option **(4)**.
Transmission charges were not abolished — **CTU charges** are ~**₹3.4 lakh/MW/month**.
xa: APGENCO thermal: **4,210 MW** (NTTPS + RTPP).
**Krishnapatnam** SDSTPS (**APPDCL**): **2,400 MW**.

72.s: With reference to PM-KUSUM in Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following figures represents the target number of farm pumps?
72.x: PM-KUSUM in Andhra Pradesh targets 2.93 lakh farm pumps. The figure of 32,000 refers to solar pumps installed earlier.
72.tq: Separate the target figure from the already-installed solar-pump figure before choosing the numerical option.
xs: PM-KUSUM in AP targets **2.93 lakh** farm pumps — option **(2)**.
**32,000** = solar pumps installed earlier; ~**5.6 GW** is AP's solar capacity.
xa: **123 MW** rooftop was installed earlier (**2024-25/2025-26**).
AP's 50,000-acre barren-land policy eases **food-vs-fuel** conflicts.

72.s: Which of the following correctly represents the national pumped-storage position?
o: 58 GW on-stream, 209 GW off-stream and approximately 7 GW installed
7 GW on-stream, 58 GW off-stream and 209 GW installed
267 GW on-stream, 7 GW off-stream and 58 GW installed
209 GW on-stream, 58 GW off-stream and 267 GW installed
72.x: The national potential includes about 58 GW on-stream and 209 GW off-stream components, while installed capacity is approximately 7 GW.
72.tq: Separate potential categories from the installed-capacity figure.
xs: PSP: **58 GW on-stream**, **209 GW off-stream**, ~**7 GW installed** — option **(1)**.
The other options jumble these numbers; total potential is **~267 GW**.
xa: ⚠ Off-stream potential (**209 GW**) far exceeds on-stream (**58 GW**).

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. An ecological community consists of all populations of different species living in an area.
2. A biome is a large region defined chiefly by its population density and sex ratio.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 1 is correct: a community is all populations of different species in an area. Statement 2 is wrong: a biome is a large region defined by climate and dominant vegetation (rainforest, tundra, desert); density and sex ratio are population attributes. Hence '1 only'; the other options are wrong.
73.tq: Community = many species' populations together; biome = climate + dominant vegetation; density/sex ratio = population attributes.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: a **community** = all populations of **different species** in an area — correct.
Statement 2: a **biome** is defined by **climate and dominant vegetation** (rainforest, tundra, desert) — wrong; density and sex ratio are **population** attributes.
xa: Order: **organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere**.
The biosphere is absent at the **poles**, highest peaks and deepest oceans.

73.s: Which one of the following represents the correct ecological order from the smallest to the largest level?
o: Organism → community → population → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere
Population → organism → community → biome → ecosystem → biosphere
Organism → ecosystem → population → community → biome → biosphere
73.x: The ecological order is organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
73.tq: Check the hierarchy sequentially from the individual level upward.
xs: Order: **organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere** — option **(2)**.
The others misplace community/population or ecosystem/biome.
xa: Full chain starts with **atoms → molecules → protoplasm → cells**.
"Ecology" was coined by **Ernst Haeckel (1869)**.
The **ecosystem** is the **basic functional unit of ecology**.

73.s: The fundamental niche of a species refers to
o: the actual range occupied after competition
the full range of conditions and resources it could use in the absence of other species
73.x: Fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources available to a species when competition and other biological limitations are absent.
73.tq: Distinguish potential range from actual range.
xs: The **fundamental niche** is the full range of conditions and resources a species could use **free from other species** — option **(4)** (**APPSC 2021**).
The range actually used under competition is the **realised niche** — option (1).
xa: **Niche breadth**: **specialists** (koala — eucalyptus) vs **generalists**.
**Hutchinson** gave the **n-dimensional niche** (**1957**).
Niche is **unique to each species**.

73.s: A koala, which feeds mainly on eucalyptus, is best described as a
73.x: A specialist uses a narrow range of resources. Dependence of the koala mainly on eucalyptus is an example of narrow niche breadth.
73.tq: Infer niche breadth from the range of resources used.
xs: The koala, eating only **eucalyptus**, is a **specialist** with **narrow niche breadth** — option **(2)**.
**Generalists** (most animals) have broad niche breadth.
xa: **Fundamental niche** = range possible without other species; **realised niche** = range used under competition.
No two species occupy the **same niche**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about the ecological niche:
1. A niche is the functional role of a species in its habitat.
2. No two species occupy exactly the same niche.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 1 is correct: the niche is the functional role ('profession') of a species, set by habitat, food, reproduction and physical-chemical factors. Statement 2 is correct: a niche is unique to each species, so no two species occupy the same niche (APPSC 2022: both correct). Hence 'Both 1 and 2'.
73.tq: Niche = profession, and it is unique to each species.
xs: Both are correct — option **(3) Both 1 and 2** (**APPSC 2022**).
Statement 1: a niche is the **functional role** ("profession") of a species — correct.
Statement 2: a niche is **unique to each species** — correct.
xa: Niche is set by habitat, food, reproduction and physical-chemical factors.
**Gause's competitive exclusion principle** relates to species competing for the same resource.
**Resource partitioning** lets competing species coexist.

73.s: Which of the following is NOT a population attribute?
73.x: Density, mortality, age structure and sex ratio are population attributes. Dominant vegetation is associated with the description of a biome.
73.tq: Find the item belonging to the neighbouring ecological level rather than the population level.
xs: **Dominant vegetation** is not a population attribute — option **(2)**; it defines a **biome**.
**Mortality**, **density** and **age structure** are population attributes (with **sex ratio**, **natality**).
xa: **J-curve** = exponential growth (dN/dt = rN).
**S-curve** = logistic growth to **carrying capacity K**.

73.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: Mortality — births per female per unit time
Carrying capacity — number of predators only
73.x: Population density is the number of individuals per unit area. Mortality refers to deaths per unit time, while natality refers to births.
73.tq: Separate the basic population attributes by their measured quantities.
xs: **Density — individuals per unit area** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Mortality** = deaths per unit time; **natality** = births (individuals per female per unit time).
**Carrying capacity K** is where logistic growth levels off, not a count of predators.
xa: **Natality** question was a **PYQ 2025** (both statements true).
**K-selected** species live near **K** (elephants, humans).

73.s: Which one of the following combinations is correctly matched?
73.x: A triangular age pyramid indicates an expanding population. Bell-shaped and urn-shaped pyramids indicate stable and declining populations respectively.
73.tq: Compare the three age-pyramid forms with their population trends.
xs: **Triangular pyramid — expanding** population is correct — option **(4)**.
**Bell** = **stable**; **urn** = **declining**.
xa: Other population attributes: **natality**, **mortality**, **density**, **sex ratio**.
**r-selected**: many small offspring, little care (insects, weeds).

73.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the exchange characteristics of ecosystems and the Earth?
o: Ecosystems are open for energy and matter, while the Earth is open for energy but nearly closed for matter
Ecosystems are open only for matter, while the Earth is closed for energy
Ecosystems are closed for both energy and matter, while the Earth is open for both
Both ecosystems and the Earth are completely closed systems
73.x: Ecosystems exchange both energy and matter with their surroundings. The Earth receives energy from outside but is nearly closed with respect to matter.
73.tq: Compare open and closed characteristics across ecosystems and the Earth.
xs: Ecosystems are **open for energy and matter**; Earth is **open for energy** but **nearly closed for matter** — option **(1)**.
The other options wrongly call ecosystems or Earth closed for energy.
xa: Primary energy source = **Sun**; flow is **unidirectional**.
Energy flow obeys the **laws of thermodynamics**.

73.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the basic functional unit of ecology?
73.x: The ecosystem - a biotic community plus its non-living surroundings linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling - is the basic functional unit of ecology (APPSC PYQ). A population is one species in an area; a biome is a large climatic-vegetation region; the biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems.
73.tq: Functional unit of ecology = ecosystem.
xs: The **ecosystem** is the **basic functional unit of ecology** (APPSC PYQ) — option **(3)**.
A **population** is one species; a **biome** is a large climate-vegetation region; the **biosphere** is the top of the hierarchy.
xa: Term coined by **Tansley**, **1935**.
Functions: **energy flow** and **nutrient cycling**.

73.s: The rate of decomposition is likely to be fastest under which of the following conditions?
o: Detritus rich in nitrogen and sugars, with a warm and moist climate
Detritus rich in chitin, with cold and dry conditions
Detritus rich in lignin, with low temperature and anaerobic conditions
Detritus poor in nitrogen, with persistent waterlogging
73.x: Decomposition is rapid when detritus contains nitrogen and sugars and the climate is warm and moist. Lignin, chitin, low temperature and anaerobic conditions slow it down.
73.tq: Identify the combination of favourable and unfavourable decomposition conditions.
xs: Decay is fastest with detritus **rich in nitrogen and sugars** in a **warm and moist** climate — option **(1)**.
**Lignin**, **chitin**, **low temperature** and **anaerobic** conditions slow it.
xa: **Rainforest**: fast litter decay → thin, nutrient-poor soil.
**Taiga**: slow decay, thick litter, acidic soil.

73.s: Competing species may coexist when they
o: avoid all interaction with other species
use different parts or forms of a shared resource
73.x: Resource partitioning permits competing species to coexist by using different portions of a resource, such as different parts of the same plant.
73.tq: Apply the ecological principle of resource partitioning.
xs: Competitors coexist by **resource partitioning** — using **different parts of a shared resource** — option **(3)**.
Example: insect pests feeding on **different parts of the same plant**.
No two species occupy **exactly the same niche** (option 2).
xa: **Gause's competitive exclusion principle** governs competition (**-/-**).
Niche is **unique to each species** (**APPSC 2022**).

73.s: The sea star Pisaster ochraceus is regarded as a keystone species because it
73.x: Pisaster ochraceus is a keystone sea star that controls mussels in intertidal zones. This example is associated with the work of Robert Paine.
73.tq: Use the species–ecological effect association rather than the general definition alone.
xs: **Pisaster ochraceus** is keystone because it **controls mussels in intertidal zones** — option **(2)** (**APPSC 2024**).
It was studied by **Robert Paine**.
Building reefs is a **foundation** role (corals); SO2 indication is a **lichen** (indicator) role.
xa: Pisaster eating mussels is also an example of **predation** (+/-).
Other keystone species: **tiger, sea otter, fig**.

73.s: Which one of the following is a foundation species?
73.x: Foundation species create or shape the habitat itself; corals and kelp are examples.
73.tq: Distinguish habitat-building species from charismatic and environmental-indicator species.
xs: **Coral** is a **foundation species** — it creates/shapes the habitat — option **(3)**.
**Lichens** and **amphibians** are **indicators**; the **giant panda** is a **flagship** species.
xa: Other foundation species: **kelp**, **dominant trees**.
Coral reefs are the **'rainforests of the sea'**.

73.s: Which pair is NOT correctly matched?
o: Keystone species — effect much larger than its abundance
Umbrella species — attracts public support mainly through charisma
Foundation species — creates or shapes habitat
73.x: Attracting public support through charisma is the role of a flagship species. An umbrella species is wide-ranging, and its protection benefits many other species.
73.tq: Find the swapped definition among closely related conservation roles.
xs: **Umbrella — charisma** is wrong — option **(2)**; drawing public support by charisma is the **flagship** role (tiger, giant panda).
An **umbrella** species is **wide-ranging**; protecting it protects many others (tiger, snow leopard).
xa: Keystone, indicator and foundation pairs in the other options are correct.
The **tiger** fits keystone, flagship and umbrella roles.

73.s: The edge effect refers to the phenomenon in which an ecotone generally has
o: fewer species than either adjoining community
only species from the larger adjoining community
more species and higher density of some species than either adjoining community
73.x: The edge effect is the increased number of species and increased density of some species in an ecotone. Such organisms are called edge species.
73.tq: Use the comparison with adjoining communities to identify the edge effect.
xs: **Edge effect**: an ecotone has **more species** and **higher density of some species** than either community — option **(4)**.
Such species are called **edge species**.
xa: Example: higher **bird density** in the forest-desert ecotone.
Ecotone conditions are **intermediate**.

73.s: Which of the following is correctly matched?
o: Artificial or man-modified ecosystem — crop field
73.x: Crop fields are artificial or man-modified ecosystems. Forests, oceans, lakes, deserts and grasslands are natural ecosystems, while a city is an extreme artificial example.
73.tq: Use the human-disturbance distinction to eliminate mismatched examples.
xs: **Crop field — artificial / man-modified** is correct — option **(3)**.
**Open ocean** is natural; **industrial estate** and **city** are artificial.
xa: The **city** is the extreme artificial example.
Natural split: **terrestrial** vs **aquatic**.

73.s: Which one of the following does NOT belong to marine ecosystems?
73.x: Rivers are freshwater ecosystems. Coral reefs, hydrothermal vents and tidal zones are marine ecosystems.
73.tq: Find the freshwater item among marine ecosystem examples.
xs: A **river** is freshwater, not marine — option **(3)**.
**Tidal zones**, **hydrothermal vents** and **coral reefs** are marine.
xa: Rivers are **lotic** freshwater (**< 5 ppt**).
Vent food chains rest on **chemosynthetic bacteria**.

73.s: Gloger’s rule primarily explains variation in which of the following characteristics in relation to climate?
73.x: Gloger’s rule relates climate to colouration; warm and humid environments are generally associated with darker colouration.
73.tq: Direct one-fact recall of a confusable rule-trait relationship.
xs: **Gloger's rule** explains **colouration** — warm-humid = **darker** — option **(3)**.
Body size = **Bergmann**; limbs = **Allen**; vertebrae = **Jordan**.
xa: **Rensch** = size dimorphism in **shorebirds**.
Asked in **APPSC 2024** as a match.

73.s: India launched its first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems at which international event and venue?
73.x: India launched its first guide to Open Natural Ecosystems at UNCCD COP17 in Ulaanbaatar.
73.tq: Match the document with the correct convention and venue.
xs: India launched its first **Open Natural Ecosystems** guide at **UNCCD COP17, Ulaanbaatar** (Aug **2026**) — option **(3)**.
The other events are not linked to this guide in the notes.
xa: ONEs = **grasslands, deserts, scrub**.
They cover over **10%** of India; less than **5%** protected.

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Xerophyte
(b) Hydrophyte
(c) Halophyte
(d) Epiphyte

List-II
(i) Saline habitat
(ii) On another plant
(iii) Dry/desert
(iv) Aquatic/wetland
73.x: Xerophytes live in deserts, hydrophytes in water, halophytes in salty places and epiphytes on other plants, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
73.tq: Recall the habitat of each plant type.
n: Xerophytes inhabit dry or desert habitats. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Hydrophytes inhabit aquatic or wetland habitats. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Halophytes inhabit saline habitats. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Epiphytes grow on another plant. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Xerophytes** — **dry or desert** habitats; **hydrophytes** — **aquatic or wetland** habitats.
**Halophytes** — **saline** habitats; **epiphytes** — **grow on another plant** for support.
xa: ⚠ **Pneumatophores**, **vivipary** = halophytes; **aerenchyma** = hydrophytes; **CAM** = xerophytes.
Xerophytes **reduce water loss**: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines, succulence (e.g. **Opuntia**).
**Phreatophytes**: **groundwater zones**, **deep roots**.

73.s: Which term refers to the transition zone between two ecosystems or communities?
73.x: An ecotone is the transition zone where two ecosystems meet, such as forest and grassland. Lentic means still water, and a sere is a stage in succession.
73.tq: Discriminate ecotone, lentic, sere and anthrome.
n: An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems or communities. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A sere is the entire sequence of communities that successively change in an area. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Lentic water is still water. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
An anthropogenic biome is also called an anthrome. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: The **ecotone** is the **transition zone** between **two ecosystems** or **communities** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Lentic** means **still water** (ponds, lakes, swamps).
A **sere** is the **entire sequence of communities** that successively change in an area; an **anthrome** is a **human-altered terrestrial biosphere**.
xa: Ecotones can be **narrow** (grassland-forest) or **wide** (forest-desert).
Ecotone examples: **mangroves** (marine and terrestrial), **estuary** (fresh and salt water), riverbank (dry and wet).
**Edge effect**: more species and higher density of some species in the ecotone — these are **edge species**.
A uniform stand of one forest type is **not** an ecotone.

73.s:
Assertion (A): A biodiversity hotspot is a biologically rich and highly threatened region.
Reason (R): To qualify as a hotspot, a region must have at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species and must have lost at least 70% of its original habitat.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true and R explains A: the hotspot criteria (Myers; Conservation International) demand both high endemism and heavy habitat loss, which is exactly why every hotspot is both rich and threatened.
73.tq: Check whether R gives the criteria that produce A.
n: A biodiversity hotspot is a biologically rich region. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A biodiversity hotspot is a highly threatened region. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: Both **A and R are true**, and **R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **biodiversity hotspot** is a **biologically rich** and **highly threatened** region.
R's criteria — at least **1,500 endemic** vascular plant species and **70%** habitat lost — make a hotspot both rich and threatened.
xa: **Endemic species** are **restricted** to a **particular geographical area**.
An **invasive alien species**, introduced outside its natural range, **adversely affects** native ecosystems or species.
**Habitat fragmentation** breaks continuous habitat into **smaller isolated patches**.

73.s:
Assertion (A): Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and the environment.
Reason (R): An ecosystem is a functional unit of organisms and the environment.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
73.x: Both are true: ecology studies how organisms relate to their environment, and an ecosystem is a working unit of organisms and environment. One defines a science and the other a unit, so R does not explain A.
73.tq: Ask whether two definitions explain each other.
n: Ecology is the study of relationships between organisms and the environment. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
An ecosystem is a functional unit of organisms and the environment. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: Both **A and R are true**, but **R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A: **ecology** is the **study of relationships** between **organisms** and the **environment**.
R: an **ecosystem** is a **functional unit** of organisms and the environment — it defines a unit, not the science.
xa: "Ecology" was coined by **Ernst Haeckel**; "ecosystem" by **Arthur Tansley** in **1935**.
The ecosystem is the **basic functional unit of ecology**.
Ecological order: **organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere**.

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Anthropogenic biome
 b. Ecological footprint
 c. Global hectare
 d. Biogeochemical cycle

List-II
 i. Unit of ecological footprint
 ii. Movement of nutrient elements through ecosystem components
 iii. Human-altered terrestrial biosphere
 iv. Human demand on Earth's ecosystems
73.x: An anthrome is a human-altered biome, the ecological footprint is human demand on nature, the global hectare is its unit, and a biogeochemical cycle moves nutrients. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
73.tq: Match each term to its meaning.
n: An anthropogenic biome is a human-altered terrestrial biosphere. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
An ecological footprint is human demand on Earth's ecosystems. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A global hectare is a unit of ecological footprint. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A biogeochemical cycle is the movement of nutrient elements through ecosystem components. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Anthropogenic biome (anthrome)** — **human-altered terrestrial biosphere**; **ecological footprint** — **human demand** on Earth's ecosystems.
**Global hectare** — **unit** of the ecological footprint; **biogeochemical cycle** — **movement of nutrient elements** through ecosystem components.
xa: **Sere**: the **entire sequence of communities** that successively change in an area.
**Biodiversity hotspot**: a **biologically rich** and **highly threatened** region.
A biogeochemical cycle is also called the **nutritional cycle**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Habitat fragmentation is the breaking of continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches.
Statement B: Species diversity is the variety of species.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: habitat fragmentation breaks a continuous habitat into small isolated patches, and species diversity is the variety of species.
73.tq: Recall the biodiversity terms.
n: Habitat fragmentation is the breaking of continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Species diversity is the variety of species. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: **Both statements are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement A: **habitat fragmentation** is the **breaking of continuous habitat** into **smaller isolated patches**.
Statement B: **species diversity** is the **variety of species**.
xa: **Endemic species** are **restricted** to a particular geographical area.
**Alien species** are introduced **outside** their natural range; invasive ones **adversely affect** native species.
**Ecological footprint** is measured in **global hectares**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The niche concept is associated with Grinnell.
II. The maximum sustainable population is called carrying capacity.
III. The biosphere comprises all ecosystems together.
IV. The niche concept is associated with A.G. Tansley.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: I, II and III are correct: Grinnell introduced the niche, carrying capacity is the largest population an area can sustain, and the biosphere is all ecosystems together. IV is false because Tansley coined 'ecosystem'.
73.tq: Match each concept to who proposed it.
n: The niche concept is associated with Grinnell. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
The maximum sustainable population is called carrying capacity. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
The biosphere comprises all ecosystems together. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I: the **niche** concept is associated with **Grinnell**.
II: the **maximum sustainable population** is **carrying capacity**; III: the **biosphere** is **all ecosystems** together.
IV is wrong: **A.G. Tansley** coined **"ecosystem"** (**1935**), not the niche.
xa: Niche proponents: **Grinnell** (**1917**, habitat niche), **Elton** (**1927**, functional niche), **Hutchinson** (**1957**, n-dimensional).
The biosphere is **absent** at the poles, highest peaks and deepest oceans.
⚠ Habitat = **address**; niche = **profession**.

73.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
73.x: Grinnell proposed the habitat niche concept in 1917. Elton is associated with the functional niche, while Hutchinson proposed the n-dimensional niche.
73.tq: Match proponents with the specific form of niche concept.
xs: **Grinnell — habitat niche** (**1917**) is correct — option **(1)**.
**Elton** = **functional niche** (**1927**); **Hutchinson** = **n-dimensional niche** (**1957**).
xa: Elton also wrote **Animal Ecology** and described the **pyramid of numbers**.
**Gause** gave the **competitive exclusion principle**.
**Robert Paine** studied the keystone sea star **Pisaster ochraceus**.

73.s: Which of the following pairs of Indian estuaries is located on the west coast?
73.x: Narmada and Tapi are major west-coast estuaries. Hooghly, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Cauvery are east-coast estuaries.
73.tq: Separate the east-coast and west-coast groups before choosing the pair.
xs: **Narmada and Tapi** are **west-coast** estuaries — option **(4)**.
**Hooghly, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery** are **east-coast**.
xa: AP has a **1,053 km** coastline.
Estuary salinity reaches **35 ppt** at the mouth.

73.s: Ramdeo Misra is popularly known as the
73.x: Ramdeo Misra is recognised as the father of Indian ecology.
73.tq: Test a national attribution against similarly worded ecological titles.
xs: **Ramdeo Misra** = **father of Indian ecology** — option **(4)**.
**Odum** = father of modern ecosystem ecology; **Hutchinson** = n-dimensional niche.
xa: **Elton** wrote **Animal Ecology (1927)**.
**Haeckel** coined "ecology"; **Tansley** coined "ecosystem" (**1935**).

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Ecologist)
a. H.C. Cowles
b. F.E. Clements
c. A.G. Tansley
d. E.P. Odum

List-II (Contribution)
i. Coined the term ecosystem
 ii. Ecosystem ecology and Fundamentals of Ecology
 iii. Succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes
 iv. Phases of succession and monoclimax theory

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
73.x: Cowles studied succession on Lake Michigan sand dunes; Clements developed phases of succession and monoclimax theory; Tansley coined ecosystem; Odum contributed to ecosystem ecology and authored Fundamentals of Ecology.
73.tq: Start from the distinctive pair Tansley–ecosystem and complete the remaining matches.
xs: **Cowles – Lake Michigan dunes (iii)**, **Clements – phases of succession, monoclimax (iv)**, **Tansley – coined ecosystem (i)**, **Odum – Fundamentals of Ecology (ii)** — option **(1)**.
Cowles **1899**; Clements **1916**; Tansley **1935**; Odum **1953**.
xa: ⚠ Fundamentals of Ecology is **Odum's**, not E. Lucy Braun's.
**Lindeman** gave the **10% law** (**1942**).

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
 a. Biosphere (term)
 b. Ecosystem
 c. Ecology
 d. Biodiversity

List-II
 i. Raymond F. Dasmann
 ii. A.G. Tansley
 iii. Eduard Suess
 iv. Reiter & Ernst Haeckel
73.x: Eduard Suess coined 'biosphere' (1875), Tansley 'ecosystem' (1935), Reiter and Haeckel 'ecology', and Dasmann 'biological diversity', giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
73.tq: Match each term to who coined it.
n: Edward Suess is associated with the biosphere reserve. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
A.G. Tansley is associated with the ecosystem. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Reiter is associated with ecology. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Ernst Haeckel is associated with ecology. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Raymond F. Dasmann is associated with biodiversity. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Biosphere** — **Eduard Suess**; **ecosystem** — **A.G. Tansley** (**1935**).
**Ecology** — **Reiter and Ernst Haeckel**; **biodiversity** — **Raymond F. Dasmann**.
xa: **Lindeman** — the **10% law** of energy transfer (**1942**).
**Grinnell** — the **niche** concept (**1917**); **Elton** — functional niche (**1927**); **Hutchinson** — n-dimensional niche (**1957**).
**E.P. Odum** — Fundamentals of Ecology (**1953**); **H.C. Cowles** — ecological succession (**1899**).
⚠ Haeckel coined "ecology" — the notes give **1869** and **1866** in different places.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about the environment:
1. Its chemical interactions include the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
2. Its biological component consists of nutrients, water and air.
3. It is the surroundings and conditions in which organisms live, and it is never static.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 3 is correct: environment means the surroundings and conditions in which organisms live, and it is never static. Statement 1 is correct: carbon and nitrogen cycles are its chemical interactions. Statement 2 is wrong: nutrients, water and air form the physical component; the biological component is the organisms. Hence 1 and 3 only.
73.tq: Physical = nutrients, water, air; biological = organisms; chemical = C and N cycles.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the environment's **chemical interactions** include the **carbon** and **nitrogen cycles**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **nutrients, water and air** form the **physical** component; the **biological** component is the **organisms**.
Statement 3 is correct: the environment is the **surroundings and conditions** in which organisms live, and it is **never static**.
xa: Categories of environment: **physical** (lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere), **biotic** (plants, animals, microbes) and **cultural** (man-made).
Primary functions: **provide resources**, **assimilate wastes**, and give **habitat** for biodiversity.
⚠ Trap: **"generating synthetic chemicals"** is **NOT** a function of the environment (APPSC **2024**).
**Habitat** always has life and suits one species; the **environment** may not have life.

73.s: Which of the following is included in the cultural category of the environment?
73.x: The cultural environment is man-made and includes social, economic and political aspects.
73.tq: Identify the man-made category rather than a natural component.
xs: **Political institutions** fall in the **cultural** (man-made) category — option **(2)**.
Cultural = **social, economic, political**; wild animals are **biotic**; atmospheric gases and soil minerals are **physical**.
xa: Physical = **lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere**.
Biotic = **plants, animals, microbes**.
Functions: resources, **assimilating wastes**, habitat for biodiversity.

73.s: Which one of the following is NOT a primary function of the environment?
73.x: The primary functions of the environment are providing resources, assimilating wastes and serving as a habitat for biodiversity. Generating synthetic chemicals is not one of them (APPSC 2024 trap).
73.tq: Resources, waste assimilation, habitat - synthetic chemicals is the odd one out.
xs: **Generating synthetic chemicals** is NOT a function — option **(3)** (**APPSC 2024** trap).
The primary functions: **provide resources**, **assimilate wastes**, **habitat for biodiversity**.
xa: Environment includes **physical**, **biotic** and **cultural** categories.
Environment is **never static**.

73.s: Which one of the following represents a functional process of an ecosystem rather than its structure?
73.x: Nutrient cycling is an ecosystem function. Species composition, trophic levels and abiotic materials are elements of ecosystem structure.
73.tq: Discriminate between the structure and function columns of an ecosystem.
xs: **Nutrient cycling** is a **function** — option **(2)**.
**Trophic levels**, **abiotic materials** and **species composition** are **structure**.
xa: Other functions: **energy flow** (one-way from the sun), primary and secondary production, self-regulation.
Nutrients **cycle** (biogeochemical cycles); energy **flows one way**.

73.s: An abiotic factor is best defined as which one of the following?
o: An organism that obtains food from dead organic matter
Any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment
A living component occupying the highest trophic level
A biological interaction between two species
73.x: An abiotic factor is any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment, such as light, temperature, water or soil.
73.tq: Use the precise definition rather than examples alone.
xs: An **abiotic factor** is **any non-living component that affects organisms or their environment** (**APPSC 2018**) — option **(2)**.
Feeding on dead matter = **saprotrophs**; species interactions are biotic.
xa: Types: **climatic**, **edaphic** (soil), **topographic**.
Abiotic factors can be **limiting or enabling**.

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Type of abiotic factor)
(a) Climatic
(b) Edaphic
(c) Topographic

List-II (Examples)
(i) Altitude, slope and aspect
(ii) Light, temperature and rainfall
(iii) Soil texture, pH and minerals

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Climatic factors include light, temperature and rainfall; edaphic factors relate to soil; topographic factors include altitude, slope and aspect.
73.tq: Start from the meaning of edaphic and topographic before matching the remaining pair.
xs: **Climatic – light, temperature, rainfall (ii)**; **Edaphic – soil texture, pH, minerals (iii)**; **Topographic – altitude, slope, aspect (i)** — option **(1)**.
Edaphic always means **soil**.
xa: Climatic factors also include **humidity** and **wind**.
**Liebig** = law of the **minimum**; **Shelford** = law of **tolerance**.

73.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism or group)
 a. Humans
 b. Saprotrophs
 c. Reptiles
 d. Camel

List-II (Characteristic)
 i. Cold-blooded
 ii. Desert-adapted
 iii. Feed on dead matter
 iv. Omnivores

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Humans are omnivores, saprotrophs feed on dead matter, reptiles are cold-blooded, and camels are adapted to desert conditions.
73.tq: Begin with the distinctive camel and saprotroph pairs, then complete the remaining matches.
xs: **Humans – omnivores (iv)**, **saprotrophs – dead matter (iii)**, **reptiles – cold-blooded (i)**, **camel – desert-adapted (ii)** — option **(1)** (**APPSC 2023**).
Saprotrophs (decomposers) are **bacteria and fungi**.
xa: Detritivores: **earthworms**, nematodes, arthropods.
Desert fauna: camels, lizards, snakes, scorpions — mostly **nocturnal**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about producers in different ecosystems:
1. At deep-sea vents, chemosynthetic bacteria such as sulphur bacteria are the producers, using chemical energy rather than light.
2. In terrestrial ecosystems, herbs, shrubs and trees are the producers.
3. In aquatic ecosystems, zooplankton are the main producers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 3 is wrong: aquatic producers are phytoplankton, algae and submerged and floating plants; zooplankton are primary consumers. Statement 2 is correct: herbs, shrubs and trees are terrestrial producers. Statement 1 is correct: chemosynthetic (e.g. sulphur) bacteria are the producers at deep-sea vents, using chemical energy. Hence 1 and 2 only.
73.tq: Phyto = producer, zoo = consumer; vents run on chemosynthesis.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: at **deep-sea vents**, **chemosynthetic bacteria** (e.g. **sulphur bacteria**) are producers using **chemical energy**, not light.
Statement 2 is correct: **herbs, shrubs and trees** are the producers of **terrestrial** ecosystems.
Statement 3 is wrong: aquatic producers are **phytoplankton**, algae and submerged/floating plants; **zooplankton** are **primary consumers**.
xa: **Diatoms and cyanobacteria** are **ocean producers**; the **copepod** is a **primary consumer**.
**Photoautotrophs** use sunlight (green plants, algae, cyanobacteria); **chemoautotrophs** use chemical oxidation (e.g. **nitrifying bacteria**).
Chemoautotrophic **bacteria in deep ocean trenches** use **hydrogen sulphide** from sea-floor cracks.
Decomposers (**saprotrophs / osmotrophs**) are **bacteria and fungi**; detritivores include earthworms, nematodes, arthropods.

73.s: Chemoautotrophic bacteria inhabiting deep ocean trenches may obtain energy by oxidising which substance released from sea-floor cracks?
73.x: Chemoautotrophic bacteria in deep ocean trenches can use hydrogen sulphide released from cracks on the sea floor as an energy source.
73.tq: Direct recall of the specialised energy source used by deep-sea chemoautotrophs.
xs: Deep-trench chemoautotrophs use **hydrogen sulphide** from sea-floor cracks — option **(4)**.
They rely on **chemical oxidation**, not sunlight.
xa: Other chemoautotrophs: **nitrifying bacteria**; **methanogen** archaea.
Vent chains rest on **chemosynthetic bacteria**.

73.s: Decomposers are regarded as a link between the biotic and abiotic components because they:
o: Convert dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients reused by producers
Prevent nutrient cycling in the soil
73.x: Decomposers release inorganic nutrients from dead organic matter, making them available again to producers and linking living and non-living components.
73.tq: Apply the link concept by tracing nutrients from dead organisms back to producers.
xs: Decomposers turn dead matter into **inorganic nutrients reused by producers** — option **(1)** — so they are the **link between biotic and abiotic** parts.
They drive, not prevent, nutrient cycling.
xa: Main decomposers: **bacteria and fungi** (saprotrophs / osmotrophs).
Nutrients **cycle** (biogeochemical cycles); energy flows **one way**.
⚠ Decomposers get **no place** in ecological pyramids despite their role.

73.s: Which of the following statements regarding ecological pyramids is correct?
o: The base represents top consumers and the apex represents producers.
The base generally represents producers and the apex represents top consumers.
Ecological pyramids have only two types.
All organisms occupy only one trophic level.
73.x: The base of an ecological pyramid represents producers and the apex represents top consumers. The three types are pyramids of number, biomass and energy.
73.tq: Use the structural rule of ecological pyramids: producers at the base and top consumers at the apex.
xs: The **base = producers**; the **apex = top consumers** — option **(2)**.
There are **three** types (number, biomass, energy), not two; a species may occupy more than one level.
xa: Count **all** organisms at a level.
**Energy pyramid** is **always upright**.

73.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Freshwater — open oceans and shallow seas
Marine water — coral reefs and open oceans
Brackish water — estuaries and mangrove swamps
73.x: Open oceans and shallow seas are marine ecosystems, not freshwater ecosystems. Springs and rivers are lotic freshwater examples, while lakes and ponds are lentic examples.
73.tq: Find the reversed category-example pair.
xs: **Freshwater — open oceans and shallow seas** is wrong — option **(1)**; those are **marine**.
Coral reefs are marine; estuaries and mangrove swamps are brackish; springs and rivers are freshwater.
xa: ⚠ **Lentic** = still; **lotic** = flowing.
Freshwater salinity: **< 5 ppt**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about forest soils:
1. Tropical rainforest soil is often thin and nutrient-poor because litter decays fast.
2. Taiga (boreal) forests show fast decay, thin litter and highly fertile soil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 1 is correct: fast litter decay in rainforests leaves thin, nutrient-poor soil. Statement 2 is wrong: taiga has slow decay, thick litter and acidic soil. Hence 1 only.
73.tq: Rainforest = fast decay, thin soil; taiga = slow decay, thick litter, acidic soil.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: in the **tropical rainforest**, **fast litter decay** leaves **thin, nutrient-poor soil**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **taiga** has **slow decay**, **thick litter** and **acidic soil**.
xa: Forest types: **tropical rainforest**, tropical deciduous (**monsoon**), temperate deciduous, **taiga / boreal** (evergreen coniferous).
The rainforest has the **highest species richness on land**.
Mature forests give little **net oxygen** (respiration balances photosynthesis) but are vital **carbon sinks**.

73.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical adaptation of desert flora?
o: Broad, thin leaves that increase water loss
73.x: Desert plants commonly have deep roots, small or spiny leaves and waxy cuticles. Broad, thin leaves would generally increase water loss.
73.tq: Identify the option that contradicts the water-conservation principle.
xs: **Broad, thin leaves** are not a desert adaptation — option **(2)**; they would lose water.
Desert plants have **deep roots**, **small or spiny leaves** and a **waxy cuticle**.
xa: **Xerophytes** also show sunken stomata, succulence and **CAM** (e.g. **Opuntia**).
Desert fauna are mostly **nocturnal** and water-saving.

73.s: Which lake zone is characterised by shallow water, light reaching the bottom and rooted plants?
73.x: The littoral zone is the shallow edge of a lake where light reaches the bottom and rooted plants commonly grow.
73.tq: Match the zone with its physical features and vegetation.

73.s: Which group of microorganisms acts as the main decomposers of dead organic matter?
73.x: Saprophytic fungi and bacteria are the main decomposers, breaking dead matter down and recycling nutrients. Lactobacillus makes curd, while Rhizobium and Anabaena fix nitrogen.
73.tq: Pick the saprophytes among microbes known for other jobs.
n: Fungi perform decomposition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
xs: **Saprophytic fungi and bacteria** are the **main decomposers** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Bacteria** and **fungi** **decompose organic matter** into **inorganic nutrients reused by producers**.
Decomposers (**saprotrophs / osmotrophs**) are the **link between biotic and abiotic** parts.
xa: Helpers: **earthworms**, nematodes, arthropods (**detritivores**).
Steps: **fragmentation** → **leaching** → **catabolism** → **humification** → **mineralisation**.
Decomposition is **slow** with **lignin, chitin**, low temperature and **anaerobic** conditions.

73.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Photoautotrophs — Chemical oxidation as the energy source
Chemoautotrophs — Sunlight as the energy source
Photoautotrophs — Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria
Archaea — All members depend on photosynthesis
73.x: Photoautotrophs use sunlight and include green plants, algae and cyanobacteria. Chemoautotrophs obtain energy through chemical oxidation, while many archaea are chemoautotrophic.
73.tq: Use the energy-source distinction to separate photoautotrophs from chemoautotrophs.
xs: **Photoautotrophs — green plants, algae, cyanobacteria** is correct — option **(3)**.
Photoautotrophs use **sunlight**; **chemoautotrophs** use **chemical oxidation** — options (1) and (2) swap them.
Many **archaea** are **chemoautotrophic** (e.g. methanogens), not photosynthetic.
xa: Chemoautotroph examples: **nitrifying bacteria**; bacteria using **hydrogen sulphide**.
Deep-sea vent producers are **chemosynthetic bacteria** (e.g. **sulphur bacteria**).

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding food chains:
1. A grazing food chain begins with living green plants.
2. A detritus food chain begins with dead organic matter.
3. In a grazing food chain, energy captured by autotrophs is transferred to herbivores.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. Grazing chains begin with living producers, whereas detritus chains begin with dead leaves, remains or other dead organic matter.
73.tq: Test the defining starting point and energy-transfer direction of each food-chain type.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **grazing** chain starts with **living green plants** — correct.
Statement 2: **detritus** chain starts with **dead organic matter** — correct.
Statement 3: **autotrophs** capture energy and pass it to **herbivores** — correct (**PYQ 2025**).
xa: ⚠ "Grazing chain begins with dead leaves" = **false** (**APPSC-G2 2025**).
Grazing example: **grass → goat → human** (**PYQ 2025**).

73.s: A food chain beginning with leaf litter and proceeding through earthworms to birds is classified as a:
73.x: A detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter such as leaf litter and proceeds through detritivores such as earthworms to higher consumers.
73.tq: Distinguish the two chains by asking whether the first component is living vegetation or dead organic matter.
xs: **Leaf litter → earthworm → bird** is a **detritus food chain** — option **(1)**.
A detritus chain begins with **dead organic matter**; a **grazing** chain begins with **living green plants**.
xa: Detritivores and decomposers form the **base of the detritus chain** and recycle all levels.
Grazing example: **grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle** (UPSC).

73.s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence in an aquatic food chain?
o: Zooplankton → phytoplankton → large fish → small fish
Large fish → small fish → zooplankton → phytoplankton
Phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish
Small fish → phytoplankton → zooplankton → large fish
73.x: Phytoplankton are producers, zooplankton are primary consumers, and small and large fish occupy progressively higher trophic positions.
73.tq: Arrange the organisms from producer to successively larger consumers.
xs: Aquatic sequence: **phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish** — option **(3)**.
Phytoplankton are **producers of the sea**; zooplankton are **primary consumers**.
xa: Pond: **phytoplankton → zooplankton → fish**, with bacteria/fungi as decomposers.
Grassland: **grass → grasshopper/rabbit → snake/hawk**.

73.s:
Which of the following organisms occupies the first trophic level in an ecosystem?
1. Phytoplankton
2. Seaweeds
3. Green plants
4. Zooplankton
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
73.x: Phytoplankton, seaweeds and green plants are producers and occupy the first trophic level. Zooplankton are primary consumers at the second trophic level.
73.tq: Separate producers from primary consumers before selecting the coded combination.
xs: **Phytoplankton, seaweeds, green plants** are **producers (T1)** — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Zooplankton** are **T2 – primary consumers**.
xa: **Chemosynthetic bacteria** (at hydrothermal vents) are also T1 producers.
T3 = carnivores (**secondary consumers**); T4 = top carnivores.

73.s: Why can the biomass pyramid in an aquatic ecosystem be inverted?
o: Fish do not consume zooplankton in aquatic ecosystems.
Energy increases at every aquatic trophic level.
Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but rapidly support larger zooplankton and fish biomass.
73.x: Phytoplankton have a small standing crop but reproduce and are consumed rapidly, allowing them to support a larger standing biomass of zooplankton and fish.
73.tq: Distinguish standing biomass from productivity and identify the fast-turnover producer explanation.
xs: **Phytoplankton** have a **small standing crop** but turn over fast, supporting larger **zooplankton/fish** biomass — option **(4)**.
So the **biomass pyramid** is inverted in the **sea**.
xa: On land (forest, grassland) the biomass pyramid is **upright**.
**Energy pyramid** is never inverted.

73.s: DDT contamination in an aquatic food chain is most directly associated with which of the following effects?
o: Thinning of bird eggshells and crashes in seabird populations
Thickening of bird eggshells and increase in seabird populations
Conversion of mercury into oxygen in seabirds
Immediate destruction of all aquatic vegetation
73.x: DDT causes thinning of bird eggshells and has been associated with crashes in seabird populations.
73.tq: Link a named pollutant with its characteristic ecological impact in an applied situation.
xs: **DDT** causes **thinning of bird eggshells** and **seabird population crashes** — option **(1)**.
It hits **fish-eating birds** at the top of aquatic chains.
xa: ⚠ Mercury → **Minamata disease**; DDT → **eggshell thinning**.
DDT is **persistent and fat-soluble**.

73.s: The association between a fig tree and a fig wasp is an example of
73.x: The fig wasp pollinates the fig and obtains a breeding site, making the association a coevolved mutualistic relationship.
73.tq: Apply the benefit-benefit relationship to a specialised natural association.
xs: **Fig and fig wasp** is **coevolved mutualism** (+/+) — option **(1)**: pollination in return for a **breeding site**.
Amensalism (-/0) and neutralism (0/0) do not fit.
xa: Other coevolved pairs: **yucca – yucca moth**; **Ophrys orchid – bee**.
**Lichen** (alga + fungus) is also mutualism.

73.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Rule — Ecogeographic trait
o: Bergmann — Number of vertebrae in fish
Allen — Body colouration in warm-humid climates
Jordan — Number of vertebrae in fish
Gloger — Sexual size dimorphism in shorebirds
73.x: Jordan's rule relates temperature to the number of vertebrae in fish; colder conditions are associated with a greater number of vertebrae. Bergmann concerns body size, Allen concerns appendages, and Gloger concerns colouration.
73.tq: Use direct rule-trait discrimination and reject the swapped associations.
xs: **Jordan's rule** links temperature to the **number of vertebrae** in fish (colder = more) — option **(3)**.
**Bergmann** = **body size**; **Allen** = **ears/limbs**; **Gloger** = **colouration**; **Rensch** = sexual size dimorphism.
xa: **APPSC 2024** answer: colouration-Gloger, vertebrae-Jordan, body size-Bergmann, shorebirds-Rensch.
Gloger: warm-humid = **darker**.

73.s:
Match the habitat group with its characteristic association:
List-I
(a) Hydrophytes
(b) Lithophytes
(c) Epiphytes
(d) Cuscuta

List-II
(i) On host plants as a stem parasite
(ii) Aquatic habitats
(iii) Rocks
(iv) Grow on another plant mainly for support
73.x: Hydrophytes grow in water, lithophytes on rocks, epiphytes on other plants for support, and Cuscuta as a stem parasite on hosts, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
73.tq: Recall the habitat of each plant type.
n: Hydrophytes inhabit aquatic habitats. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 112-114]
Lithophytes inhabit rocks. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 112-114]
Epiphytes grow on another plant mainly for physical support. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 112-114]
Cuscuta grows on host plants as a stem parasite. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 112-114]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Hydrophytes** — **aquatic** habitats; **lithophytes** — **rocks**.
**Epiphytes** — **grow on another plant** mainly for **physical support**; **Cuscuta** — a **stem parasite** on host plants.
xa: Hydrophytes have **aerenchyma** (air-filled tissue), reduced roots and thin cuticle (e.g. **Hydrilla**, lotus).
Epiphytes get **moisture and nutrients** from their **surroundings**.
**Cuscuta** is a **parasitic angiosperm**; its parasitism is a **+/-** interaction.
**Phreatophytes** live in **groundwater zones** with **deep roots**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: In the ant–fungus association, ants cultivate fungus as food.
Statement B: Fig association involves a highly specific pollination relationship between a fig and a specific wasp.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: leafcutter ants farm fungus for food, and each fig species is pollinated by its own specific fig wasp.
73.tq: Recall the examples of mutualism.
n: Fig association involves a fig and a specific wasp. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61-2 · pp 114-116]
Fig association is a highly specific pollination relationship. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61-2 · pp 114-116]
The ant cultivates the fungus as food. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61-2 · pp 114-116]
Ant–fungus symbiosis involves an ant and a fungus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #61-2 · pp 114-116]
xs: **Both statements are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement A: in the **ant–fungus symbiosis**, the **ant cultivates** the **fungus** as **food**.
Statement B: the **fig association** is a **highly specific pollination** relationship between a **fig** and a specific **fig wasp**.
xa: Coevolved plant-pollinator pairs: **fig - fig wasp**, **yucca - yucca moth**, **Ophrys orchid - bee** (sexual deceit).
In mutualism the fig wasp gets a **breeding site** for pollination (**+/+**).
**Protozoan symbiosis**: protozoa with **bacteria, algae or animals** — **mutualistic associations**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Azotobacter is associated with N₂ fixation.
Statement B: Decomposer bacteria break down organic matter.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
73.x: Both are true: free-living Azotobacter fixes nitrogen, and decomposer bacteria break down dead organic matter.
73.tq: Recall the roles of soil bacteria.
n: Azotobacter performs free-living nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Decomposer bacteria break down organic matter. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
Bacteria perform decomposition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #65 · pp 122-124]
xs: **Both statements are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement A: **Azotobacter** is associated with **N₂ fixation**.
Statement B: **decomposer bacteria** **break down** organic matter; **bacteria and fungi** are the **main decomposers**.
xa: Decomposition steps: **fragmentation** → **leaching** → **catabolism** → **humification** → **mineralisation**.
Decomposers break dead matter into **inorganic nutrients reused by producers** — the **link between biotic and abiotic** parts.
Decomposition is **fast** with nitrogen- and sugar-rich detritus in **warm and moist** climate; **slow** with **lignin, chitin**, low temperature and **anaerobic** conditions.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about the carbon cycle:
I. Respiration removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.
II. Decay of organic matter releases CO₂.
III. Photosynthesis takes up CO₂.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement I is wrong: respiration releases CO₂, as do decay and fossil-fuel combustion. Statement II is correct: decay releases CO₂. Statement III is correct: photosynthesis takes up (removes) CO₂. Hence II and III only.
73.tq: Only photosynthesis takes CO₂ in; respiration, decay and burning give it out.
xs: Statements **II and III** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
I is wrong: **respiration** **releases** CO₂, not removes it.
II is correct: **decay** **releases** CO₂ — as do respiration and **fossil-fuel combustion**.
III is correct: **photosynthesis** **takes up / removes** CO₂.
xa: The carbon cycle is **CO₂ exchange** through **biological processes**.
Mature forests are vital **carbon sinks**.
The **water cycle** is driven by **solar energy**; the **phosphorus cycle** involves **rock weathering**.

73.s:
The physical category of the environment consists of which of the following?
1. Lithosphere
2. Hydrosphere
3. Atmosphere
4. Microbes
73.x: Lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere constitute the physical category. Microbes belong to the biotic category.
73.tq: Separate physical components from living components.
xs: The physical category is **lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere** — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Microbes** belong to the **biotic** category (plants, animals, microbes).
xa: **Cultural** category = man-made: social, economic, political.
Composite nature: physical + biological + chemical interactions.
⚠ "Generating synthetic chemicals" is **NOT** a function of the environment (**APPSC 2024**).

73.s:
With reference to habitat and environment, consider the following statements:
1. A habitat always has life.
2. A habitat is suited to a particular species.
3. An environment may exist even in the absence of life.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: A habitat is a living place suited to a species, whereas environment is broader and may include conditions without life.
73.tq: Discriminate between two closely related ecological terms.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statements 1 and 2: a **habitat always has life** and **suits one species** — correct.
Statement 3: an **environment may not have life** — correct.
xa: One habitat can hold **many species**.
All habitats are environments; **not all environments are habitats**.
⚠ Habitat = **"address"**; niche = **"profession"**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about the biosphere:
1. It is absent at the poles, the highest peaks and the deepest oceans.
2. Fungal and bacterial spores occurring above 8,000 metres are dormant.
3. Energy enters the biosphere from the Sun, while nutrients are recycled within it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements correctly describe the limits and functioning of the biosphere. Solar energy enters the system, whereas nutrients undergo internal recycling.
73.tq: Combine three independent factual statements and identify the inclusive option.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: biosphere is absent at the **poles, highest peaks, deepest oceans** — correct.
Statement 2: spores above **8,000 m** are **dormant** — correct.
Statement 3: energy comes from the **sun**; nutrients are **recycled within** — correct.
xa: Earth is **open for energy** but **nearly closed for matter**.
Energy flows **one way**; nutrients **cycle** (biogeochemical cycles).

73.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. One habitat may contain many species.
2. All habitats are environments.
3. All environments are habitats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: A habitat is a particular physical place within the broader concept of environment. Thus, one habitat can contain many species and all habitats are environments, but all environments are not habitats.
73.tq: Spot the reversed universal statement in a definition-based question.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **one habitat can hold many species** — correct.
Statement 2: **all habitats are environments** — correct.
Statement 3: **not all environments are habitats** — wrong.
xa: A habitat always has **life**; an environment may not.
Habitat = **address**; niche = **profession**.

73.s:
Consider the following statements about population growth:
1. An S-shaped curve shows logistic growth that levels off at the carrying capacity K.
2. Carrying capacity is the maximum population an environment can sustain.
3. A J-shaped curve shows logistic growth that levels off at carrying capacity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
73.x: Statement 3 is wrong: the J-curve is exponential growth with unlimited resources (dN/dt = rN); levelling off belongs to the S-curve. Statement 1 is correct: the S-curve is logistic growth levelling at K (dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K). Statement 2 is correct: carrying capacity is the maximum sustainable population. Hence 1 and 2 only.
73.tq: J = exponential, unlimited; S = logistic, stops at K.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the **S-curve** is **logistic growth** levelling at **carrying capacity K** (dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K).
Statement 2 is correct: **carrying capacity** is the **maximum sustainable population**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **J-curve** is **exponential growth** with **unlimited resources** (dN/dt = rN); it does not level off.
xa: **Natality** = births; rate = **individuals produced per female per unit time**; **mortality** = deaths per unit time.
Age pyramids: **triangular** = expanding; **bell** = stable; **urn** = declining.
**r-selected** species: many small offspring, little care (insects, weeds); **K-selected**: few large offspring, much care, near **K** (elephants, humans).

73.s:
Consider the following statements regarding r-selected and K-selected species:
1. Insects and weeds commonly show r-selected characteristics.
2. Elephants and humans commonly show K-selected characteristics.
3. K-selected species generally produce few large offspring and provide considerable parental care.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
73.x: All three statements are correct. r-selected species include many insects and weeds, whereas elephants and humans illustrate the K-selected strategy of fewer offspring and greater care.
73.tq: Combine examples with the contrasting reproductive strategies.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **insects, weeds** are **r-selected** — correct.
Statement 2: **elephants, humans** are **K-selected** — correct.
Statement 3: K-selected species have **few large offspring** and **much care** — correct.
xa: r-selected: many small offspring, short life, **unstable habitats**.
K-selected species live **near K** (carrying capacity).

73.s:
