81.s: Which of the following statements about India's performance in the Sustainable Development Report 2026 is NOT correct?
o: India lagged on 13 of the 17 SDGs.
India ranked below Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka.
SDG 2 was identified as India's biggest concern.
India ranked above all its South Asian neighbours.
81.x: India ranked below Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka; therefore, it did not rank above all its South Asian neighbours.
81.tq: Find the reversed comparison in the option describing relative performance.
xs: The incorrect statement: India ranked **above all its South Asian neighbours** — option **(4)**.
India is still **below Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka**.
It lags on **13 of 17** goals, with **SDG 2** (Zero Hunger) the biggest worry — options (1)-(3) are correct.
xa: India's best-ever rank: **94th** in **2026**.
SDR scores run **0 to 100**; publisher **UN SDSN**.
Indian schemes for SDG 2: **NFSA**, **POSHAN Abhiyaan**.

81.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's SDG monitoring:
1. MoSPI develops the National Indicator Framework, while NITI Aayog coordinates SDG work.
2. The SDG-NIF Progress Report 2026 tracks 277 indicators across all 17 SDGs.
3. The SDG-NIF is modelled on the Human Development Index framework.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
81.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: MoSPI develops the NIF, NITI Aayog coordinates, and the 2026 report tracks 277 indicators. Statement 3 is wrong: it is modelled on the UN Global Indicator Framework, not the HDI. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
81.tq: NIF: MoSPI makes it, 277 indicators, modelled on UN Global Indicator Framework.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **MoSPI** develops the **NIF**; **NITI Aayog** coordinates.
**Statement 2:** correct — the **2026** report tracks **277 indicators** across all **17** SDGs.
**Statement 3:** wrong — it is modelled on the **UN Global Indicator Framework**.
xa: SDR is by **UN SDSN**.
First **SDG India Index**: **2018**.

81.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine themes used for Localised Sustainable Development Goals in Gram Panchayats?
81.x: The nine themes include women-friendly village, water-sufficient village and good governance; an industrially advanced village is not listed as a theme.
81.tq: Find the plausible-looking but unlisted theme.
xs: "**Industrially advanced village**" is not one of the **9 themes** — option **(1)**.
**Women-friendly village**, **good governance** and **water-sufficient village** are themes.
xa: Other themes: poverty-free and better livelihoods; healthy; **child-friendly**; **clean and green**.
Also: **self-sufficient infrastructure**; **socially just and secure**.
Framework of the **Ministry of Panchayati Raj**.

81.s: In the Sustainable Development Report 2026, India achieved its best-ever rank of:
81.x: India's best-ever rank is 94th, in SDR 2026. 99th was its 2025 rank, when it first entered the top 100; 109th and 112th are lower ranks from before that.
81.tq: SDR: 99th (2025, first top-100) then 94th (2026, best ever).
xs: India's best-ever SDR rank is **94th** in **2026** — option **(2)**.
The SDR is published by **UN SDSN**.
xa: India is still below **Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka**.
India lags on **13 of 17** goals; **SDG 2** is the biggest worry.
**SDR 2025** leader: **Finland** (**87**).

81.s: Which one of the following is NOT the title of a Sustainable Development Goal?
81.x: Green Economy is not one of the 17 SDG titles. The other three are SDG 12, SDG 16 and SDG 17 respectively.
81.tq: Find the odd title among exact SDG formulations.
xs: "**Green Economy**" is not an SDG title — option **(1)**.
**SDG 12** = Responsible Consumption and Production; **SDG 16** = Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions; **SDG 17** = Partnerships for the Goals.
xa: ⚠ "**Blue Economy**" and "**Digital Inclusion**" are also not SDG titles.
Blue Economy maps to **SDG 14** (Life Below Water).
There are **17** SDGs with **169** targets.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about the green economy:
1. It decouples growth from resource use and pollution and fosters green industries and green jobs.
2. It was a central theme of the Rio+20 conference in 2012.
3. Green jobs are limited to work directly related to renewable-energy generation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is correct: a green economy decouples growth from resource use and pollution and fosters green industries and jobs. Statement 2 is correct: it was a central theme of Rio+20 (2012). Statement 3 is wrong: green jobs are any work in farming, industry, services or administration that preserves or restores environmental quality. So '1 only' misses Rio+20, and options with 3 are wrong.
82.tq: Green jobs are broad (farming to administration) - 'only renewables' is the trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — a green economy **decouples** growth from resource use and pollution and fosters **green industries and green jobs**.
**Statement 2:** correct — it was the central theme of **Rio+20, 2012**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — **green jobs** are any work in **farming, industry, services or administration** that preserves or restores environmental quality.
xa: A green economy also **reduces environmental risks and ecological scarcity**.
**UNEP Green Economy Initiative**: **2008**; **PAGE**: **2013**.
**Green Skill Development Programme** (**2017**) trains youth for green jobs.

82.s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of green technology?
o: It recycles more of its waste.
It is necessarily inexpensive for developing countries.
82.x: High cost is a major barrier to green technology, particularly for developing countries; it is not necessarily inexpensive.
82.tq: Find the exception by separating core characteristics from the stated barrier.
xs: The wrong claim is that green technology is **inexpensive for developing countries** — option **(4)**; **high cost** is its main barrier (PYQ key).
Green technology does **pollute less**, **uses resources sustainably** and **recycles more of its waste** — options (1)-(3).
xa: **Green economy** fosters **green industries and green jobs** (PYQ answer).
**Green chemistry** principles: waste prevention, **atom economy**, safer solvents.
**Green Pharmacy** applies green chemistry to medicines.

82.s: Greenwashing refers to
o: the compulsory recycling of all industrial waste
making false or exaggerated claims that a product, firm or investment is environmentally friendly
the restoration of polluted water bodies through biological methods
the conversion of all investments into government securities
82.x: Greenwashing is the practice of making false or exaggerated environmental claims about a product, firm or investment.
82.tq: Distinguish misleading environmental communication from genuine environmental improvement.
xs: **Greenwashing** = **false or exaggerated claims** that a product, firm or investment is environmentally friendly — option **(2)**.
The other options describe recycling, restoration or investment changes, not greenwashing.
xa: Remedy: a clear **taxonomy** to curb greenwashing and "**transition washing**".
India still has **no final green taxonomy**.
**SEBI** regulates **ESG Rating Providers**.

82.s: The Green Skill Development Programme was launched in 2017 by the
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship alone
82.x: The Green Skill Development Programme was launched in 2017 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
82.tq: Use the ministry-and-year pair and reject the neighbouring ministry trap.
xs: The **Green Skill Development Programme** was launched in **2017** by the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change** (MoEFCC) — option **(2)**.
It was built on the **ENVIS** network, MoEFCC's information network.
xa: It trains youth for **green jobs**.
Areas: **biodiversity conservation**, **pollution monitoring**, **waste management**, forestry and wildlife.
⚠ Sequence: UNEP GEI **2008** → Rio+20 **2012** → PAGE **2013** → GSDP **2017** → European Green Deal **2019**.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about the European Green Deal:
1. It was launched in December 2019.
2. It aims at a climate-neutral European Union by 2030.
3. Its legislative package for cutting greenhouse gases by at least 55% by 2030 (vs 1990) is called 'Fit for 55'.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is correct: launched December 2019. Statement 2 is wrong: climate neutrality is targeted by 2050; 2030 is the year for the 55% cut. Statement 3 is correct: the package is 'Fit for 55'. Hence only 1 and 3; every other option includes statement 2 or leaves out 3.
82.tq: 2030 = 55% cut; 2050 = climate neutral.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — launched **December 2019**.
**Statement 2:** wrong — **climate-neutral** EU by **2050**; **2030** is the year for the **55%** cut.
**Statement 3:** correct — the package is "**Fit for 55**" (at least **55%** GHG cut by **2030** vs **1990**).
xa: Components: **Farm to Fork**, **Circular Economy Action Plan**, **Biodiversity Strategy**.
Also: **Just Transition Fund**, **Renovation Wave** (energy-efficient buildings).
It came after PAGE (**2013**) and GSDP (**2017**).

82.s: The Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE) was launched in 2013 primarily in response to
82.x: PAGE was launched in 2013 in response to the call made at Rio+20 for action towards greener and more inclusive economies.
82.tq: Link the initiative to its originating international call and distinguish it from later agreements.
xs: **PAGE** was launched in **2013** in response to the **Rio+20 call** — option **(2)**.
Paris, Montreal and Kyoto are not linked to PAGE in the notes.
xa: PAGE = **Partnership for Action on Green Economy**.
It brings together **UNEP, ILO, UNIDO, UNDP and UNITAR**.
**UNEP Green Economy Initiative** came earlier, in **2008**.

82.s: The Green Credit Programme was notified by MoEFCC in:
82.x: MoEFCC notified the Green Credit Programme in October 2023.
82.tq: Distinguish the notification year of the programme from other green-policy years.
xs: The **Green Credit Programme** was notified by MoEFCC in **October 2023** — option **(2)**.
It is a **market-based incentive** for **voluntary environmental actions** (tree plantation, water conservation).
xa: The **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme** is to be put into operation.
**RBI Green Deposit Framework**: in force since **2023**.
**Sovereign Green Bonds**: first issue **2023**.

82.s: The 12 Principles of Green Chemistry were introduced in 1998 by
o: John Maynard Keynes and Paul Warner
82.x: Paul Anastas and John Warner introduced the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry in 1998.
82.tq: Pair the correct authors with the correct year and subject.
xs: The **12 Principles of Green Chemistry** were introduced in **1998** by **Paul Anastas and John Warner** — option **(3)**.
The other name pairs are wrong.
xa: Principles include **waste prevention rather than cleanup** and **atom economy**.
Also: **safer solvents and reagents**, **energy-efficient processes**.
**Green Pharmacy** applies green chemistry to medicines.

82.s: Why are urban local bodies unable to issue municipal green bonds, as highlighted in the debate?
o: They are prohibited from undertaking environmental projects.
They can issue only social bonds under SEBI rules.
They are not permitted to collect municipal revenue.
82.x: Urban local bodies cannot issue municipal green bonds because they lack credit ratings, which are important for such borrowing.
82.tq: Identify the institutional constraint rather than confusing it with a prohibition on environmental projects.
xs: **ULBs cannot issue municipal green bonds** because they **lack credit ratings** — option **(3)**.
The notes give no legal ban on their environmental projects or revenue.
xa: Green bonds fund **renewables, green transport, climate** projects.
**Sovereign Green Bonds**: first issue **2023**, **Rs 8,000 crore**.
Another debate: **greenwashing risk** without a taxonomy.

82.s:
Consider the following statements regarding green bonds:
1. The European Investment Bank pioneered green bonds in 2007.
2. The World Bank pioneered green bonds in 2008.
3. Green bonds are intended to finance environment-friendly projects.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: All three statements are correct. The European Investment Bank pioneered green bonds in 2007, followed by the World Bank in 2008, and the proceeds support environment-friendly projects.
82.tq: Check the dates and the common purpose before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**1:** **EIB** pioneered green bonds in **2007**; **2:** **World Bank** in **2008**.
**3:** green bonds fund **environment-friendly projects** — renewables, green transport, climate.
xa: India's **Sovereign Green Bonds**: first issue **2023**, **Rs 8,000 crore**.
⚠ FIRSTs: green bond **EIB 2007**; sovereign blue bond **Seychelles 2018**.
ULBs **cannot issue municipal green bonds** — they lack credit ratings.

82.s:
With reference to India's Sovereign Green Bonds, consider the following statements:
1. They were announced in the Union Budget 2022–23.
2. Their framework was issued in 2022.
3. The first issue was made in 2023 for Rs 8,000 crore.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: The Sovereign Green Bonds were announced in Budget 2022–23, their framework was issued in 2022, and the first issue in 2023 amounted to Rs 8,000 crore.
82.tq: Use the chronological sequence of announcement, framework and first issue.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(2)**.
**1:** announced in **Budget 2022-23**; **2:** framework **2022**.
**3:** first issue **2023**, **Rs 8,000 crore**.
xa: Public financial institutions publish **Green Bond Frameworks**.
**RBI Green Deposit Framework**: in force since **2023**.
Green bond pioneers: **EIB 2007**, **World Bank 2008**.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about blue bonds:
1. Blue bonds finance ocean and water projects.
2. The world's first sovereign blue bond was issued by Seychelles in 2018.
3. India's first blue bond is being issued by the RBI for Rs 8,000 crore.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: blue bonds fund ocean and water projects, and Seychelles issued the first sovereign blue bond in 2018. Statement 3 is wrong: India's first blue bond is by Sagarmala Finance Corporation Ltd for Rs 1,000 crore (FY 2026-27); Rs 8,000 crore was the first Sovereign Green Bond issue. So '1 and 2 only'.
82.tq: Rs 8,000 crore = sovereign green bond 2023; Rs 1,000 crore = Sagarmala blue bond.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — **blue bonds** finance **ocean and water** projects.
**Statement 2:** correct — first sovereign blue bond: **Seychelles 2018**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — India's first blue bond is by **Sagarmala Finance Corporation Ltd**, **Rs 1,000 crore** (**FY 2026-27**); **Rs 8,000 crore** was the first Sovereign Green Bond.
xa: Sagarmala's blue bond due in **FY 2026-27** was in the news (**Jun 2026**).
Green bond pioneers: **EIB 2007**, **World Bank 2008**.
**Social bonds** fund housing, health, education.

82.s: The RBI Green Deposit Framework primarily enables banks to:
o: Raise deposits earmarked for green lending
Set the national climate finance taxonomy
Finance social projects without accepting deposits
82.x: The RBI Green Deposit Framework allows banks to raise deposits specifically earmarked for green lending. It has been in force since 2023.
82.tq: Identify the function of the financial regulator from the purpose of the framework.
xs: The **RBI Green Deposit Framework** lets banks **raise deposits earmarked for green lending** — option **(1)**.
It has been in force since **2023**.
xa: The national **Climate Finance Taxonomy** is the **Ministry of Finance**'s (announced **Budget 2024-25**).
Gap: **Rs 35 crore** per-borrower PSL cap.
**MSE-GIFT** is the green finance scheme for MSMEs (**2023-26**).

82.s:
Consider the following statements regarding climate finance taxonomies in India:
1. The Climate Finance Taxonomy was announced in Budget 2024–25.
2. The Ministry of Finance's Climate Finance Taxonomy exists alongside the Ministry of Steel's Green Steel Taxonomy.
3. A final green taxonomy has already been established for all sectors.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. A key gap is that a final green taxonomy has not yet been established for all sectors, making statement 3 false.
82.tq: Find the incorrect statement by testing the status claim against the stated taxonomy gap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Statement 1:** correct — announced in **Budget 2024-25**.
**Statement 2:** correct — **Ministry of Finance**'s **Climate Finance Taxonomy** + **Ministry of Steel**'s **Green Steel Taxonomy**.
**Statement 3:** wrong — there is **no final green taxonomy yet**.
xa: Another gap: **Rs 35 crore** per-borrower PSL cap.
Without a taxonomy there is **greenwashing risk**.
The taxonomy gap was discussed at the **Bonn Climate Conference 2026**.

82.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Green Hydrogen Mission:
1. Its outlay is Rs 19,744 crore.
2. Its annual target is 5 MMT.
3. It is associated with the goal of achieving net zero by 2070.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
82.x: The Green Hydrogen Mission has an outlay of Rs 19,744 crore, targets 5 MMT annually and is linked with the net-zero target for 2070.
82.tq: Verify each numerical and target statement before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Green Hydrogen Mission**: outlay **Rs 19,744 crore**; target **5 MMT a year**.
It is linked to **net zero by 2070**.
xa: **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme** is to be put into operation.
**Green Credit Programme**: notified by MoEFCC, **October 2023**.
**Sovereign Green Bonds**: first issue **2023**, **Rs 8,000 crore**.

82.s: Which of the following sets correctly represents priority waste streams for which circular-economy action plans were drawn up in India?
o: Coal, crude oil, natural gas, uranium and limestone
Food grains, cotton, jute, sugarcane and tea
Cement, glass, sand, clay and timber only
Plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres and metals
82.x: NITI Aayog and MoEFCC committees drew up action plans for priority streams including plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres and metals.
82.tq: Recall the complete named list rather than selecting a broader but unsupported group.
xs: India's priority waste streams: **plastics, e-waste, batteries, tyres, metals** — option **(4)**.
Plans were drawn up by **NITI Aayog + MoEFCC** committees.
xa: **EPR regimes**: plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries, tyres.
**EPR results (2025-26)**: **308 lakh tonnes** recycled; **296.53 lakh tonnes** of EPR certificates.
**Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy (2019)** promotes secondary raw materials.

82.s:
Consider the following statements about the Draft National Resource Efficiency Policy, 2019:
1. It was prepared by the Ministry of Steel.
2. It promotes secondary raw materials and a National Resource Efficiency Authority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the draft policy was prepared by MoEFCC (the Ministry of Steel issued the Green Steel Taxonomy). Statement 2 is correct. Hence '2 only'; '1 only', 'both' and 'neither' are wrong.
82.tq: Draft NREP 2019 = MoEFCC.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** wrong — the draft policy is by **MoEFCC**; the **Ministry of Steel** issued the **Green Steel Taxonomy**.
**Statement 2:** correct — it promotes **secondary raw materials** and a **National Resource Efficiency Authority**.
xa: The draft dates from **2019**.
NITI Aayog + MoEFCC drew up plans for **priority waste streams**.
**EPR** covers plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries, tyres.

82.s: Extended Producer Responsibility regimes cover which of the following categories?
o: Plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres
82.x: The listed EPR regimes cover plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres.
82.tq: Recognise the complete waste-category list rather than selecting a partial list.
xs: **EPR regimes** cover **plastic packaging, e-waste, batteries and tyres** — option **(2)**.
**Housing, health, education** relate to **social bonds**, not EPR.
xa: **EPR results (2025-26)**: **308 lakh tonnes** recycled.
**296.53 lakh tonnes** of EPR certificates generated.
Priority waste streams add **metals** to this list.

82.s: Why is a clear taxonomy considered necessary in relation to greenwashing?
o: To replace life-cycle assessment with a single carbon figure
To help regulators curb greenwashing and transition washing
To remove all environmental regulations from financial markets
To classify only species threatened with extinction
82.x: A clear taxonomy helps regulators identify and curb greenwashing as well as transition washing.
82.tq: Identify the regulatory purpose of classification rather than its unrelated environmental uses.
xs: A clear **taxonomy** helps regulators **curb greenwashing and "transition washing"** — option **(2)**.
It does not replace LCA, remove regulation or classify species.
xa: India has a **Climate Finance Taxonomy** (MoF) and **Green Steel Taxonomy** (Ministry of Steel), but **no final green taxonomy**.
Greenwashing risk without a taxonomy is a key **criticism**.
**BRSR** requires the **top 1,000 listed companies** to publish audited ESG metrics.

82.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ESG regulation in India:
1. Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) is set by the Reserve Bank of India.
2. Under BRSR, the top 1,000 listed companies must publish audited ESG metrics every year.
3. SEBI regulates ESG Rating Providers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
82.x: Statement 1 is wrong: BRSR is set by SEBI, not RBI. Statement 2 is correct: the top 1,000 listed companies publish audited ESG metrics yearly. Statement 3 is correct: SEBI regulates ESG Rating Providers. So '2 and 3 only'; options with 1 are wrong.
82.tq: Both BRSR and ESG raters sit with SEBI (the market regulator).
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Statement 1:** wrong — **BRSR** is set by **SEBI**, not RBI.
**Statement 2:** correct — the **top 1,000 listed companies** publish **audited ESG metrics** every year.
**Statement 3:** correct — **SEBI** regulates **ESG Rating Providers**.
xa: BRSR = **Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting**.
RBI's role: the **Green Deposit Framework** (since **2023**).
SEBI BRSR was discussed at the **Bonn Climate Conference 2026**.

82.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Component)
a. Farm to Fork
b. Circular Economy Action Plan
c. Biodiversity Strategy
d. Just Transition Fund

List-II (Content)
i. Support for affected regions
ii. Sustainable food system
iii. Protect and restore ecosystems
iv. Resource efficiency and recycling

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
82.x: Farm to Fork concerns a sustainable food system; the Circular Economy Action Plan concerns resource efficiency and recycling; the Biodiversity Strategy protects and restores ecosystems; and the Just Transition Fund supports affected regions.
82.tq: Start with the distinctive pairs such as Farm to Fork–food and Just Transition Fund–affected regions.
xs: Correct match: **a–ii, b–iv, c–iii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Farm to Fork** → **sustainable food system**; **Circular Economy Action Plan** → **resource efficiency, recycling**.
**Biodiversity Strategy** → **protect and restore ecosystems**; **Just Transition Fund** → **support for affected regions**.
xa: **Renovation Wave** → **energy-efficient buildings**.
The Green Deal (**December 2019**) aims at a **climate-neutral** EU by **2050**.
Legislative package: "**Fit for 55**".

82.s: Which one of the following best describes a circular economy?
o: An economic system based primarily on the extraction and disposal of resources
An economic system based on increasing the use of fossil fuels
An economic system built on reuse, recycling and waste minimisation
An economic system focused exclusively on reducing carbon emissions
82.x: A circular economy is built on reuse, recycling and waste minimisation. It is not exclusively focused on carbon emissions or fossil fuels.
82.tq: Use the precise definition and reject the extreme word 'exclusively'.
xs: A **circular economy** is built on **reuse, recycling and waste minimisation** — option **(3)**.
⚠ It does **not** focus **exclusively on carbon or fossil fuels**; "take and dispose" is the **linear** model.
xa: PYQ answer: it promotes the **reuse, recycling and repair** of materials to reduce waste.
In it, **waste becomes a resource**, decoupling growth from resource use.
Indian MSME scheme for circular-economy investment: **MSE-SPICE**.

82.s: Which statement best explains the relationship between green chemistry, cleaner production, EIA and LCA?
o: EIA and LCA are unrelated to sustainability and resource efficiency.
Cleaner production increases pollution so that LCA can measure it more accurately.
Green chemistry and cleaner production reduce waste and pollution across the product life cycle, thereby serving the goals of EIA and LCA.
Green chemistry deals only with final waste disposal, whereas EIA deals only with product marketing.
82.x: Green chemistry and cleaner production minimise waste and pollution and promote sustainability throughout the product life cycle, supporting the objectives of Environmental Impact Assessment and Life-Cycle Assessment.
82.tq: Trace the common life-cycle and sustainability link instead of treating the instruments as isolated concepts.
xs: **Green chemistry** and **cleaner production** reduce waste and pollution across the **product life cycle**, serving the goals of **EIA** and **LCA** — option **(3)** (PYQ key).
They **minimise** pollution, so option (2) is wrong; they are not limited to final disposal.
xa: LCA = **Life-Cycle Assessment**.
Green chemistry favours **waste prevention rather than cleanup**.
**12 Principles**: **1998**, **Anastas and Warner**.

83.s:
Ozone is concentrated predominantly in which layer of the atmosphere?

The approximate altitude range associated with this concentration is:
83.x: Ozone is concentrated mainly in the stratosphere, approximately between 10 and 50 km above Earth. This layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
83.tq: Use the location-and-range combination to distinguish the ozone layer from adjacent atmospheric layers.
xs: Ozone is concentrated in the **Stratosphere, about 10-50 km** above Earth — so option **(1)** is correct.
This ozone layer shields Earth from harmful **UV-B** radiation.
Some notes give the range as **10-40 km**; either way it is the stratosphere, not the troposphere, mesosphere or thermosphere.
xa: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**; an "ozone hole" means total ozone below **220 DU**.
The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s, reported in **1985** by the **British Antarctic Survey**.
PIB reported a dense ozone pocket at **21-23 km** over the **North Bay of Bengal** (16 Aug 2026).

83.s: An ozone hole is conventionally identified when the total column ozone falls below:

xs: An ozone hole is identified when total ozone falls below **220 Dobson Units** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Ozone is measured in the **Dobson Unit (DU)**.
xa: The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s.
First reported in **1985** by **British Antarctic Survey** scientists (some notes say discovered **1983**).

83.s: The seasonal thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica is most pronounced during:
o: Southern Hemisphere autumn, March to May
Southern Hemisphere summer, December to February
Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November
Northern Hemisphere spring, March to May

83.tq: Link the phenomenon with the correct hemisphere and season.
xs: Antarctic ozone thinning peaks in **Southern Hemisphere spring, approximately August to November** — so option **(3)** is correct.
In the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**, polar stratospheric clouds activate chlorine, which destroys ozone **when sunlight returns** in spring.
xa: Ozone hole = total ozone below **220 DU**.
First detected over **Antarctica** in the mid-1980s; reported **1985** by the British Antarctic Survey.
Antarctic ozone is projected to recover to 1980 levels only by **2066** — the latest of all regions.

83.s: Polar stratospheric clouds contribute to ozone destruction because they:
o: Absorb all incoming solar radiation before it reaches the stratosphere
Convert oxygen directly into carbon dioxide
Prevent the return of sunlight to the polar vortex
Convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold
83.x: In the extremely cold polar vortex, polar stratospheric clouds provide surfaces that convert stable chlorine into active forms. When sunlight returns, these forms catalytically destroy ozone.
83.tq: Identify the causal mechanism rather than merely the associated location.
xs: Polar stratospheric clouds **convert stable chlorine compounds into active forms on their surfaces in extreme cold** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They form in the extreme cold of the **polar vortex**; the active chlorine **destroys ozone when sunlight returns**.
So they do not block sunlight or make CO2 — the ozone loss in fact needs the return of sunlight.
xa: Chlorine and bromine atoms destroy ozone **catalytically**.
The ozone hole is seasonal: **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.
**Halons** (bromine) are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.

83.s: Which one of the following is the main cause of depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer?
83.x: CFCs release chlorine in the stratosphere under UV, and the chlorine catalytically breaks down ozone; they are the main culprit. Carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases but not the main ozone depleters, and nitrogen (N2) is an inert atmospheric gas.
83.tq: Ozone depletion = CFCs (chlorine); CO2, CH4, N2 are the usual traps.
xs: **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** are the main cause of ozone depletion — so option **(3)** is correct.
CFCs release **chlorine** in the stratosphere, which breaks down ozone.
⚠ **CO2, methane and N2** are the usual wrong options — they are not the main ozone depleters.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2025** twice.
CFC uses: refrigerators, ACs, **aerosol propellants**, foam blowing, solvents.
CFCs are also greenhouse gases — about **15%** of the greenhouse effect.

83.x: The ODS (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 were framed under the Environment (Protection) Act.

xs: The ODS (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 were framed under the **Environment (Protection) Act** — so option **(3)** is correct.

xa: Halons (except essential use): **1 Jan 2001**; CFCs in manufacturing: **1 Jan 2003**.
CTC, methyl chloroform, CFCs in MDIs: **1 Jan 2010**; methyl bromide: **1 Jan 2015**.
HCFCs allowed up to **1 Jan 2040**.

83.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: halons (bromine) are used in fire extinguishers, methyl bromide is a fumigant/quarantine agent, and CTC and methyl chloroform are solvents. Statement 4 is wrong: HFCs are non-ODS substitutes (with high global warming potential); CFCs are the main cause of ozone depletion. So '1, 2 and 3 only'.
83.tq: Reject the swapped-category statement that treats a non-ODS substitute as an ozone-depleting substance.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **halons** contain **bromine** and are used in **portable fire extinguishers**.
Statement 2 is correct: **methyl bromide** is an **agricultural fumigant** and quarantine treatment.
Statement 3 is correct: **carbon tetrachloride** and **methyl chloroform** are **solvents** and chemical feedstock.
Statement 4 is wrong: **HFCs** are **non-ODS** (but high GWP); **CFCs** are the main cause of ozone depletion.
xa: **HCFCs** are weaker ODS, an **interim/transitional CFC substitute**.
Halons are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

CFCs are also used in **foam blowing** and as **solvents**.

Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.
xa: An "**ozone hole**" = total ozone below **220 DU**.
Ozone (**O₃**) has **three oxygen atoms**; it forms by **UV radiation + O₂ → O₃**.
The **ozone layer** is in the **stratosphere** (about **10-50 km**), shielding Earth from **UV-B**.

83.s:

83.x: All four are correct: the Montreal Protocol and Vienna Convention protect the ozone layer, a British team found the Antarctic ozone hole (1985), and G.W. Kent Moore described the Tibetan ozone low.
83.tq: Recall the ozone facts.
n: The Montreal Protocol concerns ozone protection. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
The Vienna Convention concerns ozone protection. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
The Antarctic ozone hole was discovered by a British team. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
G.W. Kent Moore is associated with the Tibetan ozone hole or halo. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
xs: **All four** statements — **I, II, III and IV** — are correct, so option **(1)** is correct.
I and II: the **Montreal Protocol** and the **Vienna Convention** concern **protection of the ozone layer**.
III: the Antarctic ozone hole was first reported in **1985** by **British Antarctic Survey** scientists.
IV: the **Tibetan ozone hole** or halo is linked with **G. W. Kent Moore**.
xa: The ozone hole was first detected over **Antarctica** in the **mid-1980s**; some notes say discovered **1983**.
Seasonal thinning: **Southern Hemisphere spring, Aug-Nov**.
**Polar stratospheric clouds** convert stable chlorine into active forms that destroy ozone.

83.s:
Which of the following effects is specifically associated with exposure to UV-B radiation due to ozone depletion?

1. DNA damage in plants and animals
2. Increased incidence of skin cancer
3. Suppression of the human immune system
4. Formation of nitrogen gas in the atmosphere

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
83.x: UV-B exposure can cause DNA damage, skin cancer, eye cataracts and suppression of the human immune system. Formation of nitrogen gas is not an identified effect.
83.tq: Find the unrelated scientific effect among several consequences of the same environmental problem.
xs: UV-B effects are **DNA damage**, **skin cancer** and **immune suppression** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: UV-B causes **DNA damage in plants and animals**.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: in humans it causes **skin cancer**, **eye cataracts**, blindness and **suppression of the immune system**.
Statement 4 is wrong: **formation of nitrogen gas** is not a UV-B effect.
xa: A **1% ozone loss** raises harmful UV by about **2%**.
Crops: reduced growth and photosynthesis in **rice, wheat, corn, soybean**; a 1% UV-B rise may cut food output ~1%.
Marine: damage to **phytoplankton** and fish, shrimp, crab larvae → **food-chain disruption**.
Materials: UV degrades **wood, plastic, rubber, fabrics**.

83.s:
With reference to the destruction of stratospheric ozone, consider the following statements:
1. Ultraviolet radiation releases chlorine and bromine atoms from suitable compounds.
2. Chlorine and bromine atoms can catalytically destroy ozone molecules.
3. Each chlorine or bromine atom is consumed permanently in the first reaction and cannot participate further.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
83.x: UV radiation releases chlorine and bromine atoms, which catalytically destroy ozone. They are not necessarily consumed permanently in the first reaction, so statement 3 is false.
83.tq: Identify the false statement by testing whether the key chemical agent acts catalytically or is consumed once.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **UV** releases **chlorine and bromine atoms** from compounds like CFCs and halons.
Statement 2 is correct: these atoms destroy ozone **catalytically**.
Statement 3 is wrong: a catalyst is not used up — the same atom goes on destroying more ozone molecules.
xa: **CFCs** release chlorine in the stratosphere and are the **main cause** of ozone depletion.
**Halons** carry **bromine** and are about **100 times more potent** than CFCs.
**Polar stratospheric clouds** convert stable chlorine into active forms.

83.s:
Consider the following statements about HFCs:
1. They replaced ozone-depleting substances in air-conditioners and refrigerators.
2. They do not deplete ozone.
3. They have very high global warming potential.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: All three statements are correct: HFCs replaced ODS in cooling equipment, do not deplete ozone, and possess high global warming potential.
83.tq: Test the distinction between ozone depletion and global warming potential.
xs: All three statements are correct — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: HFCs replaced ODS in **ACs and refrigerators**.
Statement 2 is correct: HFCs **do not deplete ozone** (non-ODS).
Statement 3 is correct: HFCs have **very high global warming potential** — hence the **Kigali Amendment**.
xa: Kigali (**2016**, Rwanda) is a legally binding HFC phase-down.
MoEFCC: no environmental clearance for **new or additional HFC production** after **31 December 2027**.
⚠ **HCFCs** are weaker ODS (transitional substitutes); **HFCs** are non-ODS.

83.s:
With reference to India under the Kigali Amendment, consider the following statements:
1. India is in Group 2, along with Gulf states, Iran, Iraq and Pakistan.
2. India's baseline years are 2024-26 and its freeze year is 2028.
3. India must achieve an 80% cut in HFCs by 2045.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
83.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: 80% by 2045 is the target of Developing Group 1 (including China); India's final cut is 85% by 2047. So '1 and 2 only'.
83.tq: India: 2024-26 baseline, 2028 freeze, 85% by 2047.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: India is in **Group 2** with **Gulf states, Iran, Iraq, Pakistan**.
Statement 2 is correct: India's baseline is **2024-26** and freeze **2028**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **80% by 2045** is Developing **Group 1** (incl. China); India's final cut is **85% by 2047**.
xa: India **ratified Kigali in 2021**.
Developed countries: **85% by 2036**.

83.s:

1. It bans exports of hazardous waste from OECD/EU countries and Liechtenstein to other countries.
2. It came into force on 5 December 2019.
3. It bans exports of hazardous waste from developing countries to OECD countries.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
83.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the ban covers exports from OECD/EU and Liechtenstein to other countries and came into force on 5 December 2019. Statement 3 reverses the direction - the aim is to stop rich countries dumping on poorer ones. So '1 and 2 only'.
83.tq: The ban runs rich -> poor, never the reverse.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the Ban Amendment bans hazardous waste exports from **OECD/EU countries + Liechtenstein** to other countries.
Statement 2 is correct: it came into force on **5 December 2019**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it reverses the direction — Basel targets dumping from **rich → poorer countries**.
xa: Basel was adopted at **Basel, Switzerland, 1989**; India ratified it in **June 1992**.

India implements Basel via **Prior Informed Consent** under the **Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016**.

Desertification is associated with UNCCD. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Mercury is associated with the Minamata Convention. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is that **mercury** is linked with the **Rotterdam Convention** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Mercury** falls under the **Minamata Convention**.
The **Rotterdam Convention** covers **hazardous chemicals and pesticides** (**Prior Informed Consent**).
**Wetlands** — **Ramsar**; **POPs** — **Stockholm Convention**; **desertification** — **UNCCD**: these are correct.
xa: Minamata: adopted **2013**, in force **2017**; phase out **dental amalgam by 2034**.
Major mercury sources: **coal-fired power plants**, **artisanal and small-scale gold mining**.
Rotterdam: in force **2004**; India **acceded in 2005**.

83.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched under the Stockholm Convention?
o: Annex A — DDT limited use for malaria control
Annex B — dioxins and furans as unintentional by-products
Annex B — DDT restricted, including limited use for malaria control
83.x: DDT is listed in Annex B for restriction, with limited use permitted for malaria control. Aldrin and dieldrin are associated with Annex A, while dioxins and furans are Annex C examples.
83.tq: Check whether the example is paired with the correct annex function.
xs: **Annex B — DDT restricted, including limited use for malaria control** is correct — option **(4)** is correct.
**Annex A** (elimination) has aldrin, dieldrin, UV-328 — not DDT.
**Dioxins and furans** are **Annex C** (by-products), and **aldrin** is Annex A — so options (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: 2025 Annex A additions: **chlorpyrifos**, **long-chain PFCAs**, **medium-chain chlorinated paraffins**.
DDT, PCBs, dioxins and furans are key members of the **dirty dozen**.
India ratified Stockholm in **2006**.

83.s: Persistent Organic Pollutants are characterised by which combination of properties?
o: Toxicity, long persistence, bioaccumulation and long-distance transport
Radioactivity, water solubility and immediate evaporation
High biodegradability, low toxicity and limited mobility
Short persistence, rapid breakdown and local movement only
83.x: POPs are toxic chemicals that persist for long periods, build up in living tissue and travel long distances.
83.tq: Select the option containing the complete defining property cluster.
xs: POPs show **toxicity, long persistence, bioaccumulation and long-distance transport** — option **(1)** is correct.
POPs are toxic chemicals that **last long**, **bioaccumulate in living tissue** and **travel long distances** — the opposite of options (3) and (4).
xa: POPs are covered by the **Stockholm Convention** (adopted **2001**, in force **2004**).
Initial list: **12 POPs**, the "**dirty dozen**".
Current count: **34 chemicals**.

84.s: Which one of the following correctly describes species diversity?
o: The variety of climatic zones on Earth
Variation in genes within a single species only
Only the number of species in an area, irrespective of their abundance
The variety of species in an area, involving richness as well as abundance
84.x: Species diversity concerns the variety of species in an area and includes both species richness and abundance.
84.tq: Distinguish species diversity from the narrower concept of richness.
xs: Species diversity is **the variety of species in an area, involving richness as well as abundance** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) is wrong because it ignores **abundance**; option (2) describes **genetic** diversity.
xa: **Species richness** = number of species; **evenness** = relative abundance.
Species diversity is measured by the **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson** indices.
**Alpha** diversity = species richness within one community.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about ecosystem diversity:
1. It refers to the variety of ecosystems such as rainforests, deciduous forests and boreal ecosystems.
2. One ecosystem can always replace the functions of another ecosystem.
3. Boreal conifers cannot perform the same ecological role as tropical deciduous trees in every context.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because one ecosystem cannot simply replace another; boreal conifers cannot do the job of tropical deciduous trees in every context.
84.tq: Use the absolute word in the replacement claim as the false-statement trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems — **rainforest, deciduous, boreal**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **one ecosystem cannot replace another**.
Statement 3 is correct: **boreal conifers ≠ tropical deciduous trees** in function.
xa: Richest ecosystem on land: **tropical rainforests**; in the sea: **coral reefs**.
⚠ **Taiga, deserts and temperate forests** are the usual wrong options for richest ecosystem.
**Gamma** diversity = total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding measures of diversity:
1. Alpha diversity is the diversity within one area or community.
2. Beta diversity is the total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region.
3. Gamma diversity is the overall diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region or landscape.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is correct (alpha = within one community). Statement 2 is wrong: beta diversity is the change or turnover of species between ecosystems along a habitat gradient; regional total is gamma. Statement 3 is correct. So '1 and 3 only'.
84.tq: Alpha = within, beta = between (turnover), gamma = whole region.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **alpha** = diversity within one area or community.
Statement 2 is wrong: **beta** is the **change (turnover)** in species between ecosystems along a habitat gradient.
Statement 3 is correct: **gamma** = total diversity across a whole region or landscape.
xa: ⚠ Alpha = **within**; Beta = **between (turnover)**; Gamma = **whole region**.
These terms originated with **R.H. Whittaker**.
**Point richness** = species count at a single point.

84.s: Species richness and species evenness refer, respectively, to:
o: Relative abundance and total number of species
Total number of species and their relative abundance
Change between ecosystems and total regional diversity
84.x: Species richness is the number of species, while species evenness indicates their relative abundance. Low evenness means that a few species dominate.
84.tq: Discriminate between number and proportional distribution.
xs: Richness and evenness are the **total number of species and their relative abundance** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Low evenness** means a few species dominate.
Option (1) reverses them; option (3) describes beta and gamma diversity.
xa: Example: Forest A (2 tigers, 6 deer, 7 rabbits) is **more even** than Forest B (1, 6, 8).
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.
Functional diversity has its own **richness**, **evenness** and **divergence**.

84.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised explanation for the greater biodiversity of tropical regions?
o: Long, undisturbed evolutionary history without glaciation
Greater solar energy and higher productivity
A less seasonal and more predictable climate
Frequent continental-scale glaciation and severe seasonal fluctuations
84.x: Tropical richness is associated with long evolutionary time without glaciation, stable climate, solar energy and productivity. Frequent severe glaciation is not an explanation for tropical richness.
84.tq: Find the option that reverses the standard explanation for a biodiversity pattern.
xs: **Frequent continental-scale glaciation and severe seasonal fluctuations** is not a reason — option **(4)** is correct.
The tropics had **long, undisturbed evolutionary time** with **no glaciation**.
They have a **less seasonal, more stable** climate → niche specialisation, and **more solar energy** → higher **productivity**.
xa: **Moderate disturbance** and **habitat heterogeneity** also raise diversity.
Ant example: about **10 species** near the North Pole vs up to **2,000** at the equator.
UPPSC 2019 A/R: butterflies peak in the tropics because they **cannot tolerate low temperature**.

84.s: The most significant aspect of biodiversity is:
84.x: The most significant aspect of biodiversity is the maintenance of the ecosystem. Timber, ornamental plants and ecotourism are uses of biodiversity (productive or aesthetic values), but they are not its most significant aspect.
84.tq: Most significant aspect = maintenance of the ecosystem (UPPSC 2015).
xs: The most significant aspect is **maintenance of the ecosystem** — option **(2)** is correct (UPPSC 2015).
Timber is **productive** value; ornamentals and **ecotourism** are uses (aesthetic), not the main aspect.
xa: Role in sustainable development (APPSC 2025): **supports ecosystem services**.
Losing a **keystone species** can bring an ecosystem down (rivet popper).
**Ethical / existence** value: every species has a **right to exist**.

84.s: Which of the following crop combinations is associated with the Hindustan (Indo-Burma) centre of origin?
o: Rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper
Wheat, barley, olive, grape and cabbage
84.x: The Hindustan or Indian centre is associated with rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper. It is also associated with many pulses and citrus.
84.tq: Match a named centre with its characteristic crop group.
xs: The Hindustan centre gives **rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber and black pepper** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is also linked to **many pulses** and **citrus**.
xa: Centres identified by **N.I. Vavilov** (**8 centres**).
**Nokrek Biosphere Reserve** (Garo Hills) = **Citrus Gene Sanctuary**.
**Oryza rufipogon** is the wild ancestor of cultivated rice.

84.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Endemic species are restricted to a particular geographical area.
Invasive alien species adversely affect native ecosystems or species.
Genetic diversity refers to the variety of ecosystems.
Alien species are introduced outside their natural range.
84.x: Option C is incorrect: genetic diversity is variation within a species. The variety of ecosystems is ecosystem diversity.
84.tq: Discriminate genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
n: An endemic species is restricted to a particular geographical area. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
An alien species is introduced outside its natural range. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
An invasive alien species is an alien species that adversely affects native ecosystems or species. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Genetic diversity is variation within species. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
Ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 43-45]
xs: The **incorrect** statement is that **genetic diversity** is the **variety of ecosystems** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Genetic diversity** is **variation within species**; the variety of ecosystems is **ecosystem diversity**.
Options (1), (2), (4) correctly define **endemic species**, **invasive alien species** and **alien species**.
xa: **Species diversity**: the **variety of species**.
Genetic example: all rice varieties are **Oryza sativa** but differ in size, aroma, nutrients.
"Biodiversity" was coined by **Walter G. Rosen** (**1985**).
CBD (**1992**) definition covers diversity **within species, between species and of ecosystems**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The word 'biodiversity' was coined by Walter G. Rosen.
2. The word was popularised by E.O. Wilson.
3. The terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity originated with E.O. Wilson.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Rosen coined the word (1985) and E.O. Wilson popularised it. Statement 3 is wrong: alpha, beta and gamma diversity terms come from R.H. Whittaker. So '1 and 2 only'.
84.tq: Rosen coined, Wilson popularised, Whittaker gave alpha/beta/gamma.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **Walter G. Rosen** coined "biodiversity" in **1985**.
Statement 2 is correct: **E.O. Wilson** popularised the term.
Statement 3 is wrong: the terms alpha, beta and gamma diversity come from **R.H. Whittaker**.
xa: ⚠ **Rosen** coined; **Wilson** popularised — do not swap (UKPSC 2025).
**Wilson (1992)** estimated **10-50 million** species; **Robert May** about **7 million**.
**Paul Ehrlich** proposed the **rivet popper hypothesis**; **Humboldt** the species-area relationship.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding estimates of global biodiversity:
1. About 1.5 million living species have been described.
2. E.O. Wilson estimated that the total number of species could be 10–50 million.
3. The estimate of 10–50 million refers only to described species.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: About 1.5 million species have been described, while Wilson estimated 10–50 million species in all. Statement 3 is false because the larger estimate includes undescribed species as well.
84.tq: Reject the statement that improperly narrows the scope of a broad estimate.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: about **1.5 million** living species are described.
Statement 2 is correct: **E.O. Wilson (1992)** estimated **10-50 million** species in all.
Statement 3 is wrong: 10-50 million is the **total** estimate, far above the **1.5 million** described.
xa: **Robert May** estimated about **7 million** species.
About **300,000** fossil species are described.
India has identified about **1,50,000** living species.

84.s: The high species richness of the Himalayas is most appropriately explained by the fact that the Himalayas
o: are a meeting point of different biogeographical zones
have no seasonal variation in climate
are entirely covered by tropical rainforests
are located close to the equator
84.x: The Himalayas bring together different biogeographical zones, creating varied habitats and high species richness.
84.tq: Apply the ecological cause to a geographical case rather than selecting a location-based distractor.
xs: The Himalayas are rich because they **are a meeting point of different biogeographical zones** — option **(1)** is correct.
There the **Palearctic** and **Indo-Malayan** realms meet, bringing species from both.
xa: The **Himalaya** zone has the most faunal species in India: **30,377**.
⚠ Largest zone = **Deccan Peninsula**; most faunal species = **Himalaya**.
The Himalaya zone covers **7.2%** of India's land.

84.s:
With reference to the species-area relationship, consider the following statements:
1. It is expressed as log S = log C + Z log A, where Z is about 0.1-0.2 for most areas.
2. It was proposed by Paul Ehrlich.
3. Species richness rises with area, but only up to a limit.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the species-area relationship was proposed by Alexander von Humboldt; Paul Ehrlich proposed the rivet popper hypothesis. Statement 1 is correct: log S = log C + Z log A, with Z about 0.1-0.2 for most areas (0.6-1.2 for whole continents). Statement 3 is correct: richness rises with area only up to a limit. Hence 1 and 3 only.
84.tq: Humboldt = species-area; Ehrlich = rivet popper.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **log S = log C + Z log A**, with **Z** about **0.1-0.2** for most areas.
Statement 2 is wrong: the species-area relationship was proposed by **Alexander von Humboldt**; **Paul Ehrlich** proposed the **rivet popper hypothesis**.
Statement 3 is correct: species richness **rises with area**, but **only up to a limit**.
xa: For very large areas (whole continents), Z is **0.6-1.2**.
**R.H. Whittaker** gave the terms **alpha, beta, gamma** diversity.
⚠ **Rosen** coined "biodiversity" (**1985**); **Wilson** popularised it.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Rivet Popper Hypothesis:
1. The loss of a few species may initially appear harmless.
2. Every species has exactly the same ecological importance.
3. The loss of a keystone species may destabilise or collapse an ecosystem.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the hypothesis highlights the special importance of key or keystone species.
84.tq: Find the statement that reverses the key-species distinction.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: losing a few rivets (species) **seems harmless**.
Statement 2 is wrong: species are not equal — a **key rivet** (keystone species) matters more.
Statement 3 is correct: losing a **keystone species** can bring the ecosystem down.
xa: Proposed by **Paul Ehrlich**: ecosystem = **aeroplane**, species = **rivets**.
Each loss **weakens** the ecosystem.
Ecosystem services: **pollination**, **climate regulation**, resilience.

84.s: Who classified India into biogeographic zones and provinces in the standard scheme associated with the year 1988?
o: Rodgers and Panwar under the Wildlife Institute of India
Alexander von Humboldt under the Zoological Survey of India
Rodgers and Panwar under the Botanical Survey of India
Madhav Gadgil and Panwar under the Indian Council of Forestry Research
84.x: The classification was prepared by Rodgers and Panwar under the Wildlife Institute of India in 1988.
84.tq: Apply the ‘who–institution–year’ combination without swapping the scientific survey organisation.
xs: India's zones were classified by **Rodgers and Panwar** under the **Wildlife Institute of India** — option **(1)** is correct.
The year was **1988**; it was WII, not BSI or ZSI.
xa: Scheme: **2 realms**, **3 biomes**, **10 zones**, **25 provinces**.
**Himalaya** has the most faunal species: **30,377**.
**AP** falls in the **Deccan** biogeographic zone.

84.s: Who identified eight centres of origin of cultivated plants?
84.x: N. I. Vavilov identified eight centres of origin of cultivated plants.
84.tq: Use direct person–contribution recall.
xs: **N. I. Vavilov** identified the **8 centres of origin** of cultivated plants — option **(1)** is correct.
**E.O. Wilson** popularised "biodiversity"; **Robert May** estimated about **7 million** species.
xa: India is the **Hindustan (Indo-Burma)** centre: rice, sugarcane, pulses, mango, citrus, black pepper.
India ranks **6th** among centres of crop diversity and origin.
India has **811 cultivated crop species** + **902 crop wild relatives**.

84.s: Which pair of indices is used for measuring species diversity?
o: Simpson index and Human Development Index
84.x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.
84.tq: Start from the sure pair of recognised biodiversity indices.
xs: **Shannon-Wiener index and Simpson index** measure species diversity — option **(1)** is correct.
They combine **richness** (number of species) and **evenness** (relative abundance).
xa: **Alpha, beta, gamma** diversity terms come from **R.H. Whittaker**.
**Species-area relationship**: log S = log C + Z log A.
**Functional diversity** = range of ecological roles.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the latitudinal pattern of biodiversity:
1. Biodiversity generally decreases from the tropics towards the poles.
2. Biodiversity generally decreases from lower to higher altitudes on mountains.
3. An ant survey recorded about 2,000 species near the North Pole and about 10 species at the equator.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: Biodiversity decreases towards the poles and with increasing altitude. The ant survey recorded about 10 species near the North Pole and up to 2,000 at the equator, making statement 3 false.
84.tq: Check the direction of the gradient and detect the reversed numerical comparison.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: biodiversity falls from the **tropics toward the poles**.
Statement 2 is correct: it falls from **lower to higher altitudes**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is reversed — about **10** ant species near the North Pole vs up to **2,000** at the equator.
xa: Tropics are richest due to long **undisturbed evolutionary time**, stable climate and more solar energy.
The **Himalayas** are rich as a **meeting point of biogeographical zones**.
Moderate disturbance and habitat heterogeneity also raise diversity.

84.s: Which of the following correctly identifies the ecosystems with the greatest species richness on land and in the sea, respectively?
84.x: Tropical rainforests or tropical moist forests are the richest terrestrial ecosystems, while coral reefs are the richest marine ecosystems.
84.tq: Use the land–sea comparison to distinguish the two richest ecosystems.
xs: **Tropical rainforests and coral reefs** are the richest on land and in the sea — option **(1)** is correct.
Tropical rainforests (**tropical moist forests**) were the answer in PYQs **2017** and **2023**.
⚠ **Taiga, deserts and temperate forests** are the usual wrong options.
xa: Biodiversity is **highest in the tropics** and falls toward the poles.
India has **4 of the 36** hotspots.
India records **20,444** marine species.

84.s:
The assertion that butterflies have their maximum diversity in the tropics is best explained by which of the following reasons?
Assertion (A): The maximum number of butterfly species is found in tropical regions.
Reason (R): Butterflies generally cannot tolerate low temperatures.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
84.x: Both statements are true, and intolerance to low temperatures helps explain why butterfly diversity is highest in the warmer tropics.
84.tq: Test whether the ecological reason directly explains the geographical diversity pattern.
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
Butterflies peak in the **tropics**, and their inability to **tolerate low temperature** explains it (UPPSC 2019).
xa: Biodiversity falls from the **tropics toward the poles**.
Tropics: more **solar energy** → higher **productivity**.
Tropics: less seasonal, more **stable/predictable** climate → **niche specialisation**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about the values of biodiversity:
1. Fuelwood, fodder and wild food collected by local people for their own use are examples of productive use value.
2. Timber, fibre, medicines and genetic material sold commercially are examples of productive use value.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is wrong: goods used directly by local people and not sold (fuelwood, fodder, wild food) are consumptive use value. Statement 2 is correct: goods sold commercially (timber, fibre, medicines, genetic material) are productive use value. Hence 2 only.
84.tq: Consumptive = used, not sold; productive = sold commercially.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: fuelwood, fodder and wild food used by local people and **not sold** are **consumptive use** value.
Statement 2 is correct: **timber, fibre, medicines** and **genetic material** **sold commercially** are **productive use** value.
xa: ⚠ Consumptive = used, **not sold**; productive = **sold commercially**.
**Option value**: unknown future uses such as **undiscovered medicines** and crop genes.
**Ethical / existence** value: every species has a **right to exist**.
Rivet popper hypothesis (**Paul Ehrlich**): ecosystem = aeroplane; species = **rivets**.

84.s: The possible future use of an undiscovered medicinal compound or a new crop gene is referred to as
84.x: Option value refers to possible future benefits, including undiscovered medicines and useful crop genes.
84.tq: Recognise the future-possibility meaning of the term ‘option value’.
xs: Possible future uses like undiscovered medicines and crop genes are **option value** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Consumptive** use is current direct local use; **aesthetic** is beauty; **social** is cultural or sacred value.
xa: **Productive** use = sold commercially (timber, fibre, medicines).
**TKDL** documents traditional formulations to stop wrong patents.
**Bioprospecting** = search in nature for commercially valuable compounds + genes.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about the Dasgupta Review (2021):
1. It was prepared by Partha Dasgupta for the UK Treasury.
2. It treats nature as an asset.
3. It holds that GDP fully accounts for the depreciation of nature.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the Review argues that GDP ignores nature's depreciation. So '1 and 2 only'.
84.tq: Dasgupta: nature is an asset GDP fails to depreciate.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: it was by **Partha Dasgupta** for the **UK Treasury**.
Statement 2 is correct: it treats **nature as an asset**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it says **GDP ignores nature's depreciation**.
xa: **TEEB** (**2007**, UNEP) aims to make nature's values visible.
**LMMC** formed by the **Cancun Declaration, 2002**.
**Biological Diversity Act 2002** was **amended in 2023**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Bioprospecting is the search in nature for commercially valuable compounds and genes.
2. Biopiracy is the patenting of such resources or traditional knowledge with prior consent and compensation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: biopiracy is patenting resources or traditional knowledge WITHOUT consent or compensation. So '1 only'.
84.tq: Biopiracy = without consent or compensation.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so **1 only**, option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **bioprospecting** = search in nature for commercially valuable **compounds + genes**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **biopiracy** is patenting resources or traditional knowledge **without consent or compensation**.
xa: **Turmeric** patent revoked **1997**; **Neem** patent revoked **2000**.
**Basmati** (RiceTec): most claims withdrawn after India's challenge.
**TKDL** makes traditional knowledge **prior art** for patent offices.

84.s:
The Convention on Biological Diversity defines biodiversity as variability among living organisms from which of the following sources?
1. Terrestrial ecosystems
2. Marine and other aquatic ecosystems
3. The ecological complexes of which organisms are part
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: The CBD definition covers organisms from terrestrial, marine and other aquatic sources, together with the ecological complexes to which they belong.
84.tq: Read the definition broadly and include all listed domains.
xs: All three sources are in the CBD definition — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
The CBD (**1992**) covers organisms from **terrestrial**, **marine** and **other aquatic** sources, plus the **ecological complexes** they belong to.
It covers diversity **within species**, **between species** and **of ecosystems**.
xa: Three levels: **genetic**, **species**, **ecosystem**.
The term "biodiversity" was coined by **W.G. Rosen** (**1985**).
CBD goals: **conservation**, **sustainable use**, **fair and equitable benefit-sharing**.

84.s: Forest A contains 2 tigers, 6 deer and 7 rabbits, while Forest B contains 1 tiger, 6 deer and 8 rabbits. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Forest B is more even because it has more rabbits.
Forest A has greater species richness and Forest B has greater ecosystem diversity.
Forest A and Forest B differ in species richness but not in evenness.
Both forests have three species and 15 individuals, but Forest A is more even.
84.x: Both forests contain three species and 15 individuals. Forest A has a more equal distribution of individuals and is therefore more even.
84.tq: Separate richness from the distribution of individuals.
xs: **Both forests have three species and 15 individuals, but Forest A is more even** — option **(4)** is correct.
Richness is equal (**3** species each); Forest A (**2, 6, 7**) spreads individuals more equally than B (**1, 6, 8**).
More rabbits in B means one species dominates more — lower evenness, so option (1) is wrong.
xa: **Species evenness** = relative abundance; low evenness = a few species dominate.
**Species richness** = number of species.
Indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.

84.s: Which one of the following statements about the taxonomic composition of recorded species is correct?
o: Animals constitute over 70% of recorded species, plants account for about 22%, and insects are the richest animal group.
Plants constitute over 70% of all recorded species.
Insects constitute less than 1% of recorded animal species.
Animals and plants each constitute approximately 50% of recorded species.
84.x: Over 70% of recorded species are animals, plants account for about 22%, and insects are the richest group among animals.
84.tq: Use relative shares and the within-group comparison together.
xs: **Animals are over 70%, plants about 22%, and insects are the richest animal group** — option **(1)** is correct.
Insects make up over **70%** of animals, so option (3) is wrong; plants are not over 70%.
xa: Described species: about **1.5 million** living + **300,000** fossil.
**Wilson (1992)**: **10-50 million** species in all.
India: **Hymenoptera** (**106**) topped the new animal species of 2025.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about TEEB:
1. TEEB is hosted by UNEP.
2. It began from a G8+5 initiative in 2007.
3. It is hosted by the World Economic Forum.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: TEEB is hosted by UNEP and originated from a G8+5 initiative in 2007. Statement 3 is false because it is not hosted by the World Economic Forum.
84.tq: Apply the wrong-host organisation trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: TEEB is hosted by **UNEP**.
Statement 2 is correct: it began from a **G8+5 initiative, 2007**.
Statement 3 is wrong: ⚠ TEEB is hosted by **UNEP**, not IMF or **WEF**.
xa: Aim: **"make nature's values visible"**.
**Dasgupta Review (2021)** was for the **UK Treasury**.
**Conservation International (1998)** identified the megadiverse countries.

84.s: How many countries are recognised as the world's megadiverse countries?
84.x: There are 17 megadiverse countries. The figure 36 refers to the global number of biodiversity hotspots, not megadiverse countries.
84.tq: Distinguish the country count from the separate hotspot count.
xs: There are **17** megadiverse countries — option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **36** is the number of global **biodiversity hotspots**, not megadiverse countries.
xa: Identified by **Conservation International (1998)**.
Criteria: at least **5,000 endemic plants** + border marine ecosystems.
India is a member of the **LMMC** (Cancun Declaration, **2002**).

84.s: India's share of the world's land area, recorded species and population is approximately:
84.x: India occupies about 2.4% of the world's land area, accounts for 7–8% of recorded species and has about 18% of the world's population.
84.tq: Preserve the order of the three measures while comparing percentages.
xs: India has **2.4%** of land, **7–8%** of recorded species and **18%** of people — option **(4)** is correct.
So the order is **2.4%, 7–8% and 18%, respectively**; the other options shuffle these figures.
xa: India has about **7.5% of global fauna**; **over 30%** of its animals are endemic.
India has identified about **1,50,000** living species.
India has **4 of the 36** hotspots.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about India's biodiversity:
1. India has about 7.5% of global fauna.
2. More than 30% of India's animals are endemic.
3. India contains 4 of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All three statements are correct: India has about 7.5% of global fauna, over 30% of its animals are endemic, and it contains 4 of the 36 global hotspots.
84.tq: Verify each percentage and count independently before using the combined option.
xs: All three statements are correct — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: India has about **7.5% of global fauna**.
Statement 2 is correct: **over 30%** of India's animals are **endemic**.
Statement 3 is correct: India has **4 of the 36** hotspots.
xa: India's fauna now **1,05,953 species** (ZSI).
**2025**: India added **709 animal species** = **483** new to science + **226** new records.
**7,076** faunal species on the **IUCN Red List**.

84.s: The 17 megadiverse countries were identified by Conservation International in 1998 on the basis of which stated criteria?
o: At least 5,000 animal species and absence of marine ecosystems
At least 500 endemic plants and a completely landlocked location
At least 36 biodiversity hotspots and 18% of world population
At least 5,000 endemic plants and a coastline bordering marine ecosystems
84.x: The criteria included at least 5,000 endemic plant species and borders with marine ecosystems.
84.tq: Match the institutional criterion with both of its required conditions.
xs: Criteria: **at least 5,000 endemic plants and a coastline bordering marine ecosystems** — option **(4)** is correct.
The criteria are endemic **plants** (not animals) and **bordering** marine ecosystems (not landlocked).
xa: Identified by **Conservation International (1998)**; there are **17**.
⚠ **36** = number of global hotspots.
India is in the **LMMC** negotiating bloc.

84.s:
With reference to the natural range of Indian fauna, consider the following statements:
1. The Bactrian camel is found in Nubra Valley and also in Central Asia.
2. The one-horned rhinoceros occurs in India and Nepal.
3. The hoolock gibbon is India’s only ape.
4. Slow loris and pangolin are associated with North-East India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
84.x: All four statements are correct. The hoolock gibbon is India’s only ape, while slow loris and pangolin are associated particularly with the North-East.
84.tq: Test a list by checking each geographical range independently.
xs: All four statements are correct — so **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)** is correct.
Statements 1 and 2: the **Bactrian camel** is in **Nubra valley** and **Central Asia**; the **one-horned rhino** in **India and Nepal**.
Statement 3: the **hoolock gibbon** is **India's only ape**.
Statement 4: **slow loris and pangolin** are in the **North-East**, e.g. Manipur.
xa: The **Indian pangolin** also lives in **NSTR, AP**.
Only the **Asiatic lion** is India-only (Gir).
Hoolock gibbon lives **south of the Brahmaputra**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements about India's biodiversity additions in 2025:
1. India added 709 animal species.
2. Of these, 226 were new to science and 483 were new records for India.
3. India also added 353 plant taxa.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: 709 animal species and 353 plant taxa were added. Statement 2 swaps the figures: 483 were new to science and 226 were new records. So '1 and 3 only'.
84.tq: Bigger part (483) = new to science.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: India added **709 animal species** in 2025.
Statement 2 is wrong: it swaps the figures — **483 new to science** and **226 new records**.
Statement 3 is correct: **353 plant taxa** were added (**14** infraspecific).
xa: India's fauna is now **1,05,953 species** (ZSI).
Top state: **Kerala 98**; top group: **Hymenoptera (106)**.

84.s:
Consider the following statements regarding marsupials and India:
1. Marsupials do not occur naturally in India.
2. Marsupials thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
84.x: Marsupials do not occur naturally in India. The second statement is false because the claim that they thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators is incorrect.
84.tq: Reject an absolute ecological claim while retaining the valid distribution statement.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — so **1 only**, option **(2)** is correct (UPSC 2023).
Statement 1 is correct: **marsupials do not occur naturally in India**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the claim that they "**thrive only in montane grasslands**" is false.
xa: India has **no native kangaroos, giraffes or lemurs**.
India's realms: **Palearctic** + **Indo-Malayan**.
Only the **Asiatic lion** is found naturally in India alone.

84.s: The two biogeographical realms represented in India are
84.x: India covers the Palearctic and Indo-Malayan biogeographical realms.
84.tq: Directly distinguish the correct pair of realms from similarly named global realms.
xs: India's two realms are **Palearctic and Indo-Malayan** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **Palearctic** (Himalaya) and **Indo-Malayan** realms meet in India, so it has species from both.
xa: India: **2 realms**, **3 biomes**, **10 zones**, **25 provinces**.
**Nicobar** fauna is closest to **Malesian** (Southeast Asian) fauna.
Classified by **Rodgers and Panwar (WII, 1988)**.

84.s: Which one of the following is the largest biogeographic zone of India?
84.x: The Deccan Peninsula is the largest biogeographic zone of India and covers about 42% of the country's land area.
84.tq: Use the size comparison to distinguish the largest zone from zones known for high species richness or endemism.
xs: The **Deccan Peninsula** is India's largest zone, about **42%** of land — option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ The **Himalaya** has the most faunal species (**30,377**), but is not the largest zone.
xa: Deccan Peninsula has **5 provinces** (APPSC 2024): Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau, Deccan South.
**AP falls in the Deccan zone** — an inverted-triangle plateau between the two Ghats, mostly rain-shadow.
Deccan Peninsula faunal species: **15,539**.

84.s: Which of the following correctly lists the five provinces of the Deccan Peninsula biogeographic zone?
o: Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau and Deccan South
Western Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Plateau, Gangetic Plain and Deccan North
Central Highlands, Aravallis, Eastern Ghats, Central Plateau and Malabar
Ladakh, Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Deccan South and Nicobar
84.x: The five provinces are Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau and Deccan South.
84.tq: Recall the complete province list and reject options that insert neighbouring zones or regions.
xs: The five provinces are **Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands, Central Plateau and Deccan South** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2024).
