102.x: Statement 1 is correct: day is 6 am-10 pm. Statement 2 is correct: firecrackers are banned 10 pm-6 am. Statement 3 is wrong: the CPCB limit is 125 dB at 4 m, not 100 dB. So '1 only' misses statement 2, '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include statement 3.
102.tq: Remember the pair 6 am-10 pm day and the 125 dB at 4 m cracker limit.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1: **day** = **6 am-10 pm**.
Statement 2: firecrackers banned **10 pm-6 am**.
Statement 3 is wrong: CPCB bans crackers above **125 dB** at **4 m**, not 100.
xa: **Thrissur Pooram 2025** peaked at **122.4 dB**.
Above **85 dB** → permanent hearing loss.
**Silence zone** = at least **100 m** around hospitals, schools, courts.

102.s: Which one of the following statements regarding noise monitoring in India is correct?
o: NANMN monitors only industrial zones in two metropolitan cities.
NANMN has 100 stations in all State capitals.
NANMN has 25 stations confined to Andhra Pradesh.
NANMN has 70 stations in seven metropolitan cities.
102.x: The CPCB Real Time National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network has 70 stations in seven metros: Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Lucknow and Hyderabad.
102.tq: Use the network’s count-and-coverage combination to reject swapped figures and locations.
xs: **NANMN** has **70** real-time stations in **7 metros**, so option **(4)** is correct.
The metros: **Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Lucknow, Hyderabad**.
**25** is the number of **APPCB** real-time noise stations, not NANMN.
xa: NANMN = CPCB's **Real Time National Ambient Noise Monitoring Network**.
**Delhi**: **65-85%** of sites breach limits (**Sep 2025**).
Criticism: monitoring is **episodic**, enforcement weak.

102.s: Green mufflers used along roads generally consist of:
o: Rows of trees and shrubs that absorb noise
102.x: Green mufflers are rows of trees and shrubs along roads that help absorb noise.
102.tq: Distinguish a biological noise barrier from mechanical control devices.
xs: **Green mufflers** are **rows of trees and shrubs** along roads that **absorb noise**, so option **(4)** is correct.
**Cooling ponds** control **thermal** pollution, not noise.
xa: Other controls: **silencers/mufflers**, **sound barriers**, **green belts** along highways.
**Loudspeaker curbs** and **traffic management** also help.
Main primary source of noise = **construction** (**APPSC-G2 2025**).

102.s: The intensity of noise is measured in
102.x: Noise is measured in decibels (dB) (APPSC 2025); dB(A) is weighted to human hearing. Hertz measures frequency, sievert measures biological radiation dose and becquerel measures radioactivity.
102.tq: Noise unit = decibel; every +10 dB ≈ double loudness.
xs: Noise intensity is measured in **decibels (dB)**, so option **(1)** is correct (**APPSC 2025**).
**Sievert** measures **biological dose**; **becquerel** measures radioactive **activity**.
xa: **dB(A)** is weighted to human hearing.
Whisper ~**30 dB**; conversation ~**60 dB**.
Every **10 dB** rise ≈ loudness doubles.

102.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Rustling leaves produce about 20 dB of noise.
Statement B: A rocket engine produces about 180 dB of noise.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
102.x: Both are true: rustling leaves make about 20 dB and a rocket engine about 180 dB.
102.tq: Recall the noise levels.
n: Rustling leaves produce about 20 dB of noise. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 21-23]
A rocket engine produces about 180 dB of noise. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 21-23]
xs: **Both statements are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Rustling leaves** make about **20 dB**; a **rocket engine** about **180 dB**.
Noise is measured in **decibels (dB)**.
xa: **Green muffler** = rows of trees and shrubs along roads that absorb noise.
Every **10 dB** rise roughly **doubles** loudness.
**>85 dB** causes **permanent hearing loss**; WHO safe indoor level is **< 30 dB**.

102.s:
Consider the following statements about MARPOL 73/78:
1. It is an IMO convention.
2. It has six Annexes.
3. It permits unrestricted dumping of plastics at sea.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: MARPOL 73/78 is an IMO convention with six Annexes. It bans the dumping of plastics at sea, so statement 3 is false.
102.tq: Reject the absolute claim that reverses the convention’s central restriction on plastics.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1: **MARPOL 73/78** is an **IMO** convention against ship-based pollution.
Statement 2: it has **6 Annexes**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it **bans plastic dumping** at sea.
xa: **IMO BWM Convention** on ballast water came into force in **2017**.
**IMO** caps sulphur in ship fuel.
**GloLitter** (IMO-FAO, **2019**) targets sea-based plastic litter.

102.s: Samudra Pratap is associated with which of the following?
o: A satellite for tracking ghost nets
India’s first indigenously built Pollution Control Vessel
102.x: Samudra Pratap is India’s first indigenously built Pollution Control Vessel, built by Goa Shipyard Limited.
102.tq: Link the named vessel with its exact national distinction and function.
xs: **Samudra Pratap** is India's **first indigenously built Pollution Control Vessel**, so option **(3)** is correct.
It was built by **Goa Shipyard Ltd** (**Jun 2026**).
xa: **SARAT** app is for **oil-slick** tracking.
Oil-spill tools: **booms, skimmers, dispersants**, **Oil Zapper**.
**Ghost nets** = abandoned fishing gear that keeps trapping marine life.

102.s:
Consider the following statements about the GloLitter Partnerships:
1. It is a joint initiative of UNEP and WHO launched in 2019.
2. It is funded by Norway and India is a partner country.
3. It targets sea-based marine plastic litter from shipping and fisheries.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: GloLitter (2019) is run by the IMO and FAO, not UNEP and WHO. So '2 and 3 only'.
102.tq: GloLitter = IMO + FAO, Norway-funded, sea-based litter.
xs: **Statements 2 and 3 only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is wrong: **GloLitter Partnerships** is by the **IMO and FAO** (**2019**), not UNEP and WHO.
Statement 2 is correct: funded by **Norway**; **India** is a partner country.
Statement 3 is correct: it targets **sea-based marine plastic litter** from shipping and fisheries.
xa: **SACEP** (set up **1982**) has its secretariat in **Colombo** and **8 members** incl. India.
**MARPOL 73/78** is the **IMO** convention against ship-based pollution, with **6 Annexes**.
⚠ APPSC-G1 **2022** key accepted "UNEP initiative"; the partnership is IMO-FAO.

102.s: Microplastics are generally defined as plastic pieces having a size:
102.x: Microplastics are plastic pieces smaller than 5 millimetres.
102.tq: Use the size threshold directly and reject options that shift the unit or scale.
xs: **Microplastics** are plastic pieces **less than 5 mm**, so option **(2)** is correct.
**Microbeads** are added to **cosmetics and scrubs**.
xa: Oceans are the **final sink** for plastics.
**MARPOL** bans plastic dumping at sea.
**GloLitter** targets sea-based plastic litter.

102.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
102.x: Becquerel and curie measure activity, gray and rad measure absorbed dose, and sievert and rem measure biological dose. Rad is not a unit of activity.
102.tq: Match each unit to the quantity it measures and find the category mismatch.
xs: **Activity — Rad** is wrong, so option **(1)** is correct.
**Rad** (with **gray**) measures **absorbed dose**.
The rest are right: **sievert** = **biological dose**; **gray** = absorbed dose; **becquerel** = **activity**.
xa: **Curie** also measures activity.
**Rem** also measures biological dose.
⚠ **Decibel** is the noise unit, not a radiation unit.

102.s:
Consider the following statements about radon (Rn-222):
1. It is a radioactive noble gas originating from the Earth's crust.
2. It seeps from uranium-bearing soil and rock and from granite building materials, and builds up in closed rooms.
3. It is the leading cause of skin cancer after ultraviolet radiation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
102.x: Statement 1 is correct: radon is a radioactive noble gas from the Earth's crust. Statement 2 is correct: it seeps from uranium-bearing soil/rock and granite and accumulates indoors. Statement 3 is wrong: radon is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, not skin cancer. Hence '1 only' is incomplete and options containing 3 are wrong.
102.tq: Radon = noble gas, indoor build-up, lung cancer (second only to smoking).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1: **radon (Rn-222)** is a radioactive **noble gas** from the Earth's crust.
Statement 2: it seeps from **uranium-bearing soil/rock** and **granite** and builds up in **closed rooms**.
Statement 3 is wrong: radon is the leading cause of **lung cancer after smoking**, not skin cancer.
xa: Radon is a noble gas used to **treat cancer** (**APPSC-G1 2018**).
Radon is also an **indoor** air pollutant.
Building materials: **thorium** (**APPSC 2019** key); radon from granite.

102.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Source category)
a. Natural
b. Building materials
c. Medical
 d. Nuclear

List-II (Example)
i. X-rays and isotopes
 ii. Reactor waste and accidents
 iii. Cosmic rays and radon-222
 iv. Thorium and radon from granite
102.x: Natural sources include cosmic rays and radon-222; building materials may contain thorium and radon from granite; medical sources include X-rays and isotopes; nuclear sources include reactor waste and accidents.
102.tq: Start from the sure pair ‘medical–X-rays’ and eliminate codes that violate the remaining source categories.
xs: Correct match: **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii**, so option **(1)** is correct.
**Natural** → cosmic rays, **radon-222**; **building materials** → **thorium**, radon from granite.
**Medical** → **X-rays, isotopes**; **nuclear** → **reactor waste, accidents**.
xa: **Thorium** in building materials was the **APPSC 2019** key.
Nuclear tests release **Sr-90, Cs-137, I-131**.
Natural list also has **potassium-40** and **thorium-232**.

102.s: Which radioactive noble gas, coming from the Earth's crust, is used in the treatment of cancer?
102.x: Radon (Rn-222) is the radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer (APPSC-G1 2018); it is also a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Neon, helium and argon are noble gases but not the radioactive gas cited here.
102.tq: Radon: radioactive noble gas; treats cancer, causes lung cancer.
xs: **Radon** is the radioactive **noble gas** used to **treat cancer**, so option **(1)** is correct (**APPSC-G1 2018**).
**Neon, helium, argon** are noble gases but are not the radioactive gas cited.
xa: Radon (**Rn-222**) comes from the **Earth's crust**.
It seeps from **uranium-bearing** soil/rock and **granite** and builds up in closed rooms.
It is a leading cause of **lung cancer** after smoking.

102.s:
Consider the following statements regarding radiation safety institutions in India:
1. The AERB was set up in 1983 under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962.
2. The AERB approves the handling and disposal of radioactive waste.
3. The Environmental Survey Laboratory approves all radioactive waste disposal sites.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
102.x: Statement 1 is correct: AERB dates from 1983 under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. Statement 2 is correct: AERB approves radioactive waste handling and disposal. Statement 3 is wrong: the Environmental Survey Laboratory only monitors radiation around plants; approval rests with AERB. So '1 only' is incomplete and options with 3 are wrong.
102.tq: AERB approves; ESL monitors.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1: **AERB** was set up in **1983** under the **Atomic Energy Act 1962**.
Statement 2: AERB **approves radioactive waste handling and disposal**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **Environmental Survey Laboratory** only **monitors radiation** around plants.
xa: **NDMA guidelines** on nuclear and radiological emergencies: **2009**.
**MRDS** detect **orphan** radioactive material.
Precedent: **Mayapuri, Delhi (2010)** — **cobalt-60**.

102.s: The 2010 Mayapuri incident in Delhi was associated with which radioactive material?
102.x: The Mayapuri scrap-market incident involved an unclaimed source of cobalt-60 in 2010.
102.tq: Use the incident–radioisotope association rather than confusing it with isotopes listed under reactor waste and accidents.
xs: The **Mayapuri, Delhi (2010)** scrap-market incident involved **cobalt-60**, so option **(2)** is correct.
**I-131, Cs-137, Sr-90** are named as nuclear-test fallout, not the Mayapuri source.
xa: It is the precedent for the NDMA's **MRDS** plan.
MRDS detect **unclaimed ("orphan")** radioactive material (**APPSC 2021**).
**AERB** approves radioactive waste disposal.

102.s:
Consider the following statements about the Tummalapalle uranium mine and mill of UCIL:
1. Villagers allege groundwater contamination and skin and health problems from its tailings pond.
2. It is located in Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
102.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: Tummalapalle is in YSR Kadapa district, not Kurnool. So '1 only'.
102.tq: Tummalapalle = YSR Kadapa.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: villagers allege **groundwater contamination** and skin/health problems from the **tailings pond**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **UCIL** mine and mill is in **YSR Kadapa district**, not Kurnool.
xa: Sources of radioactive pollution include **uranium and thorium mining and refining**.
**Radon** is a leading cause of **lung cancer** after smoking.
India's first **Dark Sky Reserve** is **Hanle, Ladakh** (**2022**).

102.s: Under the NDMA plan, Mobile Radiation Detection Systems (MRDS) are provided to States and UTs mainly to
102.x: MRDS are given for metros and State capitals to detect unclaimed ('orphan') radioactive material (APPSC 2021, asked twice); the 2010 Mayapuri cobalt-60 incident is the precedent. Noise, ozone and cyclone monitoring are done by other networks.
102.tq: MRDS = orphan radioactive source detection (Mayapuri 2010).
xs: **MRDS** are meant to **detect unclaimed (orphan) radioactive material**, so option **(1)** is correct (**APPSC 2021**, asked twice).
Noise is tracked by **NANMN**; ozone by air networks — not by MRDS.
xa: MRDS go to **metros and State capitals**.
Precedent: **Mayapuri, Delhi (2010)** — **cobalt-60**.
**Environmental Survey Laboratory** monitors radiation around plants.

102.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)
(b) Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB)
(c) National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)
(d) District Administration

List-II
(i) Leads the off-site emergency
(ii) Specially trained CBRN battalions
(iii) Independent regulator for nuclear and radiation safety
(iv) Nodal technical agency and Crisis Management Group
102.x: DAE is the nodal technical agency with the crisis group, AERB the independent safety regulator, NDRF has CBRN battalions, and the district administration leads off-site emergencies. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
102.tq: Match each body to its role.
n: The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) is the nodal technical agency. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Crisis Management Group (CMG) is associated with the Department of Atomic Energy. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) is an independent regulator for nuclear and radiation safety. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) has specially trained CBRN battalions for response. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The District Administration leads the off-site emergency. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) is the nodal agency for man-made radiological emergencies in the public domain. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**DAE**: **nodal technical agency**, with the **Crisis Management Group**; **AERB**: **independent regulator** for **nuclear** and **radiation safety**.
**NDRF**: **specially trained** **CBRN battalions**; **District Administration**: **leads** the **off-site emergency**.
xa: The **District Collector** is the **Incident Commander** off-site.
**NDMA** issued the nuclear and radiological emergency guidelines in **2009**.
The **Cabinet Committee on Security** handles **nuclear**, **biological** and **chemical emergencies**.

102.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: NDMA issued the National Guidelines on Management of Nuclear and Radiological Emergencies in 2009.
Statement B: The District Collector acts as the Incident Commander during an off-site emergency.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
102.x: Both are true: NDMA issued its nuclear and radiological emergency guidelines in 2009, and the District Collector is incident commander in an off-site emergency.
102.tq: Recall the nuclear emergency setup.
n: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) issued the National Guidelines on Management of Nuclear and Radiological Emergencies in 2009. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
The District Collector is the Incident Commander for an off-site emergency. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 19-22]
xs: **Both statements are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: **NDMA** issued the **National Guidelines on Management of Nuclear and Radiological Emergencies** in **2009**.
B: the **District Collector** is the **Incident Commander** for the **off-site emergency**.
xa: **AERB** (**1983**, under the Atomic Energy Act **1962**) regulates radiation safety.
NDMA plan gives states **Mobile Radiation Detection Systems** to detect **orphan** radioactive material.
Precedent: **Mayapuri, Delhi (2010)** **cobalt-60** incident.

102.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India's designated dark-sky locations:
1. Hanle became India's first Dark Sky Reserve in 2022.
2. Hanle lies inside Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary.
3. Pench Tiger Reserve became India's first Dark Sky Park in 2024.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
102.x: Hanle in Ladakh became India's first Dark Sky Reserve in 2022 within Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary, while Pench Tiger Reserve became India's first Dark Sky Park in 2024.
102.tq: Separate the reserve, sanctuary and park facts while retaining the dates.
xs: All three statements are correct, so option **(4)** is correct.
Statements 1 and 2: **Hanle, Ladakh** = India's **first Dark Sky Reserve** (**2022**), inside **Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary**.
Statement 3: **Pench Tiger Reserve (Maharashtra)** = first **Dark Sky Park** (**2024**).
xa: ⚠ **Reserve** = Hanle (2022); **Park** = Pench (2024).
Certified by **DarkSky International**.
Ladakh has **clear skies**, **least humidity and pollution**, **high altitude**.

102.s: Which organisation certifies dark sky reserves?
102.x: Dark sky reserves, such as India's first at Hanle, Ladakh (2022), are certified by DarkSky International. IAEA, IMO and WMO deal with nuclear energy, shipping and weather respectively.
102.tq: Use the exact certifying body rather than a similarly international organisation.
xs: Dark sky reserves are certified by **DarkSky International**, so option **(2)** is correct.
**IMO** deals with shipping (MARPOL, GloLitter); the others are not linked in the notes.
xa: A reserve has a **protected natural night sky** and **controlled artificial lighting**.
India's first: **Hanle, Ladakh** (**2022**).
First Dark Sky Park: **Pench Tiger Reserve** (**2024**).

102.s: The Blue Flag is best described as:
o: A marine pollution vessel operated by Goa Shipyard
An IMO convention regulating ship emissions
A radioactive warning symbol issued by AERB
A beach eco-label awarded by the Foundation for Environmental Education
102.x: Blue Flag is a beach eco-label associated with the Foundation for Environmental Education, based in Denmark.
102.tq: Match the certification label with its issuing organisation and avoid confusing it with a treaty or vessel.
xs: **Blue Flag** is a **beach eco-label** from the **Foundation for Environmental Education (Denmark)**, so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Goa Shipyard** vessel is **Samudra Pratap**; **MARPOL** is the IMO ship-pollution convention; **AERB** regulates radiation safety.
xa: **Dead zones**: e.g. **Gulf of Mexico**.
**Microplastics** are **< 5 mm**.
**SACEP** secretariat = **Colombo**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding decomposition of biodegradable waste:
1. Aerobic decomposition produces compost.
2. Anaerobic decomposition can produce methane.
3. Biodegradable waste is mainly decomposed into simpler substances by microorganisms.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. Microorganisms decompose biodegradable matter into simpler substances; oxygen-supported decomposition produces compost, while anaerobic decomposition produces methane or biogas.
103.tq: Combine the process, condition and product statements before selecting the coded option.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **aerobic decomposition** produces **compost** — correct.
Statement 2: **anaerobic decomposition** produces **methane (CH4)**/biogas — correct.
Statement 3: biodegradable waste is decomposed by **microorganisms** (mainly **bacteria**) into simpler substances — correct.
xa: **Non-biodegradable** waste is mainly inorganic, not broken down by microbes, and accumulates in the environment.
Methods built on this: **composting** (aerobic, Indore method), **anaerobic digestion / biomethanation** (methane biogas + slurry manure).
Indian MSW is **~55-60% biodegradable**.

103.s:
For the purposes of solid-waste management, solid waste includes discarded or abandoned material in which of the following forms?
1. Solid
2. Liquid
3. Semi-solid
4. Containerised gaseous form
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: The definition includes discarded or abandoned materials that are solid, liquid, semi-solid or containerised gaseous.
103.tq: Read the legal-style definition inclusively and avoid limiting solid waste to solid matter alone.
xs: Solid waste covers discarded or abandoned materials that are **solid, liquid, semi-solid or containerised gaseous** — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
The definition is not limited to solids: all four forms are included.
xa: Categories of solid waste: **municipal**, **industrial**, **hazardous**, **biomedical**, **e-waste**, **agricultural**, **construction & demolition**, radioactive and mining.
**E-waste (ITU definition):** discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts **not meant for reuse**.
Hazardous waste also occurs as **solids, liquids, sludges and gases**.

103.s: In the composition of Indian municipal solid waste, which component accounts for approximately 55–60 per cent?
103.x: Biodegradable material constitutes approximately 55–60 per cent of Indian municipal solid waste.
103.tq: Match the percentage range with the corresponding waste component.
xs: **Biodegradable waste** makes up **~55-60%** of Indian municipal solid waste — option **(2)** is correct.
**Recyclable** waste is only **15-20%**, and **hazardous or non-recyclable** waste **15-25%**.
xa: India generates over **62 million tonnes** of MSW a year; **~60%** of all waste comes from urban areas.
Textile waste: ~**7.8 million tonnes** a year.
The waste sector = **2.56%** of India's total emissions in 2020 (**4th Biennial Update Report**).

103.s: Which of the following may be added in expanded 5R versions of the waste hierarchy?
103.x: Expanded 5R versions may add Refuse and Repurpose or, in some versions, Recover. The versions vary, but Refuse and Repurpose are stated additions.
103.tq: Identify the additional terms in an expanded version of a familiar list.
xs: Expanded **5R** versions add **Refuse** and **Repurpose** (or Recover) — option **(1)** is correct.
"**Regain**" is not part of the R-hierarchy — options (2) and (4) are wrong; Reduce and Recycle are already in the 3R.
xa: **3R = Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**; **source reduction** is the top priority.
**RRR Centre** under SBM-U 2.0 = **Reduce, Reuse, Recover**.
⚠ Trap: "Regain" is not one of the 3R (APPSC-GS 2025).

103.s: Under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, waste was required to be segregated into which three streams?
o: Biodegradable, dry and domestic hazardous waste
103.x: The three streams under the 2016 Rules were biodegradable waste, dry waste and domestic hazardous waste.
103.tq: Discriminate between the three-stream system of 2016 and the four-stream system of 2026.
xs: The **SWM Rules 2016** set three streams: **biodegradable, dry and domestic hazardous** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wet, dry, sanitary and special care** are the four streams of the **SWM Rules 2026**.
xa: **Dry** stream: plastic, paper, metal, wood.
⚠ **2000** = segregation goal; **2016** = **3 streams**; **2026** = **4 streams**.
Under 2016 Rules, used diapers/napkins went wrapped into the **dry bin**.

103.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly represents important provisions of the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016?
o: User fees, spot fines, extended producer responsibility and prohibition of untreated waste in landfills
Only centralised collection and unrestricted disposal in landfills
Import for disposal, co-processing and absence of producer responsibility
Tourist fees, biomining of legacy dumps and four-stream segregation
103.x: The 2016 Rules provided for user fees, spot fines, extended producer responsibility for producers and brand owners, and prohibited the disposal of untreated waste in landfills.
103.tq: Identify the option containing the complete set of provisions belonging to the same rules.
xs: The **SWM Rules 2016** provided **user fees, spot fines, EPR** and **no untreated waste to landfill** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Tourist fees, biomining of legacy dumps and four-stream segregation** are features of the **SWM Rules 2026** — option (4) is wrong.
**Import for disposal** is prohibited under the HOWM Rules 2016 — option (3) is wrong.
xa: The 2016 Rules came into force on **8 Apr 2016**, replacing the **2000** Rules.
They extended to **UAs, census towns, railways, airports, SEZs**, religious/historical places.
**EPR** first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (M&H) Rules 2011**.

103.s: Under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, every waste generator is required to segregate waste into which of the following four streams?
o: Wet, dry, sanitary and special care
103.x: The four streams are wet, dry, sanitary and special care waste, the last category covering domestic hazardous waste.
103.tq: Watch for the replacement of the earlier three-stream classification by the four-stream classification.
xs: The four streams under the **SWM Rules 2026** are **wet, dry, sanitary and special care** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Special care** = domestic hazardous waste (batteries, chemicals, paint cans, bulbs).
xa: **Sanitary** bin: **diapers, sanitary napkins**.
**Dry** bin: paper, plastics, metals, glass, wood; **Wet**: food scraps, peels, garden waste.
⚠ Trap: some notes still list three streams (2016); the **four-stream** rule is current.

103.s: What is the duty of a Bulk Waste Generator under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026?
o: To process wet waste on site or obtain an EBWGR certificate
To mix sanitary waste with dry recyclable waste
To send all wet waste directly to a landfill
To transfer responsibility exclusively to railways
103.x: Bulk Waste Generators must process wet waste on site or obtain an EBWGR certificate as prescribed under the 2026 Rules.
103.tq: Apply the actor-duty relationship by asking what the specified stakeholder must do.
xs: Bulk Waste Generators must **process wet waste on site** or obtain an **EBWGR certificate** — option **(1)** is correct.
Thresholds: **100 kg/day** waste, **5,000 L/day** water or **20,000 sq m**.
xa: Every generator: four-stream segregation — **wet, dry, sanitary, special care**.
Hill/island bodies: **user fee on tourists**; regulate tourist inflow.
Local bodies: map legacy dumpsites; **biomining**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 and their implementation:
1. Hill and island towns can levy user fees on tourists.
2. Environmental Compensation under the Rules is based on the precautionary principle.
3. The Supreme Court, issuing pan-India directions for implementation, treated a clean environment as part of Article 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: hill and island bodies may levy user fees on tourists and regulate inflow. Statement 2 is wrong: Environmental Compensation follows the polluter-pays principle. Statement 3 is correct: the SC treated a clean environment as part of Art. 21. So '1 only' is incomplete, and options with 2 are wrong.
103.tq: Environmental Compensation = polluter pays; clean environment = Art. 21.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **hill and island towns** can levy **user fees on tourists** — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — **Environmental Compensation** is based on the **polluter-pays principle**.
Statement 3: the **SC** issued pan-India directions and treated a clean environment as part of **Art. 21** — correct.
xa: The SWM Rules 2026 were notified under **EPA 1986**, in force **1 April 2026**.
SC order of **18 Aug 2026**: **generators**, not only sanitary workers, are responsible for waste at the threshold.
SC pulled up Union and States for not institutionalising the Rules (**1 Sep 2026**).

103.s: The primary goal of the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000 was:
103.x: The MSW (M&H) Rules 2000 primarily aimed at promoting waste segregation (APPSC-G2 2025). SUP ban came in 2022, EPR first came via the E-waste Rules 2011, and four-stream segregation is under the SWM Rules 2026.
103.tq: MSW 2000 → segregation; SWM 2016 → 3 streams; SWM 2026 → 4 streams.
xs: The **MSW (M&H) Rules 2000** primarily aimed at **promoting waste segregation** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025).
**SUP ban** came on **1 July 2022**; **EPR** first via the **E-waste Rules 2011**; **four-stream** segregation is under the **SWM Rules 2026**.
xa: ⚠ **2000** = segregation goal; **2016** = 3 streams; **2026** = 4 streams.
The 2016 Rules replaced the 2000 Rules from **8 Apr 2016**.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Bin under the 2026 Rules)
a. Wet
b. Dry
c. Sanitary
d. Special care

List-II (Examples)
i. Batteries, chemicals and paint cans
 ii. Food scraps, peels and garden waste
 iii. Diapers and sanitary napkins
 iv. Paper, plastics, metals, glass and wood

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Wet waste includes food scraps, peels and garden waste; dry waste includes paper, plastics, metals, glass and wood; sanitary waste includes diapers and napkins; special-care waste includes batteries, chemicals and paint cans.
103.tq: Begin with the distinctive sanitary and special-care pairs, then complete the remaining codes.
xs: Correct matching is **a–ii, b–iv, c–iii, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Wet**: food scraps, peels, garden waste; **Dry**: paper, plastics, metals, glass, wood.
**Sanitary**: diapers, sanitary napkins; **Special care**: batteries, chemicals, cleaning agents, paint cans, bulbs.
xa: The **SWM Rules 2026** came into force on **1 April 2026**, replacing the 2016 Rules.
Under the **2016 Rules**, used diapers/napkins were wrapped and put in the **dry** bin.
Collection chain ends at the **Material Recovery Facility** → processing → residual landfill.

103.s: Under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, used diapers and sanitary napkins were generally to be wrapped and placed in which stream?
103.x: Under the 2016 system, used diapers and sanitary napkins were generally wrapped and placed in the dry bin. The 2026 Rules provide a separate sanitary stream.
103.tq: Discriminate between the earlier three-stream rule and the later four-stream rule.
xs: Under the **SWM Rules 2016**, used diapers and sanitary napkins went wrapped into the **dry waste** bin — option **(3)** is correct.
A separate **sanitary** stream came only with the **SWM Rules 2026**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes put diapers/napkins under **domestic hazardous** (2016).
2016 streams: **biodegradable (wet), dry, domestic hazardous**.
2026 streams: **wet, dry, sanitary, special care**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding sanitary landfills:
1. Waste is compacted in cells and covered with earth daily.
2. Liners and leachate-collection systems are used.
3. The method relies mainly on containment rather than treatment.
4. It is intended for all biodegradable waste without segregation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Sanitary landfills use compacted cells, daily cover, liners and leachate collection, and rely on containment. They are not meant for all biodegradable waste without segregation.
103.tq: Find the single overbroad statement in a group describing a controlled facility.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: waste compacted in **cells**, covered with earth **daily** — correct.
Statement 2: **liners** and **leachate collection** are used — correct.
Statement 3: it relies on **containment**, not treatment — correct.
Statement 4: wrong — it is only for **residual** (non-recyclable, inert) waste, not unsegregated biodegradable waste.
xa: Sanitary landfill is the **most common and economic** method; it includes **methane and groundwater monitoring**.
Broken **glass** pieces → **landfilling** (APPSC-G2 2023 match).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about waste-to-energy technologies:
1. Incineration burns waste in oxygen and may produce steam for power generation.
2. Incineration can reduce waste volume by approximately 90 percent.
3. Incineration may generate ash and emissions.
4. Biomethanation converts wet organic waste into biogas through microbial action.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All four statements correctly describe incineration or biomethanation. Incineration produces steam, reduces volume substantially and has ash and emission concerns, while microbes convert wet organic waste into biogas.
103.tq: Test the complete technology profile rather than relying on only the principal output.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statements 1-3: **incineration** burns waste at high temperature, gives **steam for power**, cuts volume **up to 90%**, but causes **air pollution** and **ash** disposal problems.
Statement 4: **biomethanation** turns organic waste into **methane biogas** + slurry via microbes.
xa: India (Feb 2026): **21 operational WtE plants** producing **170+ MW** + **133 biogas facilities**.
AP WtE plants: **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam**.
SBM-U 2.0 target: **10,000 TPD** additional WtE capacity.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about Refuse-Derived Fuel (RDF):
1. It is made by shredding and dehydrating high-calorific MSW after removing recyclables and biodegradables.
2. It is used mainly as an alternative fuel in fertiliser plants and hospitals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct; RDF is mainly non-recyclable plastic, paper and textiles. Statement 2 is wrong: RDF is used as an alternative fuel in cement kilns and thermal power plants. So '1 only'.
103.tq: RDF -> cement kilns.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **RDF** is made by **shredding and dehydrating** high-calorific MSW, mainly non-recyclable plastic, paper, textiles.
Statement 2 is wrong: RDF is an alternative fuel in **cement kilns** and **thermal power plants**, not fertiliser plants or hospitals.
xa: Non-recyclable high-calorific dry waste goes to **RDF / co-processing in cement kilns**.
**WtE** cuts MSW volume by **~90%**.
**Biomedical waste** goes for incineration at a **CBMWTF**; **broken glass** to landfilling.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with its principal focus?
o: Total Sanitation Campaign — only construction of subsidised rural latrines
Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan — introduction of sanitation for the first time in India
Central Rural Sanitation Programme — award for ODF gram panchayats
Integrated Low Cost Sanitation — conversion of dry latrines to pour-flush latrines and liberation of manual scavengers
103.x: The Integrated Low Cost Sanitation programme focused on converting dry latrines into pour-flush latrines and freeing manual scavengers. The other options assign incorrect descriptions.
103.tq: Detect the swapped programme-focus pair.
xs: **ILCS** focused on converting **dry latrines to pour-flush** and **freeing manual scavengers** — option **(4)** is correct.
**TSC** was **demand-driven, community-led**, not just subsidised latrines (that was the **CRSP**).
**Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan** renamed TSC (**saturation approach**); the **ODF award** was **Nirmal Gram Puraskar**.
xa: **SBM** launched on **2 Oct 2014** (Gandhi Jayanti).

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026:
1. Plastics are classed as rigid, flexible and multi-layered.
2. Unmet targets may be carried forward for up to three years.
3. Plastic certificates become tradable.
4. Waste-to-energy, co-processing and waste-to-oil are permitted as end-of-life options.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The 2026 amendment includes all four measures: classification into three categories, three-year carry-forward, tradable certificates and specified end-of-life options.
103.tq: Check whether every provision in a regulatory amendment is correctly included.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statement 1: plastics classed as **rigid, flexible and multi-layered** — correct.
Statements 2-3: **carry-forward** of unmet targets up to **3 years**; **tradable plastic certificates** — correct.
Statement 4: **WtE, co-processing, waste-to-oil** allowed at end-of-life — correct.
xa: Recycled content in rigid plastics: **30% to 60% by 2028-29**.
Reuse targets (2025-26): **10%** small containers; **70%** large water packaging.
Critics say compliance was **eased** (4 Apr 2026).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about microplastics:
1. FSSAI detected microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples.
2. Microbeads in cosmetics are prohibited under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.
3. Microplastics in the Sundarbans can drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying antimicrobial-resistance genes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct: an FSSAI study found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples; the PWM Rules ban microbeads in cosmetics; and microplastics in the Sundarbans drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying AMR genes. Hence '1, 2 and 3'.
103.tq: Test findings, regulatory action and ecological consequence together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **FSSAI** found microplastics in **all tested sugar and salt samples** — correct.
Statement 2: PWM Rules ban **microbeads** in cosmetics — correct.
Statement 3: **Sundarbans** microplastics drive plastic-degrading enzymes in microbes carrying **AMR genes** — correct.
xa: Microplastics = particles **up to 5 mm**.
**National Action Plan for Marine Litter** (Dec 2025).

103.s: Which of the following best defines e-waste in the context of the ITU definition?
o: Only hazardous electronic equipment exported across borders
Only discarded computers sent for recycling
All household waste containing any metal component
Discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts not meant for reuse
103.x: E-waste consists of discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts that are not intended for reuse.
103.tq: Prefer the definition covering both equipment and parts, and excluding items meant for reuse.
xs: **ITU** defines e-waste as **discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts not meant for reuse** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is not limited to computers, exports or metal-containing household waste.
xa: **E-waste Rules 2022** cover **106 EEE** items incl. **solar PV** waste.
**Global E-waste Monitor** — **ITU and UNITAR**; **six** categories.
India = **3rd largest** e-waste generator (after China, USA).

103.s: Which organisations jointly publish the Global E-waste Monitor?
103.x: The Global E-waste Monitor is published by the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Institute for Training and Research.
103.tq: Identify the correct institutional pair instead of substituting neighbouring UN bodies.
xs: The **Global E-waste Monitor** is published by **ITU and UNITAR** — option **(2)** is correct.
UNFCCC, IUCN, UNEP and WHO are not its publishers.
xa: It uses **six categories**: cooling equipment, screens, lamps, large equipment, small equipment, IT.
The e-waste definition used is also the **ITU** one.
India: **2.2 million tonnes** (2025).

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Extended Producer Responsibility under the E-waste Rules, 2022:
1. Producers receive annual recycling targets based on earlier sales.
2. Producers register on the CPCB portal.
3. Producers may buy digital EPR certificates from registered recyclers.
4. An EPR floor price is intended to protect formal recyclers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All four statements correctly describe the EPR framework under the 2022 E-waste Rules.
103.tq: Test the complete regulatory chain from target-setting to certificate trading and price protection.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
Statement 1: annual **EPR recycling targets** based on earlier sales — correct.
Statements 2-3: register on the **CPCB portal**; buy **digital EPR certificates** from registered recyclers — correct.
Statement 4: **EPR floor price** protects formal recyclers — correct.
xa: The EPR system is built around the **circular economy**.
EPR first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (M&H) Rules 2011**.

103.s: Which new framework is associated with the Environment (Construction and Demolition Waste Management) Rules, 2025?
o: Extended Producer Responsibility for C&D waste
A national prohibition on using recycled aggregates
A complete ban on recycling construction waste
103.x: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has notified an Extended Producer Responsibility framework for C&D waste under the 2025 rules.
103.tq: Identify the policy instrument directly linked with the newer rules.
xs: MoEFCC notified an **EPR framework for C&D waste** (2026) with the **2025 Rules** — option **(2)** is correct.
The Rules promote reuse — **recycled aggregates, bricks, tiles** — so a ban on recycling is wrong.
xa: The **Environment (C&D Waste Management) Rules 2025** took effect on **1 April 2026** (3 Jan 2026).
India generates about **12 million tonnes** of C&D waste a year.
The **2016 Rules** already treated C&D waste as a **'Resource'**.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly states the urban local-government set-up in Andhra Pradesh mentioned for waste management?
o: 17 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards
113 Municipal Corporations, 17 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards
7 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 17 cantonment boards
17 Municipal Corporations, 7 municipalities and 113 cantonment boards
103.x: The stated urban set-up consists of 17 Municipal Corporations, 113 municipalities and 7 cantonment boards.
103.tq: Keep the three administrative counts matched with their correct categories.
xs: AP has **17 Municipal Corporations, 113 Municipalities and 7 Cantonment Boards** (May 2026) — option **(1)** is correct.
The other options shuffle the figures **17**, **113** and **7**.
xa: **Operation Clean Sweep** covered all **123 ULBs** (23 May-20 Jun 2026).
**94.62%** of wards have full door-to-door coverage (SES 2025-26).

103.s: The Supreme Court order of 18 August 2026 regarding responsibility for waste at the threshold held that:
o: Only Urban Local Bodies are responsible for such waste
Only sanitary workers are responsible for such waste
Responsibility begins only after waste reaches a landfill
Generators, and not only sanitary workers, are responsible for such waste
103.x: The Supreme Court held that generators, and not only sanitary workers, are responsible for waste at the threshold.
103.tq: Reject the exclusive responsibility claim by focusing on the phrase ‘not only’.
xs: The SC order of **18 Aug 2026** held that **generators**, not only sanitary workers, are responsible for waste at the threshold — option **(4)** is correct.
It was passed by the Bench of **Justice S.V.N. Bhatti**.
xa: SC pulled up Union and States for not institutionalising **SWM Rules 2026** (**1 Sep 2026**).
SC earlier gave pan-India directions; clean environment part of **Art. 21** (Feb 2026).

103.s: Which one of the following changes has been reported in the composition of rural waste?
o: A shift from municipal waste towards only industrial hazardous waste
A shift from biodegradable waste towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste
A complete disappearance of sanitary waste from rural areas
A shift from plastic waste towards exclusively biodegradable waste
103.x: Rural waste is shifting from predominantly biodegradable waste towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste.
103.tq: Identify the direction of change by comparing the earlier and emerging waste categories.
xs: Rural waste is shifting from **biodegradable** to **plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable** waste — option **(2)** is correct (5 Sep 2026).
Sanitary waste has grown, not disappeared, and the shift is away from biodegradable waste.
xa: Rural gaps: **Gram Panchayats lack capacity**; open dumping and burning continue.
Under **SWM Rules 2026**, **sanitary** waste (diapers, napkins) has its own bin.

103.s: Which of the following is an example of ‘invisible e-waste’ commonly discarded with regular waste?
o: Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories
Glass bottles, steel cans and paper cartons
Construction aggregates, fly ash and cement bags
Food scraps, garden leaves and crop residue
103.x: Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories are examples of ‘invisible e-waste’ that may be thrown into regular waste streams.
103.tq: Use the category clue and select the cluster of small electronic products.
xs: **Vapes, USB cables and LED accessories** are "invisible e-waste" — option **(1)** is correct (Jun 2026).
They are thrown into regular trash instead of reaching authorised recyclers.
xa: E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste (E-waste Rules 2022).
Citizens should deposit old electronics with **authorised recyclers** after wiping data.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the legal frameworks for which the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 serves as an umbrella?
o: Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 as the only framework
103.x: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 serves as an umbrella for frameworks including the EIA, Hazardous Waste, Coastal Regulation Zone and Contaminated Sites Rules. It is not described as an umbrella exclusively for the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026.
103.tq: Find the option that improperly uses an exclusive formulation and narrows a broader legal relationship.
xs: The odd one out is "**SWM Rules 2026 as the only framework**" — option **(1)**.
**EPA 1986** is the umbrella for **EIA, Hazardous Waste, CRZ and Contaminated Sites Rules** — not only for the SWM Rules.
xa: SWM Rules 2026 are themselves notified under **EPA 1986**.
EPA 1986 was enacted after **Bhopal**.

103.s:
How many of the following are listed as biodegradable polymers?
1. PHBV
2. PVC
3. Starch
4. Proteins
103.x: Three are biodegradable: PHBV, starch and proteins. PVC is a non-biodegradable synthetic plastic.
103.tq: Recall the biodegradable polymers.
n: PHBV is biodegradable. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Starch is biodegradable. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Proteins are biodegradable. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
PVC is a non-biodegradable synthetic plastic. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
xs: **Only three** — **PHBV**, **starch** and **proteins** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**PVC** is a **non-biodegradable** synthetic plastic.
xa: Other biodegradable polymers: **polylactic acid**, **polyglycolic acid**, **cellulose**, **Nylon-2-Nylon-6**.
Non-biodegradable: **polythene**, **PVC**, **polystyrene**, **nylon**, **Teflon**.
⚠ **Nylon-2-Nylon-6** is biodegradable but plain **nylon** is not.

103.s: The SWM Rules, 2016 are particularly associated with which key provision?
o: Prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides
Criteria for landfill and waste-processing sites
103.x: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, set criteria for landfill and waste-processing sites. HFC phase-down is the Kigali Amendment, and prior informed consent is the Rotterdam Convention.
103.tq: Match each rule or treaty to its key provision.
n: The SWM Rules were issued in 2016. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The key provision of the SWM Rules is criteria for landfill and waste-processing sites. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
xs: **SWM Rules 2016** are linked to **criteria for landfill and waste-processing sites** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Prior informed consent** for hazardous chemicals and pesticides is the **Rotterdam Convention**.
The 2016 Rules set **3 streams** (biodegradable, dry, domestic hazardous).
xa: They extended coverage beyond municipal areas to UAs, census towns, railways, airports, SEZs.
⚠ **2000** = segregation goal; **2016** = 3 streams; **2026** = 4 streams.
**SWM Rules 2026** came into force on **1 April 2026**.

103.s:
How many of the following are included under non-biodegradable waste?
1. Plastic
2. Sewage
3. DDT
4. Asbestos
103.x: Three are non-biodegradable: plastic, DDT and asbestos. Sewage is biodegradable.
103.tq: Find the biodegradable item.
n: Biodegradable waste includes sewage and domestic organic waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
Non-biodegradable waste includes plastic, DDT and asbestos. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
xs: **Only three** — **plastic**, **DDT** and **asbestos** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Sewage** is **biodegradable**: it **decomposes naturally** by **microorganisms**.
xa: Non-biodegradable items also include **tin**, aluminium foil, **glass bottles** and synthetic rubber.
**Wool** and cotton are biodegradable natural fibres.
Aerobic decomposition gives **compost**; anaerobic gives **methane (CH4)**.

103.s: Which of the following correctly shows the municipal solid-waste collection chain?
o: Door-to-door collection → segregated transport → transfer station → MRF → processing/recycling → residual landfill
Transfer station → door-to-door collection → landfill → MRF → recycling
Door-to-door collection → landfill → segregation → transfer station → MRF
MRF → door-to-door collection → segregated transport → landfill → processing
103.x: The chain begins with door-to-door collection, followed by segregated transport, transfer station, MRF, processing or recycling, and final residual landfill.
103.tq: Arrange a service chain by its operational sequence.
xs: The chain is **door-to-door collection → segregated transport → transfer station → MRF → processing/recycling → residual landfill** — option **(1)** is correct.
The landfill comes **last** and takes only residual waste — the other orders are wrong.
xa: **MRF** = **Material Recovery Facility**.
National gaps: only **68%** of ULBs notified SWM by-laws; under **45%** achieved full segregation.
AP: MRFs in **101 ULBs**; **94.62%** of wards with full door-to-door coverage.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Indore method of composting?
o: Anaerobic pits with alternate layers of municipal solid waste and night soil for four to six months
Aerobic composting in which organic waste is turned at intervals
Heating mixed waste without oxygen to obtain oil and char
103.x: The Indore method is aerobic composting in which the material is turned at intervals. The Bangalore method uses anaerobic pits with alternate layers of municipal solid waste and night soil.
103.tq: Discriminate between the closely associated Indore and Bangalore composting methods.
xs: The **Indore method** is **aerobic** composting with **turning at intervals** — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) describes the **Bangalore method** — anaerobic pits with alternate layers of MSW and **night soil**, **4-6 months**.
Options (2) and (4) describe **incineration** and **pyrolysis**.
xa: Both methods were systematised by **Howard** and developed by **Acharya and Subrahmanyam**.
Aerobic composting is **exothermic**, ending in **CO2, nitrite, nitrate** and manure.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below:

List-I (Waste)
 a. E-waste
 b. Broken glass pieces
 c. Biomedical waste
 d. Non-recyclable high-calorific dry waste

List-II (Preferred method)
 i. Incineration at a common biomedical waste treatment facility
 ii. Recycling
 iii. RDF or co-processing in cement kilns
 iv. Landfilling
103.x: E-waste is sent for recycling, broken glass pieces are landfilled, biomedical waste is incinerated at a common biomedical waste treatment facility, and high-calorific dry waste is used as RDF or co-processed in cement kilns.
103.tq: Start with the sure waste-treatment pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong pair.
xs: Correct matching is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**E-waste** → **recycling**; **broken glass** → **landfilling**.
**Biomedical waste** → **incineration at CBMWTF**; **high-calorific dry waste** → **RDF / co-processing in cement kilns**.
xa: APPSC-G2 2023 match: organic → **composting**, e-waste → recycling, hazardous → **incineration**, glass → landfilling.
**RDF** is made by **shredding and dehydrating** high-calorific MSW; used in **cement kilns** and thermal power plants.
AP: **APPCB** permitted **12 cement industries** to co-process waste.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes incineration from pyrolysis?
o: Incineration heats waste in the absence of oxygen, whereas pyrolysis uses excess oxygen
Incineration is controlled high-temperature burning, whereas pyrolysis heats waste without oxygen
Both methods are biological processes using earthworms
Both methods are restricted to inert waste in sanitary landfills
103.x: Incineration is controlled high-temperature combustion, while pyrolysis is thermal treatment in the absence of oxygen.
103.tq: Compare the defining operating condition of two similar thermal technologies.
xs: **Incineration** is controlled **high-temperature burning**; **pyrolysis** heats waste **without oxygen** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses them; **earthworms** belong to vermicomposting; **inert waste** goes to sanitary landfill.
xa: Incineration cuts volume **up to 90%**, recovers energy as steam, but causes **air pollution** and ash disposal problems.
Pyrolysis gives **gas, oil, char**; it suits mixed/contaminated streams but is **costly**.
Incineration suits **hazardous, biomedical, combustible** waste.

103.s: According to the stated healthcare-waste composition, approximately what proportion of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous waste?
103.x: Approximately 85% of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous waste, while about 15% is hazardous, including infectious, chemical and radioactive waste.
103.tq: Use the complementary proportions to distinguish the large general fraction from the smaller hazardous fraction.
xs: About **85%** of healthcare waste is **general non-hazardous** — option **(4)** is correct (WHO).
The remaining **~15%** is **hazardous** (infectious, chemical, radioactive) — option (1) is that share.
xa: India (2024): **1.89 lakh** facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.
BMW treatment aims to **prevent infection spread** and **protect human health**.

103.s: The main purpose of treating biomedical waste before disposal is to:
o: Increase the calorific value of hospital waste
Prevent the spread of infection and protect human health
Convert all biomedical waste into compost
Allow syringes to be reused safely
103.x: BMW is treated before disposal mainly to prevent infection spread and protect human health (APPSC-GS 2025) - killing pathogens, stopping syringe reuse and cutting volume and toxicity. Raising calorific value is not the aim, composting is not the route, and treatment is meant to stop syringe reuse, not enable it.
103.tq: BMW treatment → kill pathogens, stop reuse, protect health.
xs: BMW is treated before disposal to **prevent infection spread and protect human health** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
Treatment **kills pathogens**, **stops syringe reuse**, and cuts volume and toxicity — it is not for calorific value or compost.
xa: **White** bin: **sharps** — autoclave/dry heat, shredding, encapsulation.
Improper BMW/e-waste disposal releases **toxic substances into soil and water**.
BMW goes to **CBMWTFs** for incineration in AP.

103.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four classic characteristics used to identify hazardous waste?
103.x: The four classic characteristics are ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity and toxicity. Biodegradability is not one of these four classic criteria.
103.tq: Reject a familiar environmental term that does not belong to the defined list.
xs: **Biodegradability** is not a hazardous-waste criterion — option **(3)** is the answer.
The four classic criteria are **ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity**.
xa: Some notes add **explosive, infectious, radioactive**.
Examples: **lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium**, solvents, dyes, pesticides.
Forms: **solids, liquids, sludges, gases**.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly matched as a household hazardous waste?
103.x: Paints and batteries are household examples of hazardous waste. The other options generally represent biodegradable or non-hazardous household wastes.
103.tq: Match a household item with its correct waste category.
xs: **Paints and batteries** are household hazardous waste — option **(1)** is correct.
**Peels**, **paper**, **cotton**, **garden leaves** are biodegradable, non-hazardous wastes.
xa: Other household hazardous items: **fluorescent lamps**, aerosol cans, tyres, fertilisers, pesticides.
Under **SWM Rules 2026**, these go to the **special care** bin (batteries, chemicals, paint cans, bulbs).
**HOWM Rules 2024**: household **Deposition Centres**.

103.s: The principal purpose of the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 is to provide:
o: Compensation only after criminal conviction of the polluter
No-fault insurance cover and immediate relief to victims of hazardous-substance accidents
Insurance exclusively for transport of municipal waste
Long-term subsidies to industries using fly ash
103.x: The Act provides no-fault insurance cover intended to give immediate relief to victims of accidents involving hazardous substances.
103.tq: Identify the legal purpose by focusing on the beneficiary, liability basis and timing of relief.
xs: The **Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** gives **no-fault insurance** → **immediate relief** to victims of hazardous-substance accidents — option **(2)** is correct.
It does not wait for criminal conviction and is not about municipal transport or fly ash.
xa: **EPA 1986** — enacted after **Bhopal**.
**MSIHC Rules 1989** — hazardous chemicals.
**Bhopal (2-3 Dec 1984)**: **methyl isocyanate**, **5,400+** lives.

103.s: Which principle best describes the preferred approach to hazardous-waste disposal?
o: Landfilling is the first and preferred option for all hazardous waste
Hazardous waste should always be burned in open areas
Landfill is the last resort, while co-processing in cement plants and waste exchange are preferred where suitable
All hazardous waste must be discharged into surface water after dilution
103.x: Landfill is considered the last resort. APPCB prefers suitable co-processing as fuel in cement plants and exchange of waste between industries.
103.tq: Apply the waste hierarchy and reject options based on absolute or environmentally unsafe practices.
xs: **Landfill is the last resort**; **co-processing** in cement plants and **waste exchange** are preferred — option **(3)** is correct.
Open burning and discharge into water are not acceptable options.
xa: AP: **2 CHWTSDFs** (**Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**) for secure landfilling; **6 pre-processing** facilities.
**APPCB** permitted **12 cement industries** to co-process waste.
**APEMC** tracks hazardous waste with **GPS**.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Vermicompost
(b) Landfill
(c) Incineration
(d) Recycling

List-II
(i) Processing waste into usable material
(ii) Compost produced using earthworms
(iii) Controlled burning of waste
(iv) Disposal of solid waste in a designated land area
103.x: Vermicompost is made by earthworms, a landfill is a designated disposal site, incineration is controlled burning, and recycling turns waste into usable material. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
103.tq: Match each waste term to its meaning.
n: Vermicompost is compost produced using earthworms. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
A landfill is the disposal of solid waste in a designated land area. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Incineration is the controlled burning of waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Recycling is the processing of waste into usable material. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Earthworms are involved in vermicomposting. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Vermicompost**: compost made using **earthworms**; **Landfill**: disposal in a **designated land area**.
**Incineration**: **controlled burning** of waste; **Recycling**: **processing** waste into **usable material**.
xa: Incineration cuts volume **up to 90%** but causes air pollution.
**Pyrolysis** heats waste in the **absence of oxygen**.
Landfill relies on **containment**, not treatment.

103.s:
How many of the following are identified as waste-to-energy processes?

1. Pyrolysis
2. Plasma gasification
3. Compost
4. Vermicompost
103.x: Two are waste-to-energy processes: pyrolysis and plasma gasification. Compost and vermicompost turn waste into manure, not energy.
103.tq: Discriminate energy recovery from composting.
n: Pyrolysis is a waste-to-energy process. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
Plasma gasification is a waste-to-energy process. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
Compost is decomposed biodegradable waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
Vermicompost is worm compost. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
xs: **Only two** — **pyrolysis** and **plasma gasification** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are **waste-to-energy** processes; pyrolysis heats waste **without oxygen**, plasma gasification gives **syngas**.
**Compost** and **vermicompost** treat **biodegradable waste**, not energy recovery.
xa: **Pyrolysis** yields gas, oil and char and is **costly**.
**Plasma gasification** has a **Sweden** example.
**Anaerobic digestion** gives **methane** biogas + slurry.

103.s: Which alternative method is associated with oil spills and oily sludge?
103.x: Oilzapper, a mix of bacteria, cleans up oil spills and oily sludge. A microbial fuel cell treats wastewater, and EPR is a producer duty.
103.tq: Match each method to its use.
n: Oilzapper addresses oil spills and oily sludge. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
MFC addresses wastewater and electricity generation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Composting processes biodegradable waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
EPR assigns producers end-of-life responsibility. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
xs: **Oilzapper** addresses **oil spills** and **oily sludge** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**MFC** addresses **wastewater** and **electricity generation**; **EPR** assigns **producers** end-of-life responsibility.
**Composting** treats **biodegradable waste**.
xa: **Bioremediation** uses **microorganisms** for **pollutant removal**, incl. oil spills.
**Genetically engineered microbes** target **specific pollutants**.
**UV purification** targets **microorganisms** in **water**.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Bioremediation
(b) Genetically engineered microbes
(c) UV purification
(d) Pyrolysis

List-II
(i) Killing microorganisms in drinking water
(ii) Recombinant organisms such as the oil-eating 'superbug'
(iii) Thermal breakdown of waste without oxygen to recover energy
(iv) Using naturally occurring organisms to remove pollutants
103.x: Bioremediation uses naturally occurring organisms to remove pollutants, genetically engineered microbes include the oil-eating superbug, UV kills microbes in water, and pyrolysis breaks waste down without oxygen to recover energy. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
103.tq: Match each method to its use.
n: Bioremediation addresses toxic pollutants and oil spills. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Genetically engineered microbes address specific pollutants. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
UV purification addresses microorganisms in water. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Pyrolysis converts waste into energy. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Bioremediation**: **microorganisms** for **pollutant removal**; **genetically engineered microbes**: **specific pollutants**.
**UV purification**: **microorganisms** in **water**; **pyrolysis**: heat **without oxygen** to **convert waste** into **energy**.
xa: **Oilzapper** handles **oil spills** and **oily sludge**.
**Bio-asphalt** is an alternative to **petroleum-based asphalt**.
**Green Muffler** addresses **noise** and **some air pollution**.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Plasma gasification
(b) Bio-asphalt
(c) Hydrogen fuel
(d) Biofuels

List-II
(i) Ethanol and biodiesel made from biomass
(ii) Used in fuel cells that emit only water vapour
(iii) Alternative to petroleum-based asphalt
(iv) Waste-to-energy using very high-temperature plasma
103.x: Plasma gasification turns waste into energy with high-temperature plasma, bio-asphalt replaces petroleum asphalt, hydrogen powers fuel cells that emit only water, and biofuels such as ethanol and biodiesel come from biomass. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
103.tq: Match each method to its use.
n: Plasma gasification converts waste into energy. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Bio-asphalt is an alternative to petroleum-based asphalt. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Hydrogen fuel provides cleaner energy and transport. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
Biofuels are an alternative to fossil fuels. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 70-71]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Plasma gasification**: **waste-to-energy**; **Bio-asphalt**: alternative to **petroleum-based asphalt**.
**Hydrogen fuel**: **cleaner energy and transport**; **Biofuels**: an **alternative** to **fossil fuels**.
xa: **Euro/BS emission norms** address **vehicle emissions**.
**Renewable energy** addresses **fossil-fuel pollution**.
**MFC** addresses **wastewater** and **electricity generation**.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Resin code)
 a. 1
 b. 2
 c. 3
 d. 5
List-II (Plastic)
 i. PVC
 ii. PP
 iii. PET
 iv. HDPE
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Resin code 1 denotes PET, 2 denotes HDPE, 3 denotes PVC and 5 denotes PP.
103.tq: Start from the sure resin-code pair and eliminate inconsistent combinations.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii** — option **(1)**.
Resin codes: **1 PET**, **2 HDPE**, **3 PVC**, **5 PP**.
xa: Others: **4 LDPE**, **6 PS**, **7 others** incl. **polycarbonate** (BPA).
**PET** — water and soft-drink bottles; **LDPE/HDPE** — carry bags, milk bottles.
**Rigid** plastics (PET, HDPE bottles) need **30% → 60%** recycled content by 2028-29.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly states the carry-bag thickness progression under the specified plastic-waste measures?
o: 40 microns in 2011, 75 microns in 2016, 50 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022
40 microns in 2011, 50 microns in 2016, 120 microns from 30 September 2021 and 75 microns from 31 December 2022
50 microns in 2011, 40 microns in 2016, 75 microns from 31 December 2021 and 120 microns from 30 September 2022
40 microns in 2011, 50 microns in 2016, 75 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022
103.x: The stated progression is 40 microns in 2011, 50 microns in 2016, 75 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022.
103.tq: Track a sequence of dated numerical thresholds without reversing the dates.
xs: Carry-bag thickness went **40 (2011) → 50 (2016) → 75 microns (30 Sep 2021) → 120 microns (31 Dec 2022)** — option **(4)** is correct.
Options (1)-(3) jumble the **50/75** or **75/120** steps or their dates.
xa: The **75** and **120 micron** steps came from the **PWM Amendment Rules 2021** (12 Aug 2021, GSR 571(E)).
**PWM Rules 2016** also brought **50-micron packaging sheets**, a PWM fee on retailers and **plastic roads**.
AP bans SUP and carry bags **under 120 microns**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The ban on identified single-use plastic items came into force on 1 July 2022.
2. The EPR Guidelines for plastic packaging became effective in July 2022.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Both statements are correct: the SUP ban took effect on 1 July 2022 and the EPR Guidelines 2022 on plastic packaging became effective in July 2022. So 'Both 1 and 2'.
103.tq: July 2022: SUP ban + EPR Guidelines.
xs: **Both statements** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1: the **SUP ban** came into force on **1 July 2022**.
Statement 2: the **EPR Guidelines 2022** on plastic packaging became effective in **July 2022**.
xa: **PWM Amendment Rules 2021** aimed to phase out SUP by **2022**.
The SUP ban covers only **11%** of total plastic waste (CSE **2023**).

103.s: Under the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2024, which of the following is required for makers of biodegradable plastics?
o: Approval only from local village panchayats
Certification by the Central Pollution Control Board
Certification only by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
Registration with the National Disaster Management Authority
103.x: The 2024 amendment defined biodegradable plastics and required CPCB certification for their makers.
103.tq: Identify the competent certifying authority in a regulatory provision.
xs: The **PWM Amendment Rules 2024** required **CPCB certification** for makers of **biodegradable plastics** — option **(2)** is correct.
They also **defined** biodegradable plastics.
xa: Compostable plastics must meet **IS/ISO 17088**.
**FSSAI** found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt samples — a different context.
Timeline: 2016 Rules → 2021 Amendment → 2022 EPR Guidelines → **2024** Amendment → 2026 Amendment.

103.s: The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2021 aimed at phasing out identified single-use plastic items by:
103.x: The 2021 Amendment Rules (12 Aug 2021) aimed to phase out identified SUP by 2022 (APPSC-GS 2021); the ban took effect on 1 July 2022. 2020 precedes the Rules, and 2025 and 2030 are not the stated targets.
103.tq: PWM 2021 → SUP out by 2022; EPR Guidelines July 2022.
xs: The **PWM Amendment Rules 2021** aimed to phase out identified SUP by **2022** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021).
The ban duly took effect on **1 July 2022**.
xa: The 2021 Rules (**12 Aug 2021**) set carry bags at **75 microns** from 30 Sep 2021 and **120 microns** from 31 Dec 2022.
**EPR Guidelines** effective **July 2022**.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the identified single-use plastic items listed for prohibition?
o: Plastic sticks used in ear buds
103.x: Plastic ear-bud sticks, plastic flags and thermocol for decoration are included in the listed SUP items. HDPE milk bottles are not included in that list.
103.tq: Find the item outside the specified SUP list rather than choosing a prohibited item.
xs: **HDPE milk bottles** are not in the SUP ban list — option **(3)** is the answer.
Banned items include **ear buds with plastic sticks**, **thermocol for decoration** and **plastic flags**.
xa: Also banned: balloon sticks, candy and ice-cream sticks, plates, cups, cutlery, straws, stirrers, **PVC banners under 100 microns**.
**HDPE** milk/shampoo bottles are **rigid** packaging under **EPR Category I**.
In force from **1 July 2022**.

103.s: Which authorities are primarily responsible for enforcing the identified single-use plastic ban?
o: Only the Ministry of Jal Shakti
SPCBs/PCCs and local bodies, supported by national and state task forces
Only the National Disaster Management Authority
Only municipal corporations in metropolitan cities
103.x: Enforcement involves State Pollution Control Boards or Pollution Control Committees and local bodies, along with a National Level Taskforce and State Special Task Forces.
103.tq: Identify the correct combination of implementing authorities.
xs: Enforcement lies with **SPCBs/PCCs and local bodies**, backed by a **National Level Taskforce** and **State Special Task Forces** — option **(2)** is correct.
No single ministry or only metro corporations enforce it.
xa: AP enforces its SUP and **120-micron** carry-bag ban with **Revenue, Police, PCB**.
AP seizures: **5,505.06 kg** carry bags + **3,571.40 kg** SUP (SES 2025-26).
**Guntur**: complete ban from **15 Aug 2026**; fines up to **₹5,000** via **'Swachh App'**.

103.s: The identified single-use plastic ban covers approximately what proportion of total plastic waste?
103.x: The ban covers only about 11% of total plastic waste.
103.tq: Recall the precise proportion rather than assuming that the ban covers all plastic waste.
xs: The SUP ban covers only **11%** of total plastic waste — option **(2)** is correct (CSE 2023).
**5%**, **25%** and **50%** are not the stated share — the ban's reach is limited.
xa: SUP ban in force **1 July 2022**; **19 items** per most notes.
**70%+** of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers; **NAMASTE** aims to formalise them.
Packaging outside the ban is covered by **EPR Guidelines 2022**.

103.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Extended Producer Responsibility under the plastic-packaging framework?
o: Producers, Importers and Brand Owners handle covered plastic packaging not included in the SUP ban.
It transfers all plastic-waste responsibility to municipal bodies.
It applies only to consumers who purchase plastic goods.
It applies only to manufacturers of rigid plastics.
103.x: EPR applies to Producers, Importers and Brand Owners, or PIBOs, for plastic packaging not covered by the SUP ban.
103.tq: Ask who bears the responsibility and identify the correct institutional actors.
xs: Under EPR, **Producers, Importers and Brand Owners (PIBOs)** handle plastic packaging **not covered by the SUP ban** — option **(1)** is correct.
It does not shift responsibility to municipalities or consumers, and covers rigid, flexible and multi-layered plastics.
xa: Framework: **EPR Guidelines 2022**, effective **July 2022**.
Recyclers generate **EPR certificates** on the **CPCB portal** and sell them to producers.
Fewer than **50%** of producers comply with EPR.

103.s: EPR was first introduced into Indian waste law through the:
103.x: EPR first entered Indian waste law through the E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011.
103.tq: Use the exact first-introduction instrument rather than a later plastic-specific rule.
xs: EPR first entered Indian law via the **E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules 2011** — option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Some notes say the **Hazardous Wastes Rules 2016** introduced it first — not correct.
xa: SWM Rules 2016 also put **EPR** on producers/brand owners.
E-waste Rules lineage: **2011 → 2016 → 2022**.
**Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** cover batteries under EPR.

103.s:
Match the plastic category with its recycled-content target progression:
List-I (Category)
 a. Rigid
 b. Flexible, single-layer
 c. Multi-layered
List-II (2025-26 to later)
 i. 5% to 10%
 ii. 10% to 20%
 iii. 30% to 60%
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Rigid plastics have a 30% to 60% progression, flexible single-layer plastics 10% to 20%, and multi-layered plastics 5% to 10%.
103.tq: Start with the distinctive rigid-plastic percentage and complete the remaining pairs.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
xa: Rigid examples: **PET bottles**, HDPE milk/shampoo bottles; flexible: **carry bags, chips packets**.
Unmet targets can be carried forward up to **3 years** (2026 Amendment).

103.s: China's National Sword Policy of 2018 and Thailand's 2025 measure primarily restrict:
o: Domestic manufacture of all plastic products
103.x: China's National Sword Policy and Thailand's 2025 measure restrict imports of plastic waste.
103.tq: Identify the regulated activity rather than the broad environmental theme.
xs: China's **National Sword Policy (2018)** and **Thailand's 2025 ban** restrict **plastic waste imports** — option **(1)** is correct.
They do not target hospital use, domestic manufacture or microplastics in food.
xa: **Basel** amendment on **plastic waste** is now operative.
**Global Plastics Treaty** process began at **UNEA-5.2 (Nairobi, March 2022)**.
Transboundary issue = physical transfer of hazardous waste, often to **developing countries**.

103.s: UNEA-5.2, held in Nairobi in March 2022, adopted which resolution that led to the establishment of the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC)?
103.x: The UNEA-5.2 resolution titled “End Plastic Pollution” established the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee.
103.tq: Use the exact title of the resolution rather than a broad subject description.
xs: **UNEA-5.2** (Nairobi, March 2022) adopted the resolution "**End Plastic Pollution**" — option **(3)** is correct.
It set up the **Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC)**.
xa: INC venues: **Punta del Este, Paris, Nairobi, Ottawa, Busan (INC-5, 2024), Geneva (INC-5.2, Aug 2025)**.
