No agreement — sticking points: **production caps**, chemicals of concern, finance.

103.s: Which of the following persons or entities may legally deal in e-waste under the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022?
o: Only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers
103.x: The Rules permit only registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers to deal in e-waste.
103.tq: Apply the registration requirement to a practical e-waste transaction.
xs: Only **registered producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers** may deal in e-waste — option **(4)** is correct.
**Unregistered scrap dealers** and informal dismantlers are excluded.
xa: E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste.
Producers register on the **CPCB portal** and buy **digital EPR certificates**.
Rules in force **1 April 2023**.

103.s: Which of the following was issued by the CPCB in response to biomedical waste generated during the COVID-19 period?
o: Global E-waste Monitor and Basel Protocol
R2 electronics recycling code and plastic treaty guidelines
COVID19BWM tracking app and COVID-19 waste guidelines
103.x: The CPCB issued COVID-19 biomedical-waste guidelines in 2020 and introduced the COVID19BWM tracking app.
103.tq: Match the emergency, authority and digital tracking instrument.
xs: **CPCB** issued **COVID-19 waste guidelines** in **2020** and the **COVID19BWM** tracking app — option **(3)** is correct.
**Global E-waste Monitor** is by ITU/UNITAR; **R2** is an e-waste certification; **Swachh App** is Guntur's plastic-fine tool.
xa: BMW Rules 2016 use **barcoding and GPS tracking**.

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the reported compliance position concerning Extended Producer Responsibility for plastic waste?
o: Fewer than 50% of producers comply with EPR targets
EPR targets have been withdrawn for producers
More than 90% of producers comply with EPR targets
Exactly 70% of producers comply with EPR targets
103.x: Fewer than 50% of producers were reported to comply with Extended Producer Responsibility targets, leading to criticism about enforceability.
103.tq: Distinguish the compliance percentage from the separate figure relating to informal recycling.
xs: **Fewer than 50%** of producers comply with EPR — option **(1)** is correct.
EPR has not been withdrawn; **90%** and **70%** are not the stated compliance figures.
xa: EPR collection targets are hard to enforce (6 Apr 2026).
CPCB EPR portal: **69,470 producers**, **4,402 recyclers** (29 Oct 2025).
2026 Amendment allows **carry-forward** up to **3 years**.

103.s: Which of the following statements about Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is incorrect?
o: EPR concerns the producer’s responsibility for product or waste at the end of its life.
EPR makes the producer responsible for environmentally sound management of product or waste through its life cycle.
EPR was introduced under the Plastic Waste Management and Handling Rules, 2012.
EPR was introduced under the Plastic Waste Management and Handling Rules, 2011.
103.x: Option C is incorrect: Extended Producer Responsibility came in with the Plastic Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, not 2012. It makes producers responsible for their product's waste.
103.tq: Recall the EPR year, 2011.
n: Extended Producer Responsibility is a producer's responsibility for the environmentally sound management of a product or waste throughout its life cycle. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Extended Producer Responsibility makes the producer responsible for the environmentally sound management of a product or waste at the end of its life. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Extended Producer Responsibility was introduced under the Plastic Waste Management and Handling Rules, 2011. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
xs: The incorrect statement is that EPR was introduced under the **PWM Rules, 2012** — so option **(3)** is correct.
EPR was **introduced** under the **Plastic Waste Management and Handling Rules, 2011**.
Options (1) and (2) are true: EPR is the **producer's responsibility** for **environmentally sound management** through the **life cycle**, at **end of its life**.
xa: ⚠ Other notes say EPR came via the **E-waste (Management and Handling) Rules 2011**.
⚠ It is NOT the **Hazardous Wastes Rules 2016** that introduced EPR first.
The **CPCB EPR portal** lets recyclers sell **EPR certificates** to producers.

103.s: Bisphenol A (BPA) is particularly associated with which resin-code category?
103.x: Resin code 7 ('others') includes polycarbonate, which releases bisphenol A (BPA), an endocrine disruptor. PET (1), PVC (3) and PP (5) are not the BPA-linked category.
103.tq: Link a chemical concern with the correct resin category.
xs: **BPA** is linked to resin code **7**, which includes **polycarbonate** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Polycarbonate** (hard bottles, containers) releases **bisphenol A**, an **endocrine disruptor**.
**PET (1)**, **PVC (3)** and **PP (5)** are not the BPA category.
xa: **PET** leaches additives when heated.
Resin codes: 1 PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 PP, 6 PS, 7 others.

103.s: Which standard must compostable plastics meet?
103.x: Compostable plastics must meet the IS/ISO 17088 standard.
103.tq: Recall the exact technical standard rather than a general environmental certification.
xs: Compostable plastics must meet **IS/ISO 17088** — option **(3)** is correct.
The notes name no other standard for compostable plastics.
xa: **PWM Amendment Rules 2024** defined **biodegradable plastics** and required **CPCB certification** for makers.
**PWM Amendment Rules 2026**: **QR-code traceability**; classes rigid, flexible, multi-layered.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly arranged as the authorised e-waste recycling chain?
o: Producer → consumer → landfill → dismantler → recovered materials
Consumer → collection centre or producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials
Consumer → informal hub → landfill → authorised recycler → producer take-back
Consumer → authorised recycler → collection centre → informal hub → recovered materials
103.x: The authorised chain begins with the consumer and collection or producer take-back, followed by dismantling, recycling and recovery of materials.
103.tq: Follow the material flow from generation to recovery and reject informal or disposal stages.
xs: The formal chain is **consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → authorised dismantler → authorised recycler → recovered materials** — option **(2)** is correct.
Chains via **landfill** or **informal hubs** are not the authorised route.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**Urban mining** recovers iron, steel, copper, aluminium, plastics from e-waste.
AP: **Re Sustainability** MoU for e-waste collection in all **123 ULBs**.

103.s: What does the R2 Code of Practices primarily promote?
o: Environmentally responsible practices in electronics recycling
103.x: R2, or Responsible Recycling, is a code of practices promoting environmentally responsible electronics recycling.
103.tq: Expand the abbreviation and link it to its specific sector.
xs: The **R2 Code of Practices** promotes **environmentally responsible practices in electronics recycling** — option **(1)** is correct (UPSC 2021).
**R2 = Responsible Recycling**, a global certification for **e-waste recyclers**.
xa: Formal chain: consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → **authorised dismantler** → **authorised recycler** → recovered materials.
**78%** of e-waste is processed informally, by **open burning and acid baths**.
**468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the scope and compliance features of the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016?
o: They cover all healthcare facilities, use four colour categories and require bar coding.
They cover only laboratories and require no tracking mechanism.
They cover municipal waste generators and require three waste streams.
They cover only government hospitals and require ten colour categories.
103.x: The BMW Management Rules, 2016 cover 100% of healthcare facilities, use four colour categories and provide for barcoding and GPS tracking. Ten categories belonged to the 1998 Rules, and the Rules are not limited to laboratories or government hospitals.
103.tq: Reject the options that import the ten-category system of the earlier rules or the municipal three-stream system.
xs: The **BMW Rules 2016** cover **100% of healthcare facilities**, use **4 colour categories** and require **barcoding** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ten categories** belonged to the **1998** Rules; the Rules are not limited to labs or government hospitals.
**Three streams** belong to the **SWM Rules 2016**, not the BMW Rules.
xa: Tracking: **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
Scale (2024): **1.89 lakh** health-care facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.

103.s:
Match List-I (Biomedical waste) with List-II (Colour category) under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016:
List-I
a. Sharps such as needles and blades
b. Glassware and metallic implants
c. Contaminated recyclable plastics such as IV sets and catheters
d. Anatomical waste and expired medicines
List-II
i. Yellow
ii. Red
iii. White (translucent)
iv. Blue
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Sharps go to White (translucent), glassware and metallic implants to Blue, contaminated recyclable plastics to Red, and anatomical waste/expired medicines to Yellow, so a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i. Option 2 swaps sharps and glass; option 3 swaps plastics and anatomical waste; option 4 swaps sharps and plastics.
103.tq: Yellow = burn (anatomical), Red = recyclable plastics, White = sharps, Blue = glass/metal.
xs: Correct matching is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)**.
**Sharps** → **White (translucent)**; **glassware, metallic implants** → **Blue**.
**Recyclable plastics** (IV sets, catheters) → **Red**; **anatomical waste, expired medicines** → **Yellow**.
xa: ⚠ **White** = sharps; **Red** = recyclable plastics; **Blue** = glass; **Yellow** = anatomical.
BMW Rules 2016 use **4 colour categories**.
AP sends BMW to **CBMWTFs** for incineration.

103.s:
Biomedical waste may arise from the diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals. Which of the following is included in this waste stream?
1. Blood
2. Sharps
3. Cultures
4. Discarded or expired medicines
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Blood, sharps, cultures and discarded or expired medicines are all examples of biomedical waste; anatomical and chemical waste are also included.
103.tq: Check each listed source against the broad definition of waste from healthcare activity.
xs: **Blood, sharps, cultures and discarded/expired medicines** are all biomedical waste — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
BMW = waste from **diagnosis, treatment or immunisation** of humans/animals; also **anatomical** and **chemical** waste.
xa: About **85%** of healthcare waste is general non-hazardous; **~15%** hazardous (WHO).
Biomedical category examples: **syringes, gloves**.

103.s: Biomedical waste in Andhra Pradesh is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities primarily for
o: Production of RDF for cement kilns only
103.x: Biomedical waste is sent to Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facilities for incineration. It is not intended for open dumping or untreated agricultural composting.
103.tq: Identify the prescribed treatment route for a specialised waste stream.
xs: AP sends biomedical waste to **CBMWTFs** for **incineration** (2024-25) — option **(3)** is correct.
Open dumping and untreated composting are not permitted routes.
xa: **Yellow** category BMW → incineration / **plasma pyrolysis** / deep burial.
BMW Rules 2016 use **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
India (2024): **1.89 lakh** facilities generate **800+ tonnes/day**.

103.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Landfill is associated with solid waste disposal.
EPR refers to the producer's end-of-life responsibility.
R2 refers to wastewater treatment and electricity generation.
103.x: Option C is incorrect: R2 is about responsible electronics recycling. Wastewater treatment with electricity is the microbial fuel cell.
103.tq: Match each waste term to its meaning.
n: A landfill is used for solid-waste disposal. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
Extended Producer Responsibility assigns producers responsibility for end-of-life management. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
R2 is associated with electronics recycling. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
Compost is decomposed biodegradable waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
MFCs are associated with wastewater treatment and electricity generation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **R2** refers to **wastewater treatment and electricity generation** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**R2** relates to the **electronics recycling industry** — **responsible electronics recycling**.
**Wastewater** and **electricity generation** is the **MFC**.
xa: A company following the **R2 Code of Practices** can become **R2 Certified** (UPSC **2021**).
**78%** of e-waste is processed informally; hubs at **Seelampur** and **Moradabad**.
India has **468 authorised recyclers** (CPCB **2024**).

103.s: Which one of the following best illustrates the contribution of biomining of legacy waste to a circular economy?
o: It permanently stores all waste without recovery.
It increases the generation of mixed municipal waste.
It recovers useful materials from old waste dumps for productive reuse.
It replaces source reduction with open dumping.
103.x: Biomining of legacy waste supports the circular economy by recovering materials from old waste accumulations for reuse or further processing.
103.tq: Identify the option that reflects resource recovery and circularity.
xs: Biomining **recovers useful materials from old waste dumps for productive reuse**, supporting the **circular economy** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Biomining** = excavating legacy waste and separating it into **recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill**.
It does not store waste permanently, increase mixed waste or replace source reduction — options (1), (2), (4) are wrong.
xa: **Legacy waste** = old MSW piled in dumpsites for years; emits **methane**, pollutes groundwater.
**SWM Rules 2026:** legacy dumps mapped, time-bound biomining with **quarterly** reports.
AP example: **Ongole** is biomining its **Guthikondavaripalem** yard — **1.76 lakh t** of 2.56 lakh t processed.
**Urban mining** recovers iron, steel, copper, aluminium, plastics from e-waste.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Biomining of legacy waste means burning the dump in place and capping it with soil.
2. Legacy waste is old municipal solid waste piled in dumpsites for years; it emits methane and pollutes groundwater.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong: biomining excavates the legacy waste and separates it into recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill; it is not burning or capping. So '2 only'.
103.tq: Biomining = excavate and separate.
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 2 is correct: **legacy waste** is old MSW piled in dumpsites for years; it **emits methane** and **pollutes groundwater**.
Statement 1 is wrong: **biomining** excavates and separates the waste into **recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill** — not burning and capping.
xa: Biomining of legacy waste supports the **circular economy**.
**3R** = **Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**; **source reduction** is the top of the hierarchy.
⚠ "**Regain**" is not one of the 3R (APPSC-GS **2025**).

103.s:
With reference to legacy waste in Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Ongole is biomining its Guthikondavaripalem dump yard and supplying RDF to cement industries.
2. The State inherited about 108 lakh tonnes of legacy waste, as stated by the CM in Feb 2026.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: Ongole is biomining the Guthikondavaripalem yard (1.76 lakh t of 2.56 lakh t processed) and supplying RDF to cement plants. Statement 2 is correct: AP inherited 108 lakh tonnes of legacy waste. So 'Both' is right; '1 only', '2 only' and 'Neither' miss a true statement.
103.tq: Ongole → Guthikondavaripalem biomining; AP legacy waste 108 lakh t.
xs: Both statements are correct — option **(3) Both 1 and 2**.
Statement 1: **Ongole** is biomining its **Guthikondavaripalem** yard — **1.76 lakh t** of 2.56 lakh t processed; **RDF** supplied to cement plants.
Statement 2: AP inherited **108 lakh tonnes** of legacy waste (CM, Feb 2026).
xa: **Anantapur** is setting up a **170 TPD** waste-processing plant (Jul 2026).
AP: **2 CHWTSDFs** at **Anakapalli** and **SPSR Nellore**; **6 pre-processing** facilities.
AP **Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30** — guidelines via **G.O. Ms. No. 26**.

103.s:
The INC-5.2 meeting held in Geneva in August 2025 ended with no agreement. Which of the following were identified as major sticking points?
1. Production caps
2. Chemicals of concern
3. Finance
4. Establishment of informal e-waste hubs
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: Production caps, chemicals of concern and finance were the major sticking points. Informal e-waste hubs were not an issue in the INC negotiations.
103.tq: Eliminate the statement imported from a neighbouring environmental topic.
xs: **Production caps, chemicals of concern and finance** were the sticking points — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Informal e-waste hubs (**Seelampur**, **Moradabad**) are an Indian e-waste issue, not an INC sticking point.
xa: **Busan (INC-5, 2024)** also ended without agreement before Geneva.
Treaty origin: **UNEA-5.2**, Nairobi, March 2022.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT a hazardous constituent released by old computers?
103.x: Old computers can release beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury and lead, besides PCBs and PBBs. Plutonium is not included in this list.
103.tq: Find the outsider among the listed hazardous constituents.
xs: **Plutonium** is not released by old computers — option **(2)** is the answer (UPSC 2013 key).
Old computers release **beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead**, plus **PCBs, PBBs**.
⚠ Trap: NOT heptachlor, NOT plutonium.
xa: **Mercury** — brain and kidney damage; **cadmium** — kidney and bone damage.
**RoHS** limits lead, mercury, cadmium in new EEE.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Constituent)
a. Lead
b. Mercury
c. Cadmium
d. Brominated flame retardants (PBBs)

List-II (Main harm or characteristic)
i. Kidney and bone damage
ii. Persistent nature and endocrine effects
iii. Nervous-system and kidney effects
iv. Brain and kidney damage; bioaccumulation in fish

Codes:
103.x: Lead affects the nervous system and kidneys; mercury damages the brain and kidneys and bioaccumulates in fish; cadmium damages kidneys and bones; PBBs are persistent and have endocrine effects.
103.tq: Start from the sure pair, especially cadmium with kidney and bone damage.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–iv, c–i, d–ii** — option **(1)**.
**Lead** — nervous system, kidneys; **mercury** — brain and kidney damage, **bioaccumulates in fish**.
**Cadmium** — kidney and bone damage; **PBBs** — **persistent**, **endocrine effects**.
xa: Old computers also release **beryllium** and **chromium**.
**Fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain mercury; mercury products phased out under **Minamata**.

103.s: India is presently described as the world’s ______ largest generator of e-waste, after China and the United States.
103.x: India is the third-largest e-waste generator, after China and the United States.
103.tq: Read the ranking together with the named countries to avoid reversing the order.
xs: India is the **third** (3rd) largest e-waste generator, after **China** and **USA** — option **(4)** is correct.
So **second**, **fourth** and **fifth** are wrong.
xa: India's e-waste: **2.2 million tonnes (2025)**.
**First e-waste clinic**: **Bhopal**.
India also ranks third among dry MSW generators for **textile waste**.

103.s: The e-waste generation attributed to India for 2025 was approximately:
103.x: India’s e-waste generation was reported as approximately 2.2 million tonnes in 2025. The 3.54 lakh tonnes figure refers to e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021.
103.tq: Separate generation figures from collection-and-processing figures and compare their units.
xs: India generated about **2.2 million tonnes** of e-waste in **2025** — option **(2)** is correct.
**1.75 MT** is an earlier figure (Oct 2025); **1.6 MT** is recycler capacity; **3.54** lakh tonnes was processed in FY 2021.
xa: **468 authorised recyclers**, **1.6 MT** capacity (CPCB 2024).
**78%** processed informally; only **10-20%** of materials recovered.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about the E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022:
1. They were notified in November 2022 and came into force on 1 April 2023.
2. They replaced the 2016 E-waste Rules, which had in turn replaced the 2011 Rules.
3. They cover 106 EEE items but exclude solar PV modules, panels and cells.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: notified Nov 2022, in force 1 April 2023. Statement 2 is correct: they replaced the 2016 Rules, which replaced the 2011 M&H Rules. Statement 3 is wrong: the 106 EEE items include solar PV waste (modules/panels/cells). So '1 only' is incomplete and the options containing 3 are wrong.
103.tq: Remember 2011 -> 2016 -> 2022 lineage; 106 items INCLUDING solar PV.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: notified **November 2022**, in force **1 April 2023** — correct.
Statement 2: replaced the **2016** Rules, which replaced the **2011** M&H Rules — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — the **106 EEE** items **include solar PV** modules/panels/cells.
xa: Only **registered** producers, manufacturers, refurbishers, recyclers may deal in e-waste.
E-waste must **not be mixed** with other waste; enforcement by environmental compensation and audits.

103.s: Which of the following is correctly matched with the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022?
o: They replaced the 2001 rules and cover EV, portable, automotive and industrial batteries.
They replaced the 2016 E-waste Rules and cover only mobile-phone batteries.
They apply only to lead-acid batteries used in automobiles.
They exclude batteries from the EPR framework.
103.x: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 replaced the 2001 rules and cover electric-vehicle, portable, automotive and industrial batteries under EPR.
103.tq: Distinguish battery rules from e-waste rules using scope and replacement year.
xs: The **Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** replaced the **2001** rules and cover **EV, portable, automotive and industrial** batteries — option **(1)** is correct.
They bring batteries **under EPR**, so option (4) is wrong; they are not limited to lead-acid or mobile batteries.
xa: **E-waste Rules 2022** replaced the **2016** Rules (which replaced 2011).
**Household examples** of hazardous waste include **batteries**; under SWM 2026 they go to the **special care** bin.

103.s: Which pair of places is correctly associated with informal e-waste recycling hubs?
103.x: Seelampur in Delhi and Moradabad are identified as informal e-waste recycling hubs.
103.tq: Match the locations with the distinctive informal e-waste activity.
xs: **Seelampur** (Delhi) and **Moradabad** (UP) are informal e-waste hubs — option **(1)** is correct.
**Indore**, **Tirupati** and **Visakhapatnam** feature in cleanliness rankings, not as e-waste hubs.
xa: **78%** of e-waste is processed informally (Jun 2026).
Informal workers use **open burning and acid baths**.

103.s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate action for a citizen disposing of an old electronic device?
o: Burn it to recover copper and aluminium
Mix it with municipal solid waste after removing the battery
Sell or deposit it with an authorised recycler or collection centre after wiping data
Hand it over to any informal dismantler without data removal
103.x: Citizens should use authorised recyclers or collection centres and wipe personal data before handing over old electronics.
103.tq: Apply the recommended citizen action while avoiding unsafe informal handling.
xs: Citizens should **sell or deposit old electronics with authorised recyclers or collection centres** after **wiping data** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Burning** and **informal** dismantling are harmful; e-waste must **not be mixed** with MSW.
xa: "Invisible e-waste": **vapes, USB cables, LED accessories** thrown in regular trash (Jun 2026).
AP collected **60,392 kg** of e-waste (SES 2025-26).

103.s: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced which earlier rules?
o: Municipal Solid Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000
103.x: The Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Biomedical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998, which had ten categories.
103.tq: Use the predecessor-successor relationship to distinguish rules with similar environmental subject matter.
xs: The **BMW Management Rules 2016** replaced the **BMW (M&H) Rules 1998** — option **(3)** is correct.
The 1998 Rules had **10 categories**; the 2016 Rules use **4 colour categories**.
xa: Amended in **2018** and **2019**.
Cover **100%** of healthcare facilities; **barcoding and GPS tracking**.
⚠ "**10** colour-coded categories" mixes up the 1998 Rules.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fluorescent lamps and CFLs are household hazardous waste because they contain mercury.
2. Mercury-added products are being phased out under the Stockholm Convention.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct; broken lamps release mercury vapour. Statement 2 is wrong: mercury-added products are phased out under the Minamata Convention; Stockholm deals with persistent organic pollutants. So '1 only'.
103.tq: Mercury = Minamata; POPs = Stockholm.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **fluorescent lamps/CFLs** contain **mercury** = household hazardous waste; broken lamps release mercury vapour.
Statement 2 is wrong: mercury-added products are phased out under **Minamata**; **Stockholm** covers **persistent organic pollutants**.
xa: Minamata Convention (**2013**): dental amalgam phase-out by **2034**.
**PFAS** ("forever chemicals") are now listed under **Stockholm**.
Old computers release **beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead** — ⚠ NOT heptachlor or plutonium.

103.s:
With reference to the Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016, consider the following statements:
1. Imports and exports of hazardous waste follow the Basel Convention.
2. Import of hazardous waste for disposal is prohibited.
3. Co-processing is placed above prevention in the waste-management hierarchy.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because prevention is at the top of the hierarchy and co-processing occurs later, before safe disposal.
103.tq: Find the reversed hierarchy statement; the position of co-processing is the trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: imports/exports follow the **Basel** Convention — correct.
Statement 2: **import for disposal** is prohibited — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — **prevention** is at the top; **co-processing** comes just before **safe disposal**.
xa: Hierarchy: **prevention > minimisation > reuse > recycling > recovery > co-processing > safe disposal**.
**PIC** for import/export; **2024**: household **Deposition Centres**, simpler manifests.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I (Industrial waste)
a. Fly ash
b. Steel slag
c. Red mud
d. Phosphogypsum

List-II (Source industry)
i. Alumina refining
 ii. Steel plants
 iii. Coal-based thermal power plants
 iv. Phosphoric acid or phosphatic fertiliser plants

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Fly ash comes from coal-based thermal power plants, steel slag from steel plants, red mud from alumina refining, and phosphogypsum from phosphoric acid or phosphatic fertiliser plants.
103.tq: Start from the sure source-industry pair and eliminate the codes that swap industrial processes.
xs: Correct matching is **a–iii, b–ii, c–i, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Fly ash** — coal thermal plants; **steel slag** — steel plants.
**Red mud** — alumina refining; **phosphogypsum** — phosphoric acid / phosphatic fertiliser plants.
xa: Phosphogypsum reuse: gypsum substitute in cement, **soil conditioner**.
**Chromium sludge** — tanneries, electroplating.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about fly ash:
1. The Fly Ash Utilisation Notification requires its use in bricks, cement and roads within 100 km of thermal plants.
2. Fly ash can be used to make bricks and to partly replace Portland cement in concrete.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 2 is correct (UPSC 2015). Statement 1 is wrong on the distance: the notification applies within 300 km of thermal plants. So '2 only'.
103.tq: Fly ash use mandatory within 300 km.
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 2 is correct: **fly ash** is used in **building bricks** and **partly replaces Portland cement** in concrete (UPSC **2015**).
Statement 1 is wrong: the notification applies **within 300 km** of thermal plants, not 100 km.
xa: Fly ash comes from **coal-based thermal power plants**.
**Steel slag** is used in road bases, agricultural soil and cement (UPSC **2020**).
**Red mud** comes from **alumina refining**; **phosphogypsum** from phosphatic fertiliser plants.

103.s:
Steel slag can be the material for which of the following?
1. Construction of base roads
2. Improvement of agricultural soil
3. Production of cement
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: All three uses are correct (UPSC 2020): steel slag is used as road base, to improve agricultural soil and in cement production; Surat has a steel-slag road. Options leaving out any use are incomplete.
103.tq: Steel slag → roads + soil + cement (all three).
xs: All three uses are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (UPSC 2020).
Steel slag serves as **road base**, **improves agricultural soil** and is used in **cement production**.
xa: **Surat** has a **steel-slag road**.
**Fly ash** — bricks, cement, roads within **300 km** of plants.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The C&D Waste Management Rules, 2016 treat construction and demolition waste as a resource and provide for its collection, storage and reprocessing.
2. The Environment (C&D) Waste Management Rules, 2025 took effect from 1 October 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 2016 Rules treat C&D waste as a resource (collection, storage, reprocessing). Statement 2 is wrong: the 2025 Rules took effect from 1 April 2026 (1 Oct 2025 was the date in the draft SWM Rules). So only 1 is correct; '2 only', 'Both' and 'Neither' are wrong.
103.tq: New waste rules of 2025-26 (SWM 2026, C&D 2025) both start 1 April 2026.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: **C&D Rules 2016** treat C&D waste as a **'Resource'** — collection, transport, storage, re-processing — correct.
Statement 2: wrong — the **2025 Rules** took effect from **1 April 2026**; **1 Oct 2025** was the draft SWM Rules date.
xa: MoEFCC notified an **EPR framework for C&D waste** (2026).
India generates about **12 million tonnes** of C&D waste a year.

103.s:
With reference to plastic recycling and waste-pickers, consider the following statements:
1. More than 70% of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers.
2. The NAMASTE scheme aims to formalise informal workers.
3. About 15 lakh waste-pickers remain outside formal systems.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements are correct. More than 70% of recycled plastic is handled by informal workers, NAMASTE seeks to formalise them, and approximately 15 lakh waste-pickers remain outside formal systems.
103.tq: Keep distinct percentages, scheme objectives and population estimates separate while evaluating the statements.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **70%+** of recycled plastic handled by informal workers — correct.
Statement 2: **NAMASTE** scheme (2024) aims to formalise them — correct.
Statement 3: ~**15 lakh** waste-pickers outside formal systems — correct.
xa: Segregation at source is **under 25%** (Oct 2025).
**78%** of e-waste is also processed informally.

103.s: Which one of the following best describes PFAS, often referred to as “forever chemicals”?
o: They are biodegradable chemicals used exclusively in cement production
They persist in the environment, occur in products such as food packaging, and may accumulate in animal bodies
They rapidly decompose in soil and water and do not accumulate in organisms
They are radioactive substances used mainly in fluorescent lamps
103.x: PFAS are persistent chemicals found in drinking water, food and food packaging. They do not break down easily and can accumulate in animal bodies.
103.tq: Use the option that combines the defining properties and common exposure pathways.
xs: **PFAS** persist, occur in **drinking water, food and food packaging**, and **accumulate in animal bodies** — option **(2)** is correct (UPSC 2024).
They **do not break down easily** — option (3) is wrong; they are not radioactive or biodegradable.
xa: PFAS are now listed under the **Stockholm** Convention.
Stockholm now covers **34 chemicals**, incl. **chlorpyrifos** and PFAS.

103.s: In the context of transboundary movement of hazardous waste, PIC refers to:
103.x: PIC means Prior Informed Consent, a control associated with the import and export of hazardous waste.
103.tq: Break the abbreviation into its regulatory meaning before evaluating the options.
xs: **PIC** = **Prior Informed Consent** — option **(4)** is correct.
Under **HOWM Rules 2016**, imports/exports follow **Basel** with PIC.
xa: **Rotterdam** (in force **2004**) is the PIC convention for hazardous chemicals and pesticides; India acceded **2005**.
**Basel** in force **5 May 1992**; India ratified **June 1992**.

103.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: MSIHC Rules, 1989 — manufacture, storage and import of hazardous chemicals
CAEPPR Rules, 1996 — insurance compensation without fault
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 — constitution of crisis groups
Contaminated Sites Rules, 2025 — regulation of fluorescent lamp manufacture
103.x: The MSIHC Rules, 1989 address the manufacture, storage and import of hazardous chemicals. CAEPPR concerns crisis groups, while the Public Liability Insurance Act provides no-fault relief.
103.tq: Start with the sure pair and reject options that swap the functions of neighbouring legal instruments.
xs: **MSIHC Rules 1989** — **manufacture, storage, import of hazardous chemicals** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** gives **no-fault insurance** — option (3) misassigns it.
**Contaminated Sites Rules 2025** deal with suspected contaminated sites, not lamp manufacture.
xa: **Contaminated Sites Rules 2025**: district half-yearly reports; **189** hazardous chemicals.
**EPA 1986** was enacted after **Bhopal**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Stockholm Convention currently includes 34 chemicals, including chlorpyrifos and PFAS.
2. The Minamata Convention concerns mercury.
3. Dental amalgam phase-out under the Minamata framework is associated with the year 2034.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: The current figure given for Stockholm is 34 chemicals, including chlorpyrifos and PFAS. Minamata concerns mercury, and dental amalgam phase-out is targeted by 2034.
103.tq: Test the treaty’s subject together with its current chemical count and target year.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Stockholm** now covers **34 chemicals** incl. **chlorpyrifos** and **PFAS** — correct (IYB still says 23).
Statement 2: **Minamata (2013)** concerns **mercury** — correct.
Statement 3: **dental amalgam** phase-out by **2034** — correct.
xa: ⚠ **Basel** = hazardous waste; **Rotterdam** = PIC; **Stockholm** = POPs; **Minamata** = mercury.
**Coal power plants** are a big mercury source.

103.s: The global issue involved in the transboundary movement of hazardous waste refers to:
o: exchange of agricultural seeds under biodiversity agreements
movement of only biodegradable waste between rural districts
transport of clean energy equipment to developed countries
physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage, often to developing countries
103.x: Transboundary hazardous-waste movement involves the physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage, frequently to developing countries.
103.tq: Use the operational meaning of the term rather than an unrelated environmental transfer.
xs: The issue is the **physical transfer of hazardous waste for reprocessing or storage**, often to **developing countries** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025).
It is not about seeds, rural biodegradable waste or clean-energy equipment.
xa: Governed by the **Basel** Convention (1989; in force **5 May 1992**); India ratified **June 1992**.
HOWM Rules 2016 prohibit **import for disposal**.
China's **National Sword Policy (2018)** curbs plastic waste imports.

103.s:
Match List-I (Convention) with List-II (Subject):
a. Basel
b. Rotterdam
c. Stockholm
d. Minamata
i. Persistent Organic Pollutants
ii. Mercury
iii. Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes
iv. Prior Informed Consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides in trade
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
103.x: Basel (1989) covers transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, Rotterdam is the PIC convention for hazardous chemicals and pesticides, Stockholm (2001) covers POPs and Minamata (2013) covers mercury. The other codes swap Basel/Rotterdam, Stockholm/Minamata or Basel/Stockholm.
103.tq: Basel waste, Rotterdam PIC, Stockholm POPs, Minamata mercury.
xs: Correct matching is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Basel** (1989) — transboundary hazardous wastes; **Rotterdam** — **Prior Informed Consent**.
**Stockholm** (2001) — **POPs**; **Minamata** (2013) — **mercury**.
xa: Rotterdam in force **2004**; India acceded **2005**.
Stockholm now lists **34** chemicals incl. PFAS.

103.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Ramsar Convention
(b) World Heritage Convention
(c) ITPGRFA
(d) Stockholm Convention

List-II
(i) Persistent organic pollutants
(ii) Plant genetic resources
(iii) Wetlands
(iv) Natural and cultural heritage
103.x: Ramsar covers wetlands, the World Heritage Convention natural and cultural heritage, ITPGRFA plant genetic resources, and Stockholm persistent organic pollutants. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
103.tq: Match each treaty to its subject.
n: The Ramsar Convention concerns wetlands. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The World Heritage Convention concerns natural and cultural heritage. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The ITPGRFA, or International Seed Treaty, concerns plant genetic resources. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The Stockholm Convention concerns persistent organic pollutants. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Ramsar**: **wetlands**; **World Heritage Convention**: **natural and cultural heritage**.
**ITPGRFA** (the **International Seed Treaty**): **plant genetic resources**; **Stockholm**: **persistent organic pollutants**.
xa: **Stockholm Convention** (**2001**) now lists **34 chemicals** incl. chlorpyrifos and PFAS.
**Basel Convention** (**1989**) covers transboundary movement of **hazardous wastes**.
**Rotterdam Convention** (in force **2004**) covers **prior informed consent**.

103.s:
With reference to municipal solid waste in India, consider the following statements:
1. Independent estimates suggest about 60-70% of waste is collected but only 15-20% is processed.
2. As per official SBM-U figures, urban waste processing rose from 16% in 2014 to 82% in 2026.
3. Urban areas account for only about 20% of all waste generated.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: independent estimate of 60-70% collected, only 15-20% processed. Statement 2 is correct: official SBM-U figure is 16% (2014) to 82% (2026). Statement 3 is wrong: about 60% of waste comes from urban areas. So '1 only' is incomplete, and the options with 3 are wrong.
103.tq: Independent (15-20% processed) vs official (82% processed) figures differ; urban share ~60%.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: independent estimates — **60-70% collected**, only **15-20% processed** — correct.
Statement 2: official **SBM-U** figures — urban processing **16% (2014) → 82% (2026)** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — **~60%** of all waste comes from **urban areas**, not 20%.
xa: India generates over **62 million tonnes** of MSW a year (Feb 2026).
National gaps: only **68%** of ULBs notified SWM by-laws; under **45%** achieved full segregation.
Waste sector = **2.56%** of India's emissions in 2020.

103.s: Every city is intended to have a permanent RRR Centre under
o: The Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016
103.x: Every city has a permanent RRR Centre under SBM-U 2.0. RRR is expanded in the cited context as Reduce, Reuse and Recover.
103.tq: Link an institutional facility with the correct mission.
xs: A permanent **RRR Centre** in every city is set up under **Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban 2.0** — option **(4)** is correct.
RRR here = **Reduce, Reuse, Recover**.
**GOBARdhan** is a **SBM-G** biogas scheme; the **HOWM Rules 2016** deal with hazardous waste.
xa: **SBM-U 2.0** launched **1 Oct 2021**, till **2026**; **₹1.41 lakh crore** over 5 years; goal **"Garbage Free" cities**.
**Challenge Fund ₹13,029 crore** for 10 lakh+ cities (2026).
SBM-U 2.0 target: **10,000 TPD** additional WtE capacity.

103.s: Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan, introduced in 2012, was the renamed form of the:
103.x: Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan was the renamed Total Sanitation Campaign and followed a saturation approach.
103.tq: Discriminate between predecessor programmes with similar sanitation objectives.
xs: **Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (2012)** was the renamed **Total Sanitation Campaign** — option **(3)** is correct.
It followed a **saturation approach**.
xa: **TSC (1999)** was **demand-driven, community-led**.
**CRSP (1986):** subsidised rural latrines; **ILCS (1980-81):** dry latrines to pour-flush.
**SBM (2014)** followed, with toilets for all and ODF villages and cities.

103.s: Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban was launched on:
103.x: SBM-Urban was launched on 2 October 2014.
103.tq: Use the exact launch date and reject nearby national-day distractors.
xs: SBM was launched on **2 October 2014** (Gandhi Jayanti) — option **(4)** is correct.
It was **announced** on **15 Aug 2014**; some notes give that as the launch date — the launch was 2 October.
xa: **Swachh Bharat Diwas** = **2 October**.
**SBM-U** covers urban toilets + solid waste management; **SBM-U 2.0** launched **1 Oct 2021**.
**SBM-G** was also launched on **2 October 2014**.

103.s: GOBARdhan, launched in 2018 under SBM-Grameen, is associated with conversion of cattle dung, agricultural waste and solid waste into:
103.x: GOBARdhan promotes conversion of cattle dung, agricultural waste and solid waste into biogas and bio-slurry, supported by a unified portal.
103.tq: Identify the input-output relationship in a waste-to-resource initiative.
xs: **GOBARdhan** converts cattle dung, agri and solid waste into **biogas and bio-slurry** — option **(3)** is correct.
It was launched in **2018** under **SBM-G**, with a **unified GOBARdhan portal**.
xa: **SATAT + GOBARdhan** linkage targets **500 new CBG plants**.
**Anaerobic digestion** gives **methane** biogas + slurry used as manure.
**Swachhata Hi Seva** — fortnight shramdaan campaign every year since **2017**.

103.s: Swachh Bharat Mission-Grameen is implemented by the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation under the:
o: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
103.x: SBM-Grameen is run by the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation under the Ministry of Jal Shakti. The ministry was renamed in June 2019.
103.tq: Identify the authority responsible for the programme.
xs: **SBM-G** is run by the **Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation**, **Ministry of Jal Shakti** — option **(2)** is correct.
The ministry was **renamed in June 2019**; **MoHUA** runs the urban mission and Swachh Survekshan.
xa: SBM-G launched **2 October 2014**; over **10 crore** toilets by 2019-20.
DDWS prepared the **Rural Sanitation Strategy 2019-2029**.
**IHHL incentive**: **₹12,000**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Phase I of SBM-Grameen:
1. It aimed to construct over 10 crore toilets by 2019-20.
2. It aimed at making all villages open-defecation free.
3. Rural sanitation coverage increased from 39% in 2014 to 100% in 2019.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three statements correctly describe the targets and reported sanitation-coverage increase under Phase I of SBM-Grameen.
103.tq: Use the all-inclusive option after checking each numerical and outcome statement.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: over **10 crore** toilets by **2019-20** — correct (APPSC-GS 2024: ~100 million in 7 years).
Statement 2: **all villages ODF** — correct.
Statement 3: coverage **39% (2014) → 100% (2019)** — correct.
xa: Now nearly **12 crore** rural toilets (Aug 2026).
**ODF Plus** levels: **Aspiring → Rising → Model**; **95%+** villages ODF Plus (Aug 2026).

103.s:
Consider the following statements about ODF Plus villages under SBM-Grameen:
1. ODF Plus means ODF status is sustained along with management of greywater, faecal sludge and plastic waste.
2. Its three progressive levels are Model, then Rising, then Aspiring.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 reverses the order: the levels run Aspiring, then Rising, then Model (the highest). So '1 only'.
103.tq: Aspiring -> Rising -> Model.
xs: Only **statement 1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **ODF Plus** = ODF sustained + **greywater**, **faecal sludge** and **plastic waste** management.
Statement 2 is wrong: the three progressive levels run **Aspiring → Rising → Model**.
xa: **Status (Aug 2026):** **95%+ villages ODF Plus**; **5 lakh+ ODF Plus Model**.
**SBM-G** is run by the **Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti**.
**IHHL incentive** = **₹12,000**.

103.s: Under SBM-Grameen, the incentive provided for construction of an Individual Household Latrine (IHHL) is:
103.x: The IHHL incentive under SBM-G is ₹12,000. ₹6,000, ₹10,000 and ₹15,000 are not the stated amount; separately, greywater support is ₹280/capita (villages up to 5,000) and ₹660/capita (above 5,000).
xs: The **IHHL incentive** under SBM-G is **₹12,000** — option **(3)** is correct.
**₹6,000**, **₹10,000** and **₹15,000** are not the stated amount.
xa: Greywater support: **₹280/capita** (villages up to 5,000) and **₹660/capita** (above 5,000).
Over **10 crore** toilets built by 2019-20; nearly **12 crore** now.
**Rural Sanitation Strategy 2019-2029** by DDWS.

103.s: The principal target of SBM-Urban 2.0, implemented during 2021-26, is to create:
103.x: SBM-Urban 2.0, covering 2021-26, targets garbage-free cities.
103.tq: Separate the mission’s current target from the objectives of related urban programmes.
xs: SBM-U 2.0's goal is **"Garbage Free" cities** by **2026** — option **(2)** is correct.
SBM-U 2.0 runs **2021-26** and covers **all statutory towns**, not only riverfront or heritage cities.
xa: Launched **1 Oct 2021**; **₹1.41 lakh crore** over 5 years; **Centrally Sponsored**, all statutory towns.
Components: **100% source segregation**, door-to-door collection, **legacy dumpsite remediation**, C&D waste management.
**Garbage Free City** star ratings: **1, 3, 5 and 7** stars.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about SBM-Urban 2.0:
1. It was launched on 1 October 2021 and runs till 2026.
2. It has an outlay of about ₹1.41 lakh crore over five years.
3. It is a Central Sector Scheme covering only cities selected under the Smart Cities Mission.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 1 is correct: SBM-U 2.0 was launched on 1 Oct 2021, till 2026. Statement 2 is correct: the outlay is ₹1.41 lakh crore over 5 years. Statement 3 is wrong: it is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme covering all statutory towns. Hence '1 only' misses statement 2, while '2 and 3 only' and '1, 2 and 3' wrongly include statement 3.
103.tq: Scheme type trap: Centrally Sponsored + all statutory towns; dates 2021-26, ₹1.41 lakh crore.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: launched **1 Oct 2021**, runs till **2026** — correct.
Statement 2: outlay **₹1.41 lakh crore** over **5 years** — correct.
Statement 3: wrong — it is **Centrally Sponsored** and covers **all statutory towns**.
xa: Goal: **"Garbage Free" cities by 2026**.
**Challenge Fund ₹13,029 crore** for 10 lakh+ cities (2026).
Every city gets a permanent **RRR Centre** under SBM-U 2.0.

103.s: The Garbage Free City star-rating system provides which of the following ratings?
103.x: The Garbage Free City certification uses 1-star, 3-star, 5-star and 7-star ratings for waste management.
103.tq: Recall the distinctive non-consecutive rating sequence.
xs: The **Garbage Free City** star rating uses **1, 3, 5 and 7** stars — option **(3)** is correct.
The ratings measure **waste management** under SBM-U 2.0.
xa: **ODF+** — toilets functional, clean, maintained; **ODF++** — plus safe faecal sludge management.
**Water+** — used water treated before discharge.
SBM-U 2.0 goal: **"Garbage Free" cities by 2026**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about Swachh Survekshan:
1. It is run by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs under SBM-Urban and conducted by the Quality Council of India.
2. Swachh Survekshan Grameen was also launched in 2016.
3. The first Swachh Survekshan was held in 2016.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: Swachh Survekshan, the world's largest annual urban cleanliness survey, began in 2016 under MoHUA, conducted by QCI. Statement 2 is wrong: Swachh Survekshan Grameen was launched in 2018. So '1 and 3 only'.
103.tq: SS 2016 (urban, QCI); SS Grameen 2018.
xs: **Statements 1 and 3 only** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: run by **MoHUA** under SBM-U, conducted by the **Quality Council of India (QCI)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Swachh Survekshan Grameen** was launched in **2018**.
Statement 3 is correct: the first Swachh Survekshan was in **2016**.
xa: It is the world's **largest annual urban cleanliness survey**, with **160+ indicators**.
**Indore (MP)** keeps ranking **#1** as the cleanest city.
**Swachh Survekshan 2024-25** awards were conferred by the **President**.

103.s: Which of the following correctly represents the cleanest-city result for the 2023 edition of Swachh Survekshan in the 10 lakh-plus category?
103.x: Indore and Surat jointly occupied the cleanest-city position in the 2023 edition for cities with more than 10 lakh population.
103.tq: Distinguish a joint ranking from single-city results in adjacent editions.
xs: In **2023**, **Indore and Surat** were jointly the cleanest city (10 lakh+) — option **(4)** is correct.
Indore alone had topped every edition from **2017 to 2022**; 2023 was shared.
xa: **2017 to 2022**: **Indore** every year.
**2024-25**: Indore, Surat, Navi Mumbai placed in the **Super Swachh League**; **Ahmedabad** topped the regular 10 lakh+ list.
Indore topped the Super Swachh League for the **8th time** (Jul 2025).

103.s: Which one of the following cities is described as India’s model zero-waste and landfill-free city?
103.x: Indore is identified as India’s model zero-waste or landfill-free city and has repeatedly ranked first in cleanliness assessments.
103.tq: Associate the distinctive zero-waste description with the correct city.
xs: **Indore (MP)** is the model **zero-waste / landfill-free** city — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025).
**Visakhapatnam** was 'Top Impact Creator' and **Tirupati** first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar' (SS 2022).
xa: Indore topped the **Super Swachh League** for the **8th time** (Jul 2025).
Guntur Commissioner studied **Indore's model** (24 Jun 2026).
Indore uses the **Indore method** of aerobic composting — turning at intervals.

103.s: Operation Clean Sweep, launched in May 2026, is a campaign of the Municipal Administration Department for:
o: Scientific solid-waste management in Tier-1 and Tier-2 corporations
Only coastal plastic clean-up in villages
103.x: Operation Clean Sweep is the Municipal Administration Department’s campaign for scientific solid-waste management in Tier-1 and Tier-2 corporations.
103.tq: Link the campaign with its department, timing and operational scope.
xs: **Operation Clean Sweep** (May 2026) is the Municipal Administration department's drive for **scientific SWM in Tier-1/2 corporations** — option **(3)** is correct.
It covered all **123 ULBs**, **23 May-20 Jun 2026**, under **Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra**.
xa: **Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra** was launched in **January 2025**.
GVMC threatened to seal an apartment without **two segregation bins** (28 Aug 2026).
Guntur Commissioner studied **Indore's model** (24 Jun 2026).

103.s: Which statement regarding the waste hierarchy is correct?
o: Reduction at source is the top priority in the 3R approach.
Regain replaces Reduce in the standard 3R formulation.
Recycling means using an item again in its original form.
Reuse means converting waste into a different usable material.
103.x: Reduction at source is the top priority. Reuse means using an item again in its existing form, while recycling converts waste into other usable materials.
103.tq: Distinguish closely related terms by their precise meanings.
xs: **Reduction at source** is the **top priority** in the waste hierarchy — option **(1)** is correct.
**3R = Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**; "**Regain**" is not one of the 3R (APPSC-GS 2025 trap) — option (2) is wrong.
**Reuse** = using the item again in its **existing form**; **Recycling** = converting waste into **other usable materials** — options (3) and (4) swap them.
xa: **5R** adds **Refuse** and Repurpose/Recover (versions vary).
**HOWM Rules 2016 hierarchy:** prevention > minimisation > reuse > recycling > recovery > co-processing > safe disposal.
Practising 3R **reduces waste at source** (APPSC-GS 2025).

103.s: The two Common Hazardous Waste Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities (CHWTSDFs) in Andhra Pradesh are located at:
103.x: The two CHWTSDFs identified for Andhra Pradesh are located in Anakapalli and SPSR Nellore.
103.tq: Use location-based recall and distinguish the named facility sites from other Andhra Pradesh cities.
xs: AP's two **CHWTSDFs** are at **Anakapalli** and **SPSR Nellore** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are used for **secure landfilling** (2024-25).
xa: **6 pre-processing** facilities and **APEMC GPS tracking**.
AP **Circular Economy and Waste Recycling Policy 2025-30** targets industrial hazardous waste.
AP has **4,000+ industries** producing hazardous and non-hazardous waste (APPCB, 6 Feb 2026).

103.s: Which system is used by APEMC for tracking hazardous-waste movement in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Biometric tracking of every waste container
103.x: APEMC uses GPS tracking for monitoring hazardous-waste movement and management.
103.tq: Match the institution with the specific monitoring technology stated for it.
xs: **APEMC** uses **GPS tracking** of hazardous waste via GPS-fitted vehicles — option **(4)** is correct.
The **APEMC portal** tracks the movement in real time.
xa: **APCMMS** portal — real-time monitoring.
AP CHWTSDFs: **Anakapalli**, **SPSR Nellore**.
BMW Rules 2016 also use **GPS tracking** with **barcoding**.

103.s: Which agency functions as the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Andhra Pradesh State Council of Higher Education
103.x: Swachha Andhra Corporation, or SAC, is the state agency running urban sanitation under SBM-U 2.0 in Andhra Pradesh.
103.tq: Identify the correct state agency from closely related institutional names.
xs: **Swachha Andhra Corporation (SAC)** runs urban sanitation under **SBM-U 2.0** in AP — option **(2)** is correct.
For SS 2026, SAC operationalised **Project Monitoring Units in 46 ULBs**, chosen on SS 2024 ranks.
xa: **CBMWTFs** handle biomedical waste — not the sanitation agency.
AP urban profile: **17 Municipal Corporations**, **113 Municipalities**, **7 Cantonment Boards**.
**Re Sustainability MoU** covers all **123 ULBs**; **ITC MoU** covers **30 ULBs**.

103.s: Which statement correctly describes the Re Sustainability MoU in Andhra Pradesh?
o: It covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs.
It covers only 30 ULBs for rural sanitation.
It operates only the state’s WtE plants.
It tracks hazardous waste through GPS-fitted vehicles.
103.x: The Re Sustainability MoU covers all 123 ULBs for scientific e-waste collection, disposal and material recovery facilities. The 30-ULB figure relates to the ITC MoU.
103.tq: Separate similar institutional agreements by coverage and function.
xs: The **Re Sustainability MoU** covers **all 123 ULBs** for scientific **e-waste collection, disposal and MRFs** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **30-ULB** figure belongs to the **ITC MoU**; GPS tracking is done by **APEMC**.
xa: AP collected **60,392 kg** of e-waste; MRFs in **101 ULBs** (SES 2025-26).
AP WtE plants: **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam**.

103.s: Clean Andhra Pradesh, popularly known as the CLAP programme, was launched on 2 October 2021 as:
103.x: CLAP was launched on 2 October 2021 under the name Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam. Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra is a later state drive launched in January 2025.
103.tq: Use the exact official name to distinguish related sanitation initiatives.
xs: **CLAP** was launched on **2 Oct 2021** as **Jagananna Swachha Sankalpam** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra** is the later State drive, launched **January 2025**.
xa: **Operation Clean Sweep** (May 2026) runs under Swarna Andhra-Swachh Andhra.
**SBM-U 2.0** was launched a day earlier, on **1 Oct 2021**.

103.s: In Swachh Survekshan 2022, which of the following pairs of Andhra Pradesh cities and recognitions is correctly matched?
o: Visakhapatnam - 'Top Impact Creator'; Tirupati - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Tirupati - 'Top Impact Creator'; Visakhapatnam - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Vijayawada - 'Top Impact Creator'; Guntur - first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'
Visakhapatnam - cleanest city overall; Tirupati - 'Top Impact Creator'
103.x: In SS 2022, Visakhapatnam was 'Top Impact Creator' (million-plus) and Tirupati came first in 'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar' (APPSC-G1 2022 key). Option 2 swaps the two cities, option 3 names the wrong cities, and Visakhapatnam was not the overall cleanest city.
103.tq: SS 2022: Vizag = Top Impact Creator; Tirupati = Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar.
xs: In **SS 2022**, **Visakhapatnam** was **'Top Impact Creator'** (million-plus) and **Tirupati** first in **'Safai Mitra Surakshit Shehar'** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-G1 2022 key).
Option (2) swaps the two cities; option (3) names the wrong cities; Visakhapatnam was not the overall cleanest.
xa: **Indore** was the cleanest city (10 lakh+) in the **2017 to 2022** editions.
**Vijayawada** "recognised well" last year; aiming for top rank (9 Apr 2026).

103.s: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board has permitted how many cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste?
103.x: The APPCB permitted 12 cement industries to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste.
103.tq: Recall the exact institutional count and distinguish it from nearby figures.
xs: **APPCB** permitted **12 cement industries** to co-process incinerable, plastic and municipal waste — option **(2)** is correct.
**6** is the number of **pre-processing facilities** that feed them; **46** is the number of ULBs with PMUs.
xa: APPCB prefers **co-processing** as fuel in cement plants + **waste exchange**; landfill is the **last resort**.
**RDF** is used in **cement kilns**.

103.s: Which pair of Andhra Pradesh cities is associated with WtE plants?
103.x: The cited Andhra Pradesh WtE plants are located at Guntur and Visakhapatnam.
103.tq: Recall a location pair without substituting nearby urban centres.
xs: AP's **WtE plants** are at **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ongole** is linked with biomining; **Nellore** with a CHWTSDF.
xa: India: **21 operational WtE plants**, **170+ MW** (Feb 2026).
**Anantapur** is setting up a **170 TPD** waste-processing plant.

103.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the ban on single-use plastic and carry bags applies to carry bags having thickness below:
103.x: Andhra Pradesh bans single-use plastic and carry bags below 120 microns, with enforcement involving the Revenue Department, Police and Pollution Control Board.
103.tq: Distinguish the precise statutory threshold from nearby thickness values.
xs: AP bans SUP and carry bags **under 120 microns** — option **(4)** is correct.
Enforcement involves **Revenue, Police, PCB**.
xa: National carry-bag limit is also **120 microns** from **31 Dec 2022**.
AP seizures: **5,505.06 kg** carry bags + **3,571.40 kg** SUP (SES 2025-26).
**100 microns** is the limit for banned **PVC banners**.

103.s: Which State is identified as the highest solid-waste-generating State in India?
103.x: Maharashtra is identified as the highest solid-waste-generating State.
103.tq: Test the precise State association rather than the general urban-waste trend.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the highest solid-waste-generating State — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
The notes name no other State for this record, so the remaining options are not the answer.
xa: **Indore (MP)** keeps ranking **#1** as the cleanest city.
First **Swachh Survekshan**: **2016** — world's largest annual urban cleanliness survey.
India = **3rd largest** e-waste generator, after **China** and **USA**.

103.s:
Which of the following methods are used for disposal of solid waste in urban India?
1. Composting
2. Incineration
3. Landfilling
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
103.x: All three - composting, incineration and landfilling - are used in urban India (APPSC-G2 2025 key: 'all the above'). Options leaving out any one of them are incomplete; only uncontrolled dumping is described as not viable.
103.tq: Urban India: compost + incinerate + landfill - all used.
xs: **Composting, incineration and landfilling** are all used in urban India — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** (APPSC-G2 2025 key: "all the above").
Only **uncontrolled dumping** is described as **not a viable option**.
xa: **Composting** = aerobic, for biodegradable organic/wet waste; **incineration** suits hazardous, biomedical, combustible waste.
**Sanitary landfill** is the most common and economic method, for **residual** waste only.
Incineration cuts volume **up to 90%** but causes air pollution and ash disposal problems.

103.s: Which of the following correctly describes the SATAT–GOBARdhan linkage?
o: It establishes 500 new MRFs exclusively for e-waste.
It provides 500 MW from existing WtE plants only.
It targets 500 new waste-to-wealth CBG plants.
103.x: The SATAT and GOBARdhan linkage targets 500 new waste-to-wealth compressed biogas plants.
103.tq: Link two initiatives with their stated numerical target and output.
xs: The **SATAT + GOBARdhan** linkage targets **500 new waste-to-wealth (CBG) plants** — option **(4)** is correct.
**CBG plants** turn municipal **wet waste** into green fuel.
xa: **GOBARdhan (2018, under SBM-G):** cattle dung, agri and solid waste → **biogas + bio-slurry**; unified GOBARdhan portal.
**Circular Bioenergy Scheme (MoPNG)** supports **100%** scientific processing.
SBM-U 2.0 also targets **10,000 TPD** additional WtE capacity.

103.s: Nurdles are best described as:
o: Secondary microplastics formed only by tyre wear
Primary microplastic pellets generally measuring 1–5 mm
Biodegradable plastic fibres used in clothing
103.x: Nurdles are primary microplastic pellets, generally 1–5 mm in size.
103.tq: Distinguish a specific microplastic form from its sources and effects.
xs: **Nurdles** are **primary microplastic pellets** of **1-5 mm** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Tyre-wear** microplastics come from **synthetic rubber** — a different source.
xa: India's **first major nurdle landing**: **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck (LDPE, HDPE).
Microplastics = particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS 2023).

103.s: India's first major nurdle landing was reported in:
o: Kerala, from the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck
West Bengal, from a fishing vessel
103.x: The first major nurdle landing in India occurred in Kerala following the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck. The nurdles included LDPE and HDPE.
103.tq: Combine location, event and source-vessel clues.
xs: India's first major nurdle landing was in **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck — option **(1)** is correct.
The nurdles were **LDPE and HDPE**.
xa: Nurdles = primary microplastic pellets (**1-5 mm**).
**National Action Plan for Marine Litter** (Dec 2025).

103.s: Microplastics are generally defined as plastic particles of size:
103.x: Microplastics are particles up to 5 mm (APPSC-GS 2023). 'Up to 5 micrometres only' is far too narrow, while 5-50 cm and above 5 mm describe larger debris.
103.tq: Micro = up to 5 mm; nurdles 1-5 mm.
xs: Microplastics are particles **up to 5 mm** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2023).
"**Above 5 mm**" and **5-50 cm** describe larger debris; "5 micrometres only" is far too narrow.
xa: **Nurdles** = primary microplastic pellets, **1-5 mm**.
Hidden sources: **tea bags, chewing gum, wet wipes, glitter, cigarette filters, polyester clothing**.

103.s:
Consider the following statements about plastic-bag bans:
1. New Zealand became the first country to ban thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets, in 2002.
2. Bangladesh was the first country to ban thin plastic bags, in 2002.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
103.x: Statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong on the year: New Zealand's ban on thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets came in July 2023 (APPSC-GS 2022 key), not 2002. So '2 only'.
103.tq: Bangladesh 2002 (thin bags); New Zealand 2023 (produce bags).
xs: Only **statement 2** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 2 is correct: **Bangladesh** was the first country to ban thin plastic bags (**2002**).
Statement 1 is wrong: **New Zealand** banned thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets in **July 2023**, not 2002.
xa: ⚠ **Bangladesh** = first country (thin bags); **New Zealand** = first, thin produce bags in supermarkets.
India's **first major nurdle landing** was in **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck.
**Maharashtra** is the highest solid-waste-generating State (APPSC-G2 **2025** key).

103.s: According to MeitY, approximately how much e-waste was collected and processed in India in FY 2021?
103.x: MeitY put e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021 at about 3.54 lakh tonnes (APPSC-GS 2021 key). 2.2 MT (2025) and 1.75 MT are generation figures, and 35.4 lakh tonnes is ten times the stated value.
103.tq: Processed FY21 = 3.54 lakh t; generated 2025 = 2.2 MT.
xs: **MeitY**: about **3.54 lakh tonnes** of e-waste collected and processed in **FY 2021** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021 key).
**2.2 MT** (2025) and **1.75 MT** are **generation** figures; **35.4 lakh tonnes** is ten times the stated value.
xa: Only **10-20%** of materials are recovered in informal processing.
**468 authorised recyclers** (CPCB 2024).

103.s:
How many of the following are impacts of non-biodegradable plastics?

1. Persistence in the environment
2. Pollution
3. Production of microplastics
4. Landfill issues
5. Harm to wildlife
103.x: All five are impacts of non-biodegradable plastics: persistence, pollution, microplastics, landfill problems and harm to wildlife.
103.tq: Recall the effects of plastic pollution.
n: Non-biodegradable plastics persist in the environment. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics cause pollution. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics produce microplastics. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics create landfill issues. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics harm wildlife. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
xs: **All five** are impacts — so option **(4)** is correct.
Non-biodegradable plastics **persist** in the **environment** and cause **pollution**.
They produce **microplastics**, create **landfill issues** and **harm wildlife**.
xa: **Most synthetic plastics** are non-biodegradable — **polythene**, **PVC**, **polystyrene**, **Teflon**.
**Microplastics** are particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS **2023**).
FSSAI found microplastics in **all tested sugar and salt samples**.

103.s: Which of the following is compost?
o: Disposal of solid waste in a designated land area
Decomposed organic waste that becomes nutrient-rich material
103.x: Compost is organic waste that has broken down into nutrient-rich material. The other options describe landfill, recycling and incineration.
103.tq: Match each waste term to its meaning.
n: Compost is decomposed organic waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost is a nutrient-rich material. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
A landfill is the disposal of solid waste in a designated land area. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Incineration is the controlled burning of waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Recycling is the processing of waste into usable material. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost contains organic matter. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost contains nutrients. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
xs: **Compost** is **decomposed** organic waste that becomes **nutrient-rich material** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Disposal in a designated land area** is a **landfill**; **processing waste into usable material** is **recycling**.
**Controlled burning** of waste is **incineration**.
xa: **Indore method** = aerobic composting with turning at intervals.
⚠ **Bangalore method** = anaerobic pit composting, **4-6 months**.
**Vermicompost** is produced using **earthworms**.

103.s: Which of the following statements about solid waste management is incorrect?
o: It involves the collection of waste.
It involves the processing of waste.
Landfilling is the most preferred option in the waste hierarchy.
It involves the final disposal of waste.
103.x: Option C is incorrect: in the waste hierarchy landfilling is the least preferred option, after reduction, reuse, recycling and recovery. Solid waste management does involve collection, processing and disposal.
103.tq: Recall the waste hierarchy: reduce first, landfill last.
n: Solid waste requires collection. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Solid waste requires processing. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Solid waste requires disposal. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**landfilling is the most preferred option**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Reduction at source** is the top of the **waste hierarchy**; landfill is for residual waste only.
**Solid waste** does require **collection**, **processing** and **disposal**.
xa: Landfills take only **non-recyclable, non-energy-recoverable and inert** waste.
⚠ APPCB treats landfill as the **last resort**, preferring **co-processing**.
Urban India uses **composting, incineration and landfilling** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).

103.s: Which one of the following is biodegradable?
103.x: Wool is a natural fibre and is biodegradable. Aluminium foil, glass and synthetic rubber are non-biodegradable.
103.tq: Use the material-property distinction to identify the biodegradable item.
xs: **Wool** is a natural fibre and is **biodegradable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Biodegradable matter is decomposed by microorganisms, mainly **bacteria**, into simpler substances.
**Glass bottles**, metals such as **aluminium foil**, and **synthetic rubber / tyres** are all **non-biodegradable**.
xa: Other biodegradable items: food/kitchen waste, **vegetable peels**, **cow-dung**, **paddy husk**, **paper**, **sewage**, **cotton**.
**DDT** and **heavy metals** are non-biodegradable and accumulate in the environment.
⚠ Exam angle: "which is NOT biodegradable" → **tin/metal/glass/plastic**; "which IS biodegradable" → **wool, peels**.

103.s: Which one of the following is NOT biodegradable?
103.x: Tin scrap is a metal and cannot normally be decomposed by microorganisms. Paddy husk, vegetable peels and cow-dung are biodegradable.
103.tq: Find the non-biodegradable item by separating metals from organic wastes.
xs: **Tin scrap** is a metal and is **non-biodegradable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Metals (**tin**, aluminium foil, metal scrap) are not broken down by microbes and accumulate in the environment.
**Vegetable peels**, **paddy husk** and **cow-dung** are biodegradable — decomposed by bacteria.
xa: Non-biodegradable waste is mainly **inorganic**: plastics, **glass bottles**, DDT, heavy metals, synthetic rubber tyres.
Natural fibres — **wool** and **cotton** — are biodegradable, as are **paper** and **sewage**.
Aerobic decomposition of biodegradable waste gives **compost**; anaerobic gives **methane (CH4)**/biogas.

103.s:
Assertion (A): Biodegradable polymers are eco-friendly.
Reason (R): They are degraded by microorganisms.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
103.x: Both are true and R explains A: microbes break biodegradable polymers down, so they do not pile up in the environment.
103.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Biodegradable polymers are degraded by microorganisms. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Biodegradable polymers are eco-friendly. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Biodegradable polymers** are **degraded** by **microorganisms**.
Because they break down, they are **eco-friendly** and do not persist like synthetic plastics.
xa: Biodegradable polymers: **PHBV**, **Nylon-2-Nylon-6**, **polylactic acid**, **polyglycolic acid**.
They are used in **packaging**, **orthopaedic devices** and **controlled drug release**.
**Starch-blended plastics** are semi-biodegradable — **partial degradation**.

103.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: LDPE/HDPE — carry bags and milk bottles
103.x: Synthetic rubber is associated with tyres, not drinking-water bottles. LDPE/HDPE, synthetic polymers and cellulose acetate have the associations shown in the other options.
103.tq: Find the product-material mismatch among familiar plastic applications.
xs: **Synthetic rubber — drinking-water bottles** is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is the answer.
Synthetic rubber is used in **tyres** and gives **tyre-wear microplastics**; water bottles are **PET**.
The others are correct: **cellulose acetate** — cigarette filters; **synthetic polymers** — chewing-gum base; **LDPE/HDPE** — carry bags, milk bottles.
xa: **Polycarbonate** — hard bottles; releases **BPA**.
**Microplastics**: particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS 2023).

103.s: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted in the aftermath of which event?
103.x: The EPA 1986 was enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984). The Stockholm Conference and Chernobyl are not the stated trigger, and Minamata gave its name to the 2013 mercury convention.
103.tq: Bhopal 1984 → EPA 1986 → PLI Act 1991.
xs: **EPA 1986** was enacted after the **Bhopal gas tragedy** — option **(1)** is correct.
Bhopal: **2-3 Dec 1984**, Union Carbide India Ltd, **methyl isocyanate**.
xa: SWM Rules 2026 and Contaminated Sites Rules 2025 are notified under **EPA 1986**.
**Public Liability Insurance Act 1991** — no-fault relief to accident victims.
Bhopal waste (early 2025): **337 t** incinerated → ~**900 t** toxic ash.

103.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
103.x: The Bhopal disaster in December 1984 involved methyl isocyanate. The LG Polymers incident at Visakhapatnam in May 2020 involved styrene vapour.
103.tq: Use the location–date–chemical triplet to detect swapped disaster details.
xs: **Bhopal, 1984 — methyl isocyanate** is correctly matched — option **(2)**.
The Bhopal tragedy (**2-3 Dec 1984**) at **Union Carbide India Ltd** involved **methyl isocyanate**, not styrene.
xa: **5,400+** lives lost (TH).
**EPA 1986** was enacted after Bhopal.
SC asked victims' NGO to go to the **MP High Court** (Mar 2026).

103.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. CBD is associated with biodiversity.
II. UNFCCC is associated with climate change.
III. UNCCD is associated with desertification.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
103.x: All three are correct: the CBD covers biodiversity, the UNFCCC climate change, and the UNCCD desertification. These are the three Rio conventions.
103.tq: Recall the three Rio conventions.
n: The CBD concerns biodiversity. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The UNFCCC concerns climate change. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
The UNCCD concerns desertification. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 64-66]
xs: **All three — I, II and III** — are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
**CBD**: **biodiversity**; **UNFCCC**: **climate change**; **UNCCD**: **desertification**.
xa: **Vienna Convention**: **ozone protection**.
**Ramsar Convention**: **wetlands**.
⚠ **Basel** = hazardous waste; **Rotterdam** = PIC; **Stockholm** = POPs; **Minamata** = mercury.

103.s: Which one of the following statements about Swachhata Hi Seva is correct?
o: It is an award given to ODF gram panchayats.
It is a plastic-import restriction introduced in 2018.
It is a ten-year rural sanitation strategy beginning in 2019.
It is a fortnight-long shramdaan campaign conducted every year since 2017.
103.x: Swachhata Hi Seva has been observed as a fortnight shramdaan campaign every year since 2017.
103.tq: Separate a recurring campaign from strategies, awards and regulatory measures.
xs: **Swachhata Hi Seva** is a **fortnight shramdaan campaign** held **every year since 2017** — option **(4)** is correct.
