**Jennifer Doudna** and **Emmanuelle Charpentier** demonstrated it in **2012** → **Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020**.
**Cas9** = **molecular scissors**; **guide RNA** = the **navigator**.

111.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) CRISPR
(b) Cas9
(c) Guide RNA
(d) Restriction enzyme

List-II
(i) Enzyme
(ii) Specialized stretches of DNA
(iii) Guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location
(iv) Cleaves DNA into fragments
111.x: CRISPR is specialised DNA stretches, Cas9 is the enzyme, guide RNA leads Cas9 to the target and restriction enzymes cut DNA into fragments, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
111.tq: Recall the parts of CRISPR editing.
n: CRISPR consists of specialized stretches of DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Cas9 is an enzyme. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Guide RNA guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Restriction enzymes have a role in genetic engineering by cutting DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(2)**.
**CRISPR** — **specialized stretches of DNA**; **Cas9** — an **enzyme** that cuts DNA.
**Guide RNA** guides Cas9 to the desired location; **restriction enzyme** **cleaves DNA into fragments**.
xa: CRISPR is simpler, cheaper, more accurate than **ZFNs and TALENs**.
**TnpB (ICAR)**: indigenous, **smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9**.
**Base editing** converts one base to another **without double-strand breaks**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about CRISPR-Cas9:

I. It can be used to correct genetic defects.
II. It can be used to treat or prevent disease.
III. It can be used to improve crops.
IV. Its use raises ethical concerns.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: All four are correct: CRISPR can fix genetic defects, treat or prevent disease and improve crops, and it raises ethical concerns.
111.tq: Recall the uses and concerns of CRISPR.
n: CRISPR can be used to correct genetic defects. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
CRISPR can be used to treat or prevent disease. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
CRISPR can be used to improve crops. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
CRISPR raises ethical concerns. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)** **I, II, III and IV**.
**CRISPR-Cas9** can **correct genetic defects**, **treat or prevent disease** and **improve crops**.
Its use raises **ethical concerns**.
xa: It can **remove existing** or **add new** genes.
Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up = **CRISPR** (UKPSC 2025).
**He Jiankui** (China, **2018**) — "**CRISPR babies**".
**Pusa Rice DST1** is a genome-edited, **drought + salinity**-tolerant rice.

111.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Bt brinjal:
1. The GEAC recommended its release in 2009.
2. It was developed through collaboration among Mahyco, UAS Dharwad and TNAU.
3. Its principal target was the fruit and shoot borer.
4. A moratorium was imposed on it in 2010 by Jairam Ramesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: All four statements are correct. Bt brinjal was recommended by the GEAC in October 2009, developed by the stated institutions for insect resistance, and placed under a moratorium in 2010 by Jairam Ramesh.
111.tq: Check each date, institutional association, target pest and policy action before selecting the coded option.
xs: All four statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
**GEAC** recommended release in **2009**; developers **Mahyco + UAS Dharwad + TNAU**.
Target: **fruit and shoot borer**; **moratorium 2010** by **Jairam Ramesh**.
xa: India is a **centre of diversity of brinjal** — key argument against Bt brinjal.
Exam angle: Bt brinjal was "developed for" **insect resistance**.
Gene flow into **wild relatives** is the primary environmental concern (PYQ).

111.s: GM mustard DMH-11 (Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11) was developed by:
o: Delhi University (Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants)
111.x: DMH-11 was developed at Delhi University's CGMCP (Deepak Pental). MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad and TNAU developed Bt brinjal; ICAR-IARI developed genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1.
111.tq: DMH-11 = Delhi University; Bt brinjal = Mahyco.
xs: **DMH-11** was developed by **Delhi University** (**CGMCP**, Deepak Pental) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU** developed **Bt brinjal**, not GM mustard.
xa: DMH-11 = **Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11**.
GEAC approved its environmental release in **Oct 2022**.
It is **under Supreme Court consideration**.

111.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern about the cultivation of GM crops?
o: Transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives
111.x: Gene flow, the movement of transgenes by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives, is the primary environmental concern (PYQ). It can create superweeds and alter native gene pools. The other options are not GM-crop concerns.
111.tq: GM crop main worry = gene flow by pollen.
xs: The primary environmental concern of GM crops is **gene flow**: **transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives** — option **(1)** (PYQ).
Soil evaporation, ozone depletion and canal salinisation are not GM-crop concerns.
xa: Gene flow effects: invasive **superweeds**, raised **weediness**, altered **native gene pools**.
Risk is highest at a crop's **centre of origin/diversity**; India = centre of diversity of **brinjal**.
**Non-target harm**: pollinators, natural enemies, **soil nematodes/microbes**, aquatic organisms.

111.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with Pusa Rice DST1?
o: Edited version of MTU1010 — rice bred at Maruteru in Andhra Pradesh
Transgenic version of AquAdvantage — salmon bred in Punjab
Bt version of IR8 — rice bred in Colombia
Gene-drive version of MTU1010 — mosquito bred in Maruteru
111.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited version of MTU1010, an Andhra Pradesh-bred rice variety associated with Maruteru.
111.tq: Combine the crop identity, source variety and regional association in one precise match.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** is an **edited version of MTU1010**, an AP-bred rice from **Maruteru** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is **genome-edited**, not transgenic, Bt or gene-drive; **AquAdvantage** is a GM **salmon**.
xa: DST1 gives **drought + salinity** tolerance, **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
India set to commercially launch it as its **first genome-edited rice** (**1 Sep 2026**).
**SDN-1/SDN-2** edits (no foreign DNA) are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022** guidelines).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Bt toxin:
1. The inactive protoxin is activated in the acidic gut of the larva.
2. Bacillus thuringiensis forms crystal proteins (delta-endotoxins) during sporulation.
3. The activated toxin binds to midgut cells of the larva and creates pores, killing the insect.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 2 is correct: delta-endotoxins form during sporulation. Statement 3 is correct: the toxin binds midgut cells and makes pores. Statement 1 is wrong: the protoxin is activated in the alkaline (not acidic) gut of the larva. Hence '2 and 3 only'.
111.tq: Bt protoxin -> alkaline gut -> midgut pores.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)** **2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the inactive protoxin is activated in the **alkaline gut** of the larva, not acidic.
Statement 2 correct: **Bacillus thuringiensis** forms crystal proteins (**delta-endotoxins**) during **sporulation**.
Statement 3 correct: the toxin **binds midgut cells**, **creates pores** and kills the insect.
xa: **Bollgard I (2002)** = **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard II (2006)** = **Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab**.
Target trait of Bt: **insect resistance**.
Bt proteins **degrade in soil**, despite fears of persistence.

111.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Bollgard I from Bollgard II?
o: Bollgard I is herbicide-tolerant, whereas Bollgard II is drought-tolerant.
Bollgard I contains Cry1Ac, whereas Bollgard II contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.
Bollgard I contains Cry2Ab, whereas Bollgard II contains only Cry1Ac.
Both contain only Cry2Ab but differ in the host plant.
111.x: Bollgard I, introduced in 2002, contains Cry1Ac. Bollgard II, introduced in 2006, combines Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.
111.tq: Compare the versions by separating their gene composition and introduction years.
xs: **Bollgard I** has **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard II** has **Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are **insect-resistance** traits, not herbicide or drought tolerance.
xa: Bollgard I came in **2002**, Bollgard II in **2006**.
⚠ Trap: Bt cotton approval year is **2002**, not 2006.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about recombinant DNA technology:
1. Plasmids, BACs and YACs serve as vectors.
2. Antibiotic-resistance genes on plasmids are used to select transformed cells.
3. Restriction endonucleases join DNA fragments to form recombinant DNA.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: plasmids, BACs and YACs are vectors, and plasmid antibiotic-resistance genes act as selection markers. Statement 3 is wrong: restriction endonucleases cut DNA; DNA ligase joins the fragments. So 1 and 2 only; other options either drop 2 or include 3.
111.tq: Scissors = restriction endonuclease; glue = ligase.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **plasmids, BACs and YACs** are vectors.
Statement 2 correct: plasmids carry **antibiotic-resistance genes for selection**.
Statement 3 wrong: **restriction endonucleases cut** DNA; **DNA ligase joins** it.
xa: Plant vector: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** ("nature's genetic engineer").
⚠ Antibiotic-resistance **marker genes** raise fears of spreading resistance.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Bt cotton in India:
1. The approved hybrids were three MAHYCO hybrids targeting the American bollworm.
2. It was approved for commercial cultivation in 2006.
3. It is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 2 is wrong: Bt cotton was approved in March 2002 (2006 is a common trap; Bollgard II came in 2006). Statement 3 is correct: it is the first and only GM crop commercially cultivated. Statement 1 is correct: three MAHYCO hybrids against the American bollworm. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
111.tq: Bt cotton = March 2002, only commercial GM crop.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)** **1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: approved as **3 hybrids of MAHYCO** against the **American bollworm**.
Statement 2 wrong: Bt cotton was approved in **March 2002**, not 2006.
Statement 3 correct: it is the **first and only** GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
xa: ⚠ **2006** is the year of **Bollgard II**, a common trap for the approval year.
Bt cotton covers ~**10.8 million ha**, ~**90%** of cotton area.
Largest Bt cotton producer: **Maharashtra** (APPSC-G2 2017).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Bt cotton in India:
1. It covers about 90% of the country's cotton area.
2. It has cut pesticide use by about 70-80%.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: Bt cotton covers about 90% of cotton area (~10.8 million ha). Statement 2 is wrong: the cut in pesticide use is about 40-50%, not 70-80%. Hence 1 only; 'Both' and '2 only' accept the wrong figure, 'Neither' rejects a correct one.
111.tq: Bt cotton numbers: 90% of area, 40-50% less pesticide.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: Bt cotton covers ~**90%** of cotton area (~**10.8 million ha**).
Statement 2 wrong: pesticide use fell **40-50%**, not 70-80%.
xa: Benefits **varied by region**.
Problems: **pink bollworm** resistance, **secondary pests**, **seed dependency**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements regarding HTBt cotton:
1. It combines glyphosate tolerance with the Bt trait.
2. It has been approved for commercial cultivation throughout India.
3. Its approval has been pending because of weed-management and socio-economic concerns.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: HTBt cotton combines glyphosate tolerance with the Bt trait, but it is not approved in India. Approval has remained pending over weed-management and socio-economic concerns.
111.tq: Identify the false approval claim by checking the regulatory status and the stated reasons for delay.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **HTBt cotton** = **glyphosate-tolerant + Bt**.
Statement 2 wrong: **HT crops are not approved** in India; illegal HT Bt cotton is sown without approval.
Statement 3 correct: approval is **pending** over **weed-management and socio-economic** concerns.
xa: HT crops encourage heavy **glyphosate** use.
**Punjab banned glyphosate sale in 2018**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about problems with Bt cotton:
1. The pink bollworm has developed resistance to Bt toxins.
2. Sucking/secondary pests such as whitefly and mealybug have risen.
3. It has ended farmers' dependence on purchased seed and lowered input costs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 3 is wrong: high input costs and seed dependency are listed problems of Bt cotton. Statement 1 is correct: pink bollworm overcame Bt toxins. Statement 2 is correct: whitefly and mealybug, sucking pests, rose. Non-adoption of refuges is another problem. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
111.tq: Bt cotton problems: pink bollworm resistance, sucking pests, seed dependency.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(3)** **1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **pink bollworm** developed resistance to Bt toxins.
Statement 2 correct: **sucking/secondary pests** such as **whitefly** and **mealybug** rose.
Statement 3 wrong: **high input costs** and **seed dependency** are listed problems of Bt cotton.
xa: Another problem: non-adoption of **refuge** practices.
Yield rose from **190 kg/ha (2002)** to **480 kg/ha (2023)**.
Pesticide use was cut by **40-50%**.

111.s:
Which of the following are claimed environmental benefits or applications of genetically engineered crops?
1. Reduced pesticide use through Bt cotton
2. Herbicide tolerance
3. Drought tolerance
4. Stress tolerance through genome-edited crops
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
111.x: The claimed benefits include reduced pesticide use in Bt cotton, herbicide tolerance, drought tolerance and stress tolerance achieved through genome editing.
111.tq: Recognise that the broad benefits listed belong to different genetic-engineering or genome-editing approaches.
xs: All four are claimed benefits — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
Less pesticide via **Bt cotton**, plus **herbicide-tolerant** and **drought-tolerant** crops.
**Stress tolerance without transgenes**: genome-edited **Pusa Rice DST1**.
xa: Bt cotton cut pesticide use **40-50%**.
Pusa DST1 gives **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
Non-GMO route: **71 Trombay varieties** by mutation breeding.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Pusa Rice DST1:
1. It is genome-edited for drought and salinity tolerance.
2. It gives about 10-30% higher yield under stress.
3. It is a transgenic variety carrying foreign genes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Pusa Rice DST1 is genome-edited for drought + salinity tolerance with 10-30% higher yield under stress. Statement 3 is wrong: it gives stress tolerance without transgenes (no foreign DNA). So 1 and 2 only.
111.tq: Genome-edited is not transgenic.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is genome-edited for **drought + salinity** tolerance, with **10-30%** higher yield under stress.
Statement 3 wrong: it gives stress tolerance **without transgenes**.
xa: India is set to commercially launch it as its **first genome-edited rice** (1 Sep **2026**).
AP angle: it is an edited version of **MTU1010**, AP-bred at **Maruteru**.
**SDN-1** and **SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

111.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes biofortification from genetic modification?
o: GM technology uses only conventional crossing, whereas biofortification uses viral vectors.
Biofortification usually raises nutrient levels through conventional breeding, whereas GM technology inserts foreign genes.
Biofortification always requires foreign genes, whereas GM technology never changes genes.
Both terms exclusively refer to pesticide resistance.
111.x: Biofortification generally increases nutritional value through conventional breeding, while GM crops involve insertion of foreign genes.
111.tq: Separate two look-alike concepts by their defining technological method.
xs: **Biofortification** raises nutrients usually by **conventional breeding**; **GM** inserts **foreign genes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Options (1) and (3) reverse the two methods.
xa: Biofortification examples: **Dhanshakti** iron-rich pearl millet (**ICRISAT**); **high-lysine maize**.
ICAR released **524 varieties**, incl. **34 biofortified**.
**Golden Rice** is a GM route to more nutrients (beta-carotene).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about gene-drive mosquitoes:
1. A CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome, so over 90% of offspring inherit it instead of the normal 50%.
2. Population suppression aims to make the mosquito unable to support parasite development, while population modification produces sterile females.
3. 'Transmission Zero' is a Tanzania-led project on GM mosquitoes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: the drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome, giving over 90% inheritance. Statement 2 is wrong: it reverses the two types - suppression uses sterile females, modification stops the parasite developing. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only; '1 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
111.tq: Suppression = fewer mosquitoes (sterile females); modification = mosquitoes that cannot carry the parasite.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: the drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome — **over 90%** inherit it (normal **50%**).
Statement 2 wrong: it reverses the types — **suppression** = **sterile females**; **modification** = **parasite cannot develop**.
Statement 3 correct: **"Transmission Zero"** is **Tanzania-led** (20 Apr **2026**).
xa: Gene drives give "**super-Mendelian**" inheritance.
Unlike pesticides, there is **no simple recall** (14 Jul **2026**).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about site-directed nuclease (SDN) categories of gene editing in India:
1. SDN-1 makes a small change without a template or foreign DNA and is exempt from GM rules under the 2022 guidelines.
2. SDN-2 uses a template and inserts foreign DNA.
3. SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as GM.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: SDN-2 uses a template but introduces no foreign DNA, and is also exempt (2022). Statement 3 is correct: SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as GM. So 1 and 3 only; options with 2 are wrong and '1 only' misses 3.
111.tq: Only SDN-3 brings in foreign DNA - only SDN-3 is treated as GM.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: **SDN-1** = small change, no template, no foreign DNA — **exempt** (**2022**).
Statement 2 wrong: **SDN-2** uses a template but adds **no foreign DNA**, and is **exempt**.
Statement 3 correct: **SDN-3** inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as **GM**.
xa: Criticism: **GE crops bypass GMO rules**.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is genome-edited without transgenes.

111.s: Base editing differs from conventional double-strand-break editing because it:
o: Changes proteins without altering DNA bases
Converts one DNA base into another without creating double-strand breaks
Works exclusively by destroying the host cell
111.x: Base editing converts one DNA base into another without producing double-strand breaks in the DNA.
111.tq: Focus on the defining molecular distinction rather than the general purpose of gene editing.
xs: **Base editing** converts one DNA base into another **without double-strand breaks** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does change DNA bases, so (1) is wrong; it does not insert chromosomes or destroy cells.
xa: Risk: a **6-year-old** in China died (March **2025**) after a first-of-its-kind **brain base-editing therapy**.
**ContactSeek** (27 Jul **2026**) cuts off-target edits.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. CRISPR-Cas9 is simpler, cheaper and more accurate than ZFNs and TALENs and can target many genes at once.
2. A Centre of Excellence for CRISPR Innovation and Translation (CoE-CIT) is to be set up in Bengaluru.
3. TnpB is larger than Cas9 and therefore harder to deliver.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: TnpB (ICAR) is a smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 with easier delivery. So '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses the Bengaluru CoE, and options with 3 are wrong.
111.tq: CRISPR beats ZFN/TALEN; TnpB is smaller.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 correct: CRISPR-Cas9 is **simpler, cheaper, more accurate** than **ZFNs and TALENs** and targets many genes at once.
Statement 2 correct: **CoE-CIT** is to be set up in **Bengaluru**.
Statement 3 wrong: **TnpB** is **smaller** than Cas9, with **easier delivery**.
xa: CRISPR was demonstrated in **2012** by **Doudna and Charpentier**.
**SDN-1/SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about genetic medicines:
1. Engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles are used as carriers to deliver them.
2. They aim to correct or compensate for faulty genes.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Both are correct (UPSC 2026: all statements correct): genetic medicines correct or compensate for faulty genes, and they are delivered by engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles. So '2 only', '1 only' and 'Neither' are wrong.
111.tq: Genetic medicines: fix faulty genes; carriers = viruses, lipid nanoparticles.
xs: Both statements are correct — option **(3)** **Both 1 and 2**.
**Genetic medicines** **correct or compensate for faulty genes**.
Carriers are **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles** (UPSC 2026: all statements correct).
xa: **Mitochondrial replacement therapy** = "**three-parent baby**" technique.
**Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

111.s: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy is popularly known as the ____ technique, and its main ethical concern relates to ____.
o: three-parent baby; germline editing and designer babies
three-parent baby; pollen sterility in crops
synthetic-embryo; germline editing and designer babies
111.x: MRT is the 'three-parent baby' technique and raises ethical issues of germline editing and designer babies (A). B has the wrong name and concern; C has the right name but a crop issue; D has the right concern but the wrong name.
111.tq: Three parents = nuclear DNA of two parents + donor mitochondria.
xs: **Mitochondrial replacement therapy** is the **"three-parent baby"** technique, and its ethical issue is **germline editing and designer babies** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) has the wrong name and concern; option (3) has the right name but a crop issue (pollen sterility); option (4) has the right concern but the wrong name.
xa: Genetic medicines aim to **correct/compensate for faulty genes**, carried by **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles**.
Gene therapy in India is regulated by the **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
⚠ **Sterile seeds** (crop issue) belong to **V-GURT (Terminator)** technology, not to human therapy.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about synthetic biology:
1. Insulin and artemisinin have been produced by microbes.
2. Semaglutide has been grown in Bacillus thuringiensis.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: insulin and artemisinin are made by microbes. Statement 2 is wrong: semaglutide was grown in baker's yeast, not Bacillus thuringiensis (the Bt gene source). Hence 1 only.
111.tq: Semaglutide - baker's yeast.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **insulin** and **artemisinin** are produced by **microbes** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **semaglutide** is grown in **baker's yeast**, not in **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
**Bacillus thuringiensis** is the soil bacterium that is the source of the **Bt gene** (crystal **delta-endotoxins**).
xa: **Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
First human hormone by rDNA = **insulin** (UKPSC **2024**); **Humulin** marketed **1982**.
**Genetic medicines** correct or compensate for faulty genes (carriers: **engineered viruses**, **lipid nanoparticles**).

111.s:
Which of the following may be adversely affected by Bt toxins or other engineered traits?
1. Pollinators
2. Natural enemies of pests
3. Soil nematodes and microbes
4. Aquatic organisms
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
111.x: Bt toxins or other engineered traits may affect beneficial insects such as pollinators and natural enemies, soil nematodes and microbes, and aquatic organisms.
111.tq: Use an all-inclusive option when each listed ecological group is affected by the same broad concern.
xs: Bt toxins or engineered traits may harm **pollinators, natural enemies, soil nematodes/microbes and aquatic organisms** — all four, option **(3)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
This **non-target harm** is a listed environmental risk alongside **gene flow**.
xa: Bt gene source: **Bacillus thuringiensis**; protoxin activated in the **alkaline gut** of larvae, creates pores in midgut.
Bt proteins were feared to persist, but experiments show they **degrade in soil**.
**Pink bollworm** developed resistance to Bt toxins — resistance build-up is also a listed risk.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about GURT:
1. T-GURT (traitor) switches a desired trait on or off with a proprietary chemical.
2. V-GURT is commercialised in several countries though banned in India.
3. V-GURT (terminator) makes plants produce sterile seeds.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 3 is correct: V-GURT gives sterile seeds. Statement 1 is correct: T-GURT uses a proprietary chemical switch and is at research stage. Statement 2 is wrong: V-GURT is not commercialised anywhere; it is banned in India under the PPV&FR Act, 2001. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
111.tq: V-GURT = sterile seed (banned, PPV&FR 2001); T-GURT = chemical switch.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **T-GURT (Traitor)** switches a trait on/off with a **proprietary chemical**.
Statement 2 wrong: **V-GURT** is **not commercialised anywhere**; it is banned in India under the **PPV&FR Act (2001)**.
Statement 3 correct: **V-GURT (Terminator)** makes plants produce **sterile seeds**.
xa: T-GURT is still at **research stage**.
GURT ends **seed saving/replanting** and forces annual seed purchase.
**National Genebank** holds **4,70,513 accessions** (2026).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about the debate on genetic engineering:
1. Societies generally accept gene therapy but resist GM crops.
2. GM maize, soy, cotton and canola are grown and traded widely.
3. Genome-edited crops face stricter rules than GMOs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as stated in the debate. Statement 3 is wrong: the criticism is that genome-edited crops bypass GMO rules, not that they face stricter rules. So 1 and 2 only.
111.tq: Criticism of GE crops: they bypass GMO rules.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: societies **accept gene therapy but resist GM crops** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is correct: **GM maize, soy, cotton and canola** are grown and traded widely.
Statement 3 is wrong: the criticism is that genome-edited crops **bypass GMO rules**, not face stricter ones.
xa: **SDN-1** and **SDN-2** (no foreign DNA) are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**); **SDN-3** inserts foreign DNA → regulated as GM.
**Pusa Rice DST1** = India's first genome-edited rice to be launched commercially.
**Bt cotton** (**2002**) remains the **first and only** GM crop commercially cultivated in India.

111.s:
With reference to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, consider the following statements:
1. It was adopted in 2000.
2. It entered into force in 2003.
3. It governs the transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
4. India is a party to it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
111.x: The Cartagena Protocol was adopted in 2000, entered into force in 2003, governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms, and India is a party to it.
111.tq: Check each date, subject matter and membership statement before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2, 3 and 4**).
The **Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety** was adopted in **2000** and came into force in **2003**.
It governs **transboundary movement of LMOs**, and **India is a party**.
xa: It is named after **Colombia**'s Cartagena.
In India, **GEAC** approves GM releases — e.g. **GM mustard DMH-11** (environmental release **Oct 2022**), now **under Supreme Court consideration**.
First GMO: **1973**; first GM food sold: **Flavr Savr tomato** (**1994**).

111.s:
Consider the following statements about Golden Rice:
1. It carries phytoene synthase from daffodil and crtI from the bacterium Erwinia uredovora.
2. It produces beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A.
3. Golden Rice 2 takes its phytoene synthase from wheat.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 2 is correct: beta-carotene targets Vitamin A deficiency and blindness. Statement 1 is correct: daffodil phytoene synthase plus Erwinia crtI. Statement 3 is wrong: Golden Rice 2 takes phytoene synthase from maize, not wheat. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
111.tq: Golden Rice: daffodil (maize in GR2) + Erwinia crtI.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: genes are **phytoene synthase from daffodil** and **crtI** from **Erwinia uredovora**.
Statement 2 correct: Golden Rice makes **beta-carotene**, precursor of **Vitamin A**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Golden Rice 2** takes phytoene synthase from **maize**, not wheat.
xa: Golden Rice targets **Vitamin A deficiency/blindness** (APPSC 2025).
**Biofortification** usually uses **conventional breeding**, e.g. **Dhanshakti** iron-rich pearl millet.
**Edible vaccines**: transgenic potato/banana with cholera or hepatitis B antigens.

111.s:
Consider the following statements about gene flow from GM crops:
1. The risk of transgene escape is highest in a crop's centre of origin or diversity, where many wild relatives occur.
2. India being a centre of diversity of wheat was a key argument against Bt brinjal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: Statement 1 is correct: centres of origin/diversity hold many wild relatives, so risk is highest there. Statement 2 is wrong: the argument against Bt brinjal was that India is a centre of diversity of brinjal itself. Hence 1 only.
111.tq: Bt brinjal objection = India is brinjal's centre of diversity.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: risk of transgene escape is highest at a crop's **centre of origin/diversity**, with many **wild relatives** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: India is the centre of diversity of **brinjal**, not wheat — that was the key argument against **Bt brinjal**.
xa: **Bt brinjal**: GEAC recommended release **2009**; **moratorium 2010** (**Jairam Ramesh**).
Bt brinjal was developed by **Mahyco + UAS Dharwad + TNAU** against **fruit and shoot borer**.
Gene flow can create **superweeds** and alter native gene pools.

111.s: The principal concern of farmers regarding terminator technology is that it:
o: Allows farmers to reuse seed indefinitely without purchase
Increases the nutritional value of every seed
Makes all crops resistant to every insect
Prevents plants from forming viable seeds, ending normal seed saving and replanting
111.x: Terminator technology makes the next generation of seeds non-viable, preventing seed saving and replanting and potentially forcing annual purchases.
111.tq: Apply the mechanism to the farmer’s seed-saving decision.
xs: Terminator technology **prevents plants from forming viable seeds**, **ending seed saving and replanting** — option **(4)** is correct.
Farmers are forced into **annual purchase** of seed; it does not add nutrition or universal insect resistance.
xa: Terminator = **V-GURT**; **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act (2001)**; not commercialised anywhere.
**T-GURT (Traitor)**: trait controlled by a **proprietary chemical**; research stage.
Wider concerns: **seed sovereignty** and **corporate dependency**.

111.s: Which State is the largest producer of Bt cotton in India?
111.x: Maharashtra is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 2017 key). Gujarat, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh grow Bt cotton but are not the largest producer.
111.tq: Bt cotton leader = Maharashtra.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 **2017**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Punjab** is known for banning **glyphosate** sale in **2018**.
xa: Bt cotton covers ~**90%** of India's cotton area.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.
AP angle: **Pusa DST1** is an edited version of AP-bred **MTU1010**.

111.s: Mon 863, which was in the news over the safety of feeding studies, was a genetically modified:
o: Vitamin-A enriched rice targeting night blindness
111.x: Mon 863 was a Monsanto genetically modified pest-resistant maize variety directed against corn rootworm and was discussed in connection with feeding-study safety.
111.tq: Use the crop-pest association to identify the correct GM variety.
xs: **Mon 863** was a **genetically modified pest-resistant maize** (Monsanto) **against corn rootworm** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was in the news over the **safety of feeding studies** (PYQ).
**Vitamin-A rice** is **Golden Rice**, not Mon 863.
xa: **Golden Rice** makes **beta-carotene**; genes: **phytoene synthase** from daffodil + **crtI** from **Erwinia uredovora**.
GEAC cleared confined trials of Bayer's **HT + insect-resistant GM maize** at **PAU**, Kharif **2025**.
**Brazil-nut** soybean → never released (allergenicity).

111.s: Which one of the following best explains genetic homogenisation in agriculture?
o: Cultivation of many locally adapted landraces in small farms
Increase in the number of unrelated crop species in a field
Exchange of seeds among farmers without commercial restrictions
Use of uniform engineered varieties over large areas, reducing agro-biodiversity
111.x: Genetic homogenisation results when uniform varieties are widely cultivated, reducing agro-biodiversity and increasing vulnerability to new pathogens and climate shocks.
111.tq: Choose the option that contains both the process and its defining consequence.
xs: **Genetic homogenisation** = **uniform engineered varieties over large areas**, **reducing agro-biodiversity** — option **(4)** is correct.
It raises vulnerability to **new pathogens** and **climate shocks**; growing many landraces is the opposite.
xa: **Monoculture** and a few patented seed firms displace **landraces** and farmer varieties.
Safeguards: **National Genebank** (**4,70,513** accessions, **2026**), **PPV&FR Act**, **National Gene Fund**.
PYQ: **genetic modification** is the technology flagged for impact on **biodiversity**.

111.s: Which technological development has been specifically flagged for its impact on biodiversity?
111.x: Genetic modification has been identified as the technology among these options that was flagged for its potential impact on biodiversity.
111.tq: Use the exclusion pattern to distinguish the biodiversity concern from unrelated technologies.
xs: **Genetic modification** is the technology flagged for its impact on **biodiversity** (PYQ) — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ Trap: **solar panels**, **wind turbines** and **rainwater harvesting** are not the answer.
xa: GM risks to biodiversity: **gene flow**, **superweeds**, **genetic homogenisation**.
**Monoculture** displaces **landraces** and farmer varieties.
**National Genebank** holds **4,70,513** accessions (**2026**).

111.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Gene therapy is a biotechnology and genetic-engineering application.
II. Gene therapy targets genetic abnormalities or diseases.
III. The basic idea of gene therapy is to alter, replace or correct defective genetic function.
IV. Gene therapy is based on changing environmental conditions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: I, II and III are correct: gene therapy is a genetic-engineering method that corrects or replaces defective genes. IV is false because it changes genes, not the environment.
111.tq: Recall the principle of gene therapy.
n: Gene therapy is a biotechnology and genetic-engineering application. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
Gene therapy targets genetic abnormalities or diseases. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to alter defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to replace defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to correct defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
Genetic engineering is used in gene therapy. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(3)** **I, II and III only**.
**Gene therapy** is a biotechnology and genetic-engineering application targeting **genetic abnormalities or diseases**.
Its idea is to **alter, replace or correct defective genetic function**; statement IV is wrong — it is not based on environmental change.
xa: **CRISPR** has the potential to **correct genetic defects**.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
A child in China died (**March 2025**) after a first **brain base-editing therapy**.

111.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Genome sequencing provides genomic information.
II. Pharmacogenomics relates genetics to drug response.
III. Personalised or precision medicine adapts treatment using individual biological or genetic information.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
111.x: All three are correct: genome sequencing gives genetic data, pharmacogenomics links genes to drug response and precision medicine tailors treatment.
111.tq: Recall the applications of genomics.
n: Personalised or precision medicine adapts treatment using individual biological or genetic information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
Genome sequencing provides genomic information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
Pharmacogenomics links genetics to drug response. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
DNA sequencing detects sequence or variant information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
The goal of personalised medicine is more individually tailored prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(1)** **I, II and III**.
**Genome sequencing** gives **genomic information**; **pharmacogenomics** links **genetics to drug response**.
**Personalised medicine** adapts treatment using **individual biological or genetic information**.
xa: **DNA sequencing** gives sequence or **variant information**.
**Genetic testing** identifies relevant variants.
Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up = **CRISPR** (UKPSC 2025).

111.s: Which of the following statements about genetically modified organisms is incorrect?
o: Genetic engineering is used to produce a GMO.
A GMO involves a change in the genome or genetic makeup.
The transfer occurs in ways that would naturally occur.
The process may involve transferring a gene from one organism to another.
111.x: Option C is incorrect: genetic engineering moves genes in ways that would not happen naturally. A GMO has a changed genome, often from another organism.
111.tq: Check each statement for a missing "not".
n: GMO changes the genome or genetic makeup. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
GMO production uses genetic engineering. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
GMO production transfers a gene from one organism to another. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
Genetic transfer in GMO production occurs in ways that would not naturally occur. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
xs: The incorrect statement is option **(3)**: the gene transfer in a GMO occurs in ways that would **not naturally occur**.
A **GMO** has its **genome** altered through **genetic engineering** — options (1) and (2) are true.
It **transfers a gene** from one organism to another — option (4) is true.
xa: GMO is approximately **synonymous** with **transgenic organism**.
A **transgenic organism** carries a **foreign gene** for a desired characteristic or product.
Purpose: to produce **desired traits or products**.

111.s: With reference to Bt proteins in agricultural soil, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: They can be removed only by burning the crop residue.
Experiments have shown that they degrade in soil.
They are converted into glyphosate in soil.
They remain permanently active in soil after harvest.
111.x: Although persistence of Bt proteins in soil was feared, experiments have shown that they degrade in soil.
111.tq: Distinguish an experimentally established finding from an earlier environmental fear.
xs: Experiments show **Bt proteins degrade in soil** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Soil persistence was **feared**, but it is not permanent.
xa: Bt gene source: soil bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
Bt toxins may harm **non-target** organisms such as soil nematodes/microbes.
Bt cotton cut pesticide use by **40-50%**.

112.s: Which one of the following is the apex statutory body regulating genetically modified organisms in India?
o: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
112.x: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is the apex statutory body regulating GMOs in India. FSSAI, CPCB and ICAR are not the apex GMO regulator.
112.tq: Distinguish the correct regulatory authority from closely related bodies.
xs: The **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** is the **apex statutory body** that regulates GMOs in India — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**).
⚠ Trap (PYQ): **FSSAI**, **CPCB** and **ICAR** are not the GMO regulator.
xa: GEAC is constituted in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** of the **Environment (Protection) Act 1986**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
Renamed from "**Approval**" to "**Appraisal**" Committee in **2010**.

112.s: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is chaired by:
o: The Special or Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The Chairperson of the Central Pollution Control Board
The Director-General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research
112.x: GEAC is chaired by a Special or Additional Secretary of MoEFCC. A senior officer from the Department of Biotechnology serves as co-chair.
112.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' method to identify the correct chairing authority.
xs: GEAC is chaired by the **Special/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Department of Biotechnology** provides only the **co-chair**, not the chair; CPCB and ICAR have no such role.
xa: GEAC sits in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** (EPA **1986**).
It approves **field trials** and **commercial release** of GM crops.
**RCGM** (under **DBT**) monitors ongoing research and recommends to GEAC.

112.s: Which one of the following is NOT a function of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
o: Approving field trials of genetically modified crops
Approving commercial release and cultivation of GM organisms
Approving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants
Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds
112.x: GEAC deals with field trials, environmental release, commercial cultivation and large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants. Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds is not its function.
112.tq: Find the one unrelated function among powers of the same regulatory body.
xs: **Fixing the maximum retail price of commercial seeds** is not a GEAC function — option **(4)** is the answer.
GEAC approves **field trials and commercial release** of GM crops — option (1) is a function.
It approves **large-scale use, environmental release and commercial cultivation** of GMOs, and **large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms** and recombinants — options (2), (3).
xa: GEAC = **apex/statutory** GMO regulator, in **MoEFCC**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair: **DBT**.
⚠ Genome-edited **SDN-1/SDN-2** crops **skip GEAC** and need only **IBC** approval.

112.s: Which one of the following technologies has been flagged for raising concerns about biodiversity?
112.x: Genetic modification is the technology flagged for biodiversity concerns (APPSC-GS 2023), through gene flow, monoculture and loss of diversity. Drip irrigation, solar panels and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
112.tq: Biodiversity worry = genetic modification.
xs: **Genetic modification of crops** is flagged for **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Drip irrigation, rooftop solar and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xa: Concerns: gene flow, **monoculture**, loss of diversity, **genetic homogenisation**.
Primary environmental concern: **cross-pollination** to non-GM crops.
Resistance also stems from control by **big seed companies** holding patents.

112.s: The expression “designer babies” is most directly associated with which ethical debate?
o: Use of adult stem cells for tissue repair
Inspection of laboratories handling moderate-risk agents
Protection of traditional knowledge from patent claims
Use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits
112.x: “Designer babies” refers to the ethical concern that genetic technologies could be used to select or modify desired traits in human offspring.
112.tq: Translate the ethical term into its underlying biotechnology application.
xs: **"Designer babies"** refers to the **use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is tied to **germline editing**, an ethical issue in bioethics.
xa: Other ethical issues: **three-parent baby** technique, **animal cloning welfare**, **informed consent**.
**He Jiankui** (China, **2018**): human embryo editing — **"CRISPR babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** monitors genome-editing ethics.

112.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)
(b) Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA)
(c) National Green Tribunal (NGT)
(d) Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)

List-II
(i) Constituted under the Water Act, 1974
(ii) Constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
(iii) Related to genetically engineered organisms and biotechnology regulation
(iv) Established under the NGT Act, 2010
112.x: GEAC deals with genetically engineered organisms, CGWA was set up under Section 3(3) of the EPA, the NGT under the NGT Act, 2010, and the CPCB under the Water Act, 1974. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
112.tq: Match each body to its legal basis.
n: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is related to genetically engineered organisms. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is related to biotechnology regulation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Central Ground Water Authority was constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The National Green Tribunal is governed by the NGT Act, 2010. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Central Pollution Control Board was constituted under the Water Act, 1974. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Central Pollution Control Board is a statutory body. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(4)**.
**GEAC** relates to **genetically engineered organisms** and biotech regulation.
**CGWA** was constituted under **Section 3(3)** of the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**.
**NGT** — **NGT Act, 2010**; **CPCB** — **Water Act, 1974**.
xa: CGWA **regulates and controls groundwater development** and management.
GEAC is constituted in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989**.
⚠ GEAC — NOT FSSAI, CPCB or ICAR — regulates GMOs (PYQ).

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee:
I. It was constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
II. Its earlier name was the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee.
III. The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: All three are correct: GEAC was set up under the EPA, was once the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee, and was renamed 'Appraisal' in 2010.
112.tq: Recall GEAC's renaming.
n: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee was constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The earlier name of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee was the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(3)** **I, II and III**.
**GEAC** was constituted under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**.
It was earlier the **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee**, renamed **Appraisal** Committee in **2010**.
xa: GEAC is the **apex/statutory body** regulating GMOs (APPSC-G2 2023).
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
It approves **field trials and commercial release** of GM crops.

112.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: SBCC — State-level inspection, investigation and punitive action
DLC — Approval of all commercial GM releases
112.x: SBCC operates at the state level and has powers to inspect, investigate and take punitive action. DLC performs district-level monitoring, GEAC deals with environmental release and commercial use, and IBSC is institutional.
112.tq: Use the level of operation to reject swapped committee functions.
xs: **SBCC** is the **State-level** body with powers to **inspect, investigate and take punitive action** — option **(1)** is correct.
**DLC** does **district-level monitoring**, not commercial approvals; **GEAC** (MoEFCC) approves environmental release; **IBSC** is **institutional**, not international.
xa: Six tiers: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → SBCC → DLC** → expert committees.
**RCGM** under **DBT** monitors ongoing research.
Plus **rDNA Guidelines 2017**.

112.s:
Arrange the following bodies in the sequence of the six-tier biosafety system beginning with the institutional level:
A. GEAC
B. IBSC
C. DLC
D. RCGM
112.x: The sequence is IBSC, RCGM, GEAC, SBCC, DLC and expert committees. Among the listed bodies, the order is IBSC, RCGM, GEAC and DLC.
112.tq: Arrange administrative bodies by the stated regulatory progression.
xs: Order: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → DLC** (B, D, A, C) — option **(1)** is correct.
Full six-tier system: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → SBCC → DLC → expert committees**.
xa: **IBSC** = institution level, first tier; **RCGM** = **DBT**; **GEAC** = **MoEFCC**, apex.
**SBCC** = State (punitive action); **DLC** = District (field monitoring).
**RDAC** (DBT) is **advisory**, recommending safety regulations.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the GMO regulatory bodies under the Rules, 1989:
1. RDAC, under DBT, is advisory and recommends safety regulations.
2. RCGM functions under MoEFCC and approves commercial release of GM crops.
3. IBSC is the first tier, functioning at the institutional level.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: RCGM is under DBT and monitors ongoing research and advises GEAC; GEAC (MoEFCC) approves environmental release and commercial use. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
112.tq: RCGM = DBT, advises; GEAC = MoEFCC, approves.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **RDAC** (DBT) is **advisory** and recommends safety regulations — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **RCGM** is under **DBT** (Ministry of S&T); it monitors research and advises GEAC. **GEAC (MoEFCC)** approves commercial release.
Statement 3 is correct: **IBSC** is the **first tier**, at each institution.
xa: **SBCC** (State): powers to inspect, investigate and take **punitive action**.
**DLC** (District): field-level monitoring.
**IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).

112.s:
Which sequence correctly represents the regulatory pathway for a confined biotechnology crop field trial?
A. Commercial clearance
B. Confined open-plot trials at agricultural universities or ICAR plots
C. Committees’ safety assessments
D. Assessment of superiority over non-GM varieties without ecological harm
112.x: The process begins with committees’ safety assessments, followed by confined open-plot trials, evaluation of superiority without ecological harm, and only then commercial clearance.
112.tq: Arrange the process from preliminary safety review to field testing, final evaluation and clearance.
xs: Order: **committees' safety assessments → confined open-plot trials → superiority test without ecological harm → commercial clearance** (C, B, D, A) — option **(1)**.
Trials run at **agricultural universities/ICAR plots** over several seasons and locations.
xa: Trials are **Biosafety Research Level** trials (**BRL-I**, **BRL-II**).
Field trials need the **State's NOC**; several States refuse them.
GEAC approves **field trials** and **commercial release**.

112.s:
With reference to the commercial approval of Bt cotton in India, consider the following statements:
1. The initial approval covered three MAHYCO hybrids.
2. The approval was initially granted for three years.
3. Bt cotton remains the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
112.x: All three statements are correct. Three MAHYCO hybrids were initially approved for three years, and Bt cotton remains the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
112.tq: Check each statement against the approval details before selecting the complete combination.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
Statement 1: approval in **March 2002** covered **three MAHYCO hybrids**.
Statement 2: initially for **3 years**; Statement 3: Bt cotton is the **only GM crop commercially cultivated**.
xa: Leading State: **Maharashtra** (PYQ).
**Bollgard** = GM technology (PYQ); genes from **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
**DMH-11**'s commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.

112.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome editing from SDN-3 editing?
o: All three categories are treated as conventional crops
SDN-1 alone is transgenic, while SDN-2 and SDN-3 are exempted
SDN-1 and SDN-2 introduce foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 does not
SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 is transgenic
112.x: SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA and are exempted from GMO rules under the 2022 guidelines. SDN-3 is transgenic and remains under full regulatory control.
112.tq: Discriminate the paired categories by checking the presence or absence of foreign DNA.
xs: **SDN-1 and SDN-2** are **small edits without foreign DNA**, while **SDN-3 is transgenic** — option **(4)** is correct.
SDN-1/2 are **exempted** from GMO rules (**2022 guidelines**); SDN-3 stays under **full GM control** — so options (1)-(3) are wrong.
xa: Exempt GE crops **skip GEAC**; need only **IBC** approval.
Comparison: GMO = foreign gene, full **GEAC** route; SDN-1/2 = treated like **conventional crops**.
⚠ Criticism: the GE exemption is called a **"back door"**.

112.s:
Consider the following:
1. Insect resistance build-up and harm to non-target organisms
2. Weediness in wild relatives and genetic homogenisation
3. Toxicity, allergenicity and antibiotic resistance
4. Ozone depletion
Which of the above are listed as environmental or health risks of GM crops?
112.x: 1 and 2 are listed environmental risks; 3 are listed health risks. Ozone depletion (4) is not a GM-crop risk. So 1, 2 and 3 only; options with 4 are wrong and '1 and 2 only' leaves out the health risks.
112.tq: GM risks: environment (resistance, non-target, weediness, homogenisation) + health (toxicity, allergy, antibiotic resistance).
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are listed risks; **ozone depletion** is not — option **(2)**.
1 and 2 are environmental risks: **insect resistance build-up**, **non-target harm**, **weediness**, **genetic homogenisation**.
3 are health risks: **toxicity**, **allergenicity**, **antibiotic resistance**.
xa: Primary environmental concern: **gene flow/cross-pollination**.
Reasons for resistance: **monoculture**, loss of diversity, control by **patent-holding seed companies**.
Herbicide-tolerance fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

112.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Introduction of Bt cotton
B. PIL against GM crops in the Supreme Court
C. Moratorium on Bt brinjal
D. GEAC clearance of trials of 11 crops and 21 varieties
112.x: Bt cotton was introduced in 2002, the PIL was filed in 2006, the Bt brinjal moratorium was imposed in 2010, and GEAC cleared trials in 2014.
112.tq: Use the first and last events, then place the intervening years in sequence.
xs: Order: **Bt cotton (2002) → SC PIL (2006) → Bt brinjal moratorium (2010) → trials of 11 crops/21 varieties (2014)** — option **(1)** (A, B, C, D).
The **2014** clearances came when **Veerappa Moily** resumed trials (Mar and Jul).
xa: **2009**: GEAC recommends **Bt brinjal** release.
**2012**: Parliamentary Standing Committee (**37th report**) — end all GM field trials.
**2022**: GEAC clears **DMH-11** environmental release.

112.s: The 2010 decision relating to Bt brinjal included which of the following additional measures?
o: A requirement that all GM seeds be branded by the State
A transfer of field-trial approval exclusively to FSSAI
A mandatory State no-objection certificate for field trials
A permanent ban on every GM crop in India
112.x: In 2010, a State NOC was made mandatory for field trials. The decision was not a permanent ban on every GM crop or a transfer of approval to FSSAI.
112.tq: Separate the specific administrative condition from exaggerated consequences.
xs: In **2010**, along with the **Bt brinjal moratorium**, a **State NOC was made mandatory** for field trials — option **(3)** is correct.
It was not a permanent ban on all GM crops (**Bt cotton** continued), nor a shift of approvals to FSSAI.
xa: Moratorium by Minister **Jairam Ramesh**: no scientific consensus, opposition of brinjal-growing States.
Bt brinjal targets **fruit and shoot borer**; by **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended its release in **2009**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court-appointed Technical Expert Committee:
1. It recommended a 10-year moratorium on GM field trials.
2. Its recommendation amounted to a final Supreme Court verdict.
3. GM trials were halted during the relevant period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
112.x: The Technical Expert Committee recommended a 10-year moratorium and trials were halted. The recommendation was not itself a final Supreme Court verdict.
112.tq: Distinguish an expert recommendation from a judicial verdict.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **Technical Expert Committee** recommended a **10-year moratorium** on field trials — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: there was **no SC verdict** — it was only an expert panel's recommendation.
Statement 3 is correct: trials were **halted/put on hold** (**Jayanthi Natarajan**).
xa: **2012**: **37th report** of the Parliamentary Standing Committee — end all GM field trials.
**2014**: **Veerappa Moily** resumed trials; GEAC cleared **11** crops (Mar) and **21** varieties (Jul).
**2006**: PIL against GM crops in the SC.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about GM mustard DMH-11:
1. GEAC cleared its environmental release in 2022.
2. In July 2024 the Supreme Court gave a unanimous verdict approving it.
3. In July 2024 both judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the July 2024 verdict was a split verdict. Statement 3 is correct: both judges directed a national GM crop policy. So 1 and 3 only.
112.tq: July 2024 = split verdict, but common direction for a national GM policy.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: GEAC cleared **DMH-11** environmental release in **2022** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the July **2024** ruling was a **split verdict**, not unanimous approval.
Statement 3 is correct: both judges directed the Centre to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.
xa: **DMH-11** = hybrid seed system (**barnase-barstar**), **25-30%** higher yield; **Delhi University**.
Its commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013:
1. It proposed a single regulator for biotechnology.
2. It was passed by Parliament and is now in force.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Bill lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha. Hence 1 only.
112.tq: BRAI Bill = proposed single regulator, lapsed.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **BRAI Bill, 2013** proposed a **single regulator** — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the Bill **lapsed** with the **15th Lok Sabha**.
xa: **BioE3 Policy 2024** now proposes **single-window clearance** + **regulatory sandboxes**.
Overlapping regulators: **DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA**.
GM approval takes **7-10 years** vs **3-5** globally.

112.s: Which policy proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes in the biotechnology sector?
112.x: The BioE3 Policy, 2024 proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes.
112.tq: Identify the policy by pairing its year with its distinctive regulatory features.
xs: The **BioE3 Policy, 2024** proposes **single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes** — option **(3)** is correct.
**BRAI** was a **Bill (2013)** that **lapsed**, not an Act.
xa: **FSSAI GM food framework** is also of **2024**.
Delays from overlapping mandates: **7-10 years** for approval.
⚠ India has **no biosafety liability law**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about biosafety levels:
1. BSL-1 is for agents not known to cause disease.
2. BSL-2 is for lethal agents with no cure.
3. BSL-3 is for serious airborne agents such as TB.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: BSL-2 is for moderate-risk agents; lethal agents with no cure (e.g. Ebola) need BSL-4. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
112.tq: BSL rises with danger: none, moderate, serious airborne, lethal no cure.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **BSL-1** is for agents **not known to cause disease** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **BSL-2** is for **moderate-risk agents**; lethal agents with no cure need **BSL-4**.
Statement 3 is correct: **BSL-3** handles serious airborne agents like **TB**.
xa: **BSL-4**: lethal agents with no cure (e.g. **Ebola**); India: **NIV Pune**.
**DBT** handles **biocontainment**; **NCDC** handles surveillance.
**Cartagena Protocol**: adopted **2000**, in force **2003**.

112.s: Which statement correctly describes Bollgard II cotton?
o: It uses the barnase-barstar system from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
It contains only the antisense polygalacturonase gene
It contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis
It produces beta-carotene using daffodil genes alone
112.x: Bollgard II cotton contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab genes sourced from Bacillus thuringiensis. The other options describe Flavr Savr, Golden Rice or GM mustard.
112.tq: Distinguish similar GM crop technologies by their gene combinations.
xs: **Bollgard II** contains **Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Barnase-barstar** = **GM mustard DMH-11**; **antisense polygalacturonase** = **Flavr Savr**; **beta-carotene** = **Golden Rice**.
xa: **Bollgard I** has only **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard** = GM technology (PYQ).
Bt cotton trait: **bollworm** resistance.
Bt cotton approved **March 2002** — **only GM crop commercially cultivated**.

112.s: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance against the:
112.x: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance to the fruit and shoot borer insect.
112.tq: Match the crop with its target pest rather than with another Bt crop’s pest.
xs: **Bt brinjal** was developed for resistance to the **fruit and shoot borer** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Bollworm** resistance is **Bt cotton**'s trait; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr**.
xa: Developer: **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended release **2009**; **Jairam Ramesh**'s moratorium **2010**.
Gene: **Cry1Ac** from Bt.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about GM mustard DMH-11:
1. It uses the barnase-barstar system for hybrid seed production.
2. Its barnase-barstar genes come from Bacillus thuringiensis.
3. It was developed by Delhi University.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: barnase-barstar comes from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes. Statement 3 is correct. So 1 and 3 only.
112.tq: Two Bacillus: thuringiensis = Bt toxin; amyloliquefaciens = barnase-barstar.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **DMH-11** uses the **barnase-barstar** system for **hybrid seed production** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: barnase-barstar comes from **Bacillus amyloliquefaciens**; **Bacillus thuringiensis** gives **Bt** genes.
Statement 3 is correct: DMH-11 was developed by **Delhi University**.
xa: Higher yield **25-30%**.
GEAC cleared environmental release in **2022**; held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: DMH-11 carries the **bar gene**.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 is associated with which of the following traits and editing features?
o: Insect resistance; insertion of a Bt toxin gene by SDN-2
Drought and salinity tolerance; DST gene knockout by SDN-1
Higher phosphate uptake; insertion of a foreign bacterial gene
Vitamin A enrichment; mitochondrial gene replacement
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited form of MTU1010, designed for drought and salinity tolerance through DST gene knockout using SDN-1.
112.tq: Combine the crop, trait and technical method instead of relying on the variety name alone.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** gives **drought and salinity tolerance** by **DST gene knockout via SDN-1** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **CRISPR-Cas9** edit of **MTU1010**, with **no foreign DNA** — so not Bt insertion, foreign bacterial gene or vitamin A.
xa: Yield **10-30%** higher under stress; set for commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
Developer: **ICAR-IARI, Delhi**.
**Phosphate uptake** rice is **NIPGR**'s; **vitamin A** rice is **Golden Rice**.

112.s: For genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption, which approval route is indicated?
o: IBC approval without the GEAC route
Only approval from the State Pollution Control Board
Approval from the Supreme Court after public consultation
112.x: Genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption can skip the GEAC route and require IBC approval.
112.tq: Ask which authority performs the relevant regulatory function instead of assuming every biotechnology product follows the GEAC route.
xs: Genome-edited crops under the SDN-1/SDN-2 exemption need only **IBC approval** and **skip the GEAC** route — option **(1)** is correct.
No State Pollution Board or Supreme Court route is involved.
xa: **IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).
**2022 guidelines** exempt **SDN-1/SDN-2** (no foreign DNA).
**SDN-3** (transgenic) remains under full GM control.

112.s: Golden Rice is designed to enhance the biosynthesis of:
o: Beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A
112.x: Golden Rice is designed for beta-carotene biosynthesis, linked to Vitamin A nutrition.
112.tq: Match the product’s popular name with its intended nutritional trait.
xs: **Golden Rice** enhances **beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Cry toxins** = **Bt cotton**; **barnase** = **DMH-11**; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr** tomato.
xa: Genes from **daffodil** and a **soil bacterium**.
**Flavr Savr**: first commercial GM food (USA, **1994**).
Bt cotton genes: **Cry1Ac**, **Cry2Ab**.

112.s: Pusa Rice DST1 was set for commercial launch as India’s first genome-edited rice and was to be regulated like:
112.x: Pusa Rice DST1 was described as India’s first genome-edited rice for commercial launch and was to be regulated like a conventional crop.
112.tq: Test the regulatory classification rather than the biological trait.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1**, an **SDN-1** edit with no foreign DNA, is treated like **a conventional crop** — option **(1)** is correct.
SDN-1/SDN-2 crops are **exempt** from GMO rules (**2022** guidelines) and **skip GEAC**.
xa: Developer: **ICAR-IARI**; edit of **DST gene** in **MTU1010**.
**Pusa DST1/Kamala** = first genome-edited rice; commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ GE exemption criticised as a **back door**.

112.s: Which of the following is identified as a criticism of the exemption for SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited crops?
o: It creates a statutory liability law for farmers
It requires every crop to undergo Supreme Court review
It functions as a possible back door around the full GM regulatory route
It prohibits all genome-edited crops from field trials
112.x: The exemption has been criticised as a possible back door around the full GM regulatory route, with concerns about biosecurity gaps.
112.tq: Find the criticism that directly matches the stated regulatory concern rather than an unrelated consequence.
xs: The SDN-1/SDN-2 exemption is criticised as a **back door around the full GM regulatory route** — option **(3)** is correct.
There is **no liability law**, no SC review for each crop, and no ban on field trials.
xa: The exemption lets genome-edited rice **skip GM rules**; biosecurity gaps flagged.
Other criticism: **fragmented regulators**; delays yet **no liability law**.
GE crops need only **IBC** approval.

112.s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
112.x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.
112.tq: GM food = FSS Act 2006 / FSSAI.
xs: GM food, including imports, rests on the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA 1986** governs GMO release (GEAC), the **PPVFR Act 2001** plant varieties, and the **Patents Act** patents.
xa: The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**.
**FSSAI GM food framework 2024**: approval of the **competent authority**.
July **2024**: SC **split verdict** on GM mustard; Centre told to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.

112.s: Which provision of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability while permitting patenting of microbial processes?
112.x: Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability, while microbial processes can be patented.
112.tq: Distinguish closely numbered statutory provisions by their subject matter.
xs: **Section 3(j)** excludes **plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes**, but **microbial processes** can be patented — option **(1)**.
**Section 3(d)** is the anti-**evergreening** clause (new form of a known substance).
xa: UPSC **2019**: a biological process to create a seed **cannot** be patented; plant varieties **not eligible**.
**IPAB** existed then; abolished **2021**.
Plant varieties are protected instead by the **PPVFR Act 2001**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about Section 3(d) of the Patents Act:
1. It bars a patent for a new form of a known substance unless it shows enhanced efficacy.
2. In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court upheld rejection of the Glivec patent under Section 3(j), not 3(d).
3. It is meant to block evergreening.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: Sec 3(d) needs enhanced efficacy for new forms of known substances and blocks evergreening. Statement 2 is wrong: the Glivec (imatinib) rejection was upheld under Sec 3(d); Sec 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
112.tq: 3(d) = evergreening (Novartis); 3(j) = plants/animals/seeds.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Section 3(d)** bars patents for new forms of known substances without **enhanced efficacy**.
Statement 2 wrong: in **Novartis (2013)** the SC upheld rejection of **Glivec (imatinib)** under **Sec. 3(d)**.
Statement 3 correct: Section 3(d) **blocks evergreening**.
xa: **Section 3(j)**: plants, animals, seeds and **essentially biological processes** are not patentable; **microbial processes** can be.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)** over **FL-2027 (FC5)**; registration revoked in **2021**.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001:
1. It protects plant varieties and farmers' rights.
2. Under it, farmers may sell branded seed of protected varieties.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
112.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed. Hence 1 only.
112.tq: Farmers' rights: everything except selling branded seed.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **PPVFR Act 2001** protects **plant varieties and farmers' rights** (UPPSC **2021**) — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: farmers may **save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, sell** farm produce incl. seed — but **not branded seed**.
xa: The Act **bars registration** of varieties carrying **GURT**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)**: **FL-2027 (FC5)**; PPVFR Authority revoked its registration (**2021**).
⚠ Plant varieties are **not eligible** for patents under **Section 3(j)** — the PPVFR Act protects them instead.

112.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the PepsiCo potato case:
1. PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers over the FL-2027 (FC5) potato variety.
2. The suits were subsequently withdrawn.
3. The PPVFR Authority revoked the registration of the variety in 2021.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
112.x: PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers over its FL-2027 (FC5) variety, later withdrew the suits, and the PPVFR Authority revoked the registration in 2021.
112.tq: Check all stages of a legal case—claim, withdrawal and subsequent regulatory action.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
PepsiCo sued **Gujarat farmers** over its **FL-2027 (FC5)** potato (**2019**); the suits were **withdrawn**.
The **PPVFR Authority revoked its registration** in **2021**.
xa: Farmers may save, resow, exchange and sell seed — but **not branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**IPAB** was abolished in **2021**.

112.s: Which one of the following statements about the PPVFR Act and GURT is correct?
o: The Act mandates registration of all varieties carrying GURT.
The Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT.
The Act has no provision concerning GURT.
The Act permits registration only when farmers cannot save seed.
112.x: The PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying Genetic Use Restriction Technology. This reflects concerns over seed dependency and loss of farmers' seed-saving rights.
112.tq: Watch for the reversed legal relationship between a statute and a controversial technology.
xs: The **PPVFR Act bars registration of varieties carrying GURT** — option **(2)** is correct.
So it neither mandates such registration nor is silent on GURT.
xa: GURT/**terminator seeds** yield **sterile seeds** → fresh seed every season.
Farmers' rights: **save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share, sell** seed — not **branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** (UPPSC **2021**).

112.s: Which of the following is NOT an objection raised by farmers against GURT or terminator seeds?
o: Guaranteed improvement in farmers' autonomy over seed supply
Higher recurring costs of purchasing seed
112.x: Farmers' objections include dependency on companies, recurring costs and loss of seed-saving. Guaranteed improvement in seed autonomy is contrary to these objections.
112.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of the stated social and economic concerns.
xs: **Guaranteed improvement in farmers' autonomy over seed supply** is not an objection — it is the opposite — option **(3)**.
Real objections: **seed dependency** on companies, **costs**, and **loss of seed-saving** — options (1), (2), (4).
xa: Terminator seeds yield **sterile seeds** → farmers buy fresh seed each season.
The **PPVFR Act** bars registration of GURT varieties.
Debate also flags **farmer seed dependency**, **public mistrust**, **labelling** debates.

112.s:
Consider the following statements about the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety:
1. It is supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
2. It was adopted in 2000 and entered into force in 2003.
3. It covers the transboundary movement of LMOs and has an Advance Informed Agreement procedure.
